definition: To lower oneself or someone else in dignity or respect.
examples: He refused to abase himself by begging for his job back.
The show seems designed to abase its contestants for laughs.
etymology: From Old French abaissier 'to lower', based on Late Latin bassus 'short, low'.

definition: To become less intense, severe, or widespread.
examples: We waited in the cabin for the storm to abate before driving home.
Her anger began to abate once she heard the full story.
etymology: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down', from Latin ab- + battuere 'to beat'.

definition: To give up a throne, duty, or responsibility.
examples: The king chose to abdicate rather than accept the new constitution.
Parents can't simply abdicate their role in their children's education.
etymology: From Latin abdicare, 'to renounce', from ab-, 'away', + dicare, 'to proclaim'.

definition: Arranged alphabetically, or relating to the basic rudiments of learning.
examples: She wrote an abecedarian poem, each line starting with the next letter.
His grasp of statistics is merely abecedarian.
etymology: From Late Latin abecedarius, formed from the letters A, B, C, D.

definition: In bed, especially resting or sleeping late.
examples: He lay abed until noon on Sundays.
With the flu, she stayed abed all week.
etymology: From Old English on bedde 'in bed'.

definition: A departure from what is normal, expected, or typical, often a temporary one.
examples: The cold week in July was an aberration in an otherwise hot summer.
Scientists treated the odd reading as an aberration until it appeared again.
etymology: From Latin aberrare, 'to wander away', from ab- 'away' + errare 'to wander'.

definition: To encourage or help someone do something, usually wrong.
examples: Anyone who helped him escape will be charged, since it is a crime to abet a fugitive.
Lax rules only abet the bad habits of a few landlords.
etymology: From Old French abeter, from a- 'toward' + beter 'to bait'.

definition: A state of temporary suspension or inactivity.
examples: The construction project was held in abeyance until the city approved new funding.
Their old rivalry fell into abeyance during the championship season.
etymology: From Anglo-French abeiance, 'suspension', from Old French abeer, 'to gape at, aspire to'.

definition: To regard with deep disgust and hatred.
examples: I abhor the way some fans treat referees.
Most writers abhor clichés in their own work.
etymology: From Latin abhorrere, from ab- 'away from' + horrere 'to shudder'.

definition: Lasting for a long time; enduring.
examples: She has an abiding love of the sea.
His abiding interest was medieval history.
etymology: From abide, from Old English abidan 'to wait'.

definition: Extremely bad, miserable, or hopeless.
examples: The rescue workers found the animals living in abject conditions.
The first attempt was an abject failure, but we learned a lot.
etymology: From Latin abjectus, 'cast away', from abicere, 'to throw away'.

definition: To formally renounce a belief, claim, or habit.
examples: After the scandal, he publicly abjured his old methods.
She decided to abjure sugar for the entire month of January.
etymology: From Latin abjurare, from ab- 'away' + jurare 'to swear'.

definition: The act of washing oneself, often as a ritual.
examples: The morning ablution in the icy stream woke us up fast.
Each ablution before prayer follows a set order.
etymology: From Latin ablutio, from abluere 'to wash away'.

definition: Skillfully and competently.
examples: The understudy ably filled in for the lead actor.
She was ably assisted by two interns.
etymology: From able, from Old French able, from Latin habilis 'handy', plus the suffix -ly.

definition: The act of denying oneself pleasures or rights, often for a belief or cause.
examples: The monk's life of abnegation left him with few possessions and fewer comforts.
Her abnegation of personal ambition allowed the whole team to succeed.
etymology: From Latin abnegatio, 'denial', from abnegare, 'to refuse, deny'.

definition: To formally put an end to a law, system, or practice.
examples: The new board voted to abolish the dress code for remote staff.
Several cities have moved to abolish late fees at their libraries.
etymology: From French abolir, from Latin abolere 'to destroy, do away with'.

definition: Causing moral revulsion, or simply very unpleasant.
examples: The prison conditions were abominable.
The weather at the reunion was abominable.
etymology: From Latin abominabilis, from abominari 'to deprecate as an ill omen'.

definition: To exist in large numbers or great quantity.
examples: Rumors abound whenever the company skips its quarterly call.
In late spring, wildflowers abound along the ridge trail.
etymology: From Old French abonder, from Latin abundare 'to overflow', from ab- 'from' + unda 'wave'.

definition: Legitimate, honest, and open.
examples: Everything about the deal was aboveboard.
Keep the bidding process aboveboard.
etymology: From above + board, originally of card players keeping their hands above the table.

definition: Harsh and rude in manner; also, able to scrape or grind.
examples: His abrasive style alienated his co-workers.
Use an abrasive pad to remove the rust.
etymology: From Latin abras-, from abradere 'to scrape off'.

definition: Side by side; also, up to date with the latest news.
examples: Cyclists rode three abreast down the lane.
She reads daily to stay abreast of the field.
etymology: From a- 'on' + breast.

definition: To shorten a text or speech while keeping its meaning.
examples: The publisher decided to abridge the novel for younger readers.
Please abridge your remarks; we're short on time.
etymology: From Old French abregier, from Late Latin abbreviare 'to shorten'.

definition: To repeal or do away with a law, agreement, or responsibility.
examples: The new treaty will abrogate the old trade restrictions.
Parents cannot simply abrogate their duty to supervise young children.
etymology: From Latin abrogare, from ab- 'away' + rogare 'to propose a law'.

definition: Sudden and unexpected, or short and rude in manner.
examples: The bus came to an abrupt stop, and everyone lurched forward.
His abrupt reply made me think he was annoyed.
etymology: From Latin abruptus, 'broken off', from abrumpere.

definition: To leave hurriedly and secretly, often to avoid arrest or with stolen goods.
examples: The treasurer tried to abscond with the club's funds.
Our cat likes to abscond with socks from the laundry basket.
etymology: From Latin abscondere, 'to hide away'.

definition: To declare someone free from blame, guilt, or obligation.
examples: Apologizing doesn't absolve you of fixing the mess.
The report seemed designed to absolve management of any responsibility.
etymology: From Latin absolvere 'to set free', from ab- 'from' + solvere 'to loosen'.

definition: To leave abruptly; to make off.
examples: Party guests began to absquatulate once the karaoke started.
He tends to absquatulate whenever the check arrives.
etymology: A mock-Latin American coinage of the 1830s, playing on ab- and squat.

definition: To deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something, or from voting.
examples: Two members chose to abstain rather than vote against their friend.
I try to abstain from coffee after noon so I can actually sleep.
etymology: From Old French abstenir, from Latin abstinere 'to hold back', from abs- 'from' + tenere 'to hold'.

definition: Sparing in eating and drinking; moderate in indulging in pleasures.
examples: The abstemious host served only water and plain bread at the feast.
He led an abstemious life, avoiding sweets, alcohol, and late nights.
etymology: From Latin abstemius, 'temperate', from abs- 'away from' + temetum 'strong drink'.

definition: The practice of refraining from something, especially alcohol or food.
examples: After a month of abstinence, the first coffee tasted amazing.
Total abstinence isn't required; moderation works too.
etymology: From Latin abstinentia, from abstinere 'to hold back'.

definition: Existing as an idea rather than as something concrete or physical.
examples: Freedom is an abstract concept that's hard to define.
The museum's top floor is devoted to abstract painting.
etymology: From Latin abstractus 'drawn away', from abs- 'from' + trahere 'to draw'.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is deep, complex, or obscure.
examples: The professor's abstruse lecture on quantum field theory baffled even the graduate students.
She avoided abstruse jargon so that every reader could follow her argument.
etymology: From Latin abstrusus, 'hidden', from abstrudere, 'to conceal, thrust away'.

definition: An absence of willpower or the ability to act decisively.
examples: Deep abulia kept him on the couch for weeks.
Some brain injuries cause abulia.
etymology: From Greek aboulia 'ill-advisedness', from a- 'without' + boulē 'will'.

definition: Present in large, more than sufficient amounts.
examples: Tomatoes are abundant at the farmers market in August.
She has abundant energy for a Monday morning.
etymology: From Latin abundant-, present participle of abundare 'to overflow'.

definition: Extremely bad; appalling.
examples: The team's defense was abysmal last season.
Cell service in the canyon is abysmal.
etymology: From obsolete abysm 'abyss', from Old French abisme.

definition: A very deep chasm, or a situation that seems bottomless and hopeless.
examples: The hikers peered into the abyss below the cliff.
After the layoffs, he felt he was staring into an abyss.
etymology: From Greek abussos 'bottomless', from a- 'without' + bussos 'depth'.

definition: To agree to a demand or request, or to take up an office.
examples: The landlord would not accede to our request for a new fridge.
She is expected to accede to the throne next year.
etymology: From Latin accedere 'to come to', from ad- 'to' + cedere 'to go'.

definition: To make something more noticeable or prominent.
examples: A bright scarf can accentuate the color of your eyes.
The new lighting accentuates the room's high ceilings.
etymology: From Medieval Latin accentuare, from Latin accentus 'accent'.

definition: Enthusiastic public praise or approval.
examples: Her debut album won wide acclaim from critics and fans alike.
The chef shrugged off the acclaim and went back to the kitchen.
etymology: From Latin acclamare 'to shout at', from ad- 'to' + clamare 'to shout'.

definition: An upward slope.
examples: The cyclists slowed on the long acclivity.
The cottage stood at the top of a gentle acclivity.
etymology: From Latin acclivitas, from acclivis 'sloping upward'.

definition: An award or expression of high praise.
examples: The bakery's sourdough earned accolades from every food critic in town.
Her favorite accolade was a handwritten note from a former student.
etymology: From French accolade, 'embrace', from Latin ad- 'to' + collum 'neck'.

definition: To make room for or adjust to fit someone's needs or wishes.
examples: The hotel can accommodate up to two hundred guests.
We moved the meeting to accommodate the team in Tokyo.
etymology: From Latin accommodare 'to make fit', from ad- 'to' + commodus 'fitting'.

definition: A person who helps another commit a crime or mischief.
examples: The thief's accomplice was waiting in the getaway car.
My sister was my accomplice in every childhood prank.
etymology: From Middle English complice, from Late Latin complex 'allied', with the a- probably from the article a.

definition: In a way that suits the situation, or as a result.
examples: The forecast calls for snow, so dress accordingly.
Prices rose, and accordingly, sales dipped.
etymology: From according, from Old French acorder 'to agree', plus the suffix -ly.

definition: To approach and speak to someone boldly or aggressively.
examples: Reporters tried to accost the senator in the hallway.
Street vendors accost tourists near the station.
etymology: From Latin accostare 'to come side by side', from costa 'rib, side'.

definition: Required or expected to explain and take responsibility for one's actions.
examples: Voters want leaders who stay accountable after the election.
As project lead, I'm accountable for hitting the deadline.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman acontable, from Old French aconter 'to count, reckon'.

definition: Additional items of dress or equipment that go with an activity.
examples: She arrived with all the accoutrements of a serious birder.
The kitchen had all the accoutrements a baker could want.
etymology: From French accoutrement, from accoutrer 'to clothe, equip'.

definition: Gradual growth through the addition of new layers or parts.
examples: The code grew by accretion until no one understood it.
Each accretion of silt made the riverbank taller.
etymology: From Latin accretio, from accrescere 'to grow'.

definition: To accumulate or come about gradually, especially as payments or benefits.
examples: Interest will accrue daily on the unpaid balance.
Small advantages accrue over time.
etymology: From Old French acreue, from acreistre 'to increase', from Latin accrescere.

definition: To gather or pile up gradually over time.
examples: Dust tends to accumulate behind the bookshelf.
It's easy to accumulate subscriptions you never use.
etymology: From Latin accumulare 'to heap up', from ad- 'to' + cumulus 'heap'.

definition: Spiritual or mental sloth; listless apathy toward life.
examples: Lockdown brought a creeping acedia to the whole household.
Medieval monks feared acedia more than hunger.
etymology: From Late Latin acedia, from Greek akēdia 'carelessness', from a- 'without' + kēdos 'care'.

definition: Sharp and cutting in tone or wit.
examples: Her acerbic reviews are feared by every chef in town.
He has an acerbic sense of humor that not everyone gets.
etymology: From Latin acerbus 'sour, harsh'.

definition: Slightly sour, or sharp and biting in manner.
examples: The wine had an acidulous finish.
Her acidulous remarks kept the panel on edge.
etymology: From Latin acidulus 'slightly sour', from acidus 'sour'.

definition: The highest point of achievement or excellence.
examples: Winning the national title was the acme of her coaching career.
Many critics consider that album the acme of 1970s songwriting.
etymology: From Greek akmē, 'highest point, prime'.

definition: A devoted follower or assistant.
examples: The guru arrived with an acolyte carrying his bags.
Every acolyte of the chef copies her plating style.
etymology: From Medieval Latin acolytus, from Greek akolouthos 'follower'.

definition: To accept or agree to something reluctantly, without protest.
examples: After hours of argument, the board finally decided to acquiesce to the union's demands.
He would rather acquiesce than start another fight about the thermostat.
etymology: From Latin acquiescere, 'to rest, find repose in', from ad- + quiescere 'to be quiet'.

definition: Eager to gain wealth or possessions.
examples: The acquisitive firm bought three rivals in a year.
His acquisitive streak filled the garage with junk.
etymology: From Late Latin acquisitivus, from acquirere 'to acquire'.

definition: To declare someone not guilty of a charge; also, to conduct oneself in a certain way.
examples: The jury voted to acquit the defendant.
Rookies rarely acquit themselves so well in a final.
etymology: From Old French acquiter, from Medieval Latin acquitare 'to pay a debt'.

definition: Unpleasantly bitter or stinging to smell or taste.
examples: Acrid smoke from the wildfire hung over the valley.
An acrid smell rose from the overheating laptop.
etymology: From Latin acer 'sharp, pungent', formed on the pattern of acid.

definition: Bitter, angry feeling or harsh, resentful language, especially in a dispute.
examples: The divorce proceedings were marked by acrimony from the very first meeting.
Despite the acrimony of the campaign, the two rivals shook hands afterward.
etymology: From Latin acrimonia, 'sharpness, pungency', from acer, 'sharp'.

definition: Sharpness of vision, hearing, or thought.
examples: Hawks have remarkable visual acuity.
Her political acuity made her a great strategist.
etymology: From Medieval Latin acuitas, from Latin acuere 'to sharpen'.

definition: Sharpness and good judgment, especially in practical matters.
examples: Her business acumen turned a small food truck into a chain of restaurants.
You don't need financial acumen to stick to a simple monthly budget.
etymology: From Latin acumen, 'sharpness, point', from acuere 'to sharpen'.

definition: Severe, intense, or sharply felt, especially when sudden.
examples: There is an acute shortage of nurses in rural areas.
Dogs have an acute sense of smell.
etymology: From Latin acutus 'sharpened', from acuere 'to sharpen'.

definition: A short, familiar saying that expresses a general truth.
examples: My grandmother lived by the adage that you should never go to bed angry.
The old adage about measuring twice and cutting once saved our bookshelf project.
etymology: From French adage, from Latin adagium, 'proverb'.

definition: Refusing to change one's mind.
examples: She was adamant that she had locked the door.
The kids were adamant about camping in the backyard.
etymology: From Greek adamas, 'untamable, unbreakable', a name for a legendary hard stone.

definition: Unbreakable or utterly unyielding.
examples: Her adamantine resolve carried her through medical school.
The fortress had adamantine walls.
etymology: From Greek adamantinos, from adamas, 'untameable; the hardest metal'.

definition: Able to adjust easily to new conditions.
examples: Raccoons are adaptable animals that thrive in cities.
We need an adaptable plan in case it rains.
etymology: From adapt, from Latin adaptare 'to fit to', plus the suffix -able.

definition: Confused and unable to think clearly.
examples: I was too addled from jet lag to read the map.
His addled excuse made no sense.
etymology: From addle egg 'rotten egg', from Old English adela 'liquid filth'.

definition: Very skilled and capable at something that takes practice.
examples: She is adept at calming nervous clients before important presentations begin.
After years of travel, he became adept at packing everything into one small bag.
etymology: From Latin adeptus, 'having attained', the past participle of adipisci 'to attain'.

definition: Good enough for a purpose, though not outstanding.
examples: The hotel was adequate, but the view was the real reason we stayed.
Make sure you get adequate sleep before the exam.
etymology: From Latin adaequatus 'made equal', from ad- 'to' + aequus 'equal'.

definition: To stick firmly to something, or to follow a rule or belief closely.
examples: All vendors must adhere to the new safety guidelines.
This tape won't adhere to a damp wall.
etymology: From Latin adhaerere, from ad- 'to' + haerere 'to stick'.

definition: Someone who supports a particular party, person, or set of ideas.
examples: She's a devoted adherent of the slow-food movement.
Each adherent of the theory had a slightly different version.
etymology: From Latin adhaerent-, from adhaerere 'to stick to'.

definition: Next to or very near something else.
examples: We booked adjacent seats so the kids could sit together.
The café is adjacent to the train station.
etymology: From Latin adjacent-, from adjacere 'to lie near', from ad- 'to' + jacere 'to lie'.

definition: To pause or end a meeting or session until a later time.
examples: Let's adjourn and pick this up tomorrow.
The judge will adjourn the trial until Monday.
etymology: From Old French ajorner 'to set a day', from a- 'to' + jorn 'day'.

definition: To make a formal judgment on a disputed matter.
examples: A panel will adjudicate the contract dispute.
Who gets to adjudicate the baking contest?
etymology: From Latin adjudicare, from ad- 'to' + judicare 'to judge'.

definition: Something added as a supplement, or a non-permanent faculty member.
examples: Therapy is a useful adjunct to medication.
She teaches as an adjunct at two colleges.
etymology: From Latin adjunctus 'joined to', from adjungere.

definition: To urge or command someone solemnly.
examples: The coach adjured the team to stay calm in the final minutes.
I adjure you to read the contract carefully before signing it.
etymology: From Latin adjurare, 'to swear to'.

definition: Used to concede that something is true.
examples: Admittedly, I've never actually read the book.
The plan is admittedly risky, but it could pay off.
etymology: From admit, from Latin admittere 'to let in'.

definition: To scold someone gently but firmly, or to warn them earnestly.
examples: The teacher did admonish the class to stop talking during the exam.
My doctor will admonish me again if I skip my walks.
etymology: From Old French amonester, from Latin admonere, 'to warn', from ad- + monere 'to advise'.

definition: To decorate or make more beautiful.
examples: Strings of lights adorn every balcony in December.
She likes to adorn her notebooks with stickers.
etymology: From Latin adornare, from ad- 'to' + ornare 'to decorate'.

definition: Clever or skillful in using the hands or mind.
examples: She is adroit at defusing tense conversations.
The adroit pianist made the difficult piece look effortless.
etymology: From French à droit, 'according to right, properly'.

definition: Excessive admiration or praise.
examples: The young striker basked in the adulation of the crowd.
Fame brings adulation but also scrutiny.
etymology: From Latin adulatio, from adulari 'to fawn upon'.

definition: Praising someone excessively.
examples: The biography is so adulatory it reads like an ad.
Adulatory fans lined the red carpet.
etymology: From Latin adulatorius, from adulari 'to fawn upon'.

definition: To make something impure by adding an inferior substance.
examples: Some sellers adulterate olive oil with cheaper oils.
Don't adulterate good whiskey with soda.
etymology: From Latin adulterare 'to corrupt'.

definition: To outline roughly or hint at something that will come.
examples: The memo seemed to adumbrate sweeping changes to the company's structure.
Early clouds adumbrate the storm that will hit by evening.
etymology: From Latin adumbrare, 'to shade in, sketch', from umbra, 'shadow'.

definition: The arrival or beginning of something important.
examples: The advent of smartphones changed how we navigate cities.
Since the advent of streaming, few people buy DVDs.
etymology: From Latin adventus 'arrival', from advenire 'to come to'.

definition: Happening by chance or from outside rather than by design.
examples: Their meeting was adventitious, a delayed train and two empty seats.
Adventitious roots sprouted along the stem.
etymology: From Latin adventicius 'coming from abroad', from advenire 'to arrive'.

definition: Involving or marked by opposition and conflict.
examples: The negotiations grew more adversarial each week.
Courts in the US follow an adversarial system.
etymology: From adversary, from Latin adversarius 'opponent', plus the suffix -al.

definition: Harmful, unfavorable, or working against one's interests.
examples: The drug has few adverse side effects.
The flight was canceled due to adverse weather.
etymology: From Latin adversus 'turned against', from advertere 'to turn toward'.

definition: Difficult or unlucky circumstances that test a person.
examples: The team showed real grit in the face of adversity.
Adversity taught her more than any classroom did.
etymology: From Old French adversite, from Latin adversitas, from adversus 'opposed'.

definition: To refer to something in speaking or writing.
examples: She did not advert to the scandal in her speech.
Let me advert briefly to last year's figures.
etymology: From Latin advertere 'to turn toward'.

definition: After careful consideration; deliberately.
examples: I use the word "disaster" advisedly.
She chose her words advisedly in the hearing.
etymology: From advised, from Old French aviser 'to look at', plus the suffix -ly.

definition: A person who publicly supports or speaks up for a cause or another person.
examples: She became a fierce advocate for better bike lanes.
Every patient deserves an advocate in the hospital.
etymology: From Old French avocat, from Latin advocatus 'one called to help', from advocare 'to summon'.

definition: Protection, backing, or sponsorship of a person or group.
examples: The program runs under the aegis of the health ministry.
Under her aegis, the lab doubled in size.
etymology: From Greek aigis, the shield of Zeus or Athena.

definition: A large nest of a bird of prey, or a high, remote home.
examples: Eagles returned to the same aerie every spring.
His penthouse was an aerie above the city.
etymology: From Medieval Latin aeria, probably from Old French aire 'lair'.

definition: A particular set of principles or a recognizable style of beauty and taste.
examples: The café has a cozy, plant-filled aesthetic.
His photos share a moody, rain-soaked aesthetic.
etymology: From Greek aisthētikos 'of sense perception', from aisthanesthai 'to perceive'.

definition: Belonging to or appearing in summer.
examples: Aestival storms roll in every August afternoon.
The garden's aestival blooms faded by September.
etymology: From Latin aestivalis, from aestas 'summer'.

definition: Friendly, easy to talk to, and pleasant in manner.
examples: The affable shop owner greeted every customer by name and asked about their families.
His affable personality made him an instant favorite among the new employees.
etymology: From Latin affabilis, 'easy to speak to', from affari 'to speak to'.

definition: Behavior or speech that is artificial and meant to impress.
examples: His British accent was pure affectation; he grew up in Ohio.
She wore reading glasses as an affectation.
etymology: From Latin affectatio, from affectare 'to aim at'.

definition: A natural liking for or sense of connection with someone or something.
examples: She has an affinity for old maps and forgotten towns.
I felt an instant affinity with the other night owls on the team.
etymology: From Old French afinite, from Latin affinitas 'relationship by marriage', from affinis 'bordering on'.

definition: To state firmly or publicly support something as true or valid.
examples: The court will likely affirm the earlier ruling.
Good mentors affirm your strengths before pointing out weaknesses.
etymology: From Latin affirmare, from ad- 'to' + firmare 'to make firm'.

definition: A sudden rush of creative inspiration.
examples: She wrote the song in a single afflatus at 3 a.m.
Waiting for afflatus is a poor writing schedule.
etymology: From Latin afflatus 'a breathing on', from afflare 'to blow on'.

definition: To cause pain, suffering, or trouble to someone or something.
examples: Droughts continue to afflict the region every summer.
Writer's block can afflict even veteran novelists.
etymology: From Latin afflictare 'to knock about', from affligere 'to dash down'.

definition: Wealthy and comfortable, with plenty of money.
examples: The school sits in an affluent suburb with tree-lined streets.
Affluent buyers snapped up the lakefront homes.
etymology: From Latin affluent-, from affluere 'to flow toward, abound'.

definition: A public brawl that disturbs the peace.
examples: Two fans were charged with affray after the match.
The affray spilled out of the tavern into the square.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman afrayer 'to disturb, frighten'.

definition: An action or remark that causes outrage or offense.
examples: The new fees were an affront to longtime members.
She took the late reply as a personal affront.
etymology: From Old French afronter 'to slap in the face', from a front 'to the face'.

definition: A knowledgeable and enthusiastic fan of an activity.
examples: He's a jazz aficionado with thousands of records.
Any coffee aficionado will notice the difference.
etymology: From Spanish aficionado 'amateur, devotee', from afición 'fondness'.

definition: In preparation or progress, often secretly.
examples: Plans are afoot to turn the warehouse into lofts.
I could tell something was afoot from their whispers.
etymology: From a- 'on' + foot.

definition: The period or consequences following a major, usually unpleasant, event.
examples: In the aftermath of the flood, neighbors cleared the streets together.
Nobody wanted to deal with the aftermath of the failed launch.
etymology: From after + obsolete math 'a mowing'; it originally meant a second crop of grass after the first was cut.

definition: Wide open in wonder or surprise, usually of the mouth.
examples: The kids watched the fireworks, mouths agape.
She stood agape at the size of the bill.
etymology: From a- 'on' + gape.

definition: A person who never laughs.
examples: Even the agelast in the front row cracked a smile.
My boss is an agelast who treats jokes as wasted time.
etymology: From Greek agelastos 'not laughing', from a- 'not' + gelan 'to laugh'.

definition: The bringing up to date of an institution's ideas or practices.
examples: The museum is undergoing a long-overdue aggiornamento.
The party's aggiornamento alienated older members.
etymology: From Italian aggiornamento 'updating'; it became famous through the Second Vatican Council.

definition: To increase the power, status, or wealth of, or to make something seem greater than it is.
examples: He used the charity event to aggrandize himself rather than help others.
The museum's label tends to aggrandize a rather ordinary vase.
etymology: From French agrandir, from Latin grandis, 'large'.

definition: To make a problem or injury worse, or to annoy someone.
examples: Running on that ankle will only aggravate the sprain.
Loud chewing seems to aggravate everyone in the office.
etymology: From Latin aggravare 'to make heavier', from ad- 'to' + gravis 'heavy'.

definition: A whole formed by combining several separate elements.
examples: Their aggregate score over two games was 4–2.
In the aggregate, the changes saved millions.
etymology: From Latin aggregare 'to herd together', from grex 'flock'.

definition: Feeling resentment at having been treated unfairly.
examples: Aggrieved customers flooded the comments with complaints.
He sounded aggrieved that no one had thanked him.
etymology: From aggrieve, from Old French agrever 'to make heavier'.

definition: Filled with horror or shock.
examples: She was aghast at the price of concert tickets.
We stood aghast as the tree fell onto the car.
etymology: From obsolete agast 'frightened', from Old English gæstan 'to frighten'.

definition: Able to move or think quickly and easily.
examples: The goalkeeper was remarkably agile for his size.
Small startups can be more agile than large firms.
etymology: From French agile, from Latin agilis, from agere 'to do, drive'.

definition: Political propaganda, especially in art or literature.
examples: The film is less a drama than two hours of agitprop.
Early Soviet posters were classic agitprop.
etymology: From Russian agitprop, short for agitatsiya-propaganda 'agitation-propaganda'.

definition: An extra name or nickname, often earned by some achievement.
examples: Scipio earned the agnomen Africanus after his victory.
"The Bus" became the running back's lasting agnomen.
etymology: From Latin agnomen, from ad- 'to' + nomen 'name'.

definition: Believing that God's existence cannot be known; also, not tied to any one option.
examples: Our tool is platform agnostic and runs anywhere.
She was raised Catholic but is agnostic now.
etymology: Coined by T. H. Huxley in 1869 from Greek agnōstos 'unknown'.

definition: Very eager or curious to hear or see something.
examples: The whole office was agog over the rumored merger.
Kids sat agog as the magician produced a rabbit.
etymology: From Old French en gogues 'in merriment'.

definition: Relating to farming, farmland, or rural life.
examples: The region shifted from an agrarian economy to manufacturing.
Agrarian reform was a key campaign issue.
etymology: From Latin agrarius, from ager 'field'.

definition: Rural or rustic; unpolished.
examples: The inn had an agrestic charm, all hay bales and lanterns.
His agrestic manners amused the city guests.
etymology: From Latin agrestis 'of the fields', from ager 'field'.

definition: In poor health, or in a weak, failing condition.
examples: She moved home to care for her ailing father.
The new CEO was hired to rescue the ailing chain.
etymology: From ail, from Old English eglan 'to trouble'.

definition: An illness, usually a minor one.
examples: Grandma had a home remedy for every ailment.
A sore throat is a minor ailment, but it ruined her week.
etymology: From ail, from Old English eglan 'to trouble', plus the suffix -ment.

definition: Slightly open.
examples: Leave the door ajar so the cat can get in.
The window was ajar, letting in the smell of rain.
etymology: From a- 'on' + obsolete char 'a turn', from Old English cerr.

definition: With hands on hips and elbows turned outward.
examples: She stood arms akimbo, waiting for an explanation.
The toddler planted himself, arms akimbo, in the doorway.
etymology: From Middle English in kenebowe, of uncertain origin.

definition: Similar in nature or character; related.
examples: Learning to code is akin to learning a new language.
The feeling was akin to stepping off a roller coaster.
etymology: From a contraction of the phrase of kin.

definition: Acting against one's better judgment through weakness of will.
examples: Eating the whole bag of chips at midnight was pure akrasia.
Philosophers have long puzzled over akrasia: why do we do what we know is bad for us?
etymology: From Greek akrasia, 'lack of self-control'.

definition: Smooth and white like the translucent mineral alabaster.
examples: The statue's alabaster skin glowed in the candlelight.
Her alabaster complexion burned in minutes.
etymology: From Greek alabastros, a vessel for perfume often made of the stone.

definition: Cheerful readiness and eagerness to act or respond quickly.
examples: She accepted the invitation with alacrity and was packed within the hour.
The staff responded with alacrity when the manager asked for volunteers.
etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, 'lively, eager'.

definition: A seemingly magical transformation; originally, the medieval quest to turn metals into gold.
examples: Some kitchen alchemy turned leftovers into a feast.
Medieval alchemy laid groundwork for modern chemistry.
etymology: From Old French alquemie, via Medieval Latin from Arabic al-kīmiyā'.

definition: Depending on chance or luck.
examples: The composer used dice to create aleatory music.
Startup success is more aleatory than founders admit.
etymology: From Latin aleatorius, from aleator 'dice player', from alea 'die'.

definition: An old distilling apparatus, or anything that refines or transforms.
examples: The novel passes family history through the alembic of memory.
An alchemist's alembic sat on the museum shelf.
etymology: From Medieval Latin alembicus, from Arabic al-anbīq, from Greek ambix 'cup'.

definition: A line of verse with twelve syllables, or six iambic feet.
examples: Classical French tragedy is written in the alexandrine.
Each stanza of the Spenserian form ends with an alexandrine.
etymology: From French alexandrin, from Old French poems about Alexander the Great written in this meter.

definition: In the open air.
examples: We dined alfresco on the patio under string lights.
The orchestra performed alfresco in the park.
etymology: From Italian al fresco, 'in the fresh (air)'.

definition: Proof that someone was elsewhere when a crime happened, or any convenient excuse.
examples: The suspect's alibi fell apart under questioning.
"The dog ate it" is the oldest alibi in the book.
etymology: From Latin alibi 'elsewhere'.

definition: To make someone feel isolated, unwelcome, or no longer friendly.
examples: Constant price hikes will alienate loyal customers.
He didn't mean to alienate his friends, but the jokes went too far.
etymology: From Latin alienare 'to estrange', from alienus 'belonging to another'.

definition: To diminish or put to rest a fear, worry, or suspicion.
examples: The doctor's calm explanation allayed my fears about the surgery.
The company issued a statement to allay concerns about data privacy.
etymology: From Old English alecgan, 'to put down, lay aside'.

definition: A claim that someone has done something wrong, typically made without proof.
examples: The senator denied every allegation in the report.
Each allegation will be investigated thoroughly.
etymology: From Latin allegatio, from allegare 'to cite, adduce'.

definition: According to what has been claimed but not proven.
examples: The painting was allegedly hidden in an attic for fifty years.
The suspect allegedly took the bike, but no one saw him.
etymology: From allege, from Anglo-French alegier, influenced by Latin allegare 'to cite'.

definition: Loyalty or commitment to a person, group, or cause.
examples: Fans switch allegiance the moment a team starts losing.
Her allegiance to the old neighborhood never faded.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman ligeance, from Old French lige 'liege', influenced by allegeance.

definition: A story in which characters and events symbolize a deeper meaning.
examples: Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution.
The film works as an allegory about climate change.
etymology: From Greek allēgoria 'speaking otherwise', from allos 'other' + agoreuein 'to speak publicly'.

definition: To make pain, worry, or a problem less severe.
examples: A warm bath can help alleviate sore muscles.
The new bus line should alleviate traffic downtown.
etymology: From Late Latin alleviare, 'to lighten', from levis 'light'.

definition: To set aside or distribute something for a particular purpose.
examples: We allocate a small part of each paycheck to savings.
The city will allocate more money to park maintenance next year.
etymology: From Medieval Latin allocare, from ad- 'to' + locare 'to place'.

definition: To give or assign a share of something.
examples: We allot ten minutes to each speaker.
The city will allot more money to parks next year.
etymology: From Old French aloter, from a- 'to' + loter 'to divide by lot'.

definition: To mention something indirectly rather than stating it outright.
examples: In her speech, she would only allude to the troubles of the past year.
The title alludes to an old fairy tale.
etymology: From Latin alludere, 'to play with, refer to', from ad- + ludere 'to play'.

definition: The quality of being powerfully attractive or tempting.
examples: The allure of a long weekend at the beach was hard to resist.
For many travelers, the allure of Kyoto lies in its quiet temples.
etymology: From Old French aleurer, 'to attract, lure', from a- + leurre 'lure'.

definition: An indirect reference to something.
examples: The title is an allusion to a Beatles song.
She made a passing allusion to her divorce.
etymology: From Latin allusio, from alludere 'to play with, refer to'.

definition: Up in the air or overhead.
examples: The champion held the trophy aloft for the cameras.
Hawks circled aloft, riding the warm air.
etymology: From Old Norse á lopti 'in the air'.

definition: Distant and uninvolved; not friendly or forthcoming.
examples: He seemed aloof at first, but he was just shy.
The cat stayed aloof, watching the guests from the bookshelf.
etymology: From a- 'on' + luff 'windward direction', originally a nautical order to steer into the wind.

definition: The rosy light on mountain peaks around sunrise or sunset.
examples: The alpenglow turned the peaks pink as we ate dinner.
Photographers wait hours for the alpenglow.
etymology: A partial translation of German Alpenglühen 'Alps glow'.

definition: A noisy argument or minor fight.
examples: Police were called after an altercation in the parking lot.
A brief altercation over the armrest delayed takeoff.
etymology: From Latin altercatio, from altercari 'to wrangle'.

definition: The state of being other or different.
examples: The essay explores the alterity of the immigrant experience.
Travel forces you to confront alterity.
etymology: From Late Latin alteritas, from Latin alter 'other'.

definition: Showing unselfish concern for the well-being of others.
examples: Donating a kidney to a stranger is a deeply altruistic act.
Her altruistic nature led her to volunteer every weekend.
etymology: From French altruisme, from Italian altrui 'of others'.

definition: To combine separate parts into a single whole.
examples: The two unions voted to amalgamate.
The chef likes to amalgamate flavors from several cuisines.
etymology: From amalgam, from Medieval Latin amalgama, a mercury alloy.

definition: A person employed to take dictation or copy manuscripts.
examples: Late in life, the nearly blind poet relied on his daughter as his amanuensis.
With voice dictation software, my phone has become a tireless amanuensis.
etymology: From Latin (servus) a manu, 'secretary', literally 'by hand', + -ensis.

definition: Unfading and everlasting; also, deep purplish-red.
examples: The poet promised her an amaranthine love.
The sky turned amaranthine at dusk.
etymology: From amaranth, a legendary unfading flower, from Greek amarantos 'unfading'.

definition: To gather or collect a large amount over time.
examples: It took her decades to amass that record collection.
Few investors amass a fortune overnight.
etymology: From French amasser, from a- 'to' + masser 'to heap up'.

definition: Relating to sexual love or desire.
examples: The letters reveal the poet's amatory adventures.
Peacocks perform an elaborate amatory display.
etymology: From Latin amatorius, from amator 'lover'.

definition: The mood or atmosphere of a place.
examples: The restaurant's candlelit ambiance made it perfect for an anniversary dinner.
We added plants and warm lamps to improve the ambiance of the office.
etymology: From French ambiance, from ambiant 'surrounding', from Latin ambire 'to go around'.

definition: Relating to the surrounding environment, such as its light, sound, or temperature.
examples: The café plays soft ambient music all day.
Store chocolate at ambient temperature, not in the fridge.
etymology: From Latin ambient-, from ambire 'to go around'.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not clear in meaning.
examples: The contract's wording was ambiguous, so each side read it differently.
The film ends on an ambiguous note, leaving viewers to decide what really happened.
etymology: From Latin ambiguus, 'doubtful', from ambigere, 'to wander about, be uncertain'.

definition: The scope, extent, or bounds of something.
examples: Questions about pay fall outside the ambit of this review.
The new law widens the ambit of the city's housing office.
etymology: From Latin ambitus, 'a going around', from ambire, 'to go around'.

definition: Having mixed or conflicting feelings about something or someone.
examples: I feel ambivalent about moving, excited about the job but sad to leave my friends.
Voters seemed ambivalent about the proposal and split almost evenly.
etymology: From Latin ambi- 'both' + valentia, 'strength', coined in early 20th-century psychology.

definition: Exceptionally delicious or fragrant.
examples: An ambrosial smell drifted from the bakery.
Those peaches were ambrosial.
etymology: From ambrosia, the food of the Greek gods, from Greek ambrotos 'immortal'.

definition: Relating to walking, or able to walk.
examples: The patient is ambulatory and can go home today.
He led an ambulatory life, never long in one city.
etymology: From Latin ambulatorius, from ambulare 'to walk'.

definition: A surprise attack by people lying in wait.
examples: The reporters set up an ambush outside the courthouse.
The cat waited under the couch, planning an ambush.
etymology: From Old French embusche, from embuschier 'to place in a wood', from bois 'wood'.

definition: To make a bad or difficult situation better.
examples: New funding should ameliorate the shortage of nurses in rural clinics.
Planting trees can ameliorate the heat in crowded city neighborhoods.
etymology: From French améliorer, from Old French meillor, 'better', from Latin melior.

definition: Open and responsive to suggestion; willing to cooperate.
examples: The landlord was amenable to letting us paint the walls.
Most people are amenable to change if you explain the reasons.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman French amener, 'to bring to', from mener, 'to lead'.

definition: To make changes to a document or law in order to improve or correct it.
examples: We need to amend the contract before anyone signs.
Lawmakers voted to amend the zoning rules.
etymology: From Old French amender, from Latin emendare 'to correct', from e- 'out of' + menda 'fault'.

definition: A feature that makes a place more comfortable or pleasant.
examples: A rooftop pool is the building's best amenity.
Free laundry is a rare amenity in student housing.
etymology: From Latin amoenitas 'pleasantness', from amoenus 'pleasant'.

definition: Having a friendly, good-natured, and agreeable disposition.
examples: Our neighbors are amiable people who always wave and offer to help with the garden.
The two rivals had an amiable chat after the match despite the tense final.
etymology: From Late Latin amicabilis, 'friendly', from Latin amicus 'friend'.

definition: Friendly and without serious disagreement.
examples: The roommates reached an amicable agreement about chores.
Their breakup was surprisingly amicable.
etymology: From Late Latin amicabilis, from amicus 'friend'.

definition: Not quite right; wrong or out of place.
examples: She sensed something amiss when the lights were off.
A thank-you note wouldn't go amiss.
etymology: From Old Norse á mis 'so as to miss'.

definition: Friendly relations between people or countries.
examples: The treaty ushered in an era of amity.
The neighbors lived in quiet amity for decades.
etymology: From Old French amitie, from Latin amicus 'friend'.

definition: An official pardon for offenses, or a period when penalties are waived.
examples: The library declared an amnesty on overdue books.
Thousands applied under the government's tax amnesty.
etymology: From Greek amnēstia 'forgetfulness'.

definition: In a frenzied, wild, or uncontrolled way.
examples: The toddlers ran amok in the toy store.
Budgets can run amok without careful tracking.
etymology: From Malay amok 'rushing in a frenzy'.

definition: Lacking any sense of right and wrong.
examples: The film's villain is charming but amoral.
Markets are amoral; people have to supply the ethics.
etymology: From a- 'not' + moral.

definition: Showing or feeling romantic or sexual desire.
examples: The pigeons on my balcony were in an amorous mood.
He wrote amorous letters every week of the war.
etymology: From Old French amorous, from Latin amor 'love'.

definition: Without a clear shape, structure, or definition.
examples: The project's goals remain amorphous.
An amorphous blob of fog crept over the bay.
etymology: From Greek amorphos 'shapeless', from a- 'without' + morphē 'form'.

definition: A sense of one's own worth; self-esteem.
examples: Losing to his younger brother wounded his amour-propre.
Flattery soothed the minister's amour-propre.
etymology: From French amour-propre 'self-love'.

definition: Enough or more than enough; plentiful.
examples: There is ample parking behind the theater.
You'll have ample time to ask questions after the talk.
etymology: From French ample, from Latin amplus 'large, spacious'.

definition: To make something louder, stronger, or more significant.
examples: Social media can amplify a minor mistake into a scandal.
We need a speaker to amplify the guitar.
etymology: From Old French amplifier, from Latin amplificare, from amplus 'large'.

definition: A military advance inland, or any difficult journey or expedition.
examples: Our road trip became an anabasis through mountain passes.
Xenophon's Anabasis describes a long anabasis and retreat.
etymology: From Greek anabasis 'going up', from anabainein 'to go up'.

definition: Something out of place in time, especially something that belongs to an earlier era.
examples: A wristwatch in a film about ancient Rome would be an anachronism.
Some critics call the monarchy an anachronism in a modern democracy.
etymology: From Greek anakhronismos, from ana- 'against' + khronos 'time'.

definition: A sentence that abruptly shifts to a different grammatical structure.
examples: "If you think I'm going to — well, forget it" is an anacoluthon.
The speech's one anacoluthon made it sound unscripted.
etymology: From Greek anakolouthon 'lacking sequence', from an- 'not' + akolouthos 'following'.

definition: The moment in a story when a character makes a critical discovery or recognizes the truth.
examples: The anagnorisis comes when the detective realizes she has been chasing her own brother.
Oedipus's anagnorisis is one of the most devastating scenes in Greek tragedy.
etymology: From Greek anagnōrisis, 'recognition', from anagnōrizein, 'to recognize'.

definition: Comparable in certain respects, making a comparison useful.
examples: A cell's nucleus is analogous to a control room.
The situation is analogous to the housing bubble of 2008.
etymology: From Greek analogos 'proportionate'.

definition: A comparison that explains one thing by pointing out its similarity to another.
examples: The teacher used an analogy to plumbing to explain electric current.
Every analogy breaks down if you push it far enough.
etymology: From Greek analogia 'proportion', from ana- 'according to' + logos 'ratio, reason'.

definition: Recollection, especially of a supposed previous existence, or a patient's medical history.
examples: The doctor began with a careful anamnesis.
Plato believed learning was a kind of anamnesis.
etymology: From Greek anamnēsis 'remembrance', from anamimnēskein 'to remind'.

definition: The repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.
examples: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight…" is a famous anaphora.
The speechwriter leaned heavily on anaphora.
etymology: From Greek anaphora 'carrying back', from ana- 'back' + pherein 'to carry'.

definition: Lacking order or control; chaotic and free-wheeling.
examples: The band's anarchic live shows were legendary.
The first week of the startup was anarchic.
etymology: From anarchy, from Greek anarkhia 'lack of a leader'.

definition: Something or someone strongly disliked or detested.
examples: Waste of any kind is anathema to the thrifty chef.
Compromise was anathema to the party's hardliners, who wanted total victory.
etymology: From Greek anathema, 'a thing devoted, accursed', later used for ecclesiastical curses.

definition: A person's family descent or line of ancestors.
examples: A DNA kit revealed some surprising ancestry.
The family traces its ancestry to a fishing village in Portugal.
etymology: From Old French ancesserie, from ancestre 'ancestor', from Latin antecessor 'one who goes before'.

definition: A person who withdraws from society for religious reasons; a hermit.
examples: During exam week she lived like an anchorite in the library.
A medieval anchorite was sealed into a cell beside the church.
etymology: From Greek anakhōrētēs, from anakhōrein 'to retire'.

definition: Providing support to a main activity; secondary.
examples: The hospital hired more ancillary staff such as porters and cleaners.
Merchandise is an ancillary source of income for the band.
etymology: From Latin ancillaris, from ancilla 'maidservant'.

definition: A short, amusing or interesting story about a real person or event.
examples: He opened his speech with an anecdote about his first day on the job.
Grandpa's favorite anecdote involves a goat, a wedding, and a lost hat.
etymology: From Greek anekdota, 'things unpublished', from an- 'not' + ekdotos 'given out'.

definition: Lacking energy or vigor; also, suffering from anemia.
examples: Economists expect anemic growth next quarter.
The sequel had an anemic plot.
etymology: From anemia, from Greek anaimia 'lack of blood'.

definition: Full of twists and turns; winding.
examples: We followed an anfractuous mountain road for hours.
His anfractuous explanation lost everyone.
etymology: From Late Latin anfractuosus, from Latin anfractus 'a bending'.

definition: A deep feeling of anxiety or dread, often about life in general.
examples: The album captures teenage angst perfectly.
There was a lot of angst in the office before the reorg.
etymology: From German Angst 'fear'.

definition: Severe mental or physical pain and distress.
examples: You could hear the anguish in his voice on the phone.
Waiting for the test results was pure anguish.
etymology: From Old French anguisse, from Latin angustia 'tightness, distress'.

definition: The inability to feel pleasure.
examples: Anhedonia is a common symptom of depression.
Even his favorite music couldn't pierce the anhedonia.
etymology: Coined in French by Théodule Ribot in 1896 from Greek an- 'without' + hēdonē 'pleasure'.

definition: To criticize or comment unfavorably.
examples: The reviewer chose to animadvert on the novel's clumsy dialogue.
It is unkind to animadvert on someone's accent.
etymology: From Latin animadvertere, 'to turn the mind to'.

definition: Full of life and energy, or made using animation.
examples: They got into an animated debate about pineapple on pizza.
The studio's new animated film opens Friday.
etymology: From Latin animare 'to give life to', from anima 'breath, soul'.

definition: Strong hostility or dislike.
examples: There was no animosity between the rivals after the match.
Years of animosity made the merger difficult.
etymology: From Late Latin animositas, from animosus 'spirited'.

definition: Strong hostility or ill will, often driving someone's actions.
examples: There was no personal animus behind the critique; it was purely about the data.
Years of rivalry left a lingering animus between the two families.
etymology: From Latin animus, 'mind, spirit, passion'.

definition: Historical records, or the recorded history of a field.
examples: The game will go down in the annals of sports history.
Her research fills a gap in the annals of medicine.
etymology: From Latin annales libri 'yearly books', from annus 'year'.

definition: To toughen glass or metal by heating and slow cooling; to strengthen.
examples: Glassblowers anneal each piece overnight.
Hardship can anneal a person's resolve.
etymology: From Old English onælan 'to set on fire', from on + ælan 'to burn'.

definition: To add notes or comments to a text or diagram.
examples: I like to annotate the margins of library books in pencil.
Please annotate the screenshot so the bug is obvious.
etymology: From Latin annotare, from ad- 'to' + notare 'to mark'.

definition: To declare something legally invalid.
examples: They asked the court to annul the marriage.
The board voted to annul the disputed election.
etymology: From Late Latin annullare, from ad- 'to' + nullum 'nothing'.

definition: Ring-shaped.
examples: We watched an annular eclipse turn the sun into a ring of fire.
The tree's annular growth rings told its age.
etymology: From Latin annularis, from anulus 'little ring'.

definition: Inoffensive and bland, unlikely to provoke.
examples: The press release was full of anodyne phrases that said nothing.
The band traded its edgy sound for anodyne pop.
etymology: From Greek anōdunos, 'painless'.

definition: To smear with oil in a ceremony, or to choose someone as a successor.
examples: Critics were quick to anoint her the next great novelist.
Priests anoint the new king with holy oil.
etymology: From Old French enoint 'anointed', from Latin inungere, from in- 'upon' + ungere 'to smear'.

definition: Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected.
examples: The data contained one anomaly that the team could not explain.
A warm day in January is an anomaly in this part of the country.
etymology: From Greek anomalos, 'uneven, irregular', from an- 'not' + homalos 'even'.

definition: A condition of social instability and alienation caused by a breakdown of shared values.
examples: The novel captures the anomie of young workers drifting between gig jobs in a vast city.
Sociologists linked the rise in loneliness to a creeping anomie in the suburbs.
etymology: From French anomie, from Greek anomia, 'lawlessness'.

definition: Soon; shortly.
examples: I must go now, but I'll see you anon.
More details will follow anon.
etymology: From Old English on āne, 'in one'.

definition: Relating to geese, or silly like a goose.
examples: His anserine honk of a laugh filled the room.
The pond's anserine residents hissed at joggers.
etymology: From Latin anserinus, from anser 'goose'.

definition: Occurring before a war, especially the American Civil War.
examples: The town is full of antebellum mansions.
She studies antebellum politics in the South.
etymology: From Latin ante bellum 'before the war'.

definition: A thing or event that comes before and often leads to another.
examples: The telegraph was an antecedent of the internet.
Every crisis has an antecedent if you look closely.
etymology: From Latin antecedent-, from antecedere 'to go before'.

definition: Extremely old-fashioned or outdated, as if from before the biblical Flood.
examples: His antediluvian computer took ten minutes just to open a spreadsheet.
The club's antediluvian rules still banned women from the main dining room.
etymology: From Latin ante- 'before' + diluvium 'flood'.

definition: Having human characteristics attributed to an animal, object, or god.
examples: The cartoon features an anthropomorphic toaster.
Ancient myths are full of anthropomorphic gods.
etymology: From Greek anthrōpomorphos, from anthrōpos 'human' + morphē 'form'.

definition: To expect or predict something and prepare for it in advance.
examples: We didn't anticipate such a long line at the border.
Good waiters anticipate what you need before you ask.
etymology: From Latin anticipare 'to take before', from ante- 'before' + capere 'to take'.

definition: A remedy that counteracts a poison, or anything that relieves a bad situation.
examples: A long walk is my antidote to a stressful day.
The hospital keeps an antidote for snake bites on hand.
etymology: From Greek antidoton 'given against', from anti- 'against' + didonai 'to give'.

definition: A contradiction between two beliefs or conclusions that each seem reasonable.
examples: Freedom versus security is a classic antinomy.
Kant described an antinomy at the heart of reason.
etymology: From Greek antinomia, from anti- 'against' + nomos 'law'.

definition: A deep-seated feeling of dislike.
examples: Her antipathy toward meetings is well known.
There's a long-standing antipathy between the two families.
etymology: From Greek antipatheia, from anti- 'against' + pathos 'feeling'.

definition: A short chant or response sung alternately by two groups.
examples: The choir sang an antiphon across the cathedral.
Their argument became an antiphon of blame.
etymology: From Greek antiphōna 'harmonies', from anti- 'in return' + phōnē 'sound'.

definition: On the exact opposite side of the globe, or diametrically opposed.
examples: Their views on the budget were antipodal.
New Zealand is roughly antipodal to Spain.
etymology: From antipodes, from Greek antipous 'having the feet opposite'.

definition: Old-fashioned or outdated.
examples: The bank still uses an antiquated computer system.
His views on marriage seem antiquated.
etymology: From Latin antiquare 'to make old', from antiquus 'ancient'.

definition: The direct opposite of something, or a contrast between two ideas.
examples: His quiet, careful style is the antithesis of his brother's loud showmanship.
The poem sets youth against age, making each the antithesis of the other.
etymology: From Greek antithesis, 'opposition', from anti- 'against' + tithenai 'to place'.

definition: Using an epithet in place of a proper name, or a proper name as a general term.
examples: Calling a skilled lover "a Casanova" is antonomasia.
"The Bard" for Shakespeare is a common antonomasia.
etymology: From Greek antonomasia, from antonomazein 'to name instead'.

definition: Swiftly; at a fast pace.
examples: Construction of the new library is proceeding apace.
Research in the field continues apace.
etymology: From Old French à pas, 'at a pace'.

definition: A lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern about things that matter.
examples: Voter apathy meant that fewer than a quarter of residents turned out.
Years of failure had left the team in a state of apathy.
etymology: From Greek apatheia, 'freedom from suffering', from a- 'without' + pathos 'feeling'.

definition: The top or highest point of something.
examples: The band was at the apex of its fame in 1999.
The wolf is the apex predator in this forest.
etymology: From Latin apex 'peak, tip'.

definition: The point in an orbit farthest from the sun.
examples: Earth reaches aphelion in early July.
At aphelion, the comet moves slowest.
etymology: From Greek apo- 'away from' + hēlios 'sun'.

definition: A short, witty statement of a general truth.
examples: "Less is more" is an aphorism every designer knows.
Her speech was packed with one aphorism after another.
etymology: From Greek aphorismos 'definition', from aphorizein 'to define'.

definition: Relating to bees.
examples: The garden is an apian paradise in July.
Researchers study apian navigation.
etymology: From Latin apianus, from apis 'bee'.

definition: Calm self-confidence and poise in a difficult or stressful situation.
examples: She handled the surprise question with aplomb and never lost her smile.
The waiter recovered from the spilled tray with remarkable aplomb.
etymology: From French aplomb, 'perpendicularity', from à plomb, 'according to the plumb line'.

definition: Describing or predicting total destruction or the end of the world.
examples: The wildfire left an apocalyptic orange sky over the city.
Some forecasts are needlessly apocalyptic.
etymology: From Greek apokalupsis 'revelation', from apokaluptein 'to uncover'.

definition: The loss of sounds or letters from the end of a word.
examples: "Photo" from "photograph" is an example of apocope.
Casual speech is full of apocope.
etymology: From Greek apokopē 'a cutting off'.

definition: Widely told as true but probably invented or of doubtful origin.
examples: The story that he wrote the song in ten minutes is probably apocryphal.
Many apocryphal quotes get credited to Mark Twain or Einstein.
etymology: From Greek apokruphos, 'hidden, obscure', from apo- 'away' + kruptein 'to hide'.

definition: Clearly established or beyond dispute.
examples: He spoke with apodictic certainty about matters he barely knew.
The proof is apodictic; no counterexample exists.
etymology: From Greek apodeiktikos, from apodeiknunai 'to demonstrate'.

definition: The highest point or climax of something.
examples: The empire reached its apogee in the second century.
Her career hit its apogee with the Oscar win.
etymology: From Greek apogaion 'away from the earth'.

definition: A formal written defense of one's beliefs or conduct.
examples: His memoir is an apologia for a controversial career.
The essay reads as an apologia for fast fashion.
etymology: From Greek apologia 'a speech in defense'.

definition: The tendency to perceive meaningful patterns in random information.
examples: Seeing faces in electrical outlets is a harmless form of apophenia.
Conspiracy theories often feed on apophenia.
etymology: From German Apophänie, coined by Klaus Conrad from Greek apophainein, 'to make manifest'.

definition: Overcome with anger; furious.
examples: My dad was apoplectic when he saw the phone bill.
The coach looked apoplectic after the missed call.
etymology: From Greek apoplēktikos, from apoplēssein 'to disable by a stroke'.

definition: Ending in doubt or an unresolved puzzle.
examples: Many of Plato's dialogues are aporetic, ending without an answer.
The film's aporetic ending frustrated audiences.
etymology: From Greek aporētikos, from aporia 'difficulty, impasse'.

definition: An irresolvable puzzle or doubt, especially one that stalls an argument.
examples: The seminar ended in aporia, with nobody able to define justice to everyone's satisfaction.
Her essay deliberately leads the reader into an aporia about free will.
etymology: From Greek aporia, 'difficulty, perplexity', from aporos, 'impassable'.

definition: Of coloring that warns predators an animal is toxic or dangerous.
examples: The poison dart frog's aposematic blue warns birds away.
Wasps wear aposematic stripes.
etymology: From Greek apo- 'away' + sēma 'sign', coined in the late 19th century.

definition: Breaking off suddenly in speech, leaving a thought unfinished.
examples: "Why, you little…" is a classic aposiopesis.
The novelist uses aposiopesis to show the character's panic.
etymology: From Greek aposiōpēsis, from aposiōpan 'to become silent'.

definition: The abandonment of a belief, cause, or principle one once held.
examples: For a lifelong baseball fan, rooting for the rival team felt like apostasy.
Her apostasy from the strict diet began with a single cookie.
etymology: From Greek apostasia, 'defection', from apo- 'away' + stasis 'standing'.

definition: An old-fashioned word for a pharmacist, or the shop they run.
examples: The apothecary mixed a tonic for her cough.
The old apothecary jars now hold cookies.
etymology: From Late Latin apothecarius 'storekeeper', from Greek apothēkē 'storehouse'.

definition: A short, witty saying that expresses a general truth.
examples: 'Well begun is half done' is my grandmother's favorite apothegm.
The book collects apothegms from ancient philosophers.
etymology: From Greek apophthegma, from apophthengesthai 'to speak out'.

definition: The highest or most perfect example, or the raising of someone to godlike status.
examples: The film was the apotheosis of the director's career, praised by every critic.
Ancient emperors sometimes sought apotheosis, hoping to be worshipped as gods after death.
etymology: From Greek apotheosis, 'deification', from apotheoun, 'to deify'.

definition: Meant to ward off evil or bad luck.
examples: She hung an apotropaic charm by the front door.
Gargoyles may have had an apotropaic purpose.
etymology: From Greek apotropaios 'averting evil', from apotrepein 'to turn away'.

definition: To fill someone with shock and disgust.
examples: The conditions at the shelter would appall anyone who saw them.
Her rudeness never fails to appall me.
etymology: From Old French apalir 'to grow pale', from a- 'to' + palir 'to be pale'.

definition: Land or income granted to royal children, or a natural perk of a position.
examples: A corner office was the appanage of senior partners.
The prince received a modest appanage.
etymology: From French apanage, from Medieval Latin appanare 'to provide with bread'.

definition: Clearly visible or understood; also, seeming real but possibly not so.
examples: It was apparent that nobody had read the agenda.
For no apparent reason, the printer started working again.
etymology: From Old French aparant, from Latin apparere 'to appear'.

definition: To calm or satisfy someone by giving in to their demands.
examples: The airline offered vouchers to appease angry passengers.
You can't appease a toddler by negotiating.
etymology: From Old French apaisier, from a- 'to' + pais 'peace'.

definition: A name or title; also, a protected name for a wine's region of origin.
examples: He earned the appellation "the Professor" for his careful style.
Only wine from that region can use the appellation Champagne.
etymology: From Latin appellatio, from appellare 'to address, call'.

definition: A part attached to something larger, often seen as secondary.
examples: Octopuses can regrow a lost appendage.
The committee became a mere appendage of the mayor's office.
etymology: From append, from Latin appendere 'to hang on', plus the suffix -age.

definition: Understanding a new experience by relating it to what one already knows.
examples: Apperception explains why experts notice details beginners miss.
Each reader's apperception colors the poem.
etymology: From French aperception, from Latin ad- 'to' + percipere 'to perceive'.

definition: Relevant or appropriate to a particular case.
examples: Fill in only the sections that are applicable to you.
The discount isn't applicable on sale items.
etymology: From Medieval Latin applicabilis, from Latin applicare 'to attach, apply'.

definition: Apt; well suited to the circumstances.
examples: She ended her speech with an apposite quote from Maya Angelou.
His comment was apposite and brief.
etymology: From Latin appositus, from apponere, 'to apply'.

definition: To judge the value, quality, or condition of something.
examples: We hired an expert to appraise the antique ring.
She paused to appraise the room before speaking.
etymology: From apprize, from Old French aprisier, influenced by praise.

definition: To arrest someone, or to grasp the meaning of something.
examples: Police were able to apprehend the suspect within hours.
It took me years to fully apprehend what she meant.
etymology: From Latin apprehendere, from ad- 'toward' + prehendere 'to seize'.

definition: Anxious or worried that something bad may happen.
examples: I was apprehensive about my first day at the new job.
Investors remain apprehensive ahead of the rate decision.
etymology: From Medieval Latin apprehensivus, from Latin apprehendere 'to seize, grasp'.

definition: A person learning a trade by working under a skilled expert.
examples: She spent two years as an apprentice to a master carpenter.
The apprentice watched every cut the chef made.
etymology: From Old French aprentis, from aprendre 'to learn', from Latin apprehendere 'to grasp'.

definition: To inform or tell someone about something.
examples: Please apprise me of any changes to the schedule.
Doctors must apprise patients of the risks.
etymology: From French appris, past participle of apprendre 'to learn, teach'.

definition: Warm praise or official approval, especially from someone in authority.
examples: The plan won the approbation of the committee after a short discussion.
She glowed with the teacher's approbation after reading her poem aloud.
etymology: From Latin approbatio, from approbare, 'to approve'.

definition: An accessory associated with a particular activity or style.
examples: A leather briefcase was the final appurtenance of his new job.
Every appurtenance of luxury filled the yacht.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman apurtenance, from Latin appertinere 'to belong to'.

definition: The warmth of the sun on a winter day.
examples: We sat on the bench enjoying the January apricity.
The cat followed the apricity across the floor.
etymology: From Latin apricitas 'sunniness', from apricus 'sunny'.

definition: Fitting or relevant to the situation.
examples: His joke was oddly apropos, given the weather.
The quote felt apropos for a graduation speech.
etymology: From French à propos 'to the purpose'.

definition: Fitting or appropriate in the circumstances; also, likely to do something.
examples: "Organized chaos" is an apt description of our kitchen.
Teenagers are apt to sleep in on weekends.
etymology: From Latin aptus 'fitted', past participle of apere 'to fasten'.

definition: A natural ability or talent for something.
examples: He showed an early aptitude for music, picking out songs on the piano by ear.
The test measures your aptitude for spatial reasoning.
etymology: From Late Latin aptitudo, 'fitness', from Latin aptus 'fit'.

definition: A personal name that suits its owner's job or traits.
examples: A dentist named Dr. Payne has a perfect aptronym.
Usain Bolt's surname is a famous aptronym.
etymology: A 20th-century coinage blending apt and -onym 'name'.

definition: Like an eagle, especially of a nose that is hooked or curved.
examples: The actor's aquiline nose made him perfect for the role of a Roman senator.
She had sharp, aquiline features.
etymology: From Latin aquilinus, from aquila 'eagle'.

definition: Trembling, especially with excitement.
examples: The crowd was aquiver as the countdown began.
Her voice was aquiver with emotion.
etymology: From a- 'in' + quiver.

definition: An ornate design of intertwined lines, or a ballet pose on one leg.
examples: The dancer held an arabesque for what felt like forever.
Every tile bore a blue arabesque.
etymology: From French arabesque, from Italian arabesco 'in the Arabic style'.

definition: A person with authority to settle disputes or judge what is acceptable.
examples: She became an arbiter of taste in the fashion world.
The court is the final arbiter of the law.
etymology: From Latin arbiter 'judge, supreme ruler'.

definition: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason or system.
examples: The deadline seemed arbitrary, since nothing special happened on that date.
Judges should not make arbitrary decisions that ignore the evidence.
etymology: From Latin arbitrarius, 'depending on the will of an arbiter', from arbiter, 'judge'.

definition: Relating to trees, or living in them.
examples: Sloths are arboreal and rarely touch the ground.
The trail winds through an arboreal tunnel.
etymology: From Latin arboreus, from arbor 'tree'.

definition: Idyllically rural and peaceful.
examples: The painting shows an arcadian scene of shepherds and streams.
They left the city for an arcadian life on a farm.
etymology: From Arcadia, a mountainous region of Greece idealized by poets as a pastoral paradise.

definition: Understood by few; mysterious or secret in nature.
examples: The arcane rules of cricket confused the visiting tourists, who gave up halfway through.
He studied arcane texts on alchemy in the dusty library basement.
etymology: From Latin arcanus, 'hidden, secret', from arca, 'chest'.

definition: A deep secret or mystery known only to a few.
examples: The recipe is a family arcanum.
Tax law is an arcanum to most people.
etymology: From Latin arcanum 'secret thing', from arcanus 'hidden'.

definition: Very old or old-fashioned, and no longer in common use.
examples: The office still runs on an archaic filing system.
"Thou" sounds archaic to modern ears.
etymology: From Greek arkhaikos 'old-fashioned', from arkhaios 'ancient'.

definition: A perfect typical example, or an original model.
examples: He is the archetype of the absent-minded professor.
The trickster is an archetype found in many myths.
etymology: From Greek arkhetupon 'pattern', from arkhe- 'primitive' + tupos 'model'.

definition: In a playfully teasing or knowingly mischievous way.
examples: She raised an eyebrow archly at his excuse.
"Busy weekend?" he asked archly.
etymology: From arch 'chief, roguish', from the prefix arch- as in arch-rogue, plus the suffix -ly.

definition: Showing intense passion, enthusiasm, or devotion.
examples: He was an ardent supporter of the local team, attending every home game.
Her ardent belief in the cause carried her through years of setbacks.
etymology: From Latin ardens, 'burning', from ardere, 'to burn'.

definition: Great enthusiasm or passion.
examples: Her ardor for the project never wavered.
Rain did little to dampen the fans' ardor.
etymology: From Latin ardor, from ardere 'to burn'.

definition: Requiring great effort and endurance; very difficult and tiring.
examples: The arduous climb to the summit took nearly nine hours in freezing wind.
Writing a doctoral thesis is an arduous process that tests even the most patient students.
etymology: From Latin arduus, meaning 'steep' or 'difficult'.

definition: Silvery, or made of silver.
examples: The lake had an argentine sheen under the moon.
The trout's argentine scales glittered in the net.
etymology: From Latin argentinus, from argentum 'silver'.

definition: A large merchant ship, or a rich supply of something.
examples: An argosy of treats arrived from Grandma.
Shakespeare's Antonio waits on every argosy at sea.
etymology: From Italian Ragusea 'ship of Ragusa', the old name of Dubrovnik.

definition: The jargon or slang of a particular group.
examples: Skateboarders have an argot all their own, full of terms like 'kickflip' and 'grind.'
The startup's argot of 'synergies' and 'pivots' baffled the new intern.
etymology: From French argot, originally 'the slang of thieves', of uncertain origin.

definition: In a way that can be reasonably argued or supported.
examples: She is arguably the best player on the team.
This is arguably the most important decision of the year.
etymology: From argue, from Latin arguere 'to make clear'.

definition: Shrewd and sharp-witted; also, shrill.
examples: The argute lawyer spotted the loophole instantly.
An argute whistle cut through the noise.
etymology: From Latin argutus 'clear, sharp', from arguere 'to make clear'.

definition: Having very little rain; dry and barren, or lacking interest.
examples: Cacti thrive in the arid climate of Arizona.
The lecture was arid and full of jargon.
etymology: From Latin aridus, from arere 'to be dry'.

definition: Correctly or properly.
examples: If I heard you aright, the meeting is canceled.
She set the crooked frame aright.
etymology: From Old English on riht 'in the right way'.

definition: The complete set of tools or resources available for a task.
examples: Antibiotics remain central to the doctor's armamentarium.
Sarcasm is the main weapon in her rhetorical armamentarium.
etymology: From Latin armamentarium 'arsenal', from armamenta 'implements'.

definition: To call someone before a court to answer a charge.
examples: Prosecutors will arraign the suspect on Monday.
The court will arraign all three defendants together.
etymology: From Old French araisnier, from Latin ad- 'to' + ratio 'reason, account'.

definition: Complete and utter, used of something bad.
examples: That's arrant nonsense, and you know it.
He was an arrant coward when it counted.
etymology: A variant of errant, originally in phrases like arrant thief 'wandering thief'.

definition: An impressive range or orderly arrangement of things.
examples: The shop sells a dazzling array of spices.
An array of solar panels covers the roof.
etymology: From Old French areer 'to arrange', ultimately of Germanic origin.

definition: An ambitious newcomer to wealth or status, seen as pushy or vulgar.
examples: Old-money families snubbed the arriviste and his yacht.
She was dismissed as an arriviste by the art establishment.
etymology: From French arriviste, from arriver 'to arrive'.

definition: To claim or seize something without justification.
examples: The committee chair tried to arrogate the power to approve every expense.
She arrogates credit for ideas that came from her interns.
etymology: From Latin arrogare, 'to claim for oneself'.

definition: Clever and skillful, sometimes in a sly or crafty way.
examples: Her artful dodge of the question impressed the journalists.
The chef made an artful arrangement of the dessert.
etymology: From art + the suffix -ful.

definition: To express an idea clearly in words.
examples: She struggled to articulate why the plan made her uneasy.
A good cover letter should articulate what you bring to the role.
etymology: From Latin articulare, 'to utter distinctly', from articulus 'small joint'.

definition: Clever or cunning devices used to trick or deceive others.
examples: The charm of his performance felt like pure artifice once you saw it twice.
She wrote plainly, without artifice, and readers trusted her for it.
etymology: From Latin artificium, 'craftsmanship', from ars, 'art', + facere, 'to make'.

definition: A skilled worker who makes things by hand.
examples: Each mug is shaped by a local artisan.
The market was full of artisan bread and cheese.
