I used ice cream as a bribe to get the kids into the car.
etymology: From Old French bribe 'bread given to a beggar'.

definition: Miscellaneous small ornaments of little value.
examples: Grandpa's den was crammed with bric-a-brac.
The yard sale was mostly bric-a-brac and old books.
etymology: From obsolete French à bric et à brac 'at random'.

definition: A piece of brick thrown as a weapon, or a harsh criticism.
examples: The film drew brickbat after brickbat from critics.
Each brickbat on social media stung the author.
etymology: From brick + bat 'piece'.

definition: Something created from whatever diverse materials happen to be available.
examples: The treehouse was a charming bricolage of old doors, pallets, and rope.
Her playlist is a bricolage of jazz, folk, and video game soundtracks.
etymology: From French bricolage, from bricoler, 'to do odd jobs, tinker'.

definition: To show resentment or anger, especially at an insult.
examples: Many staff bridle at the idea of tracking their hours.
She tends to bridle when anyone questions her figures.
etymology: From Old English bridel, the headgear for a horse; the sense of anger comes from a horse jerking its head.

definition: A member of a gang that robs travelers in remote areas.
examples: A brigand stopped the coach at the mountain pass.
The film's hero is a charming brigand.
etymology: From Italian brigante 'foot soldier', from brigare 'to contend'.

definition: An old word for sulfur, linked with hellfire and fiery preaching.
examples: The preacher delivered a sermon full of fire and brimstone.
The volcano's vents smelled of brimstone.
etymology: From Old English brynstan, probably from bryne 'burning' + stan 'stone'.

definition: Brownish or tawny with streaks of another color.
examples: A brindled greyhound slept by the fire.
The brindled cow stood apart from the herd.
etymology: An alteration of the older word brinded 'streaked'.

definition: The edge of a steep place, or the point just before something happens.
examples: The species was pulled back from the brink of extinction.
The two countries were on the brink of war.
etymology: From Middle English, of Scandinavian origin.

definition: Pushing a dangerous situation to the edge to force concessions.
examples: Budget talks turned into a game of brinkmanship.
Cold War brinkmanship nearly ended in disaster.
etymology: From brink + -manship; it was popularized in the 1950s in discussions of Cold War policy.

definition: Vigor, vivacity, and style.
examples: The orchestra played with great brio.
She tackled the presentation with brio.
etymology: From Italian brio 'liveliness'.

definition: Quick and energetic, or pleasantly cold and fresh.
examples: We took a brisk walk before breakfast.
Business at the food truck was brisk all afternoon.
etymology: Probably from French brusque 'lively, fierce'.

definition: To react with sudden anger or offense, or for hair to stand up stiffly.
examples: Many teachers bristle at the idea of more testing.
I watched the cat's fur bristle at the stranger.
etymology: From Middle English bristel, from Old English byrst 'bristle'.

definition: Hard but easily broken, or fragile under pressure.
examples: Old plastic gets brittle in the sun.
Their truce was brittle from the start.
etymology: From Old English breotan 'to break up'.

definition: To bring up a difficult or sensitive subject for discussion.
examples: I wasn't sure how to broach the topic of splitting the rent.
She finally broached the idea of moving abroad with her parents.
etymology: From Old French broche, 'spit, pointed tool', originally meaning to pierce a cask.

definition: In general terms, without going into detail; also, widely.
examples: Broadly speaking, the plan makes sense.
She smiled broadly when she saw the cake.
etymology: From broad, from Old English brad, plus the suffix -ly.

definition: A fierce verbal or written attack.
examples: The op-ed was a broadside against the mayor.
She fired a broadside at her critics on social media.
etymology: From broad + side, originally the firing of all guns on one side of a warship.

definition: Gigantic; enormous.
examples: The restaurant serves brobdingnagian portions.
A brobdingnagian cruise ship blocked the harbor view.
etymology: From Brobdingnag, the land of giants in Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726).

definition: A trite and unoriginal statement meant to soothe.
examples: "Everything happens for a reason" is a hollow bromide.
The speech was one bromide after another.
etymology: From the chemical bromide, once used as a sedative.

definition: To think deeply and unhappily about something.
examples: Don't brood over one bad review.
He tends to brood for days after losing a game.
etymology: From Old English brod 'offspring'; the sense of worrying comes from a hen sitting on eggs.

definition: To tolerate or allow something, usually used in the negative.
examples: The coach will brook no excuses for missed practice.
She would not brook any interruption.
etymology: From Old English brucan 'to use, enjoy'.

definition: A noisy and overexcited reaction or commotion.
examples: The referee's call caused a brouhaha that lasted well after the final whistle.
All the brouhaha over the new logo faded within a week.
etymology: From French brouhaha, probably imitative in origin.

definition: To intimidate someone with stern words or looks.
examples: Salespeople tried to browbeat us into buying the warranty.
A good coach doesn't browbeat players.
etymology: From brow + beat, from the idea of overpowering someone with frowns.

definition: To look through things casually, or for animals to feed on leaves.
examples: I like to browse used bookstores on rainy days.
Deer browse the shrubs at the edge of the yard.
etymology: From Old French brost 'young shoot', probably of Germanic origin.

definition: To spread a report or rumor widely.
examples: Insiders bruit the name of the next CEO.
Don't bruit our plans about before they're final.
etymology: From French bruit 'noise', from bruire 'to roar'.

definition: Wintry; belonging to winter.
examples: Brumal winds rattled the windows all night.
The forest lay under a brumal hush.
etymology: From Latin brumalis, from bruma 'winter solstice'.

definition: Cheap, showy, and fake.
examples: The stall sold brummagem jewelry to tourists.
His brummagem charm fooled no one.
etymology: From a dialect form of Birmingham, England, once known for counterfeit coins.

definition: The worst part or chief impact of something.
examples: Coastal towns bore the brunt of the hurricane.
Junior staff took the brunt of the budget cuts.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in Middle English.

definition: Abrupt or curt in manner or speech.
examples: The receptionist's brusque reply made me feel unwelcome.
He's brusque on the phone but kind in person.
etymology: From French brusque, 'lively, fierce', from Italian brusco, 'sour'.

definition: Habitual grinding of the teeth, especially during sleep.
examples: Stress-induced bruxism wore down his molars.
The dentist prescribed a night guard for her bruxism.
etymology: From Greek brukhein 'to gnash the teeth'.

definition: A pirate, or a daring and ruthless adventurer in business.
examples: The financier was a buccaneer who loved hostile takeovers.
A buccaneer once hid treasure on this island, or so the legend goes.
etymology: From French boucanier, a hunter who cured meat on a boucan, a wooden frame.

definition: To bend and collapse under pressure, or to fasten with a buckle.
examples: The shelf began to buckle under the weight of books.
Don't buckle under pressure from the other bidders.
etymology: From Old French boucle, from Latin buccula 'cheek strap of a helmet'.

definition: Pleasantly rural or pastoral, like idealized countryside life.
examples: They retired to a bucolic village surrounded by meadows and grazing sheep.
The painting captured a bucolic scene of farmers resting beneath an oak tree.
etymology: From Greek boukolikos, 'of herdsmen', from boukolos, 'cowherd'.

definition: To move slightly, or to change an opinion.
examples: The rusty bolt wouldn't budge.
Despite the protests, the council refused to budge.
etymology: From French bouger 'to stir', based on Latin bullire 'to boil'.

definition: Something that lessens a shock or forms a protective barrier.
examples: Keep a cash buffer for unexpected bills.
The trees act as a buffer against highway noise.
etymology: Probably from the obsolete verb buff, imitative of the sound of a soft blow.

definition: A ridiculous but amusing person; a clown.
examples: He played the buffoon to hide his nerves.
The sitcom's dad is a lovable buffoon.
etymology: From French bouffon, from Italian buffone 'jester'.

definition: An object of exaggerated fear or a recurring problem.
examples: Inflation is the perennial bugaboo of central banks.
The printer jam is the office bugaboo.
etymology: Probably from bugbear and boo, related to dialect words for a goblin.

definition: A persistent source of annoyance or fear.
examples: Parking is the biggest bugbear for residents.
Grammar errors are my editor's favorite bugbear.
etymology: From obsolete bug 'bogey' + bear; it once meant an imaginary monster used to scare children.

definition: Round and swollen in shape.
examples: The cartoon villain had a bulbous red nose.
Bulbous lamps hung over the bar.
etymology: From Latin bulbosus, from bulbus 'onion, bulb'.

definition: Large size or mass, or the greater part of something.
examples: The bulk of the work is already done.
We buy rice in bulk to save money.
etymology: From Old Norse búlki 'cargo'.

definition: Large and awkward to handle or move.
examples: The bulky sofa wouldn't fit up the stairs.
Bulky winter coats take up half the closet.
etymology: From bulk, from Old Norse búlki 'cargo', plus the suffix -y.

definition: To force something through without regard for objections.
examples: The developer tried to bulldoze the plan through the council.
Don't bulldoze your teammates in meetings.
etymology: An American word of uncertain origin, first meaning to intimidate by violence.

definition: Confident and optimistic, especially about rising prices.
examples: Analysts are bullish on the electric car market.
She's bullish about the team's chances this year.
etymology: From bull, in the stock-market sense of one who expects prices to rise, plus -ish.

definition: A defensive wall, or a person or thing that protects against danger.
examples: A free press is a bulwark against corruption.
The dunes serve as a bulwark against storm surges.
etymology: From Middle Dutch bolwerc, related to bole 'tree trunk' and work.

definition: A humorous word for an umbrella.
examples: Don't forget your bumbershoot; it's pouring.
He twirled a striped bumbershoot down the street.
etymology: An American alteration of umbrella, with -shoot from parachute.

definition: Acting in a confused, clumsy, or incompetent way.
examples: The bumbling detective somehow solves every case.
A bumbling response made the crisis worse.
etymology: From bumble, probably imitative.

definition: Useless or tedious printed material; paperwork.
examples: The welcome pack was mostly marketing bumf.
I recycle the bumf before opening real mail.
etymology: British slang, short for bum-fodder, a joking term for toilet paper.

definition: Self-assertive in an irritating, pushy way.
examples: The bumptious new manager rearranged everyone's desks without asking.
A bumptious fan kept shouting advice at the players.
etymology: A humorous formation from bump, on the pattern of fractious.

definition: To carry out a task clumsily or incompetently.
examples: Rushing the launch could bungle the whole project.
Somehow they managed to bungle a simple coffee order.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: Foolish or insincere talk; nonsense.
examples: The miracle diet is pure bunkum.
His theory sounded like bunkum to the panel.
etymology: From Buncombe County, North Carolina, whose congressman gave a pointless speech in 1820 for his voters' sake.

definition: Able to float, or cheerful and optimistic.
examples: Salt water makes swimmers more buoyant.
She was in a buoyant mood after the interview.
etymology: From Spanish boyante 'floating', from boyar 'to float'.

definition: A heavy load, or a responsibility that causes worry or hardship.
examples: Student debt is a burden for many graduates.
She didn't want to be a burden to her family.
etymology: From Old English byrthen, related to bear.

definition: A system run by officials, often criticized for excessive rules and paperwork.
examples: Getting a permit means wading through layers of bureaucracy.
The startup tried to avoid bureaucracy as it grew.
etymology: From French bureaucratie, from bureau 'office, desk' + Greek-derived -cratie 'rule'.

definition: To grow or increase rapidly; to flourish.
examples: The city's food scene continues to burgeon, with new restaurants opening weekly.
Wildflowers burgeon across the hills each April after the winter rains.
etymology: From Old French burjon, 'bud, shoot', possibly of Germanic origin.

definition: A respectable citizen of a town, often middle class.
examples: Every burgher in town turned out for the parade.
Rembrandt painted many a prosperous burgher.
etymology: From Middle Dutch burgher, from burg 'borough'.

definition: To quietly suppress or avoid something, such as an inquiry.
examples: The committee tried to burke the awkward report.
Don't burke the question; answer it.
etymology: From William Burke, executed in Edinburgh in 1829 for murdering people by smothering.

definition: A parody that mocks serious subjects, or a variety show with comic acts.
examples: The play is a burlesque of corporate life.
They caught a burlesque show in New Orleans.
etymology: From Italian burlesco, from burla 'mockery'.

definition: Large, strong, and heavily built.
examples: A burly bouncer stood at the door.
The burly chef had surprisingly delicate hands.
etymology: From Middle English borlich 'stately', probably from an Old English source.

definition: To polish by rubbing, or to enhance a reputation.
examples: The craftsman burnished the brass doorknob until it gleamed.
The charity gala was meant to burnish the company's image.
etymology: From Old French burniss-, from brunir, 'to make brown, polish'.

definition: A thick-soled boot worn by ancient tragic actors, or tragedy itself.
examples: The actor traded comedy for the buskin late in his career.
Ancient Greek tragedians wore the buskin to appear taller.
etymology: Probably from Old French bouzequin, of uncertain origin.

definition: A kiss, especially a playful one.
examples: She gave her grandson a buss on the cheek.
A quick buss and he was out the door.
etymology: Probably imitative; first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: Full of busy, energetic activity.
examples: The bustling market smelled of spices and grilled meat.
Our sleepy town is now a bustling tech hub.
etymology: From bustle, probably from obsolete buskle 'to prepare'.

definition: To stop someone and hold them in conversation, often unwillingly.
examples: Lobbyists try to buttonhole senators in the hallway.
Uncle Joe will buttonhole you about crypto at dinner.
etymology: An alteration of buttonhold, from the act of grasping someone's coat button.

definition: To strengthen or support an argument, structure, or position.
examples: She buttressed her proposal with data from three pilot programs.
New funding will buttress the clinic's outreach efforts.
etymology: From Old French bouterez, 'thrusting', from bouter, 'to push'.

definition: A trendy word or phrase used more to impress than to inform.
examples: "Synergy" is the buzzword everyone in the office loves to hate.
The pitch deck had a buzzword on every slide.
etymology: From buzz + word, a 20th-century American coinage.

definition: Belonging to an earlier time.
examples: The diner looks like a relic from a bygone era.
He loves the bygone glamour of old Hollywood.
etymology: From by + gone.

definition: A secondary result produced alongside the main one.
examples: Sawdust is a byproduct of the lumber mill.
Better sleep was a happy byproduct of quitting caffeine.
etymology: From by- 'secondary' + product.

definition: Brooding, passionate, and romantically rebellious, like Lord Byron's heroes.
examples: He cultivated a byronic air with his scarf and scowl.
Heathcliff is the classic byronic hero.
etymology: From Lord Byron (1788–1824), the English Romantic poet.

definition: A person who is present at an event but does not take part.
examples: A bystander filmed the whole incident on her phone.
No one wants to be the bystander who does nothing.
etymology: From the verb phrase stand by, plus the suffix -er.

definition: Excessively complicated and hard to navigate.
examples: Getting a refund involved a byzantine set of forms.
The office politics were byzantine.
etymology: From Byzantium, the old name of Istanbul, whose imperial bureaucracy was famously complex.

definition: A small secret group plotting to advance its own interests.
examples: In the novel, a cabal of librarians secretly decides which books get published.
The memo hinted that a cabal of executives had planned the merger in private.
etymology: From French cabale, from medieval Latin cabbala, from Hebrew qabbālāh, 'tradition'.

definition: A hidden store of items, or a computer memory area holding data for quick access.
examples: Police found a cache of stolen phones in the garage.
Clearing your browser cache might fix the page.
etymology: From French cacher, 'to hide'.

definition: Prestige or distinction that sets something apart.
examples: Being featured in the magazine gave the tiny bakery real cachet.
Vinyl records have regained cachet among young music fans.
etymology: From French cachet, 'seal', from cacher, 'to press'.

definition: Severe wasting of the body from chronic illness.
examples: Doctors watched for signs of cachexia in the patient.
The novel describes the hero's slow cachexia.
etymology: From Greek kakhexia, from kakos 'bad' + hexis 'condition'.

definition: To laugh loudly and without restraint.
examples: The audience began to cachinnate at the clown's pratfall.
Old friends cachinnate over the same stories every reunion.
etymology: From Latin cachinnare, 'to laugh loudly', probably imitative.

definition: An evil spirit, or a malevolent person.
examples: Villagers blamed a cacodemon for the failed harvest.
The tyrant was a cacodemon in a tailored suit.
etymology: From Greek kakodaimōn, 'evil spirit'.

definition: An irresistible urge to do something, especially something unwise.
examples: He suffers from a cacoethes for buying gadgets he never uses.
Her cacoethes for writing produced forty unfinished novels.
etymology: From Greek kakoēthes, 'bad habit', from kakos 'bad' + ēthos 'character'.

definition: Bad handwriting or bad spelling.
examples: The doctor's cacography made the prescription a riddle.
Texting has made cacography almost fashionable.
etymology: From Greek kakos 'bad' + -graphia 'writing'.

definition: A harsh, jarring mixture of loud and unpleasant sounds.
examples: A cacophony of car horns greeted us as we left the station.
The kindergarten band produced a cacophony of banging, honking, and giggles.
etymology: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos 'bad' + phone 'sound'.

definition: Very pale, thin, or bony, like a corpse.
examples: After the flu, he looked cadaverous for weeks.
A cadaverous butler opened the creaking door.
etymology: From Latin cadaver 'corpse', from cadere 'to fall'.

definition: The rhythm and rise and fall of a voice, piece of music, or routine.
examples: The poet read with a slow, hypnotic cadence that silenced the room.
The team settled into a steady cadence of weekly releases.
etymology: From Italian cadenza, from Latin cadere, 'to fall'.

definition: To ask for something, especially food or money, without intending to repay.
examples: He'd always cadge a cigarette and never buy his own.
Freelancers learn to cadge free coffee at every conference.
etymology: Probably a back-formation from cadger, an old word for a traveling dealer.

definition: A small core group of trained people who can lead or expand an organization.
examples: A cadre of veteran engineers trained the new hires.
She built a loyal cadre of volunteers who ran every fundraiser.
etymology: From French cadre 'frame', from Italian quadro, from Latin quadrum 'square'.

definition: A pause or break, especially in the middle of a line of verse.
examples: The poem's caesura falls right after 'stop'.
The war created a caesura in her career.
etymology: From Latin caesura, 'a cutting', from caedere 'to cut'.

definition: A contemptible or cowardly person.
examples: The knight called his fleeing rival a caitiff.
Only a caitiff would abandon his crew in a storm.
etymology: From Old Northern French caitif 'captive', from Latin captivus.

definition: To persuade someone to do something through flattery or gentle coaxing.
examples: She managed to cajole her brother into driving her to the airport.
Salespeople often cajole shoppers with compliments and small discounts.
etymology: From French cajoler, 'to chatter like a jay, coax', of uncertain origin.

definition: An event that causes great and often sudden damage or distress.
examples: The flood was a calamity for every farm along the river.
Forgetting the rings felt like a calamity until the best man found a spare pair.
etymology: From Latin calamitas, 'disaster, misfortune'.

definition: The level of someone's ability or the quality of something.
examples: We rarely get applicants of her caliber.
The film's acting was of a caliber rarely seen in comedies.
etymology: From French calibre, possibly from Arabic qālib 'mold'.

definition: To adjust something carefully so that it measures or responds accurately.
examples: Technicians calibrate the scales every morning before the first shipment arrives.
A good teacher learns to calibrate feedback to each student's confidence.
etymology: Formed from caliber, the bore of a gun, since it first meant measuring gun barrels.

definition: Misty, dim, or dark.
examples: We stumbled through the caliginous forest at dusk.
The novel opens in a caliginous London fog.
etymology: From Latin caliginosus, from caligo 'mist, darkness'.

definition: Having well-shaped buttocks.
examples: The museum's callipygian Venus draws a curious crowd.
Gym ads promise a callipygian figure in six weeks.
etymology: From Greek kallipygos, from kallos 'beauty' + pygē 'buttocks'.

definition: Showing no sympathy or concern for the feelings of others.
examples: His callous remark about the layoffs shocked everyone in the room.
Years in the emergency room had not made her callous toward suffering.
etymology: From Latin callosus, 'hard-skinned', from callum, 'hard skin'.

definition: Young and inexperienced, lacking maturity or worldly knowledge.
examples: The callow intern confidently offered advice to executives with thirty years of experience.
Looking back, she cringed at her callow belief that success would come easily.
etymology: From Old English calu, 'bald', later meaning unfledged, hence immature.

definition: A phrase borrowed by translating it word for word from another language.
examples: 'Flea market' is a calque of French marché aux puces.
German Wolkenkratzer is a calque of English 'skyscraper'.
etymology: From French calque, 'a copy, tracing'.

definition: A false statement made to damage someone's reputation.
examples: The senator dismissed the rumor as pure calumny.
He endured years of calumny before his name was cleared.
etymology: From Latin calumnia, 'trickery, false accusation'.

definition: Mutual trust and friendship among people who spend time together.
examples: The camaraderie on the night shift made long hours feel shorter.
Hiking clubs offer exercise and a sense of camaraderie.
etymology: From French camaraderie, from camarade 'comrade'.

definition: A small group of secret, unofficial advisers to a ruler.
examples: A camarilla of old friends made the real decisions.
The prime minister's camarilla met in his kitchen.
etymology: From Spanish camarilla, 'little room', a diminutive of cámara 'chamber'.

definition: Coloring or covering that helps something blend into its surroundings.
examples: The moth's speckled wings are perfect camouflage against tree bark.
His cheerful small talk was camouflage for how nervous he felt.
etymology: From French camoufler, 'to disguise', popularized during World War I.

definition: A bell tower, especially one standing apart from a church.
examples: The campanile in Venice towers over St. Mark's Square.
The university's campanile chimes every quarter hour.
etymology: From Italian campanile, from campana 'bell'.

definition: The art or study of bell ringing.
examples: His interest in campanology began in the church tower.
Campanology involves complex ringing patterns.
etymology: From Late Latin campana 'bell' + -logy 'study'.

definition: The common people regarded with contempt; the rabble.
examples: The aristocrat sneered at the canaille outside his gates.
Snobs dismiss online fandom as the canaille.
etymology: From French, from Italian canaglia 'pack of dogs', from cane 'dog'.

definition: An unfounded rumor or false story.
examples: The canard that we only use ten percent of our brains refuses to die.
She spent the interview patiently debunking an old canard about her family.
etymology: From French canard, 'duck', also 'hoax'.

definition: Honest and direct in speech, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: Thank you for being candid about the problems with my draft before I submitted it.
The actor gave a candid interview about his struggles early in his career.
etymology: From Latin candidus, 'white, pure, sincere', from candere 'to shine'.

definition: Honest, open, and sincere expression, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: I appreciated her candor when she said the first draft was weak.
He spoke with refreshing candor about his mistakes as a young manager.
etymology: From Latin candor, 'whiteness, sincerity', from candere, 'to shine, be white'.

definition: Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business.
examples: A canny investor, she sold right before the crash.
The canny coach saved his best player for the final quarter.
etymology: Originally Scots, from can in its old sense 'to know how'.

definition: A body of works or rules accepted as authoritative or genuine.
examples: Fans argue whether the spin-off counts as canon.
Her novels have entered the literary canon.
etymology: From Greek kanōn, 'measuring rod, rule'.

definition: Melodious and resonant.
examples: The canorous call of a thrush filled the garden.
Her canorous voice made even the menu sound like poetry.
etymology: From Latin canorus, from canere 'to sing'.

definition: Bad-tempered, argumentative, and uncooperative.
examples: The cantankerous old printer jams whenever we're on deadline.
Our cantankerous neighbor complains about every leaf on his lawn.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly from Middle English contack 'strife'.

definition: A magic spell, or a mischievous trick.
examples: The witch muttered a cantrip over the cauldron.
Hiding his keys was her favorite cantrip.
etymology: A Scots word of unknown origin.

definition: To go around asking people for votes, opinions, or support.
examples: Volunteers will canvass the neighborhood every Saturday until the election.
Before choosing a caterer, we decided to canvass the whole office for ideas.
etymology: Originally a variant spelling of canvas; the sense of soliciting votes developed later.

definition: The maximum amount something can hold or produce, or a person's ability to do something.
examples: The concert hall was filled to capacity.
She has a remarkable capacity for forgiveness.
etymology: From Latin capacitas, from capax 'able to hold', from capere 'to take'.

definition: An ornamental covering for a horse, or rich, showy clothing.
examples: The knight's horse wore a scarlet caparison.
She arrived in full caparison of silk and pearls.
etymology: From French caparasson, from Spanish caparazón, probably related to capa 'cape'.

definition: To take advantage of something, or to write a word with a capital letter.
examples: The team failed to capitalize on its early lead.
Smart brands capitalize on viral moments within hours.
etymology: From capital, from Latin capitalis, from caput 'head'.

definition: To cease resisting and give in to a demand or opponent.
examples: After hours of pleading, my parents finally capitulated and got a dog.
The company refused to capitulate to the unreasonable demands.
etymology: From Medieval Latin capitulare, 'to draw up under headings', from capitulum, 'chapter'.

definition: A lively, free-form piece of music, or a fanciful painting of imagined scenes.
examples: The pianist encored with a dazzling capriccio.
Canaletto painted a capriccio mixing real and invented ruins.
etymology: From Italian capriccio, 'whim'.

definition: Given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior.
examples: The capricious weather ruined our picnic plans three weekends in a row.
A capricious boss can make it impossible to know what is expected.
etymology: From Italian capriccio, 'sudden start, whim', perhaps literally 'shiver' or 'goat leap'.

definition: The crowning achievement or final element of something.
examples: The bridge was the capstone of her engineering career.
Seniors present a capstone project before graduating.
etymology: Originally the top stone of a wall or structure.

definition: Tending to find fault and raise petty objections.
examples: The captious critic pounced on every tiny error in the otherwise fine film.
Her captious questions seemed designed to trap the speaker, not to learn.
etymology: From Latin captiosus, 'sophistical, deceptive', from capere, 'to take'.

definition: To hold someone's attention completely by being charming or fascinating.
examples: The street magician managed to captivate a crowd of bored commuters.
Few podcasts captivate me the way that true-crime series did.
etymology: From Late Latin captivare, 'to take captive', from captivus 'captive'.

definition: A hard protective shell, or an emotional defense someone presents to the world.
examples: The crab retreated under its carapace.
His sarcasm is a carapace over real shyness.
etymology: From French carapace, from Spanish carapacho.

definition: Relating to prisons or imprisonment.
examples: The book examines the carceral system in America.
Some schools feel almost carceral, with locked gates and guards.
etymology: From Latin carcer, 'prison'.

definition: Of the greatest importance; fundamental.
examples: The cardinal rule of improv is to say yes.
Lying to a client is a cardinal sin in this business.
etymology: From Latin cardinalis, from cardo 'hinge', that on which something turns.

definition: A picture or description that exaggerates certain features for comic effect.
examples: A street artist drew a caricature of me with an enormous chin.
The sitcom reduces every lawyer to a greedy caricature.
etymology: From Italian caricatura, from caricare 'to load, exaggerate'.

definition: A set of tuned bells played from a keyboard.
examples: The carillon played a Beatles song at noon.
Students gather on the lawn to hear the carillon.
etymology: From French carillon, from Old French quarregnon 'a peal of four bells'.

definition: The killing of many people, or widespread destruction.
examples: Reporters described the carnage after the bombing.
The toddler's birthday party left carnage in the living room.
etymology: From French, from Italian carnaggio, from Latin caro, carn- 'flesh'.

definition: To strike a surface and rebound off it.
examples: Watch the puck carom off the boards and into the net.
Ideas carom around the room during a good brainstorm.
etymology: From Spanish carambola, a billiards shot.

definition: To drink and party noisily.
examples: Sailors carouse in the harbor bars on shore leave.
They used to carouse until dawn in their twenties.
etymology: From German gar aus, 'all out', as in emptying a cup.

definition: To complain or find fault constantly about trivial things.
examples: Critics carp about the font while ignoring the content.
He'll carp about the seating chart no matter where we put him.
etymology: From Old Norse karpa 'to brag', later influenced by Latin carpere 'to pluck, slander'.

definition: An outsider who moves somewhere seeking political or financial gain.
examples: Locals dismissed the candidate as a carpetbagger.
No carpetbagger understands this valley like we do.
etymology: First used of Northerners who went South after the Civil War, carrying carpetbag luggage.

definition: A group of businesses or criminals acting together to control prices or trade.
examples: An oil cartel can drive up prices overnight.
The drug cartel controlled the border town.
etymology: From French cartel, from Italian cartello, 'placard, written challenge'.

definition: Fortune-telling with playing cards or tarot cards.
examples: Her aunt practiced cartomancy at the kitchen table.
Cartomancy had a revival in Victorian parlors.
etymology: From French carte 'card' + Greek manteia 'divination'.

definition: An oval frame enclosing a royal name in hieroglyphs, or any ornamental scroll-shaped frame.
examples: The cartouche spelled out Cleopatra's name.
A gilded cartouche framed the map's title.
etymology: From French cartouche 'cartridge', from Italian cartoccio 'paper cone'.

definition: A carved female figure used as a column to support a building.
examples: Each caryatid on the Erechtheion balances a roof on her head.
A stone caryatid holds up the porch of the old bank.
etymology: From Greek karyatides, 'maidens of Karyai', a town in Laconia.

definition: A series of things that follow quickly one after another, like water falling down steps.
examples: One missed flight set off a cascade of cancellations across the country.
A cascade of curls fell over her shoulders when she pulled out the clip.
etymology: From French cascade, from Italian cascata, from cascare 'to fall'.

definition: Built with battlements like a castle.
examples: The castellated mansion looked absurd in the suburbs.
A castellated tower rose above the village.
etymology: From Medieval Latin castellatus, from castellum 'castle'.

definition: To criticize or reprimand someone severely.
examples: The press did castigate the senator for ignoring the report's warnings.
Coaches shouldn't castigate young players for honest mistakes.
etymology: From Latin castigare, 'to correct, punish', from castus 'pure' + agere 'to drive'.

definition: A person killed or injured in an accident or war, or anything lost as a result of an event.
examples: The first casualty of the budget cuts was the art program.
Each casualty was flown to the nearest hospital.
etymology: From Medieval Latin casualitas, from casus 'chance, accident'.

definition: Clever but misleading reasoning, especially about moral questions.
examples: His defense of the bonus was pure casuistry.
Lawyers slipped into casuistry when the facts ran out.
etymology: From casuist, from Spanish casuista, from Latin casus 'case'.

definition: A descent, especially a hero's journey into the underworld.
examples: Dante's Inferno is the most famous catabasis in literature.
The film's middle act is a catabasis into the city's sewers.
etymology: From Greek katabasis, 'a going down'.

definition: The misuse of a word, or a strained, mixed metaphor.
examples: 'The leg of a table' began as a kind of catachresis.
'We must grasp the root of this bottleneck' is a catachresis editors cut.
etymology: From Greek katakhrēsis, 'misuse'.

definition: A sudden, violent upheaval or disaster.
examples: An asteroid triggered the cataclysm that ended the dinosaurs.
The war was a cataclysm that reshaped the continent.
etymology: From Greek kataklysmos 'deluge', from kata- 'down' + klyzein 'to wash'.

definition: A decorated raised platform on which a coffin rests during a funeral.
examples: The president's coffin lay on a black catafalque.
Soldiers stood watch beside the catafalque all night.
etymology: From Italian catafalco, of uncertain origin.

definition: A person or event that triggers important change or action.
examples: The scandal became the catalyst for a complete overhaul of the agency.
Her speech was the catalyst that finally got the neighbors organized.
etymology: From Greek katalysis, 'dissolution', from kata- 'down' + lysis 'loosening'; the chemistry sense came first.

definition: Motionless and unresponsive, as if in a stupor.
examples: After the all-nighter, I sat catatonic in front of the TV.
The defeat left the fans in a catatonic silence.
etymology: From catatonia, coined in German from Greek kata- 'down' + tonos 'tension'.

definition: A well-known phrase repeatedly associated with a person or group.
examples: The comedian's catchphrase ended up on T-shirts everywhere.
Every campaign needs a catchphrase people can chant.
etymology: Formed from catch + phrase.

definition: To question someone closely and systematically, or to instruct by question and answer.
examples: Reporters began to catechize the minister about the deal.
My grandmother would catechize every boyfriend I brought home.
etymology: From Greek katēkhizein, 'to instruct orally'.

definition: In an absolute and unconditional way.
examples: The company categorically denied the rumors.
I can categorically say I never touched your sandwich.
etymology: From Greek kategorikos, 'accusatory, affirmative', + -ly.

definition: To sort things or people into groups according to shared features.
examples: It is tempting to categorize every coworker as either an ally or a rival.
The app tries to categorize your spending, but it thinks coffee is groceries.
etymology: From category, from Greek katēgoria, 'assertion, accusation'.

definition: The curve formed by a chain or cable hanging freely between two points.
examples: Power lines sag in a gentle catenary.
Gaudí used the inverted catenary in his arches.
etymology: From Latin catena, 'chain'.

definition: To provide food for an event, or to provide what a particular group wants.
examples: A local taqueria will cater the office party.
The hotel tries to cater to business travelers.
etymology: From obsolete cater, 'a buyer of provisions', from Old French acater 'to buy'.

definition: To make a shrill, howling, wailing noise.
examples: The alley cats began to caterwaul just after midnight.
The toddler caterwauled when his balloon floated away.
etymology: From Middle English caterwawen, probably from cat + an imitative verb meaning 'to wail'.

definition: The release of strong or pent-up emotions, bringing relief.
examples: Writing the letter, even unsent, gave her a sense of catharsis.
The final scene of the play offers the audience a powerful catharsis.
etymology: From Greek katharsis, 'cleansing', from katharos, 'pure'.

definition: The investment of emotional energy in a person, object, or idea.
examples: His cathexis on the old car baffled his family.
Fandom can be a powerful cathexis.
etymology: From Greek kathexis 'holding', used to translate Freud's German term Besetzung.

definition: Wide-ranging and broad in tastes or interests.
examples: Her catholic taste in music runs from Bach to bluegrass.
He's a catholic reader who'll pick up anything.
etymology: From Greek katholikos, 'universal'.

definition: A supposed remedy for all ills; a panacea.
examples: Exercise is the closest thing we have to a catholicon.
He sold a dubious catholicon from the back of a wagon.
etymology: From Greek katholikon, 'universal (remedy)'.

definition: A closed meeting of a party or faction to choose candidates or set policy.
examples: The caucus ran past midnight in a school gym.
She chairs the senate's rural caucus.
etymology: An American coinage of the 1700s, of uncertain origin.

definition: An informal chat, or a light conversational essay.
examples: Her weekly causerie in the paper covered gardens and gossip.
After dinner came a pleasant causerie by the fire.
etymology: From French causerie, 'chat', from causer 'to talk'.

definition: Bitingly sarcastic, or capable of burning and corroding by chemical action.
examples: The critic's caustic review left the director furious for weeks.
Wear gloves when handling caustic cleaners, because they can burn skin.
etymology: From Greek kaustikos, 'capable of burning', from kaiein, 'to burn'.

definition: Showing a careless lack of concern about something important.
examples: His cavalier attitude toward deadlines frustrated the team.
She was cavalier about safety until she nearly fell off the ladder.
etymology: From Italian cavaliere, 'horseman, knight'.

definition: A warning or condition that limits what was just said.
examples: The deal sounds great, with one caveat: you have to pay for a full year upfront.
She agreed to help us move, with the caveat that she'd leave by six.
etymology: From Latin caveat, 'let him beware', from cavere 'to beware'.

definition: Huge, hollow, and dark, like a cave.
examples: Our footsteps echoed in the cavernous warehouse.
He let out a cavernous yawn.
etymology: From Latin caverna, from cavus 'hollow'.

definition: To raise petty objections.
examples: Critics may cavil at the ending, but the film is a triumph.
Let's not cavil over a few cents on the bill.
etymology: From Latin cavillari, 'to jest, quibble'.

definition: To jump or dance around excitedly; to behave in a lively, carefree way.
examples: Otters cavort in the shallow water all afternoon.
Tabloids love photos of celebrities who cavort on yachts.
etymology: An American coinage, perhaps an alteration of curvet, a horse's leap.

definition: To bring or come to an end; to stop.
examples: The factory will cease operations next spring.
His ability to fall asleep anywhere will never cease to amaze me.
etymology: From Latin cessare, 'to stop, delay'.

definition: To give up power, territory, or a right, usually reluctantly.
examples: The losing nation was forced to cede two provinces.
Don't cede the argument just because he talks louder.
etymology: From Latin cedere, 'to yield, go away'.

definition: A pale gray-green color, or pottery with a glaze of that color.
examples: The bowl's celadon glaze looked like seawater.
She painted the kitchen a soft celadon.
etymology: From Céladon, a shepherd in d'Urfé's French romance L'Astrée who wore pale green.

definition: Swiftness of movement or action.
examples: The waiter cleared the table with astonishing celerity.
The bill passed with unusual celerity.
etymology: From Latin celeritas, from celer 'swift'.

definition: Relating to the sky or heavens, or supremely beautiful.
examples: Sailors once steered by celestial navigation.
The choir's celestial harmonies filled the church.
etymology: From Latin caelestis, from caelum 'sky, heaven'.

definition: A small, exclusive group of writers or thinkers.
examples: The poet belonged to a Parisian cenacle that met in cafés.
A cenacle of coders gathered in her garage.
etymology: From Latin cenaculum 'dining room', the upper room of the Last Supper.

definition: A member of a religious community living together, as opposed to a hermit.
examples: The cenobite rose each night for prayers with his brothers.
Unlike the hermit, the cenobite shares meals and work.
etymology: From Greek koinobion 'convent', from koinos 'common' + bios 'life'.

definition: A monument honoring people buried elsewhere, especially war dead.
examples: Wreaths were laid at the cenotaph on Remembrance Day.
The village cenotaph lists forty names.
etymology: From Greek kenos 'empty' + taphos 'tomb'.

definition: To remove or suppress parts of speech, writing, or media judged unacceptable.
examples: The network chose to censor two words from the live broadcast.
Authoritarian governments often censor news about protests.
etymology: From Latin censor, a Roman magistrate who took the census and supervised public morals.

definition: Severely critical and quick to find fault.
examples: Her censorious aunt commented on every outfit.
The internet can be a censorious place.
etymology: From Latin censorius, 'of a censor'.

definition: To criticize someone severely and formally.
examples: The board voted to censure the treasurer for misusing funds.
Congress may censure a member without expelling him.
etymology: From Latin censura 'judgment', from censere 'to assess'.

definition: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical.
examples: The film is cerebral, more puzzle than thriller.
She's a cerebral player who wins chess games with patience.
etymology: From Latin cerebrum, 'brain'.

definition: A burial cloth or shroud.
examples: The mummy was wrapped in a linen cerement.
Fog lay over the town like a gray cerement.
etymology: From cere 'to wrap in waxed cloth', from Latin cera 'wax'.

definition: To officially confirm that something is true or meets a standard.
examples: An inspector must certify the elevator before it opens.
States certify election results within weeks.
etymology: From Late Latin certificare, from certus 'sure'.

definition: Absolute certainty or conviction.
examples: He spoke with a certitude that unsettled the jury.
Science trades certitude for evidence.
etymology: From Late Latin certitudo, from certus 'sure'.

definition: Deep sky-blue in color.
examples: The lake was a startling cerulean under the summer sun.
She painted the nursery a soft cerulean.
etymology: From Latin caeruleus, 'dark blue'.

definition: To feel irritated or impatient because of restrictions; to rub until sore.
examples: Creative people often chafe at strict dress codes.
New boots will chafe your heels on a long hike.
etymology: From Old French chaufer 'to heat', from Latin calefacere 'to make warm'.

definition: Worthless material separated from what is valuable; grain husks.
examples: A good editor separates the wheat from the chaff.
Wind blew the chaff across the threshing floor.
etymology: From Old English ceaf, 'husks'.

definition: A feeling of annoyed disappointment or embarrassment after a failure or mistake.
examples: To her chagrin, she realized she had been wearing mismatched shoes all day.
He read the error message with chagrin, knowing he had deleted the wrong file.
etymology: From French chagrin, 'sorrow, distress', possibly from chagrin 'rough leather'.

definition: A person who changes opinions or behavior to suit circumstances; a color-changing lizard.
examples: The politician is a chameleon who agrees with every crowd.
As an actor, she's a chameleon who vanishes into roles.
etymology: From Greek khamaileōn, literally 'ground lion'.

definition: Dispirited and dejected.
examples: The chapfallen team trudged off the field.
He looked chapfallen when the gallery said no.
etymology: From chap 'jaw' + fallen; Shakespeare uses it in Hamlet.

definition: An absurd pretense meant to look genuine.
examples: The public consultation was a charade; the decision was already made.
They kept up the charade of a happy marriage for years.
etymology: From French charade, of uncertain origin, possibly from Provençal charrado 'conversation'.

definition: A compelling charm that inspires devotion or attention in others.
examples: The new manager's charisma won over the team within a week.
Great teachers often have a quiet charisma that keeps students listening.
etymology: From Greek kharisma, 'gift of grace', from kharis 'grace, favor'.

definition: A noisy mock serenade with pots and pans, or any loud din.
examples: Neighbors staged a charivari outside the newlyweds' window.
The construction site was a charivari of hammers and radios.
etymology: From French charivari, of uncertain origin.

definition: A person who falsely claims special knowledge or skill.
examples: The miracle-cure salesman was a charlatan with a ring light.
Real experts admit doubt; a charlatan never does.
etymology: From French, from Italian ciarlatano, from ciarlare 'to babble'.

definition: Relating to death or corpses; ghastly.
examples: Monks stacked bones in the charnel house beneath the chapel.
A charnel stench rose from the battlefield.
etymology: From Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnalis 'of the flesh'.

definition: Cautiously reluctant or wary about doing something.
examples: Investors are chary of startups without revenue.
She's chary of giving out her phone number.
etymology: From Old English cearig 'sorrowful, careful', from caru 'care'.

definition: A deep crack in the earth, or a profound difference between people or groups.
examples: A rope bridge spans the chasm.
There's a chasm between what voters want and what they get.
etymology: From Greek khasma, 'gaping hollow'.

definition: To make someone humbler or more restrained, especially through failure.
examples: Defeat seemed to chasten the young champion.
Nothing will chasten him like a bad review.
etymology: From Old French chastier, from Latin castigare 'to correct'.

definition: To scold or criticize someone severely.
examples: The coach would chastise the rookie in front of the team for every error.
Editorials chastise the city for its slow snow removal.
etymology: From Middle English chastisen, related to chasten, from Latin castigare 'to correct'.

definition: The mistress of a large house, or a clasp at the waist holding keys.
examples: The chatelaine greeted guests in the great hall.
She ran the estate like a true chatelaine.
etymology: From French châtelaine, 'lady of the castle'.

definition: Having a changeable luster, like a cat's eye in the dark.
examples: The chatoyant gemstone flashed gold, then green.
Her silk scarf had a chatoyant sheen.
etymology: From French chatoyer, 'to shine like a cat's eye', from chat 'cat'.

definition: A personal possession, or a person treated as property.
examples: Under old laws a wife was treated as her husband's chattel.
The landlord seized every chattel the tenant owned, down to the toaster.
etymology: From Old French chatel 'property', related to cattle and capital.

definition: Aggressive or prejudiced belief in the superiority of one's own group, nation, or sex.
examples: The memo dripped with casual chauvinism.
National chauvinism made the treaty talks impossible.
etymology: Named after Nicolas Chauvin, a probably legendary French soldier famed for fanatical loyalty to Napoleon.

definition: Marked by periods of trouble or mixed fortune; also patterned in squares.
examples: The candidate has a checkered past with several bankruptcies.
We spread a checkered blanket on the grass.
etymology: From checker, from Old French eschequier 'chessboard'.

definition: To hold something dear and protect it lovingly.
examples: I cherish the letters my grandfather wrote from the war.
Cherish the slow mornings while the kids are small.
etymology: From Old French cherir, from cher 'dear', from Latin carus.

definition: The dramatic treatment of light and shadow in art.
examples: Caravaggio's paintings are famous for their bold chiaroscuro.
The photographer used a single lamp to create a moody chiaroscuro on her subject's face.
etymology: From Italian chiaroscuro, from chiaro 'bright' + oscuro 'dark'.

definition: A figure of speech that repeats words in reverse order, as in 'eat to live, not live to eat'.
examples: 'Ask not what your country can do for you' is a famous chiasmus.
Her speech ended on a neat chiasmus that drew applause.
etymology: From Greek khiasmos, 'crosswise arrangement', from the letter chi (X).

definition: Trickery or deception; also a tight S-bend on a racetrack.
examples: The deal was built on legal chicane.
Drivers brake hard for the chicane before the straight.
etymology: From French chicaner, 'to quibble'.

definition: Clever trickery or deception, especially in legal or political matters.
examples: The contract was riddled with legal chicanery meant to cheat small investors.
He won the election through chicanery, including fake endorsements and false rumors.
etymology: From French chicanerie, from chicaner, 'to quibble', of uncertain origin.

definition: To scold someone mildly.
examples: My grandmother would chide us for slouching at dinner.
Fans chide the team on social media after every loss.
etymology: From Old English cidan, 'to quarrel, complain'.

definition: The belief in a coming thousand-year age of peace.
examples: Early chiliasm expected the new age within a generation.
Tech optimism can sound like secular chiliasm.
etymology: From Greek khilias, 'a thousand'.

definition: A hoped-for thing that is wildly unrealistic or illusory.
examples: A perfectly bug-free app is a chimera.
For years he chased the chimera of overnight fame.
etymology: From Greek khimaira 'she-goat', a fire-breathing monster of myth with lion, goat and serpent parts.

definition: Imaginary or wildly unrealistic; existing only as a fanciful dream.
examples: Her chimerical plans for a floating city never left the sketchbook.
The investors dismissed the idea as chimerical, with no basis in real technology.
etymology: From Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth, with the suffix -ical.

definition: Cheap and of poor quality, or stingy.
examples: The hotel's chintzy curtains barely closed.
Don't be chintzy with the tip.
etymology: From chintz, a printed cotton fabric, from Hindi chhīṇṭ.

definition: Cheerful and lively.
examples: How are you so chipper at six in the morning?
The chipper barista knew every regular's name.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly from English dialect kipper 'lively'.

definition: Courteous, gallant behavior, originally the code of medieval knights.
examples: Holding the door is a small act of chivalry.
Chivalry is not dead; it just splits the bill now.
etymology: From Old French chevalerie, from chevalier 'knight', from Latin caballarius 'horseman'.

definition: Easily angered; bad-tempered.
examples: The choleric chef threw a pan across the kitchen.
His choleric emails were best read after lunch.
etymology: From Greek kholē 'bile'; choler was the bodily humor once thought to cause anger.

definition: To design dance steps, or to plan an event in precise detail.
examples: She was hired to choreograph the musical's big finale.
The campaign tried to choreograph every handshake.
etymology: From Greek khoreia 'dance' + graphein 'to write'.

definition: To laugh in a gleeful, breathy way.
examples: Kids chortle at the cartoon's slapstick.
I heard him chortle behind his newspaper.
etymology: Coined by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871), blending chuckle and snort.

definition: Relating to or devoted to making money.
examples: The festival lost its soul to chrematistic sponsors.
Aristotle distrusted purely chrematistic trade.
etymology: From Greek khrēmatistikos, from khrēmata 'money, goods'.

definition: A collection of selected passages, often used for learning a language.
examples: The professor assigned a Latin chrestomathy.
Mencken compiled a chrestomathy of his own essays.
etymology: From Greek khrēstomatheia, from khrēstos 'useful' + mathein 'to learn'.

definition: Lasting a long time or recurring constantly, especially of an illness or problem.
examples: She has dealt with chronic back pain since the car accident.
The city's chronic housing shortage keeps pushing rents higher.
etymology: From Greek khronikos, 'of time', from khronos 'time'.

definition: To record a series of events in detail and in order.
examples: Her blog set out to chronicle a year of living without plastic.
The documentary tries to chronicle the band's rise and fall.
etymology: From Anglo-French cronicle, ultimately from Greek khronika 'annals', from khronos 'time'.

definition: Arranged in the order in which events happened.
examples: The museum tells the artist's story in chronological order, room by room.
Please put the receipts in chronological sequence before you scan them.
etymology: From Greek khronos 'time' + logos 'account'.

definition: Relating to the underworld or the depths of the earth.
examples: The cave tour had an eerie, chthonic atmosphere.
Hades is the chief chthonic deity of Greek myth.
etymology: From Greek khthōn, 'earth'.

definition: Rude, mean-spirited, and ill-mannered, especially in refusing to be gracious.
examples: It would be churlish to refuse a gift offered so kindly.
His churlish reply to the waiter embarrassed everyone at the table.
etymology: From Old English ceorl, 'a peasant, free man of low rank', plus -ish.

definition: Shameless audacity, whether admirable or outrageous.
examples: It took chutzpah to ask the CEO for a ride home.
He had the chutzpah to bill us for his own mistake.
etymology: From Yiddish khutspe, from Hebrew ḥuṣpāh 'insolence'.

definition: A guide who explains the sights and history to visitors.
examples: Our cicerone knew every fresco in Florence.
She played cicerone to her cousins on their first trip to New York.
etymology: From Italian, after Cicero, alluding to the eloquence of tour guides.

definition: Ash-gray in color.
examples: The cinereous vulture circled above the cliffs.
A cinereous dawn crept over the city.
etymology: From Latin cinereus, from cinis 'ash'.

definition: Longer than necessary because it goes around rather than straight.
examples: The taxi took a circuitous route to raise the fare.
She gave a circuitous answer that never quite said no.
etymology: From Latin circuitus, 'a going around'.

definition: To move or pass freely from place to place or person to person.
examples: Rumors began to circulate before the CEO had even left the building.
Open the windows to let fresh air circulate through the room.
etymology: From Latin circulari, 'to form a circle', from circulus 'small ring'.

definition: To walk all the way around something, often as a ritual.
examples: Pilgrims circumambulate the shrine seven times.
The dog likes to circumambulate the yard before lying down.
etymology: From Latin circum 'around' + ambulare 'to walk'.

definition: The use of many words to say something that could be said simply.
examples: The politician's circumlocution avoided the question without ever refusing to answer it.
After a long circumlocution, he finally admitted that he had forgotten the report.
etymology: From Latin circumlocutio, from circum- 'around' + loqui 'to speak'.

definition: To sail or travel all the way around something; to find a way around an obstacle.
examples: She hopes to circumnavigate the globe alone.
We tried to circumnavigate the paperwork entirely.
etymology: From Latin circum 'around' + navigare 'to sail'.

definition: To restrict something within limits.
examples: The new rules circumscribe what reporters can film.
Don't let fear circumscribe your ambitions.
etymology: From Latin circumscribere, 'to draw a line around'.

definition: Careful to consider possible consequences before acting or speaking.
examples: Be circumspect about what you post online, since employers may read it.
The diplomat was circumspect, offering no comment until all the facts were known.
etymology: From Latin circumspectus, 'looked around', from circum 'around' + specere 'to look'.

definition: Suggesting something indirectly rather than proving it; depending on circumstances.
examples: The case against him is purely circumstantial.
Muddy boots by the door are circumstantial evidence that he went out.
etymology: From Latin circumstantia, from circumstare 'to stand around'.

definition: To find a way around an obstacle or rule.
examples: They built a detour to circumvent the flooded bridge.
Some apps try to circumvent privacy settings to collect data.
etymology: From Latin circumvenire, 'to surround', from circum, 'around', + venire, 'to come'.

definition: A fortress protecting a city, or a stronghold of a belief or institution.
examples: The citadel sits high above the old harbor.
The library was a citadel of quiet in a noisy town.
etymology: From Italian cittadella, 'little city'.

definition: To quote or mention something as evidence or as a source.
examples: Be sure to cite every study you mention in the report.
Critics cite the ending as the film's only real weakness.
etymology: From Latin citare, 'to summon, set in motion'.

definition: Relating to a city, its citizens, or the duties of citizenship.
examples: Voting in local elections is a basic civic duty.
The new library has become the town's civic heart.
etymology: From Latin civicus, from civis 'citizen'.

definition: Polite, respectful behavior, especially in disagreement.
examples: The debate ended without a shred of civility.
Basic civility costs nothing.
etymology: From Latin civilitas, from civis 'citizen'.

definition: Seemingly able to perceive the future or things beyond normal senses.
examples: I'm not clairvoyant, but I'd bet the meeting runs late.
Her clairvoyant read of the market made her rich.
etymology: From French clair 'clear' + voyant 'seeing'.

definition: Urgently demanding attention; insistent.
examples: There is a clamant need for affordable housing.
Clamant voices outside demanded the mayor resign.
etymology: From Latin clamare, 'to cry out'.

definition: To climb awkwardly using both hands and feet.
examples: Kids clamber over the fallen tree like it's a jungle gym.
We had to clamber up the rocks to reach the waterfall.
etymology: From Middle English, probably related to climb.

definition: A loud, confused noise, or a strong public demand.
examples: The clamor of the market woke us at dawn.
There's growing clamor for a bike lane on Main Street.
etymology: From Latin clamor, from clamare 'to cry out'.

definition: Kept secret, often because the activity is illegal or forbidden.
examples: The two leaders held a clandestine meeting in a hotel basement.
They ran a clandestine radio station from an abandoned farmhouse.
etymology: From Latin clandestinus, 'secret, hidden', from clam, 'secretly'.

definition: A loud, continuous clanging noise.
examples: The clangor of the shipyard never stopped.
Church bells rang out in joyful clangor.
etymology: From Latin clangor, from clangere 'to resound'.

definition: Tending to stick together in a group and exclude outsiders.
examples: The village was clannish and wary of newcomers.
Some lab teams get clannish about their data.
etymology: From clan, from Scottish Gaelic clann 'family, offspring'.

definition: Pretentious or foolish talk meant to impress.
examples: The pitch was full of marketing claptrap.
Don't believe that claptrap about getting rich quick.
etymology: Originally a theatrical trick to win applause, a 'trap' to catch a 'clap'.

definition: A group hired to applaud, or a set of sycophantic followers.
examples: The tenor's claque cheered every note.
A claque of yes-men surrounded the CEO.
etymology: From French claquer, 'to clap'.

definition: Loud, clear, and rousing.
examples: The speech was a clarion call for climate action.
Her clarion voice carried across the stadium.
etymology: From Medieval Latin clario, a shrill trumpet, from Latin clarus 'clear'.

definition: The quality of being clear, easy to see, or easy to understand.
examples: Her essay has a clarity that makes complex ideas feel simple.
A long walk gave him the clarity he needed to make the decision.
etymology: From Latin claritas, from clarus 'clear, bright'.

definition: To arrange or assign things into groups by shared qualities.
examples: Biologists classify whales as mammals, not fish.
How would you classify a hot dog: sandwich or not?
etymology: From class, from Latin classis, a division of the Roman people.

definition: Relating to a cloister, or confined and secluded.
examples: The library had a claustral hush.
After the city, island life felt claustral.
etymology: From Latin claustrum, 'enclosure'.

definition: To split something apart with force, or oddly also to cling closely to.
examples: One swing of the axe was enough to cleave the log.
Some people cleave to old traditions long after they fade.
etymology: Two Old English verbs merged: cleofan 'to split' and clifian 'to adhere'.

definition: A split, crack, or indentation.
examples: Water trickled from a cleft in the rock.
He has a deep cleft in his chin.
etymology: From Middle English clift, related to cleave 'to split'.

definition: Mercy or leniency, especially from someone in authority.
examples: The governor granted clemency to the elderly prisoner.
The referee showed some clemency and let the late goal stand.
etymology: From Latin clementia, from clemens, 'mild, merciful'.

definition: An ancient clock measuring time by the flow of water.
examples: Athenian courts timed speeches with a clepsydra.
The museum's bronze clepsydra still drips steadily.
etymology: From Greek klepsydra, from kleptein 'to steal' + hydōr 'water'.

definition: A short comic poem of two rhyming couplets about a famous person.
examples: She wrote a clerihew about Napoleon's height.
Each clerihew begins with the subject's name.
etymology: Named after Edmund Clerihew Bentley, who invented the form.

definition: Educated people considered as a class; the intelligentsia.
examples: The clerisy debated the novel long before the public read it.
Podcasts have created a new kind of clerisy.
etymology: Popularized by Coleridge, from German Klerisei, ultimately from Latin clericus 'cleric'.

definition: A phrase or idea used so often that it has lost its force or originality.
examples: Calling the game 'a tale of two halves' is a sports cliche.
The movie avoids every romantic cliche except the airport chase.
etymology: From French cliché, a printing term for a cast metal plate used to reproduce text repeatedly.

definition: The customers or clients of a business, considered as a group.
examples: The café's clientele is mostly students and night-shift nurses.
The salon caters to a wealthy clientele.
etymology: From French clientèle, from Latin clientela, from cliens 'client'.

definition: The most intense or important point of a story, event, or process.
examples: The novel reaches its climax in a thunderstorm on the cliffs.
The festival's climax was a fireworks show over the bay.
etymology: From Greek klimax, 'ladder'.

definition: A small, unpredictable swerve that produces change.
examples: One chance meeting was the clinamen that redirected her life.
Lucretius gave atoms a clinamen so the world could begin.
etymology: Latin 'inclination', the poet Lucretius's term for the swerve of atoms.

definition: Coldly efficient and detached, or relating to medical treatment.
examples: The striker was clinical in front of goal.
Her clinical tone made the breakup even worse.
etymology: From Greek klinē 'bed', referring to bedside medical care.

definition: A small, exclusive group of people who keep others out.
examples: The popular clique always sat at the table by the window.
Even the office has a clique that plans lunches without inviting anyone else.
etymology: From French clique, of uncertain origin.

definition: To shut oneself or someone away from the world.
examples: Writers often cloister themselves in cabins to finish books.
Don't cloister the kids indoors all summer.
etymology: From Latin claustrum, 'enclosure', from claudere 'to shut'.

definition: An absurdly idealized world of fantasy.
examples: If you think rents will fall, you're living in cloud-cuckoo-land.
The plan was drafted in cloud-cuckoo-land.
etymology: A translation of Greek Nephelokokkygia, the sky city in Aristophanes' comedy The Birds.

definition: Influence or power, especially in politics or business.
examples: As the biggest client, they have a lot of clout in setting deadlines.
The neighborhood association gained clout after hundreds of residents joined.
etymology: From Old English clut, 'lump, patch'; the sense of 'influence' arose in the 20th century.

definition: Unpleasantly sweet or sentimental to the point of disgust.
examples: The cloying perfume filled the elevator and left everyone wincing.
Critics found the film's cloying romance too sugary to enjoy.
etymology: From cloy, from Middle English acloyen, 'to nail up, clog', from Latin clavus, 'nail'.

definition: An assistant, especially a bishop assisting another bishop.
examples: The aging archbishop was given a coadjutor.
She served as a loyal coadjutor to the director.
etymology: From Latin coadjutor, from co- + adjuvare 'to help'.

definition: To change from liquid to a thickened, semi-solid state.
examples: Blood begins to coagulate within minutes.
Heat the milk slowly or the proteins will coagulate.
etymology: From Latin coagulare, from coagulum 'rennet'.

definition: To come together to form one mass or whole.
examples: Several small groups coalesced into a single campaign.
Her scattered ideas began to coalesce into a novel.
etymology: From Latin coalescere, from co-, 'together', + alescere, 'to grow'.

definition: An alliance of groups or parties joining forces for a shared purpose.
examples: A coalition of parents pushed for safer crosswalks.
The two parties formed a coalition to govern.
etymology: From Latin coalescere, 'to grow together'.

definition: To gently persuade someone to do something.
examples: We coaxed the shy kitten out from under the couch with treats.
She tried to coax her friend into joining the choir.
etymology: From obsolete cokes, 'a fool', originally meaning to pet or fondle.

definition: Arrogantly overconfident.
examples: The cocksure rookie promised to win the title in his first year.
Don't be so cocksure; the exam is harder than it looks.
etymology: Formed from cock + sure; the exact sense of the first element is uncertain.

definition: A concluding section of a piece of music, story, or event.
examples: The song ends with a quiet piano coda.
The final chapter is a bittersweet coda set decades later.
etymology: From Italian coda, 'tail', from Latin cauda.

definition: To treat someone too indulgently or protectively.
examples: Don't coddle the interns; let them make mistakes.
Some parents coddle their kids well into college.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; perhaps related to caudle, a warm drink for invalids.

definition: An ancient manuscript in book form rather than a scroll.
examples: Scholars spent years deciphering the Mayan codex.
The codex replaced the scroll in late antiquity.
etymology: From Latin codex, 'block of wood, book'.

definition: An addition or supplement to a will or document.
examples: A late codicil left the house to the gardener.
The treaty included a codicil on fishing rights.
etymology: From Latin codicillus, a diminutive of codex 'book'.

definition: To arrange rules or practices into a formal, written system.
examples: The team finally decided to codify its unwritten rules.
Lawmakers want to codify the court's ruling into statute.
etymology: From code, from Latin codex 'book, tablet'.

definition: To force someone to do something by using threats or pressure.
examples: No one should coerce an employee into working unpaid overtime.
The scammers tried to coerce her into sending gift cards.
etymology: From Latin coercere, 'to restrain', from co- 'together' + arcere 'to shut in'.

definition: Of the same age, era, or duration.
examples: The temple is coeval with the earliest pyramids.
Jazz and cinema are roughly coeval art forms.
etymology: From Late Latin coaevus, from co- 'together' + aevum 'age'.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
examples: She made a cogent case for moving the launch to autumn.
The lawyer's cogent argument persuaded even the skeptical jurors.
etymology: From Latin cogens, 'compelling', from cogere, 'to drive together, force'.

definition: To think deeply about something.
examples: Let me cogitate on your offer over the weekend.
Philosophers cogitate on questions that may have no answers.
etymology: From Latin cogitare, 'to think'.

definition: Related in origin, especially of words descended from the same root.
examples: English 'night' and German 'Nacht' are cognate words.
Chemistry and alchemy are cognate disciplines.
etymology: From Latin cognatus, 'related by birth'.

definition: Relating to thinking, learning, remembering, and understanding.
examples: Sleep loss affects cognitive performance more than people realize.
Chess is a cognitive workout disguised as a game.
etymology: From Latin cognoscere, 'to get to know'.

definition: Aware of or having knowledge of something.
examples: Be cognizant of the time difference when you call.
The council is cognizant of residents' concerns.
etymology: From Old French conoissant, from Latin cognoscere 'to get to know'.

definition: A nickname or surname, originally a Roman's third name.
examples: 'The Iron Lady' became her lasting cognomen.
Caesar was a cognomen before it became a title.
etymology: From Latin cognomen, from co- + nomen 'name'.

definition: People who are especially well informed about a particular subject.
examples: Among coffee cognoscenti, this tiny roaster is legendary.
The film flopped at the box office but was adored by the cognoscenti.
etymology: From obsolete Italian cognoscente, 'one who knows', from Latin cognoscere, 'to know'.

definition: Logical and well organized, so that all the parts fit together clearly.
examples: After the shock, he was barely coherent and could not explain what had happened.
A coherent argument moves step by step from evidence to a clear conclusion.
etymology: From Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together', from co- 'together' + haerere 'to stick'.

definition: Forming a united, well-connected whole.
examples: After the retreat, the team felt more cohesive.
The album is a cohesive collection of songs about home.
etymology: From Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together'.

definition: A group of people who share a characteristic or go through something together.
examples: Our graduating cohort still meets for dinner every spring.
The study followed a cohort of ten thousand nurses.
etymology: From Latin cohors, a division of a Roman legion.

definition: To happen at the same time or to match exactly.
examples: Our vacation will coincide with the cherry blossom season.
Their tastes in music rarely coincide, so road trips get loud.
etymology: From Medieval Latin coincidere, from co- 'together' + incidere 'to fall upon'.

definition: To gather and arrange information or pages in order.
examples: Volunteers collate the survey answers into one spreadsheet.
Set the printer to collate the handouts.
etymology: From Latin collatus, past participle of conferre 'to bring together'.

definition: Property pledged to a lender as security for a loan.
examples: They used the house as collateral to start the restaurant.
Without collateral, the bank refused to lend him anything.
etymology: From Medieval Latin collateralis, from com- 'together' + lateralis 'of the side'.

definition: Shared or done by all members of a group together.
examples: The team let out a collective groan.
Climate change demands collective action.
etymology: From Latin collectivus, from colligere 'to gather together'.

definition: Marked by friendly cooperation and shared responsibility among colleagues.
examples: The lab has a collegial atmosphere where everyone shares ideas.
Despite their disagreement, the debate stayed collegial.
etymology: From Latin collegialis, from collegium, 'association'.

definition: Used in ordinary, informal conversation rather than formal writing.
examples: The translation sounds stiff because it avoids colloquial phrases.
'Gonna' is fine in colloquial speech but not in a contract.
etymology: From Latin colloquium, 'conversation'.

definition: A formal conversation or dialogue.
examples: The two philosophers held a long colloquy on free will.
Their colloquy over dinner lasted until midnight.
etymology: From Latin colloquium, 'conversation'.

definition: Secret cooperation for a dishonest or illegal purpose.
examples: The airlines were fined for collusion on ticket prices.
The referee denied any collusion with the gamblers.
etymology: From Latin colludere, 'to play together'.

definition: A note at the end of a book about its production, or a publisher's emblem.
examples: The colophon notes the typeface and paper used.
A tiny penguin colophon sat on the spine.
etymology: From Greek kolophōn, 'summit, finishing touch'.

definition: Eager or ready to argue or fight.
examples: The senator grew combative when reporters asked about the budget.
My combative uncle can turn a chat about weather into a debate.
etymology: From combat, from French combattre, from Latin com- + battuere 'to beat'.

definition: Able to catch fire easily; also likely to erupt in anger or conflict.
examples: Keep combustible materials away from the furnace.
The meeting grew combustible once budgets came up.
etymology: From Latin comburere, 'to burn up'.

definition: Pleasant to look at; attractive.
examples: The novel's comely heroine wins every suitor's heart.
It was a comely little cottage with blue shutters.
etymology: From Old English cymlic, 'lovely, beautiful'.

definition: An item of food.
examples: The deli stocks every imported comestible you can imagine.
Not a single comestible was left after the party.
etymology: From Latin comedere, 'to eat up'.

definition: A punishment or fate that someone deserves.
examples: The bully finally got his comeuppance in the last episode.
Audiences love watching a villain's comeuppance.
etymology: An American coinage of the 1800s from come up + -ance.

definition: Courtesy and mutual consideration between people or nations.
examples: The two senators maintained a rare comity despite their differences.
The neighborhood association works to preserve comity among residents.
etymology: From Latin comitas, 'courteousness', from comis, 'courteous'.

definition: To take possession of something by force or authority, often for official use.
examples: The detective had to commandeer a taxi to chase the suspect.
My kids commandeer the TV every Saturday morning.
etymology: From Afrikaans kommandeer, ultimately from French commander 'to command'.

definition: To honor the memory of a person or event with a ceremony or object.
examples: The town plants an oak each year to commemorate the founders.
A new stamp will commemorate the moon landing's anniversary.
etymology: From Latin commemorare, 'to bring to mind', from com- + memorare 'to relate'.

definition: To begin, especially in a formal way.
examples: The ceremony will commence at noon, rain or shine.
Construction will commence once the permits arrive.
etymology: From Old French comencier, ultimately from Latin com- + initiare 'to begin'.

definition: To praise formally or publicly.
examples: The mayor commended the firefighters for their quick response.
I commend you for speaking up in the meeting.
etymology: From Latin commendare, 'to entrust, recommend'.

definition: Living alongside another species and benefiting without harming it.
examples: Most gut bacteria are commensal.
Sparrows have a commensal relationship with cities.
etymology: From Medieval Latin commensalis, from com- + mensa 'table'.

definition: Matching in size, amount, or importance; proportionate.
examples: Salary will be commensurate with experience, according to the job posting.
The punishment should be commensurate with the seriousness of the offense.
etymology: From Late Latin commensuratus, from com- 'together' + mensurare 'to measure'.

definition: Threatening or denunciatory.
examples: The landlord sent another comminatory letter.
His comminatory tone silenced the meeting.
etymology: From Latin comminari, 'to threaten'.

definition: To mix or blend together.
examples: Never commingle client money with your own.
In the story, myth and memory commingle.
etymology: From com- 'together' + mingle.

definition: To express sympathy or share someone's sorrow.
examples: We met for coffee to commiserate about our rejected applications.
