Fans of the losing team commiserated outside the stadium.
etymology: From Latin commiserari, from com-, 'with', + miserari, 'to lament'.

definition: Roomy and comfortable.
examples: The old farmhouse has a commodious kitchen.
She traded her cramped car for a commodious van.
etymology: From Latin commodus, 'convenient, suitable'.

definition: A basic good that can be bought and sold, or anything treated as valuable and tradable.
examples: Coffee is a commodity traded on markets around the world.
In a busy family, quiet time becomes a rare commodity.
etymology: From Latin commoditas, 'convenience', from commodus 'suitable'.

definition: Ordinary and not at all unusual.
examples: Video calls, once a novelty, are now commonplace.
His commonplace opinions never sparked much debate.
etymology: A translation of Latin locus communis, itself rendering Greek koinos topos, 'a general theme'.

definition: The general welfare of the public.
examples: Clean water serves the commonweal.
Leaders must weigh private interest against the commonweal.
etymology: From common + weal 'well-being'.

definition: Shared by or belonging to all members of a group.
examples: The dorm has a communal kitchen that is never quite clean.
Singing in a choir is a deeply communal pleasure.
etymology: From Late Latin communalis, from communis 'common'.

definition: To keep things in separate mental categories, especially difficult feelings.
examples: Surgeons learn to compartmentalize their fear.
I try to compartmentalize work so it doesn't follow me home.
etymology: From compartment, from Late Latin compartiri 'to divide'.

definition: Deep sympathy for others' suffering, together with a wish to help.
examples: The nurse treated every frightened patient with compassion.
Real compassion means showing up, not just sending thoughts.
etymology: From Late Latin compassio, from compati 'to suffer with'.

definition: To force or strongly push someone to do something.
examples: No one can compel you to share your diary.
I felt compelled to write the author a thank-you note.
etymology: From Latin compellere, 'to drive together', from com- + pellere 'to drive'.

definition: Containing much information in a concise form.
examples: The guide is a compendious account of Alpine trails.
Her compendious notes saved the whole class.
etymology: From Latin compendiosus, 'brief', from compendium 'a saving'.

definition: A collection of concise but detailed information about a subject.
examples: The guide is a compendium of every trail in the national park.
Her notebook became a compendium of family recipes and stories.
etymology: From Latin compendium, 'a saving, a shortening', from compendere, 'to weigh together'.

definition: To make up for a loss or weakness, or to pay someone for work or harm.
examples: The airline offered vouchers to compensate passengers for the delay.
He tells loud jokes to compensate for feeling shy.
etymology: From Latin compensare, 'to weigh one thing against another'.

definition: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something well.
examples: She's a competent pilot who stays calm in turbulence.
We need a competent electrician, not my cousin with a YouTube tutorial.
etymology: From Latin competere, 'to be suitable', literally 'to strive together'.

definition: To gather information or items from several sources into one collection.
examples: I need to compile a list of everyone attending the reunion.
Researchers compile weather records going back two centuries.
etymology: From Latin compilare, which originally meant 'to plunder'.

definition: Smugly satisfied with how things are, and so careless about possible problems.
examples: The champions grew complacent after three easy wins and were stunned by a late defeat.
Don't get complacent about your health just because you feel fine today.
etymology: From Latin complacere, 'to please greatly', from com- + placere 'to please'.

definition: Willing to please others or go along with their wishes.
examples: The complaisant host agreed to every request.
A complaisant board approved the merger without debate.
etymology: From French complaire 'to please', from Latin complacere.

definition: To complete or enhance something by adding qualities it lacks.
examples: A crisp white wine will complement the grilled fish.
Her patience seems to complement his restless energy.
etymology: From Latin complementum, 'that which fills up', from complere 'to fill'.

definition: Involved with others in wrongdoing, even if only by staying silent.
examples: Anyone who knew about the fraud and stayed silent was complicit.
The company was complicit in hiding the safety defects from regulators.
etymology: From Late Latin complex, 'closely connected', from com- 'together' + plicare 'to fold'.

definition: To act according to a rule, request, or order.
examples: All restaurants must comply with the new safety code by June.
When the officer asked for his license, he was quick to comply.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin complere, 'to fill up, fulfill'.

definition: To behave or conduct oneself in a certain way.
examples: Players must comport themselves with dignity off the field.
Diplomats must comport themselves carefully at state dinners.
etymology: From Latin comportare, 'to bring together'.

definition: The state of being calm and in control of oneself.
examples: She kept her composure even when the microphone died mid-speech.
After the bad call, the goalkeeper lost his composure.
etymology: From compose, from Latin componere 'to put together', + -ure.

definition: To grasp the meaning or nature of something.
examples: It's hard to comprehend the size of the universe.
I couldn't comprehend why he left without a word.
etymology: From Latin comprehendere, 'to seize, grasp'.

definition: Including all or nearly all the elements or aspects of something.
examples: The guide offers a comprehensive list of hiking trails in the park.
We need a comprehensive plan, not another quick fix.
etymology: From Latin comprehendere, 'to grasp, take in'.

definition: To consist of or be made up of certain parts.
examples: The tour will comprise five cities in ten days.
Volunteers comprise most of the shelter's staff.
etymology: From French compris, past participle of comprendre 'to include'.

definition: Resulting from or acting on an urge that is hard to resist.
examples: He's a compulsive checker who looks at his phone every few minutes.
The thriller is so compulsive that I finished it by sunrise.
etymology: From Latin compellere, 'to drive together, force'.

definition: Required by law or a rule; mandatory.
examples: Attendance at the safety briefing is compulsory.
Many countries have compulsory military service.
etymology: From Medieval Latin compulsorius, from compellere 'to compel'.

definition: A pang of guilt or uneasiness about doing something wrong.
examples: He lied to his clients without compunction and slept soundly each night.
She felt a flicker of compunction as she deleted her sister's message.
etymology: From Latin compunctio, 'a pricking', from compungere, 'to prick sharply'.

definition: The mental drive or effort that leads to purposeful action.
examples: Psychologists separate thought, feeling, and conation.
Without conation, good intentions never become habits.
etymology: From Latin conatio, from conari 'to try'.

definition: To link things together in a chain or series.
examples: The program will concatenate the two files.
Writers concatenate small scenes into a story.
etymology: From Latin concatenare, from catena 'chain'.

definition: To hide something or keep it from being known.
examples: She tried to conceal her smile while he opened the gift.
Heavy makeup can't conceal how tired the actor looks.
etymology: From Latin concelare, from com- + celare 'to hide'.

definition: To admit that something is true, often reluctantly, or to admit defeat.
examples: I'll concede that your shortcut was faster.
The candidate conceded the race late on election night.
etymology: From Latin concedere, 'to yield', from com- + cedere 'to go'.

definition: Excessive pride in oneself; also an elaborate or fanciful idea in art.
examples: His conceit made him impossible to coach.
The novel's central conceit is a house that remembers.
etymology: From conceive; it originally meant simply 'a thought or notion'.

definition: Planned or carried out jointly, or with great determination.
examples: It will take a concerted effort to clean up the river.
She made a concerted attempt to read more books this year.
etymology: From concert, from Italian concertare 'to bring into agreement'.

definition: Something given up or granted to settle a disagreement.
examples: As a concession to the neighbors, the bar closes its patio at ten.
The union won a major concession on overtime pay.
etymology: From Latin concessio, from concedere 'to yield'.

definition: Intended to make peace or reduce hostility.
examples: He sent a conciliatory text after the argument.
The company struck a conciliatory tone with the union.
etymology: From Latin conciliare, 'to bring together, win over'.

definition: Elegant harmony and fit of parts, especially in style.
examples: The essay has a concinnity that hides how hard it was to write.
Architects admired the concinnity of the façade.
etymology: From Latin concinnitas, 'elegance', from concinnus 'well put together'.

definition: Giving a lot of information clearly in very few words.
examples: Her concise summary captured the whole report in just three sentences.
Keep your emails concise so busy colleagues will actually read them to the end.
etymology: From Latin concisus, 'cut short', from concidere 'to cut off'.

definition: A private meeting, especially of cardinals choosing a pope.
examples: The conclave elected a new pope on the second day.
Department heads held a conclave behind locked doors.
etymology: From Latin conclave, 'a room that can be locked', from clavis 'key'.

definition: To invent a story or plan, or to make a dish by mixing ingredients.
examples: The kids managed to concoct an elaborate excuse for the broken lamp.
He likes to concoct strange smoothies from whatever is in the fridge.
etymology: From Latin concoquere, 'to cook together'.

definition: Naturally accompanying or associated with something else.
examples: Fame brings concomitant pressures.
Rapid growth and its concomitant traffic changed the town.
etymology: From Latin concomitari, 'to accompany', from comes 'companion'.

definition: Agreement or harmony between people or groups.
examples: The neighbors lived in rare concord.
The treaty promised lasting concord between the nations.
etymology: From Latin concordia, from com- 'together' + cor 'heart'.

definition: A formal agreement, especially between a church and a state.
examples: Napoleon signed a concordat with the pope in 1801.
The universities reached a concordat on shared research.
etymology: From Latin concordatum, 'something agreed upon'.

definition: Strong desire, especially sexual longing.
examples: Medieval sermons warned against concupiscence.
The poem throbs with barely hidden concupiscence.
etymology: From Latin concupiscere, 'to desire eagerly'.

definition: To agree with an opinion or decision.
examples: The second doctor didn't concur with the first diagnosis.
I concur: the meeting should have been an email.
etymology: From Latin concurrere, 'to run together'.

definition: To express strong disapproval of something, or to sentence someone to punishment.
examples: World leaders were quick to condemn the attack.
Don't condemn the whole series because of one weak season.
etymology: From Latin condemnare, from com- + damnare 'to condemn'.

definition: To make something shorter or more compact without losing its essentials.
examples: Can you condense this report into a single page?
Steam will condense on the cold bathroom mirror.
etymology: From Latin condensare, from densus 'thick'.

definition: Acting as though one is superior to others.
examples: The salesman used a condescending tone when explaining the engine.
Don't be condescending; she knows more about this than you do.
etymology: From condescend, from Late Latin condescendere 'to stoop'.

definition: Fitting and deserved, especially of a punishment.
examples: The fraudster received condign punishment.
Losing the election was condign for such arrogance.
etymology: From Latin condignus, 'very worthy'.

definition: Depending on certain requirements being met.
examples: The job offer is conditional on a background check.
A parent's love shouldn't be conditional.
etymology: From Latin condicio, 'agreement, stipulation'.

definition: An expression of sympathy to someone grieving.
examples: She wrote a heartfelt note of condolence to the widow.
Her letter of condolence meant more to the family than any flowers.
etymology: From Late Latin condolere, 'to suffer with'.

definition: To accept or allow behavior that is considered wrong.
examples: The school does not condone cheating of any kind.
By staying silent, they seemed to condone the bullying.
etymology: From Latin condonare, 'to give up, forgive'.

definition: A leader of mercenary soldiers, especially in Renaissance Italy.
examples: The condottiere switched sides whenever the pay improved.
He ran the hostile takeover like a modern condottiere.
etymology: From Italian, from condotta 'contract of hire'.

definition: Making a certain good result easy or likely to happen.
examples: A quiet room with soft light is conducive to deep sleep.
The open office was not conducive to concentration, so many people wore headphones.
etymology: From Latin conducere, 'to lead together', from con- + ducere 'to lead'.

definition: A channel through which something, such as water or information, is passed.
examples: The assistant served as a conduit between the director and the crew.
Old pipes beneath the street act as a conduit for rainwater.
etymology: From Old French conduit, from Latin conductus, 'led together'.

definition: To chat informally, or to invent false memories without intending to deceive.
examples: The neighbors confabulate over the fence every evening.
Patients with certain brain injuries may confabulate details of their past.
etymology: From Latin confabulari, 'to talk together'.

definition: A sweet treat, or an elaborately made, delicate creation.
examples: The bakery's newest confection is a lavender macaron.
Her wedding dress was a confection of lace and tulle.
etymology: From Latin confectio, from conficere 'to prepare, put together'.

definition: To discuss something together, or to grant a title or honor.
examples: The lawyers asked for a moment to confer.
The university will confer an honorary degree on the author.
etymology: From Latin conferre, 'to bring together'.

definition: A trusted person with whom one shares secrets.
examples: Her sister has always been her closest confidant.
The president's longtime confidant knew about the plan.
etymology: From French confident, from Italian confidente, ultimately from Latin confidere 'to trust'.

definition: To tell someone a secret or private matter because you trust them.
examples: Teenagers rarely confide in their parents about crushes.
She needed someone to confide in after the breakup.
etymology: From Latin confidere, 'to trust fully'.

definition: To take someone's property away by authority.
examples: Teachers confiscate phones that ring during exams.
Customs officers may confiscate undeclared fruit.
etymology: From Latin confiscare, 'to lay up in the treasury', from fiscus 'treasury'.

definition: A large, destructive fire that spreads widely.
examples: A small spark grew into a conflagration that swept across the dry hills.
The Great Fire of London was a conflagration that destroyed much of the city.
etymology: From Latin conflagratio, from conflagrare, 'to burn up', from com- + flagrare 'to blaze'.

definition: To combine two or more distinct ideas into one, often mistakenly.
examples: People often conflate being busy with being productive.
The article conflates two very different studies.
etymology: From Latin conflare, 'to fuse', from con-, 'together', + flare, 'to blow'.

definition: The meeting point of two rivers, or a coming together of things.
examples: The city grew at the confluence of two rivers.
A confluence of bad luck sank the business.
etymology: From Latin confluere, 'to flow together'.

definition: To behave according to accepted rules or the expectations of a group.
examples: Teenagers feel enormous pressure to conform.
All new buildings must conform to the earthquake code.
etymology: From Latin conformare, 'to shape after'.

definition: To surprise or confuse someone, especially by defying expectations.
examples: The underdog continues to confound the experts.
Results like these confound simple explanations.
etymology: From Latin confundere, 'to pour together, mix up'.

definition: To prove a person or argument wrong.
examples: New fossils confute the old theory.
She set out to confute every claim in the pamphlet.
etymology: From Latin confutare, 'to check, silence'.

definition: To thicken or solidify, or to take definite shape.
examples: Leftover gravy will congeal in the fridge overnight.
Loose ideas began to congeal into a real plan.
etymology: From Latin congelare, 'to freeze together'.

definition: A person or thing of the same kind or class as another.
examples: The lion and its congener the tiger share a genus.
This startup is a congener of every other delivery app.
etymology: From Latin congener, from con- + genus 'kind'.

definition: Pleasant and friendly, or well suited to one's tastes.
examples: The hosts were congenial and made everyone feel at home.
She found the small town a congenial place to write.
etymology: From con- 'together' + Latin genialis 'of one's nature'.

definition: Present from birth, or deeply ingrained in someone's character.
examples: The baby was born with a congenital heart defect.
He's a congenital optimist.
etymology: From Latin congenitus, 'born together with'.

definition: A disorderly collection or heap of things.
examples: The attic held a congeries of trunks, toys, and letters.
The law is a congeries of outdated rules.
etymology: From Latin congeries, 'heap', from congerere 'to pile up'.

definition: A crowded or blocked condition, as in traffic or the nose.
examples: Rush-hour congestion turned a ten-minute drive into an hour.
Steam helps relieve nasal congestion from a cold.
etymology: From Latin congestio, from congerere 'to heap up'.

definition: A large corporation formed from many different companies.
examples: A media conglomerate bought the local newspaper.
The conglomerate owns everything from cereal to cruise ships.
etymology: From Latin conglomerare, 'to roll together', from glomus 'ball of yarn'.

definition: To gather together into a crowd or group.
examples: Pigeons congregate wherever tourists eat lunch.
Guests always congregate in the kitchen at parties.
etymology: From Latin congregare, 'to herd together', from grex 'flock'.

definition: In agreement or harmony; in geometry, identical in shape and size.
examples: His actions are rarely congruent with his speeches.
The two triangles are congruent.
etymology: From Latin congruere, 'to agree, meet together'.

definition: An opinion or conclusion formed from incomplete information rather than proof.
examples: Whether the ruins were a temple is pure conjecture, since no records survive.
Her theory remains conjecture until someone can test it.
etymology: From Latin coniectura, 'a throwing together', from conicere, 'to infer, throw together'.

definition: To make something appear as if by magic, or to call it up in the mind.
examples: The smell of cinnamon can conjure memories of winter holidays.
The magician conjured a dove from an empty hat.
etymology: From Old French conjurer, from Latin conjurare 'to swear together'.

definition: To secretly allow or plot wrongdoing.
examples: The guards seemed to connive at the smuggling.
Two employees would connive to steal inventory.
etymology: From Latin connivere, 'to shut the eyes', as in winking at wrongdoing.

definition: A person with expert knowledge and refined taste in an art, food, or drink.
examples: As a coffee connoisseur, he can tell the roast's origin by smell alone.
The gallery owner is a true connoisseur of early photography.
etymology: From French connoisseur, from Old French connoistre, 'to know', from Latin cognoscere.

definition: An idea or feeling a word suggests beyond its literal meaning.
examples: 'Cheap' has a negative connotation that 'affordable' avoids.
The word home carries a connotation of warmth.
etymology: From Medieval Latin connotare, 'to mark along with', from notare 'to mark'.

definition: Relating to marriage or married life.
examples: Their connubial bliss lasted fifty years.
The sitcom mines connubial squabbles for laughs.
etymology: From Latin conubium 'marriage', from nubere 'to marry'.

definition: Relationship by blood or descent.
examples: Old laws barred marriage within certain degrees of consanguinity.
There's a consanguinity between the two languages.
etymology: From Latin consanguinitas, from sanguis 'blood'.

definition: The inner sense of right and wrong that guides a person's behavior.
examples: His conscience wouldn't let him keep the extra change.
She voted with her conscience, not her party.
etymology: From Latin conscientia, 'knowledge within oneself'.

definition: Careful and thorough, taking great care to do tasks properly.
examples: A conscientious student, he rechecked every answer before handing in the exam.
The conscientious nurse documented each change in the patient's condition without fail.
etymology: From Latin conscientia, 'knowledge, moral sense', from conscire 'to be aware'.

definition: To declare something sacred, or dedicate it to a purpose.
examples: The bishop came to consecrate the new chapel.
She chose to consecrate her life to medicine.
etymology: From Latin consecrare, from sacer 'sacred'.

definition: Following one after another without a break.
examples: It rained for nine consecutive days in April.
The team won its third consecutive championship.
etymology: From Latin consecutus, past participle of consequi 'to follow closely'.

definition: General agreement among a group of people.
examples: After an hour of debate, the family reached a consensus on where to eat.
The scientific consensus is that regular exercise improves sleep.
etymology: From Latin consensus, 'agreement', from consentire 'to agree'.

definition: Important because it has significant results.
examples: This could be the most consequential election in decades.
Choosing a college felt like a hugely consequential decision.
etymology: From Latin consequentia, from consequi 'to follow closely'.

definition: To protect something from harm or use it carefully so it is not wasted.
examples: Turn off the lights to conserve energy.
Marathoners conserve their strength for the final miles.
etymology: From Latin conservare, 'to keep safe'.

definition: Careful not to inconvenience or hurt others.
examples: It was considerate of you to bring extra chairs.
Considerate neighbors keep the music down after ten.
etymology: From Latin considerare, 'to examine closely'.

definition: A trusted adviser, originally to a Mafia boss.
examples: The senator's consigliere drafted every speech.
In the film, the consigliere is the calmest man in the room.
etymology: From Italian consigliere, 'counselor'.

definition: To send something away or hand it over, often to an unpleasant place or fate.
examples: Streaming may consign the DVD to history.
I'll consign these old clothes to the thrift store.
etymology: From Latin consignare, 'to mark with a seal'.

definition: Comfort received after a loss or disappointment.
examples: The only consolation for missing the bus was the sunrise.
Her friends' kind messages were a real consolation.
etymology: From Latin consolatio, from consolari 'to comfort'.

definition: To combine things into a single, stronger whole, or to make a position more secure.
examples: We plan to consolidate three small offices into one downtown.
After winning the primary, she worked to consolidate her support.
etymology: From Latin consolidare, 'to make firm', from solidus 'solid'.

definition: In agreement or harmony with something.
examples: The ruling is consonant with earlier decisions.
Her lifestyle is consonant with her values.
etymology: From Latin consonare, 'to sound together'.

definition: To associate or keep company with someone, often disreputable.
examples: Mobsters consort with corrupt politicians in the film.
He was warned not to consort with known gamblers.
etymology: From Latin consors, 'sharer, partner'.

definition: A broad summary or overview of a subject.
examples: The first chapter offers a conspectus of the whole field.
Her lecture gave a brisk conspectus of Roman history.
etymology: From Latin conspectus, 'a view, survey', from conspicere 'to look at'.

definition: Easy to notice; standing out.
examples: He felt conspicuous in a suit when everyone else wore jeans.
The new sign is in a conspicuous spot by the entrance.
etymology: From Latin conspicuus, 'visible', from conspicere 'to look at attentively'.

definition: To plan secretly with others to do something, often harmful.
examples: The siblings conspire every year to surprise their mom.
Weather and traffic seemed to conspire against us.
etymology: From Latin conspirare, 'to breathe together, agree'.

definition: Anxious alarm or dismay, often at something unexpected.
examples: To the coach's consternation, the star player missed the bus.
The sudden schedule changes caused consternation among the staff.
etymology: From Latin consternatio, from consternare 'to throw into confusion'.

definition: A voter represented by an elected official, or one part of a whole.
examples: The senator returned every constituent's call.
Hydrogen is a constituent of water.
etymology: From Latin constituere, 'to set up, establish'.

definition: To limit or restrict what someone or something can do.
examples: A tight budget will constrain our choice of venue.
Don't let old habits constrain your thinking.
etymology: From Old French constraindre, from Latin constringere 'to bind tightly'.

definition: Helpful and intended to improve something rather than tear it down.
examples: Her feedback was blunt but constructive.
Let's have a constructive conversation instead of trading insults.
etymology: From Latin construere, 'to heap together, build'.

definition: To interpret a statement or action in a particular way.
examples: My silence was construed as agreement.
Please don't construe my feedback as criticism of you personally.
etymology: From Latin construere, 'to build, construct'.

definition: An established custom having the force of law.
examples: By long consuetude, the eldest son spoke first.
Village consuetude decided who could graze the common.
etymology: From Latin consuetudo, 'custom'.

definition: Showing complete skill; perfect of its kind.
examples: She's a consummate professional who never misses a deadline.
The actor gave a consummate performance.
etymology: From Latin consummare, 'to complete', from summa 'sum, total'.

definition: To make something impure or unsafe by adding a harmful substance.
examples: A single leaking tank can contaminate an entire aquifer.
Wash the cutting board so raw chicken doesn't contaminate the salad.
etymology: From Latin contaminare, 'to defile, corrupt'.

definition: To treat or regard with contempt.
examples: Prophets often contemn the comforts of the city.
She seemed to contemn anyone who hadn't read Proust.
etymology: From Latin contemnere, 'to despise'.

definition: To think about something carefully and at length.
examples: She sat on the dock to contemplate her next move.
I can't even contemplate running a marathon right now.
etymology: From Latin contemplari, 'to observe', related to templum, a space marked out for watching omens.

definition: Belonging to the present time, or living or happening at the same time as something else.
examples: The gallery shows contemporary art from local painters.
Shakespeare was roughly contemporary with Cervantes.
etymology: From Medieval Latin contemporarius, from com- 'together' + tempus 'time'.

definition: A feeling that someone or something is worthless and deserves scorn.
examples: She looked at the parking ticket with open contempt.
Rolling your eyes during an apology signals contempt.
etymology: From Latin contemptus, from contemnere 'to scorn'.

definition: To struggle against a difficulty, or to argue that something is true.
examples: Farmers here contend with drought every summer.
Critics contend that the law will raise prices.
etymology: From Latin contendere, 'to stretch out, strive'.

definition: Likely to cause disagreement, or inclined to argue.
examples: Zoning is the most contentious issue in town.
The contentious debate ran three hours over.
etymology: From Latin contentio, 'strife, effort'.

definition: Sharing a border or touching; next in sequence.
examples: Shipping is free within the contiguous United States.
The two farms are contiguous, separated only by a fence.
etymology: From Latin contiguus, from contingere 'to touch'.

definition: A possible future event that must be prepared for.
examples: We packed rain jackets as a contingency for the hike.
Every wedding planner needs a contingency plan for bad weather.
etymology: From Latin contingere, 'to touch, happen to'.

definition: The unbroken, consistent existence or operation of something over time.
examples: Keeping the same coach gives the team some continuity.
Fans spotted a continuity error: his tie changes color mid-scene.
etymology: From Latin continuitas, from continuus 'uninterrupted'.

definition: To twist or bend out of normal shape.
examples: Yoga teachers contort their bodies into impossible poses.
Don't contort the facts to fit your theory.
etymology: From Latin contorquere, 'to twist'.

definition: Goods brought in or out of a place illegally.
examples: Guards found contraband hidden in a hollowed-out book.
Candy was contraband at summer camp.
etymology: From Spanish contrabanda, from Italian contrabbando, 'against the decree'.

definition: To say the opposite of what someone else has said, or to be inconsistent with something.
examples: The security footage seems to contradict his story.
It's rude to contradict your host in front of the guests.
etymology: From Latin contradicere, 'to speak against'.

definition: An odd or complicated device or machine.
examples: He built a contraption to feed the cat while we traveled.
The coffee contraption has more dials than a cockpit.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; perhaps a blend of contrive, trap and invention.

definition: Combining independent melodies or elements that play against each other.
examples: Bach's contrapuntal writing weaves four voices at once.
The film's contrapuntal storylines meet only at the end.
etymology: From Italian contrappunto, 'counterpoint'.

definition: A person who deliberately opposes popular opinion.
examples: A natural contrarian, he bought stocks when everyone sold.
Every book club needs a contrarian to stir things up.
etymology: From contrary, from Latin contrarius 'opposite'.

definition: On the other hand; in the opposite way.
examples: Some people relax by running; contrariwise, I relax by napping.
'Contrariwise,' said Tweedledee, 'if it was so, it might be.'
etymology: From contrary + -wise.

definition: Opposite in nature or direction, or stubbornly inclined to disagree.
examples: Contrary to popular belief, bats are not blind.
My contrary little brother says no to everything.
etymology: From Latin contrarius, from contra 'against'.

definition: To violate a law, rule, or principle.
examples: Parking on the sidewalk contravenes city regulations.
The decision appeared to contravene the spirit of the agreement.
etymology: From Latin contravenire, from contra, 'against', + venire, 'to come'.

definition: A minor dispute or an unfortunate, awkward mishap.
examples: A brief contretemps over seating delayed the wedding dinner.
After the contretemps at the ticket booth, the evening went smoothly.
etymology: From French, 'out of time', originally a fencing term.

definition: Sincere remorse for having done wrong.
examples: His apology showed genuine contrition, not just embarrassment.
She expressed contrition for missing the deadline and offered to stay late.
etymology: From Latin contritio, 'grinding', from conterere, 'to grind down'.

definition: To arrange or bring about something cleverly or artificially.
examples: She managed to contrive a meeting with the director.
Screenwriters contrive coincidences to move the plot.
etymology: From Old French controver, 'to invent, find'.

definition: Stubbornly disobedient, especially toward authority or a court.
examples: The contumacious witness refused again to answer the judge's questions.
His contumacious attitude toward every rule got him expelled from school.
etymology: From Latin contumax, 'stubborn, insolent', of uncertain origin.

definition: Insolent, insulting treatment or language.
examples: Hamlet laments 'the proud man's contumely'.
She endured the critics' contumely with grace.
etymology: From Latin contumelia, 'insult, abuse'.

definition: A confusing problem or puzzling question with no easy answer.
examples: Choosing between a higher salary and a shorter commute is a real conundrum.
The mystery of the missing keys remained a conundrum until we checked the freezer.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first appeared in 17th-century English as a slang word, possibly a joke.

definition: A large urban area formed when several towns merge.
examples: The conurbation stretches eighty miles along the coast.
Suburbs grew until the two cities formed one conurbation.
etymology: Coined in the early 1900s from con- 'together' + Latin urbs 'city'.

definition: To recover health gradually after illness or injury.
examples: She went to her parents' farm to convalesce after surgery.
Athletes convalesce faster with proper sleep.
etymology: From Latin convalescere, 'to grow strong', from valere 'to be well'.

definition: To come together, or call people together, for a formal meeting.
examples: The committee will convene again after the holidays.
The mayor plans to convene a panel of experts on flooding.
etymology: From Latin convenire, 'to come together'.

definition: Following accepted customs or standards rather than doing something new.
examples: They skipped the conventional wedding and eloped to Iceland.
Conventional wisdom says to buy a house, but renting suits her fine.
etymology: From Latin conventio, 'assembly, agreement', from convenire 'to come together'.

definition: To come together from different directions toward a single point.
examples: Three highways converge just north of the city.
Fans from across the country converge on the stadium every October.
etymology: From Late Latin convergere, 'to incline together'.

definition: Familiar with or knowledgeable about something.
examples: You need to be conversant with the new software.
He's conversant in three languages.
etymology: From Old French conversant, from Latin conversari 'to associate with'.

definition: A social gathering for discussing art, literature, or science.
examples: The society's annual conversazione showcased new inventions.
Her salon was a lively conversazione of poets.
etymology: From Italian conversazione, 'conversation'.

definition: In an opposite way; on the other hand.
examples: Some people relax by reading; conversely, others need to move.
Warm air rises; conversely, cool air sinks.
etymology: From Latin conversus, 'turned around'.

definition: To communicate an idea, feeling, or message.
examples: Her smile conveyed how relieved she was.
It's hard to convey sarcasm in a text message.
etymology: From Old French conveier, from Medieval Latin conviare 'to escort', from via 'way'.

definition: A firmly held belief, or a formal finding that someone is guilty of a crime.
examples: She spoke with such conviction that the room went quiet.
His conviction was overturned on appeal.
etymology: From Latin convictio, 'proof', from convincere 'to prove, overcome'.

definition: Friendly, lively, and enjoyable in company.
examples: The dinner party had a convivial mood that lasted past midnight.
He's a convivial host who remembers every guest's name.
etymology: From Latin convivialis, from convivium, 'feast'.

definition: Extremely complicated and difficult to follow.
examples: The plot is so convoluted that I needed a diagram.
They gave a convoluted explanation for the late fee.
etymology: From Latin convolvere, 'to roll together'.

definition: In excellent order; completely fine.
examples: The mechanic checked everything and said it was copacetic.
Once the bill was paid, everything was copacetic again.
etymology: American slang from the early 1900s, of unknown origin.

definition: Existing in large amounts; plentiful.
examples: She took copious notes during the lecture and filled half a notebook.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of garlic.
etymology: From Latin copiosus, 'plentiful', from copia, 'abundance'.

definition: A small group of trees or bushes.
examples: Deer sheltered in a copse at the edge of the field.
We picnicked beside a copse of birches.
etymology: A variant of coppice, from Old French copeiz 'cut wood'.

definition: A woman who flirts lightheartedly to win admiration.
examples: The play's coquette strings along three suitors.
She played the coquette at parties but was fiercely private.
etymology: From French, the feminine of coquet, a diminutive of coq 'rooster'.

definition: Warm, polite, and friendly in a sincere but often formal way.
examples: The two leaders shared a cordial handshake before the talks began.
She sent a cordial invitation to every neighbor on the street.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cordialis, 'of the heart', from Latin cor 'heart'.

definition: A line of people, vehicles, or barriers surrounding an area to guard it.
examples: Police set up a cordon around the burning building.
Fans pushed against the cordon to see the band.
etymology: From French cordon 'ribbon', from corde 'rope'.

definition: An essential part on which something is built or depends.
examples: Trust is the cornerstone of any good friendship.
Affordable housing became the cornerstone of her campaign.
etymology: From corner + stone, originally the stone at the corner of a building's foundation.

definition: An abundant supply of good things.
examples: The farmers market is a cornucopia of summer fruit.
The archive holds a cornucopia of forgotten letters.
etymology: From Latin cornu copiae, 'horn of plenty'.

definition: A natural consequence or result that follows from something else.
examples: A corollary of remote work is that clear writing matters more than ever.
Higher prices were the inevitable corollary of the shortage.
etymology: From Latin corollarium, 'money paid for a garland, gratuity', from corolla, 'little crown'.

definition: A funeral song or lament, especially in Scotland or Ireland.
examples: The piper played a coronach over the grave.
Wind in the glen sounded like a coronach.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic corranach, 'dirge'.

definition: Relating to the physical body rather than the mind or spirit.
examples: The ghost story plays with corporeal and spiritual worlds.
Hunger is the most corporeal of needs.
etymology: From Latin corporeus, from corpus 'body'.

definition: A glowing electrical discharge on a ship's mast in storms; St. Elmo's fire.
examples: Sailors took the corposant on the mast as an omen.
A blue corposant flickered along the rigging.
etymology: From Portuguese corpo santo, 'holy body'.

definition: Large and heavy in body.
examples: The novel's corpulent villain wheezes up every staircase.
A corpulent cat sprawled across the windowsill.
etymology: From Latin corpulentus, from corpus 'body'.

definition: To gather a group together and keep it in one place.
examples: Teachers corral the kids onto the bus.
It took an hour to corral everyone for the group photo.
etymology: From Spanish corral, 'enclosure for livestock'.

definition: To have a mutual relationship in which one thing changes along with another.
examples: Ice cream sales correlate with sunburns, but one doesn't cause the other.
Researchers want to correlate screen time with sleep quality.
etymology: A back-formation from correlation, from Medieval Latin correlatio.

definition: An error to be corrected in a printed work, often listed separately.
examples: The journal published a corrigendum fixing the chart.
A corrigendum was slipped into every copy of the book.
etymology: From Latin corrigendum, 'thing to be corrected', from corrigere.

definition: Capable of being corrected or reformed.
examples: The puppy's habits are bad but corrigible.
Teachers believe every student is corrigible.
etymology: From Latin corrigere, 'to correct'.

definition: To confirm or support a statement or finding with additional evidence.
examples: Two independent witnesses were able to corroborate her account of the accident.
Later studies did corroborate the original findings.
etymology: From Latin corroborare, 'to strengthen', from com- + roborare 'to make strong', from robur 'strength'.

definition: To wear away gradually, especially by chemical action, or to weaken slowly.
examples: Salt air will corrode the bike chain unless you oil it.
Small lies can corrode trust over time.
etymology: From Latin corrodere, 'to gnaw to pieces', from rodere 'to gnaw'.

definition: Willing to act dishonestly for money or personal gain; also damaged or unusable, as data.
examples: A corrupt official sold building permits to the highest bidder.
The file is corrupt and won't open.
etymology: From Latin corruptus, past participle of corrumpere 'to destroy, spoil'.

definition: To sparkle or flash, or to be brilliantly witty.
examples: Sunlight coruscated on the ripples of the lake.
Her conversation seemed to coruscate with clever jokes.
etymology: From Latin coruscare, 'to glitter'.

definition: Relating to or resembling crows or ravens.
examples: The poet had a corvine fondness for shiny things.
Corvine intelligence rivals that of apes.
etymology: From Latin corvinus, from corvus 'raven'.

definition: Wild and frenzied, as in ecstatic dancing.
examples: The crowd fell into a corybantic frenzy when the drums started.
Their corybantic celebrations lasted until sunrise.
etymology: From the Corybantes, priests of the goddess Cybele known for wild dancing.

definition: Affecting only appearance rather than substance.
examples: The redesign was purely cosmetic; the app is just as slow.
Repairs to the bumper are only cosmetic.
etymology: From Greek kosmētikos, from kosmein 'to arrange, adorn'.

definition: A theory or myth about the origin of the universe.
examples: Every culture has a cosmogony, from Genesis to the Big Bang.
The Norse cosmogony begins with fire and ice.
etymology: From Greek kosmogonia, from kosmos 'world' + gonos 'birth'.

definition: Familiar with many cultures, or including people from many countries.
examples: London's cosmopolitan food scene spans every continent.
Travel made her cosmopolitan and curious.
etymology: From Greek kosmopolitēs, 'citizen of the world'.

definition: To pamper and protect someone excessively.
examples: Luxury hotels cosset guests with heated towels.
Don't cosset the puppy, or it will never sleep alone.
etymology: Originally a noun for a lamb raised by hand as a pet.

definition: A person who sells fruit and vegetables from a street cart.
examples: A costermonger shouted prices from his barrow.
Dickens's London teemed with every kind of costermonger.
etymology: From costard, a large apple, + monger 'trader'.

definition: Constipated; figuratively, slow or reluctant, especially with words or money.
examples: The costive spokesman offered three words and left.
Costive investors held back funding for months.
etymology: From Old French costivé, from Latin constipatus 'pressed together'.

definition: A small, exclusive group of people with shared interests.
examples: The singer arrived with a coterie of stylists and assistants.
A coterie of devoted fans meets every year to reread the novels together.
etymology: From French coterie, originally 'an association of tenants'.

definition: Having the same boundaries, extent, or duration.
examples: The school district is coterminous with the city.
His career was nearly coterminous with the magazine's life.
etymology: From co- 'together' + Latin terminus 'boundary'.

definition: To express something in a particular style or language.
examples: Diplomats couch threats in polite language.
She tried to couch the criticism as a suggestion.
etymology: From Old French coucher, 'to lay down'.

definition: To tolerate or approve of something.
examples: The principal would not countenance bullying of any kind.
I cannot countenance spending that much on a phone case.
etymology: From Old French contenance, 'bearing', from Latin continentia.

definition: To act against something in order to reduce or cancel its effect.
examples: A pinch of sugar can counteract the acidity of tomatoes.
Stretching helps counteract hours of sitting.
etymology: From counter- 'against' + act.

definition: Relating to what did not happen but might have.
examples: Historians love counterfactual questions like 'What if Rome never fell?'
The study compares results with a counterfactual baseline.
etymology: From counter- 'against' + factual.

definition: To cancel an order, especially by issuing a new one.
examples: The general was quick to countermand the retreat.
Only the principal can countermand a teacher's decision.
etymology: From Latin contra 'against' + mandare 'to command'.

definition: A person or thing holding the same role or position in a different setting.
examples: The foreign minister met her French counterpart in Paris.
The tablet app is faster than its desktop counterpart.
etymology: From counter- 'opposite' + part; it first referred to a duplicate copy of a legal document.

definition: Having the opposite of the intended effect.
examples: Yelling at a toddler to calm down is usually counterproductive.
Working through lunch can be counterproductive.
etymology: From counter- 'against' + productive.

definition: To offset or counteract with equal force.
examples: Tariffs were meant to countervail foreign subsidies.
Nothing could countervail the charm of his apology.
etymology: From Anglo-French contrevaloir, from Latin contra valere 'to be worth against'.

definition: A sudden seizure of government power, or a notable success.
examples: The army staged a coup at dawn.
Landing the interview was a real coup for the young reporter.
etymology: From French coup, 'blow, stroke'.

definition: Polite, respectful, and considerate toward others.
examples: The courteous driver waved us across the busy street.
Even when customers yell, she stays courteous.
etymology: From Old French corteis, 'courtly', from cort 'court'.

definition: A formal, solemn agreement or promise.
examples: The homeowners' covenant bans purple houses.
They saw marriage as a covenant, not a contract.
etymology: From Old French covenant, from convenir 'to agree'.

definition: Secret or hidden, not openly done.
examples: The agency ran a covert operation for years.
She shot me a covert glance across the meeting table.
etymology: From Old French covert 'covered', past participle of covrir 'to cover'.

definition: To strongly desire something, especially something that belongs to someone else.
examples: Collectors covet the rare first edition.
I covet my neighbor's vegetable garden.
etymology: From Old French coveitier, from Latin cupiditas 'desire'.

definition: To crouch or shrink back in fear.
examples: Our dog will cower under the bed during thunderstorms.
Employees shouldn't have to cower before their boss.
etymology: From Middle English, of Scandinavian origin.

definition: A vain, conceited man overly concerned with his looks.
examples: The coxcomb checked his reflection in every window.
Only a coxcomb would wear a cravat to a barbecue.
etymology: From cock's comb, the cap worn by a professional fool.

definition: Pretending to be shy, or reluctant to give details.
examples: She gave a coy smile and changed the subject.
The studio is being coy about the sequel.
etymology: From Old French coi 'quiet', from Latin quietus.

definition: To trick or deceive.
examples: The con artist cozened tourists out of their money.
Don't let flattery cozen you into a bad deal.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Cramped and hard to read, as handwriting; or ill-tempered.
examples: The will was written in a crabbed hand.
The crabbed old critic hated every new play.
etymology: From crab, perhaps from the crab's sideways gait and pinching claws.

definition: Steep and rocky, or rugged and deeply lined, as a face.
examples: Goats picked their way along the craggy cliffs.
The actor's craggy face suited the Western.
etymology: From crag, a word of Celtic origin.

definition: Uncomfortably small or crowded, with too little room to move.
examples: Six of us lived in a cramped apartment above the bakery.
My legs ached after the cramped twelve-hour flight.
etymology: From cramp, a word of Germanic origin.

definition: Sickness or discomfort from excessive eating or drinking.
examples: New Year's morning brought a wave of crapulence.
He blamed his crapulence on the oysters, not the wine.
etymology: From Latin crapula 'intoxication', from Greek kraipalē 'hangover'.

definition: Lacking sensitivity, refinement, or intelligence.
examples: Joking about money at a funeral was crass.
The ad campaign was crass and quickly pulled.
etymology: From Latin crassus, 'thick, solid'.

definition: Contemptibly lacking in courage.
examples: The craven official blamed his staff for the scandal.
It was a craven decision to cancel the show under pressure.
etymology: From Middle English cravant, 'defeated', of uncertain origin.

definition: Belief in or acceptance of something as true.
examples: New evidence lends credence to her theory.
Don't give credence to rumors on anonymous forums.
etymology: From Medieval Latin credentia, from credere 'to believe'.

definition: Able to be believed or trusted because it seems reasonable.
examples: The witness gave a credible account that matched the security camera footage.
Without a credible source, the rumor should not be shared online.
etymology: From Latin credibilis, from credere 'to believe'.

definition: Deserving praise, though not outstanding.
examples: The team finished in a creditable third place.
He gave a creditable performance in a tough role.
etymology: From credit, from Latin credere 'to believe, trust'.

definition: A statement of beliefs or guiding principles.
examples: 'Leave it better than you found it' is her credo.
The startup's credo is printed on every mug.
etymology: From Latin credo, 'I believe'.

definition: Too ready to believe things.
examples: Credulous fans believed the fake trailer was real.
Scammers target credulous retirees.
etymology: From Latin credulus, from credere 'to believe'.

definition: Having battlements with regular gaps along the top of a wall.
examples: The crenellated walls glowed at sunset.
Kids built a crenellated sandcastle with a moat.
etymology: From French créneler, from crenel 'notch'.

definition: Relating to twilight, or active at dawn and dusk.
examples: Deer are crepuscular animals, most often seen at dawn and dusk.
The painting glows with crepuscular light.
etymology: From Latin crepusculum, 'twilight'.

definition: A gradual increase in loudness or intensity.
examples: The orchestra built to a thunderous crescendo.
Complaints reached a crescendo before the manager quit.
etymology: From Italian crescendo, 'increasing', from Latin crescere 'to grow'.

definition: A metal basket or cup holding fire, used as a torch or beacon.
examples: A cresset blazed on the castle wall.
Guards lit each cresset as night fell.
etymology: From Old French craisset, from craisse 'grease'.

definition: Sad and disappointed.
examples: He looked crestfallen when the trip was canceled.
The crestfallen players walked slowly off the field.
etymology: From crest + fallen, originally of a fighting rooster with drooping crest.

definition: A narrow crack or opening.
examples: A lizard vanished into a crevice in the wall.
Crumbs collect in every crevice of the car seat.
etymology: From Old French crevace, from crever 'to burst', from Latin crepare.

definition: A standard by which something is judged or decided.
examples: Price was the main criterion when we chose a laptop.
Kindness should be a criterion for any babysitter.
etymology: From Greek kritērion, 'means of judging', from kritēs 'judge'.

definition: A detailed evaluation of something's strengths and weaknesses.
examples: The writing workshop ended with a group critique of each story.
His critique of the plan was sharp but fair.
etymology: From French critique, from Greek kritikē (tekhnē), 'the art of judging'.

definition: A prehistoric stone monument, such as a circle of standing stones or a tomb.
examples: Sheep grazed around the ancient cromlech.
The cromlech's capstone weighs several tons.
etymology: From Welsh crom 'bent' + llech 'flat stone'.

definition: Unfairly giving jobs or favors to friends and associates.
examples: Critics called the appointment blatant cronyism.
Cronyism had hollowed out the agency's expertise.
etymology: From crony, old Cambridge slang from Greek khronios 'long-lasting', meaning an old friend.

definition: To transfer pollen between plants, or to share ideas across fields.
examples: Bees cross-pollinate the orchard every spring.
The lab mixes artists and engineers to cross-pollinate ideas.
etymology: From cross + pollinate, from Latin pollen 'fine flour'.

definition: An odd, whimsical notion or fixed eccentric preference.
examples: One crotchet of hers is refusing to eat anything blue.
He had a crotchet about never using elevators.
etymology: From Old French crochet, 'small hook'.

definition: Irritable and easily annoyed.
examples: The crotchety ferry captain barked at every tourist.
I get crotchety when I skip lunch.
etymology: From crotchet, 'a whim or odd notion'.

definition: A severe test or trial that forges something new; also a pot for melting metal.
examples: The pandemic was a crucible for small businesses.
Her leadership was forged in the crucible of the campaign.
etymology: From Medieval Latin crucibulum, a melting pot or lamp.

definition: Shaped like a cross.
examples: The cathedral has a cruciform floor plan.
A cruciform scar marked the old oak.
etymology: From Latin crux 'cross' + forma 'shape'.

definition: A person skilled at creating or solving crossword puzzles.
examples: A dedicated cruciverbalist, she finishes the Sunday puzzle in pen.
The newspaper hired a cruciverbalist to design themed grids.
etymology: A modern coinage from Latin crux 'cross' + verbum 'word'.

definition: A determined campaign for a cause or against something seen as wrong.
examples: Her crusade against single-use plastic began on a beach cleanup.
He launched a personal crusade to save the old theater.
etymology: From French croisade and Spanish cruzada, from Latin crux 'cross'.

definition: The most important or difficult point of a problem or issue.
examples: The crux of the problem is that nobody owns the project.
Let's skip the small details and get to the crux of the argument.
etymology: From Latin crux, 'cross'.

definition: Having a hidden or puzzling meaning that is hard to understand.
examples: He left a cryptic note on the fridge that no one could decode.
Her cryptic smile gave no hint of whether she approved of the plan.
etymology: From Late Latin crypticus, from Greek kryptos, 'hidden'.

definition: Mistaking a forgotten memory for a new, original idea.
examples: The songwriter blamed cryptomnesia for the familiar melody.
Cryptomnesia explains why some 'original' jokes sound borrowed.
etymology: From Greek kryptos 'hidden' + mnēsis 'memory'.

definition: A short, thick club used as a weapon; figuratively, a means of attack.
examples: The guard carried a heavy wooden cudgel.
The scandal became a cudgel for his opponents.
etymology: From Old English cycgel.

definition: A piece of armor covering the chest and back.
examples: The soldier's polished cuirass gleamed in the sun.
She wore her confidence like a cuirass.
etymology: From French cuirasse, ultimately from Latin corium 'leather'.

definition: Relating to cooking or the kitchen.
examples: Lyon is known as France's culinary capital.
His culinary skills end at toast.
etymology: From Latin culinarius, from culina 'kitchen'.

definition: To select from a large group, or to reduce a group by removing some members.
examples: Editors cull the best letters for the weekend issue.
Each spring I cull my closet of things I never wear.
etymology: From Old French coillir, from Latin colligere 'to gather'.

definition: To reach a final high point or result after a long process.
examples: The long negotiations will culminate in a signing ceremony next Friday.
Months of training culminate in a single race on Sunday morning.
etymology: From Late Latin culminare, 'to crown', from Latin culmen 'peak, summit'.

definition: Deserving blame or responsibility for a fault or wrongdoing.
examples: The court found the driver culpable for the crash because he was texting.
I feel partly culpable, since I knew about the problem and said nothing.
etymology: From Latin culpabilis, from culpa, 'fault, blame'.

definition: The person or thing responsible for a crime, fault, or problem.
examples: The culprit behind the missing cookies had crumbs on his shirt.
A loose wire turned out to be the culprit.
etymology: Thought to come from 'cul. prit', an abbreviation used by clerks in Anglo-French court proceedings.

definition: To develop or improve something, such as a skill, habit, or relationship, with care.
examples: She tried to cultivate patience by meditating for ten minutes each morning.
Good managers cultivate trust long before a crisis arrives.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cultivare, 'to till', from Latin cultus, past participle of colere, 'to tend, till'.

definition: Large, heavy, or complicated, and therefore hard to use.
examples: The old vacuum was too cumbersome to carry upstairs.
The application process is cumbersome and full of paperwork.
etymology: From Middle English cumber, 'to hinder', + -some.

definition: Increasing by one addition after another.
examples: The cumulative effect of small savings can be enormous.
The final exam is cumulative, covering the whole semester.
etymology: From Latin cumulare, 'to heap up', from cumulus 'heap'.

definition: A person who delays or procrastinates, sometimes strategically.
examples: The chess player was a cunctator who let opponents overreach.
I'm a cunctator by nature; taxes wait until April.
etymology: Latin 'delayer', the nickname of the Roman general Quintus Fabius Maximus.

definition: Clever at achieving goals through deceit or trickery.
examples: The cunning fox slipped past the farm dogs every night.
It was a cunning plan to get free dessert.
etymology: From Middle English, related to Old English cunnan 'to know'; it once meant simply 'learned'.

definition: Strong greed for money or possessions.
examples: The king's cupidity drove him to tax his people until they had nothing left.
Their cupidity blinded them to the obvious risks of the get-rich-quick scheme.
etymology: From Latin cupiditas, 'passionate desire', from cupidus, 'desirous', from cupere, 'to desire'.

definition: To carefully select and arrange items for a collection, exhibit, or list.
examples: She was hired to curate the museum's photography wing.
Influencers curate their feeds so that every photo matches.
etymology: A back-formation from curator, from Latin curare 'to take care of'.

definition: To keep something in check or under control.
examples: The city wants to curb noise from late-night construction.
Try to curb your spending until payday.
etymology: From Old French courbe 'bent', from Latin curvus; it first named a strap used to check a horse.

definition: A rare, unusual, or intriguing small object.
examples: Each curio in the shop, from brass compasses to glass eyes, has a tag.
A dusty curio sat on her grandfather's desk.
etymology: A shortening of curiosity.

definition: A bad-tempered, stubborn person, often an older one.
examples: The lovable curmudgeon next door secretly feeds every stray cat.
He plays the office curmudgeon, but he remembers everyone's birthday.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first recorded in the late 1500s.

definition: Done quickly and without attention to detail.
examples: A cursory glance at the report was enough to spot several errors.
The inspector gave the building only a cursory check before signing off.
etymology: From Latin cursorius, 'of a runner', from cursor, 'runner', from currere, 'to run'.

definition: Rudely brief in speech or manner.
examples: Her curt reply made it clear she was annoyed.
The clerk gave a curt nod and kept typing.
etymology: From Latin curtus, 'cut short'.

definition: To cut short or reduce something.
examples: The storm curtailed our camping trip by two days.
The company had to curtail travel to save money.
etymology: From obsolete curtal, 'a horse with a docked tail', influenced by tail.

definition: The land immediately surrounding a house, legally part of the home.
examples: The court ruled the shed was within the curtilage.
Police need a warrant to search the curtilage.
etymology: From Old French courtillage, from courtil 'small court'.

definition: Consisting of or bounded by curved lines.
examples: The museum's curvilinear walls contain no right angles.
Art nouveau loves curvilinear forms.
etymology: From Latin curvus 'curved' + linea 'line'.

definition: A point of transition between two states or periods.
examples: We're on the cusp of a breakthrough.
Born on the cusp of two zodiac signs, she claims both.
etymology: From Latin cuspis, 'point, apex'.

definition: A person responsible for looking after something, such as a building or valuable property.
examples: The school custodian knows every squeaky door by heart.
The museum sees itself as a custodian of the region's history.
etymology: From Latin custodia, 'guarding', from custos 'guardian'.

definition: According to the usual practices of a society or person.
examples: It's customary to tip about twenty percent here.
He arrived with his customary bag of oranges.
etymology: From Medieval Latin customarius, from Old French custume 'custom'.

definition: A pickpocket or thief.
examples: A cutpurse worked the crowd at the hanging.
Watch your wallet; every market has its cutpurse.
etymology: From the old practice of cutting purses that hung from belts.

definition: Fiercely and ruthlessly competitive.
examples: The restaurant business in this city is cutthroat.
Our family board games get surprisingly cutthroat.
etymology: From cut + throat; it originally described a murderer.

definition: The most advanced or innovative in a field.
examples: The lab uses cutting-edge imaging to study the brain.
Their cutting-edge design looked dated within five years.
etymology: From the sharp edge of a blade, which leads the cut.

definition: Occurring in repeated cycles.
examples: Construction work is cyclical, booming and busting with the economy.
Fashion is cyclical: flared jeans always come back.
etymology: From Greek kyklos, 'circle'.

definition: Enormous, especially of masonry made of huge irregular stones.
examples: The fortress walls are built of cyclopean blocks.
A cyclopean storm front swallowed the horizon.
etymology: From the Cyclopes of Greek myth, giants once credited with building such walls.

definition: A large circular painting viewed from within, or a curved stage backdrop.
examples: The Gettysburg cyclorama surrounds viewers with battle.
Lighting turned the cyclorama from dawn to dusk.
etymology: From Greek kyklos 'circle' + horama 'view'.

definition: Believing that people are motivated mainly by self-interest; distrustful of sincerity.
examples: Years in politics made him cynical about every promise.
It's hard not to feel cynical when ads call a sale 'once in a lifetime' every week.
etymology: From cynic, from Greek kynikos 'doglike', a nickname for philosophers who scorned convention.

definition: A person or thing that is the center of attention or admiration.
examples: The glowing sculpture became the cynosure of the entire exhibition.
As the youngest finalist, she was the cynosure of every camera at the event.
etymology: From Greek kunosoura, 'dog's tail', a name for the constellation Ursa Minor.

definition: To take part in an activity casually or superficially rather than seriously.
examples: She likes to dabble in watercolors on rainy weekends.
Many founders dabble in several ideas before committing to one.
etymology: From obsolete Dutch dabbelen, a frequentative of dabben 'to dab, splash'.

definition: An inner or attendant spirit that inspires or guides a person.
examples: Socrates claimed a daemon warned him against wrong choices.
Her creative daemon seemed to wake only after midnight.
etymology: From Latin daemon, from Greek daimōn 'divinity, guiding spirit'.

definition: A brief or casual involvement, especially a romantic one.
examples: His dalliance with politics lasted one campaign.
The tabloids hinted at a summer dalliance.
etymology: From dally, from Old French dalier 'to chat', plus -ance.

definition: To bounce a young child playfully on one's knee or in one's arms.
examples: Grandpa loved to dandle the baby on his knee.
She dandled her nephew while telling him stories.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Neat and trim in dress and appearance, especially of a man.
examples: He looked dapper in his three-piece suit.
A dapper old man tipped his hat as we passed.
etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch dapper 'strong, stout'.

definition: Willing to take bold risks or to do something unconventional.
examples: The rescue team made a daring climb up the frozen cliff.
Her daring design choices made the tiny apartment feel huge.
etymology: From the verb dare, from Old English durran 'to venture, have courage'.

definition: Wicked, cruel, and cowardly.
examples: The villain hatched a dastardly plot to steal the crown.
Stealing a kid's lunch is a dastardly act.
etymology: From dastard 'coward', probably from dazed + -ard.

definition: Seeming difficult or intimidating to deal with.
examples: Moving across the country alone felt daunting.
The reading list for the course was daunting.
etymology: From daunt, from Old French danter, from Latin domitare 'to tame'.

definition: Showing fearlessness and determination.
examples: The dauntless climbers pushed on through the snowstorm.
She was dauntless in her search for the truth.
etymology: From daunt, 'to intimidate', from Latin domitare, 'to tame', + -less.

definition: To waste time or move slowly.
examples: Don't dawdle, or we'll miss the bus.
The kids dawdled on the way home from school.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 17th century.

definition: To amaze or overwhelm someone with brilliance, skill, or beauty.
examples: The young pianist managed to dazzle the judges in under five minutes.
Fancy graphics alone won't dazzle investors who want real numbers.
etymology: A frequentative of daze, from Middle English dasen 'to stun'.

definition: A situation in which no progress can be made because neither side will give in.
examples: Talks between the union and the company ended in deadlock.
The jury remained in deadlock after three days.
etymology: From dead + lock.

definition: Deliberately impassive or expressionless, especially when being funny.
examples: Her deadpan delivery made the joke even funnier.
He gave a deadpan reply that left us unsure if he was joking.
etymology: From dead + pan, slang for 'face'; American, from the 1920s.

definition: A scarcity or lack of something that is needed.
examples: The town's dearth of affordable housing pushed many young families to move away.
A dearth of good ideas left the writers staring at a blank board.
etymology: From Middle English derthe, 'costliness, scarcity', related to dear.

definition: A sudden and total failure that causes embarrassment or chaos.
examples: The product launch was a debacle, with the website crashing within minutes.
After the debacle at the final, the coach resigned the next morning.
etymology: From French débâcle, 'breaking up of ice in a river', from débâcler 'to unbar'.

definition: To lower the quality, value, or character of something.
examples: Rulers would debase the coinage by mixing in cheap metal.
Constant clickbait can debase public conversation.
etymology: Formed in English from de- + base 'low'.

definition: To make someone or something seriously weak or unable to function well.
examples: A long bout of the flu can debilitate even the healthiest athlete.
Constant budget cuts began to debilitate the once-proud public library system.
etymology: From Latin debilitare, 'to weaken', from debilis 'weak'.

definition: Confident, stylish, and charming, especially of a man.
examples: He looked debonair in his vintage tuxedo.
The debonair host made every guest feel welcome.
etymology: From Old French debonaire, from de bon aire 'of good disposition'.

definition: To emerge from a narrow or confined space into a wider, open area.
examples: At dawn the troops would debouch onto the plain.
Here the creek begins to debouch into the bay.
etymology: From French déboucher, from dé- + bouche 'mouth'.

definition: To question someone about a task they have just completed to learn from it.
examples: Let's debrief after the launch while it's still fresh.
Officials will debrief the astronauts when they land.
etymology: Formed in English from de- + brief, first used in military contexts in the 1940s.

definition: Scattered fragments or rubbish left after something has been broken or destroyed.
examples: Volunteers cleared debris from the beach after the storm.
A piece of debris cracked the windshield on the highway.
etymology: From French débris, from obsolete débriser 'to break down'.

definition: To show that a claim or belief is false.
examples: The article debunks several myths about cracking your knuckles.
It took scientists only a day to debunk the viral video.
etymology: From de- + bunk 'nonsense', short for bunkum.

definition: Luxuriously self-indulgent, or marked by moral or cultural decline.
examples: We shared a decadent chocolate cake for dessert.
Critics called the court's lifestyle decadent and wasteful.
etymology: From French décadent, from Medieval Latin decadentia 'decay'.

definition: Undoubtedly and noticeably; to a clear degree.
examples: The second album is decidedly darker than the first.
The weather turned decidedly cold after lunch.
etymology: From decided, from decide, via French from Latin decidere 'to cut off', plus -ly.

definition: To kill or destroy a large proportion of something.
examples: A new fungus could decimate the region's banana crops.
Budget cuts threaten to decimate the city's arts programs.
etymology: From Latin decimare 'to take one in ten', from decimus 'tenth'; a Roman punishment of mutinous legions.

definition: To work out the meaning of something hard to read or understand.
examples: I couldn't decipher the doctor's handwriting.
It took weeks to decipher what the new manager actually wanted.
etymology: From de- + cipher, modeled on French déchiffrer.

definition: Able to make decisions quickly, or settling an issue clearly.
examples: A decisive leader doesn't wait for every last detail.
Her goal in the final minute was decisive.
etymology: From Medieval Latin decisivus, from Latin decidere 'to decide'.

definition: A downward slope.
examples: The cottage sat at the foot of a grassy declivity.
We sledded down the gentlest declivity we could find.
etymology: From Latin declivitas, from de- 'down' + clivus 'slope'.

definition: To remove unnecessary items from a space to make it tidier.
examples: I spent Sunday trying to declutter the garage.
It helps to declutter your inbox before a big week.
etymology: Formed in English from de- + clutter.

definition: To extract the essence of something by boiling it down.
examples: Herbalists decoct the bark to make a bitter tonic.
Editors decoct a messy draft into its strongest pages.
etymology: From Latin decoct-, past participle stem of decoquere 'to boil down'.

definition: In keeping with good taste and polite behavior; proper.
examples: The gala was a decorous affair until the band arrived.
She gave a decorous nod to the visiting dignitaries.
etymology: From Latin decorus 'seemly, becoming', from decor 'beauty'.

definition: Polite, proper behavior that suits a formal or serious occasion.
examples: The judge demanded decorum and warned the crowd to stop shouting.
She kept her decorum even when the dinner conversation turned rude.
etymology: From Latin decorum, 'what is fitting', from decor 'beauty, grace'.

definition: An official order issued by a legal or ruling authority.
examples: The governor issued a decree closing all schools.
By royal decree, the holiday was extended by a day.
etymology: From Old French decre, from Latin decretum 'something decided', from decernere 'to decide'.

definition: Worn out or ruined because of age or neglect.
examples: We drove a decrepit van across three states.
The decrepit pier was finally torn down.
etymology: From Latin decrepitus, perhaps from de- + crepare 'to creak'.

definition: To publicly denounce something as bad or wrong.
examples: Doctors decry the rise of unproven health fads.
It's easy to decry social media while scrolling it all day.
etymology: From French décrier, from Old French descrier 'to cry down'.

definition: To devote time, effort, or oneself wholly to a particular purpose.
examples: She chose to dedicate her Saturdays to the community garden.
We need to dedicate one engineer to fixing bugs full time.
etymology: From Latin dedicare 'to proclaim, consecrate', from de- + dicare 'to declare'.

definition: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from evidence.
examples: From the muddy boots, she deduced that he'd been in the garden.
Can you deduce the answer from the clues?
etymology: From Latin deducere, 'to lead down', from de- + ducere 'to lead'.

definition: To regard or judge something in a particular way.
examples: Use whatever method you deem best.
The bridge was closed until engineers could deem it safe.
etymology: From Old English dēman 'to judge', related to doom.

definition: A flaw or imperfection that makes something faulty.
examples: A tiny defect in the chip caused the recall.
The jacket was half price because of a small defect in the zipper.
etymology: From Latin defectus, from deficere 'to fail, desert'.

definition: To throw someone or something out of a window.
examples: The enraged rock star threatened to defenestrate the hotel television.
Historians recall how rebels chose to defenestrate the royal officials in Prague in 1618.
etymology: From Latin de- 'out of' + fenestra 'window'.

definition: To put something off until later, or to yield to someone else's judgment.
examples: She deferred her college start for a year to travel.
On medical questions, I defer to my doctor.
etymology: From Latin differre, 'to delay', and deferre, 'to carry down, submit'.

definition: Polite respect shown by yielding to another person's wishes or opinion.
examples: The young lawyer spoke with deference to the senior judge.
In deference to her grandmother, she changed out of her ripped jeans.
etymology: From French déférence, from déférer 'to yield', from Latin deferre 'to carry away'.

definition: Openly resisting authority or refusing to obey.
examples: The toddler gave a defiant shake of his head at bedtime.
Despite the losses, the coach struck a defiant tone at the press conference.
etymology: From French défiant, from défier 'to challenge', from Old French desfier.

definition: The amount by which something, especially money, falls short of what is needed.
examples: The city faces a budget deficit of nearly ten million dollars.
After a week of poor sleep, I was running a serious energy deficit.
etymology: From Latin deficit 'it is lacking', from deficere 'to fail, leave'.

definition: Final and authoritative, settling a matter conclusively.
examples: The lab results gave a definitive answer at last.
Her book is considered the definitive guide to sourdough.
etymology: From Latin definitivus, from definire 'to set bounds to'.

definition: To cause something to change direction, or to avoid blame or questions.
examples: The goalie managed to deflect the shot over the bar.
He tried to deflect criticism by blaming the old management.
etymology: From Latin deflectere 'to bend away', from de- + flectere 'to bend'.

definition: To provide money to pay a cost or expense.
examples: A small grant will defray the cost of travel.
Bake sales help defray the price of team uniforms.
etymology: From French défrayer, from Old French frai 'cost, expense'.

definition: Quick, neat, and skillful in movement or handling a situation.
examples: With a deft flick of the wrist, the chef flipped the omelet.
She gave a deft answer that avoided the trap hidden in the question.
etymology: From Middle English deft, a variant of 'daft' in its older sense 'gentle, fitting'.

definition: No longer existing, operating, or in use.
examples: The defunct factory is now an art studio.
The app relies on a defunct service that shut down years ago.
etymology: From Latin defunctus 'dead', past participle of defungi 'to discharge, finish'.

definition: To reduce the danger or tension in a difficult situation.
examples: A well-timed joke can defuse an awkward meeting.
The manager stepped in to defuse the argument between the two teams.
etymology: Formed in English from de- 'remove' + fuse, originally meaning to remove the fuse from an explosive.

definition: To lower the quality, condition, or dignity of something or someone.
examples: Cheap plastic will degrade in the sun within a few months.
Constant interruptions degrade the quality of everyone's work.
etymology: From Old French degrader, from Late Latin degradare 'to reduce in rank'.

definition: To split open along a natural line, as a seed pod does when ripe.
examples: The pods dehisce in late summer and scatter their seeds.
Watch a poppy capsule dehisce under the microscope.
etymology: From Latin dehiscere 'to gape open', from hiscere 'to begin to gape'.

definition: Of a word whose meaning depends on context, like here, now, or you.
examples: This and that are deictic words that point to things.
A deictic phrase like over there needs a gesture.
etymology: From Greek deiktikos 'able to show', from deiknunai 'to show'.

definition: To treat or worship someone as a god.
examples: Fans tend to deify their favorite athletes.
Ancient Romans would deify emperors after their deaths.
etymology: From Old French deifier, from Latin deificare, from deus 'god'.

definition: To do something one considers beneath one's dignity.
examples: The celebrity didn't deign to reply to fan letters.
The cat finally deigned to sit on my lap.
etymology: From Old French deignier, from Latin dignari, 'to deem worthy'.

definition: A person skilled in witty and learned conversation at the dinner table.
examples: Every dinner party needs at least one deipnosophist.
My uncle, a born deipnosophist, held court over dessert.
