examples: The instructions were explicit: no phones during the exam.
Be explicit about what you need from the team.
etymology: From Latin explicitus, past participle of explicare 'to unfold'.

definition: In a clear and direct way, leaving no room for confusion.
examples: The sign explicitly says no dogs allowed.
I explicitly asked you to call before coming over.
etymology: From Latin explicitus, 'unfolded', from explicare.

definition: To make full use of something, or to take unfair advantage of someone.
examples: Scammers exploit people's fear of losing their bank accounts.
The team learned to exploit gaps in the opposing defense.
etymology: From Old French esploit 'success, achievement', from Latin explicitum 'unfolded'.

definition: A person who supports and promotes an idea or practices an art skillfully.
examples: She was an early exponent of remote work.
He is the finest living exponent of flamenco guitar.
etymology: From Latin exponere 'to put forth, explain'.

definition: Growing faster and faster, so that the rate of increase itself keeps rising.
examples: The app saw exponential growth after one celebrity posted about it.
Compound interest produces exponential gains over decades.
etymology: From exponent, from Latin exponere 'to put forth'.

definition: A detailed explanation, or the background information at the start of a story.
examples: The film spends too long on exposition before anything happens.
Her exposition of the tax code was surprisingly clear.
etymology: From Latin expositio, from exponere 'to set forth'.

definition: To express strong disapproval or disagreement.
examples: The customer expostulated with the manager about the long wait.
She began to expostulate that the rules were unfair.
etymology: From Latin expostulare, 'to demand, complain'.

definition: To explain or present an idea in detail.
examples: My uncle likes to expound on economics at Thanksgiving.
The author will expound her theory in a new book.
etymology: From Old French espondre, from Latin exponere 'to put forth'.

definition: Effectively conveying thoughts or feelings.
examples: The actor has wonderfully expressive eyebrows.
Her expressive drawings say more than any caption could.
etymology: From French expressif, from Latin expressus 'pressed out'.

definition: For a specific purpose, or in a clear and direct way.
examples: The room was designed expressly for recording music.
The sign expressly forbids swimming after dark.
etymology: From express, from Latin expressus, 'clearly presented', + -ly.

definition: To take property from its owner, especially for public use.
examples: The government moved to expropriate farmland for the new highway.
Revolutionaries vowed to expropriate the factories.
etymology: From Medieval Latin expropriare, from ex- 'from' + proprium 'property'.

definition: To erase or remove something completely.
examples: She petitioned the court to expunge her old arrest record.
No amount of scrubbing could expunge the smell of smoke.
etymology: From Latin expungere 'to mark for deletion by points', from pungere 'to prick'.

definition: To remove offensive or objectionable material from a text.
examples: The school board voted to expurgate the novel's racier scenes.
Victorian editors would expurgate even Shakespeare.
etymology: From Latin expurgare 'to cleanse thoroughly', from purgare 'to purify'.

definition: Extremely beautiful, delicate, or finely made.
examples: The bride wore an exquisite lace veil that had belonged to her grandmother.
The chef pays exquisite attention to detail.
etymology: From Latin exquisitus 'sought out', from exquirere 'to search out'.

definition: To drain of blood, or figuratively, to drain of vitality.
examples: Without a tourniquet, the wounded soldier could exsanguinate in minutes.
Endless budget cuts threaten to exsanguinate the arts program.
etymology: From Latin exsanguinatus 'drained of blood', from sanguis 'blood'.

definition: Still in existence; surviving.
examples: Only three copies of the original map are extant.
It is the oldest extant recording of the song.
etymology: From Latin exstare 'to stand out, exist'.

definition: Spoken or done without preparation.
examples: When the slides failed, she spoke extempore for half an hour.
The jazz trio played extempore all night.
etymology: From Latin ex tempore 'on the spur of the moment', literally 'out of the time'.

definition: To speak or perform without preparation; to improvise.
examples: When the teleprompter failed, the host had to extemporize.
The jazz trio extemporized for twenty minutes.
etymology: From Latin ex tempore, 'out of the time'.

definition: Covering a large area or including a great amount.
examples: The storm caused extensive damage along the coast.
He has extensive experience managing remote teams.
etymology: From Late Latin extensivus, from extendere 'to stretch out'.

definition: Making a fault or offense seem less serious or more forgivable.
examples: Late work is accepted only in extenuating circumstances.
The judge considered his illness an extenuating factor.
etymology: From Latin extenuare 'to make thin', from tenuis 'thin'.

definition: To root out and destroy completely.
examples: The gardener vowed to extirpate every weed from the vegetable beds.
The new manager tried to extirpate the culture of gossip.
etymology: From Latin exstirpare, from stirps, 'stem'.

definition: Divination by examining the entrails of sacrificed animals.
examples: Babylonian priests practiced extispicy on sheep livers.
Reading quarterly earnings sometimes feels like extispicy.
etymology: From Latin extispicium, from exta 'entrails' + specere 'to look at'.

definition: To praise something enthusiastically and at length.
examples: Reviewers continue to extol the novel's vivid characters and its unforgettable final chapter.
My uncle will extol the virtues of cast-iron pans to anyone willing to listen.
etymology: From Latin extollere, 'to lift up', from ex- 'up' + tollere 'to raise'.

definition: To obtain something by force, threats, or intimidation.
examples: The hackers tried to extort a ransom from the hospital.
Gangs extort protection money from local shop owners.
etymology: From Latin extorquere 'to wrest out', from torquere 'to twist'.

definition: To remove or take out something, often with effort.
examples: The dentist had to extract two wisdom teeth.
It took an hour to extract a straight answer from him.
etymology: From Latin extrahere, from ex- 'out' + trahere 'to draw'.

definition: To hand over an accused person to the country where the crime was committed.
examples: Spain agreed to extradite the fugitive to the United States.
Some countries refuse to extradite their own citizens.
etymology: A back-formation from extradition, from French, from Latin ex- 'out' + traditio 'delivery'.

definition: Existing outside or beyond the physical world.
examples: Mystics claim access to extramundane realms.
The painting has an extramundane stillness.
etymology: From Late Latin extramundanus, from extra 'outside' + mundus 'world'.

definition: Irrelevant or not belonging to the matter at hand.
examples: Cut any extraneous detail from your cover letter.
The microphone picked up extraneous noise from the street.
etymology: From Latin extraneus 'external', from extra 'outside'.

definition: To estimate or conclude something by extending known information.
examples: You can't extrapolate national trends from one small town.
Economists extrapolate future growth from current data.
etymology: From extra- 'outside' + a shortened form of interpolate.

definition: Spending or using much more than is necessary or reasonable.
examples: They threw an extravagant party with ice sculptures and a live band.
A new car every year seems a bit extravagant.
etymology: From Medieval Latin extravagari 'to wander outside', from vagari 'to wander'.

definition: To free someone or something from a difficult situation or tangle.
examples: It took ten minutes to extricate the kite from the branches.
She managed to extricate herself from an awkward conversation.
etymology: From Latin extricare, 'to disentangle', from ex- + tricae 'perplexities'.

definition: Coming from outside rather than from within.
examples: Grades are an extrinsic reward; curiosity is the intrinsic one.
The bridge failed because of extrinsic factors like flooding.
etymology: From Late Latin extrinsecus 'outer', from Latin extrinsecus 'from outside'.

definition: An outgoing person who gains energy from being around others.
examples: As a true extrovert, she was recharged by a crowded party.
Even an extrovert needs a quiet evening now and then.
etymology: From extro- 'outward' + Latin vertere 'to turn'; popularized by psychologist Carl Jung's types.

definition: Full of lively, joyful energy and enthusiasm.
examples: The exuberant crowd cheered and danced long after the band left the stage.
Her exuberant laugh filled the whole room and made everyone smile.
etymology: From Latin exuberare, 'to be abundant', from ex- 'thoroughly' + uber 'fertile'.

definition: To display a quality or feeling strongly, or to discharge something slowly.
examples: Good leaders exude calm when things go wrong.
Pine trees exude sticky resin in summer.
etymology: From Latin exsudare 'to sweat out', from sudare 'to sweat'.

definition: To show or feel great triumphant joy.
examples: Fans poured into the streets to exult in the championship win.
It's unkind to exult over a rival's failure.
etymology: From Latin exsultare 'to leap up', from saltare 'to jump'.

definition: The cast-off skins or shells of animals such as insects and snakes.
examples: Dragonfly exuviae clung to the reeds by the pond.
The attic held the exuviae of my childhood: trophies, comics, a broken kite.
etymology: From Latin exuviae 'things stripped off', from exuere 'to take off'.

definition: A thing that is very ugly to look at, especially a building.
examples: The rusting billboard is an eyesore on an otherwise lovely road.
Neighbors called the half-built mansion an eyesore.
etymology: From eye + sore, originally meaning something that irritates the eye.

definition: A small island in a river.
examples: Swans nest on a willowy eyot in the Thames.
We rowed out to the eyot for a picnic.
etymology: From Old English iggath, from ieg 'island'.

definition: To invent something false in order to deceive, or to build something from parts.
examples: The reporter was fired for trying to fabricate quotes from sources.
The workshop can fabricate custom steel brackets in a single afternoon.
etymology: From Latin fabricare 'to make', from fabrica 'workshop'.

definition: The front of a building, or a false outward appearance.
examples: Behind her cheerful facade, she was worried about her exams.
The old bank's stone facade was restored to its original color.
etymology: From French façade, from Italian facciata, from faccia 'face'.

definition: One side or aspect of something complex.
examples: Customer service is just one facet of running a small bakery.
Each facet of the cut diamond caught the light differently.
etymology: From French facette, a diminutive of face 'face'.

definition: Playfully joking in a way that is not serious, often at the wrong time.
examples: Please do not be facetious; this is a serious matter.
His facetious reply made the class laugh and the teacher frown.
etymology: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, 'a jest'.

definition: Too simple, ignoring the real complexity of an issue; also achieved too easily.
examples: He offered a facile solution to a deeply complicated problem.
Critics dismissed the film's facile happy ending.
etymology: From Latin facilis 'easy', from facere 'to do'.

definition: To make a process or action easier or help it run smoothly.
examples: A good teacher will facilitate discussion rather than simply giving a lecture.
New software should facilitate faster communication between the two offices.
etymology: From French faciliter, from Latin facilis 'easy'.

definition: An exact copy, especially of a document or artwork.
examples: The museum sells a facsimile of the original manuscript.
The restaurant is a facsimile of a 1950s diner.
etymology: From Latin fac simile 'make like'.

definition: Inclined to split into quarreling groups.
examples: The party was too factious to agree on a candidate.
A factious board rarely gets anything done.
etymology: From Latin factiosus, from factio 'faction'.

definition: Artificially created rather than natural or genuine.
examples: The marketing team whipped up a factitious sense of urgency.
Critics dismissed the scandal as a factitious controversy.
etymology: From Latin facticius 'made by art', from facere 'to make'.

definition: An employee who does all kinds of work.
examples: The theater's factotum built sets, sold tickets, and fixed the plumbing.
As the office factotum, she knew where everything was kept.
etymology: From medieval Latin, from fac 'do!' + totum 'the whole thing'.

definition: Based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning.
examples: The argument is fallacious because it assumes what it tries to prove.
Fallacious claims about vaccines spread quickly online.
etymology: From Latin fallaciosus, from fallacia 'deceit'.

definition: A widely held but mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning.
examples: It is a fallacy that you lose most of your body heat through your head.
Her argument rested on the fallacy that what is popular must be true.
etymology: From Latin fallacia 'deceit', from fallere 'to deceive'.

definition: Capable of making mistakes.
examples: Even the best doctors are fallible.
Memory is fallible, so write the details down.
etymology: From Medieval Latin fallibilis, from Latin fallere 'to deceive'.

definition: The unpleasant consequences of an event; also radioactive dust after a nuclear blast.
examples: The political fallout from the scandal lasted for months.
Scientists measured fallout in the soil near the test site.
etymology: From fall + out, first used of radioactive debris in the 1950s.

definition: Left unplanted to recover, or inactive for a time.
examples: The farmer let the north field lie fallow for a year.
After a fallow period, her creativity came roaring back.
etymology: From Old English fealgian, 'to break up land for sowing'.

definition: To alter information or documents in order to deceive; also to prove false.
examples: The lab was caught trying to falsify its test results.
A single counterexample is enough to falsify the theory.
etymology: From Medieval Latin falsificare, from Latin falsus 'false'.

definition: To lose strength or momentum, or to speak or move hesitantly.
examples: Sales began to falter once the novelty of the app wore off.
He saw her voice falter as she reached the hardest part of the speech.
etymology: From Middle English, of uncertain origin.

definition: A person with extreme, uncritical enthusiasm for a cause or hobby.
examples: My uncle is a baseball fanatic who never misses a game.
A fanatic will not listen to any argument against his beliefs.
etymology: From Latin fanaticus 'inspired by a god', from fanum 'temple'.

definition: Imaginative but unrealistic; or decorated in an unusual, whimsical way.
examples: The idea of retiring at thirty seemed fanciful.
The cake was topped with fanciful sugar flowers.
etymology: From fancy, a contraction of fantasy, + -ful.

definition: A showy display or celebration that draws attention to something.
examples: The new library opened with little fanfare on a rainy Tuesday.
Trumpets played a short fanfare as the graduates walked in.
etymology: From French fanfare, probably imitative of the sound of trumpets.

definition: Arrogant boasting or bragging.
examples: The general's fanfaronade did not hide his poor strategy.
Beneath the fanfaronade, he was deeply insecure.
etymology: From French fanfaronnade, from fanfaron 'braggart', from Spanish fanfarrón.

definition: Shy and sullen, or wild and unsociable.
examples: The farouche young poet barely spoke at the dinner.
Her farouche manner hid a warm heart.
etymology: From French farouche 'wild, shy', from Late Latin forasticus 'living out of doors'.

definition: A confused mixture or jumble.
examples: The report was a farrago of half-truths and wild guesses.
His excuse was such a farrago that nobody bothered to argue.
etymology: From Latin farrago, 'mixed fodder', from far, 'grain'.

definition: Very careful about details and difficult to please.
examples: The fastidious editor checked every comma twice before finally approving the book for print.
She is fastidious about keeping her desk perfectly organized, down to the last paper clip.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus, 'disdainful', from fastidium 'loathing'.

definition: To understand something difficult after much thought.
examples: I can't fathom why anyone would wake up at 4 a.m. for fun.
It's hard to fathom how big the universe is.
etymology: From Old English fæthm, 'outstretched arms', later a unit for measuring water depth.

definition: Prophetic; concerned with foretelling fate.
examples: The old woman's fatidic warnings haunted the village.
There was something fatidic about that strange dream.
etymology: From Latin fatidicus, from fatum 'fate' + dicere 'to say'.

definition: Silly and pointless, showing a lack of thought or intelligence.
examples: His fatuous remarks at the meeting wasted everyone's time and lowered their patience.
She wore a fatuous grin while delivering the worst news of the quarter.
etymology: From Latin fatuus, 'foolish, silly'.

definition: To flatter someone excessively to win favor.
examples: Reporters began to fawn over the young star.
I won't fawn over the boss just to get a raise.
etymology: From Old English fagnian 'to rejoice', related to fain.

definition: Loyalty sworn to a lord or ruler; faithfulness.
examples: The knights swore fealty to their new king.
Party members were expected to show fealty to the leader.
etymology: From Old French feaulte, from Latin fidelitas 'faithfulness'.

definition: Possible to do or achieve in a practical way.
examples: Is it feasible to finish the whole project by the end of the month?
Engineers found a feasible way to bring clean water to the village.
etymology: From Old French faisable, 'doable', from faire 'to do', from Latin facere.

definition: An achievement that takes great skill, courage, or strength.
examples: Finishing the marathon on a broken toe was quite a feat.
Getting three toddlers to nap at the same time is no small feat.
etymology: From Old French fait, from Latin factum 'a thing done'.

definition: Feverish, or marked by intense nervous excitement.
examples: The final days of the campaign had a febrile energy.
A febrile crowd waited outside the store for the launch.
etymology: From Latin febris, 'fever'.

definition: Lacking initiative or responsibility; weak and ineffective.
examples: The feckless manager forgot meetings and blamed his staff for the chaos.
She was tired of her feckless brother borrowing money and never repaying it.
etymology: From Scots feck, 'effect, value', shortened from effect, plus -less.

definition: Highly fertile; able to produce abundant growth, offspring, or ideas.
examples: The river valley's fecund soil made it the region's best farmland.
She had a fecund imagination that produced a new story idea each morning.
etymology: From Latin fecundus, 'fruitful'.

definition: To pretend to feel or have something.
examples: She tried to feign surprise at the party.
Don't feign interest if you're bored.
etymology: From Old French feindre, from Latin fingere 'to form, contrive'.

definition: Lively, determined, and ready to argue or fight.
examples: The feisty little terrier barked at every passing truck.
She gave a feisty speech defending the local library.
etymology: From US dialect feist 'small dog'.

definition: Producing or aiming at happiness.
examples: Utilitarians judge acts by their felicific consequences.
The festival was designed with a purely felicific purpose.
etymology: From Latin felix 'happy' + -ficus 'making'; known from the 'felicific calculus' of utilitarian ethics.

definition: Well chosen or suited to the occasion; pleasing and fortunate.
examples: Her toast included a felicitous quote about friendship.
The pairing of spicy food and cold cider was felicitous.
etymology: From Latin felicitas, 'happiness', from felix, 'happy'.

definition: Great happiness; also a skill for finding the right words.
examples: They wished the couple lifelong felicity.
She writes with a felicity of phrase that few can match.
etymology: From Latin felicitas, from felix 'happy, lucky'.

definition: The arrangement of windows in a building.
examples: The architect praised the building's elegant fenestration.
Poor fenestration left the hallway dark all day.
etymology: From Latin fenestra 'window'.

definition: Wild, especially after escaping from domestication.
examples: Feral cats roam the abandoned lot.
The kids were feral by the last week of summer.
etymology: From Latin fera 'wild animal'.

definition: Savagely fierce, violent, or intense.
examples: A ferocious storm knocked out power across the county.
The two teams have a ferocious rivalry.
etymology: From Latin ferox 'fierce'.

definition: To search persistently for something, usually used with 'out'.
examples: Good reporters ferret out the facts officials want hidden.
It took an hour to ferret through the drawers for the receipt.
etymology: From the animal ferret, used to drive rabbits from burrows, from Latin fur 'thief'.

definition: Containing iron, or having the reddish-brown color of rust.
examples: The cliffs glowed with ferruginous streaks at sunset.
The spring water had a ferruginous taste.
etymology: From Latin ferrugo 'rust', from ferrum 'iron'.

definition: Showing very strong, passionate, and sincere feeling.
examples: She is a fervent supporter of the local team and never misses a game.
They made a fervent plea for help as the flood waters rose.
etymology: From Latin fervens, 'boiling, glowing', from fervere 'to boil'.

definition: Intensely enthusiastic or passionate, sometimes excessively.
examples: The rally drew a fervid crowd of supporters.
His fervid imagination filled notebooks with stories.
etymology: From Latin fervidus, from fervere 'to boil'.

definition: To decorate lavishly with chains of flowers, ribbons, or lights.
examples: Neighbors festoon their porches with lights every December.
Fans festoon the stadium in team colors.
etymology: From French feston, from Italian festone, from festa 'feast'.

definition: Smelling extremely unpleasant.
examples: A fetid smell came from the blocked drain.
The swamp's fetid air made us gag.
etymology: From Latin fetidus, from fetere 'to stink'.

definition: To restrict someone's freedom, originally with chains on the feet.
examples: Outdated rules fetter innovation at the company.
Artists should not let fear of criticism fetter them.
etymology: From Old English feter 'shackle', related to foot.

definition: Condition or state of health and spirits, usually in the phrase 'in fine fettle'.
examples: Grandpa was in fine fettle at his ninetieth birthday.
The team arrived in good fettle for the final.
etymology: From Middle English fettel 'to make ready', perhaps from Old English fetel 'belt'.

definition: A long, bitter quarrel between people, families, or groups.
examples: The two families have had a feud over the fence for decades.
Their online feud grew uglier with every post.
etymology: From Old French feide, of Germanic origin and related to foe.

definition: Strange and otherworldly; also, in older use, fated to die.
examples: The singer had a fey, dreamy quality on stage.
In the old ballad, the warrior grows fey before his last battle.
etymology: From Old English fæge 'doomed to die'.

definition: A complete and often embarrassing failure.
examples: The product launch turned into a fiasco when the website crashed.
Our attempt at a homemade wedding cake was a total fiasco.
etymology: From Italian fiasco 'bottle', via the phrase far fiasco 'to make a bottle', meaning to fail.

definition: An official order or decision issued by authority, often without consultation.
examples: The new policy was imposed by executive fiat.
Prices cannot be fixed by fiat forever.
etymology: From Latin fiat 'let it be done'.

definition: Changing often and unpredictably, especially in loyalty or affection.
examples: The fickle crowd cheered him one week and booed him loudly the next.
Spring weather in the mountains is famously fickle, so pack for both sun and snow.
etymology: From Old English ficol, 'deceitful, treacherous'.

definition: Faithfulness and loyalty; also accuracy in copying or reproducing something.
examples: The translation is praised for its fidelity to the original.
Her fidelity to old friends never wavered.
etymology: From Latin fidelitas, from fides 'faith'.

definition: To make small restless movements, usually from nervousness or boredom.
examples: Kids tend to fidget during long church services.
He began to fidget with his pen as the interview went on.
etymology: From the obsolete verb fidge 'to twitch'.

definition: Involving trust, especially the duty to manage money or property for another person.
examples: Trustees have a fiduciary duty to act in the beneficiaries' interest.
The advisor was sued for breaching her fiduciary obligations.
etymology: From Latin fiduciarius, from fiducia 'trust'.

definition: Extremely cruel, or extremely clever and complicated.
examples: The puzzle was fiendish, and nobody solved it.
The villain hatched a fiendish plot.
etymology: From fiend, from Old English feond 'enemy', + -ish.

definition: Something that exists only in the imagination.
examples: The noise in the attic was a figment of your imagination.
The promised bonus turned out to be a figment.
etymology: From Latin figmentum, from fingere 'to form, contrive'.

definition: Using words in a non-literal, metaphorical way.
examples: 'Drowning in paperwork' is a figurative expression.
The museum has mostly figurative paintings of people.
etymology: From Late Latin figurativus, from figura 'shape, figure'.

definition: A person who holds a title but has no real power.
examples: The chairman is a figurehead; the real decisions happen elsewhere.
Many modern monarchs serve mainly as a national figurehead.
etymology: Originally the carved figure on the prow of a ship.

definition: To steal something small or of little value, casually.
examples: Kids used to filch candy from the corner shop.
Someone tried to filch my pen during the meeting.
etymology: From Middle English filchen, of unknown origin.

definition: Relating to or befitting a son or daughter.
examples: He visited his mother every Sunday out of filial devotion.
Confucian ethics place great weight on filial piety.
etymology: From Latin filius 'son' and filia 'daughter'.

definition: A long speech or tactic used to delay or block a vote in a legislature.
examples: The senator launched a filibuster that lasted all night.
Reformers want to end the filibuster entirely.
etymology: From Spanish filibustero, from Dutch vrijbuiter 'freebooter, pirate'.

definition: Delicate ornamental work of fine twisted wire; any delicate tracery.
examples: The necklace was made of silver filigree.
Frost left a filigree of ice on the window.
etymology: From earlier filigreen, from Italian filigrana, from Latin filum 'thread' + granum 'seed'.

definition: Something that adds stimulus or excitement; a boost.
examples: The tax cut gave a fillip to holiday spending.
A squeeze of lime adds a fillip of flavor.
etymology: Probably imitative; originally a flick of the finger against the thumb.

definition: To obtain something through cleverness or trickery.
examples: He managed to finagle two extra tickets to the show.
She will finagle a way out of jury duty somehow.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from English dialect fainaigue 'to cheat'.

definition: Skill and delicacy in handling something.
examples: She handled the angry customer with real finesse.
The chef plated each dessert with remarkable finesse.
etymology: From French finesse, 'fineness, delicacy', from fin 'fine'.

definition: Fussy and hard to please, or requiring great attention to detail.
examples: My cat is finicky and refuses any food but salmon.
Setting up the old printer is a finicky job.
etymology: From finical 'overly particular', probably from fine.

definition: Having limits or bounds; not endless.
examples: We have a finite amount of money left for the trip.
Fossil fuels are a finite resource that will eventually run out.
etymology: From Latin finitus, past participle of finire 'to finish'.

definition: The sky or the heavens; also a sphere of influence.
examples: Stars glittered across the firmament.
She is a rising star in the literary firmament.
etymology: From Latin firmamentum, from firmare 'to strengthen'.

definition: Relating to government revenue or financial matters.
examples: The fiscal year for the company ends in June.
Lawmakers argued over fiscal policy late into the night.
etymology: From Latin fiscus 'purse, treasury'.

definition: Able to be split, especially of rock or of atoms in nuclear fission.
examples: Uranium-235 is a fissile material.
The slate is fissile and breaks into thin sheets.
etymology: From Latin fissilis, from findere 'to split'.

definition: Inclined to split into separate parts or factions.
examples: The fissiparous club split into three rival groups.
Rock bands can be notoriously fissiparous.
etymology: From Latin fissus 'split' + parere 'to bear'.

definition: In an irregular, interrupted way.
examples: I slept fitfully the night before the exam.
The old engine ran fitfully and then died.
etymology: From fitful, from fit 'a sudden bout' + -ful.

definition: To focus obsessively on one thing.
examples: Try not to fixate on the one bad review among a hundred good ones.
Toddlers often fixate on a single favorite toy for weeks.
etymology: From fix + -ate, ultimately from Latin fixus 'fixed'.

definition: Soft and limp; also lacking force or energy.
examples: The balloons were flaccid by the next morning.
Critics called the sequel a flaccid imitation of the original.
etymology: From Latin flaccidus, from flaccus 'flabby'.

definition: To whip or flog, often as religious penance; figuratively, to punish harshly.
examples: Medieval penitents would flagellate themselves in public.
There's no need to flagellate yourself over one mistake.
etymology: From Latin flagellare 'to whip', from flagellum 'whip'.

definition: Becoming tired, weaker, or less effective.
examples: A cup of coffee revived my flagging energy.
The ad campaign aimed to boost flagging sales.
etymology: From the verb flag 'to droop, become feeble'.

definition: Extremely wicked or criminal.
examples: The historian catalogued the tyrant's flagitious deeds.
No excuse can soften such a flagitious betrayal.
etymology: From Latin flagitiosus, from flagitium 'shameful crime'.

definition: Shockingly obvious and done openly without shame.
examples: The referee ejected him from the game immediately for a flagrant foul on the goalkeeper.
It was a flagrant violation of the privacy rules, and nobody tried to hide it.
etymology: From Latin flagrare, 'to blaze, burn', so 'blazing' into view.

definition: The best or most important product, store, or item in a group.
examples: The company opened its flagship store on Fifth Avenue.
This phone is the brand's flagship, packed with every new feature.
etymology: Originally the ship carrying the flag of a fleet's commander.

definition: To wave or swing wildly; also to struggle without direction.
examples: The toddler began to flail when we took away his toy.
Without a plan, new managers often flail.
etymology: From the noun flail, a threshing tool, from Latin flagellum 'whip'.

definition: A natural talent or stylish, distinctive quality.
examples: She has a real flair for turning leftovers into great meals.
The designer added some flair to the plain office with bold rugs.
etymology: From French flair 'sense of smell', from flairer 'to smell'.

definition: Showy, bold, and attracting attention.
examples: The singer was known for his flamboyant costumes.
Her flamboyant handwriting filled half the card.
etymology: From French flamboyant 'flaming', first used of a Gothic architectural style with flame-like tracery.

definition: A person who strolls idly around a city, observing its life.
examples: He became a flaneur of Paris, wandering the arcades for hours.
Every flaneur needs comfortable shoes and no schedule.
etymology: From French flâneur, from flâner 'to stroll, lounge'.

definition: To be positioned at both sides of something or someone.
examples: Two tall oaks flank the front door of the old house.
Bodyguards flank the senator wherever she goes.
etymology: From the noun flank, from Old French flanc 'side'.

definition: Foolish talk; utter nonsense.
examples: The salesman's pitch was pure flapdoodle.
Don't believe that flapdoodle about miracle diets.
etymology: A fanciful coinage first recorded in the 19th century.

definition: To show off something in a way meant to impress others.
examples: He likes to flaunt his new car in front of the neighbors.
If you trained that hard for those muscles, go ahead and flaunt them.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: To strip the skin off; also to criticize harshly.
examples: Critics will flay the director for this sequel.
Hunters flay the animal before cooking it.
etymology: From Old English flean 'to skin'.

definition: A young bird just learning to fly, or anything new and inexperienced.
examples: The startup was still a fledgling when the big investors arrived.
A fledgling hopped across the lawn, testing its wings.
etymology: From fledge 'to grow feathers' + the diminutive suffix -ling.

definition: Lasting only a very short time.
examples: We caught a fleeting glimpse of the whale before it dove.
Fame on social media is usually fleeting.
etymology: From fleet 'to pass swiftly', from Old English fleotan 'to float'.

definition: A frivolous, flighty, overly talkative person.
examples: She was no flibbertigibbet; she ran the company with an iron hand.
The play's comic relief is a flibbertigibbet of a maid.
etymology: Probably imitative of meaningless chatter; recorded in Middle English as flepergebet.

definition: Weak, thin, or easily broken; also unconvincing.
examples: That flimsy umbrella turned inside out in the first gust.
The judge rejected his flimsy excuse for missing court.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the early 18th century.

definition: To make a quick, involuntary movement from pain or fear.
examples: She didn't flinch when the nurse gave her the shot.
A good negotiator won't flinch at a high opening offer.
etymology: From Old French flenchir 'to turn aside'.

definition: Not showing proper seriousness or respect.
examples: His flippant reply to the complaint made things worse.
Don't be flippant about a friend's illness.
etymology: From flip + -ant, originally meaning 'nimble, talkative'.

definition: Woolly or fluffy, like tufts of wool.
examples: Flocculent clouds drifted across the summer sky.
A flocculent mold grew on the forgotten bread.
etymology: From Latin floccus 'tuft of wool'.

definition: Overly elaborate or ornate; also reddish in complexion.
examples: The speech was full of florid language and empty promises.
His florid face grew redder as he argued.
etymology: From Latin floridus 'flowery', from flos 'flower'.

definition: A collection of literary extracts; an anthology.
examples: The monk compiled a florilegium of sayings from the Church Fathers.
Her commonplace book became a florilegium of favorite lines.
etymology: From Latin flos 'flower' + legere 'to gather', modeled on Greek anthologia.

definition: The period during which a person whose dates are uncertain was active.
examples: The scribe's floruit is placed around 1150.
Scholars disagree about the poet's floruit.
etymology: From Latin floruit 'he or she flourished', from florere 'to flourish'.

definition: Floating wreckage, or odds and ends of little value.
examples: Flotsam from the shipwreck washed up for weeks.
The attic was full of the flotsam of three generations.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from floter 'to float'.

definition: To move in an exaggerated way that shows annoyance.
examples: She liked to flounce out of the room whenever she lost an argument.
Don't flounce off just because you didn't get your way.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly Scandinavian.

definition: To struggle clumsily or be confused about what to do.
examples: Without clear instructions, new hires tend to flounder for weeks.
I watched him flounder through questions he had not prepared for.
etymology: Possibly a blend of founder and blunder.

definition: To grow or develop successfully and vigorously.
examples: Tomatoes flourish in full sun.
Small businesses flourished after the new bridge opened.
etymology: From Old French florir, from Latin florere 'to bloom'.

definition: To openly disregard a rule, law, or convention.
examples: Some drivers flout the speed limit near the school.
The designer loves to flout fashion conventions.
etymology: Probably from Dutch fluiten, 'to whistle, hiss at'.

definition: To rise and fall irregularly in amount or level.
examples: Prices for fresh fruit tend to fluctuate with the seasons.
Her mood fluctuated wildly during exam week.
etymology: From Latin fluctuare, 'to move like a wave', from fluctus 'wave'.

definition: A lucky or unusual event that happens by chance.
examples: Was his perfect score a fluke, or is he really that good at chess?
The team's first win looked like a fluke, but they kept on winning.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first used in the 19th century for a lucky shot in billiards.

definition: Empty flattery or meaningless nonsense; originally a sweet pudding.
examples: Ignore the flummery in the press release.
His toast was flowery flummery with no real feeling.
etymology: From Welsh llymru, a soft dish made from oatmeal.

definition: To confuse or bewilder completely.
examples: The riddle seemed to flummox even the adults.
Simple tax forms still flummox me every year.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, probably from English dialect; first recorded in the 19th century.

definition: A sudden short burst of activity, or a light fall of snow.
examples: The announcement set off a flurry of phone calls.
A flurry of snow drifted past the window.
etymology: Probably imitative, from the obsolete verb flurr 'to fly up'.

definition: To make someone nervous or confused.
examples: Hecklers tried to fluster the comedian, but she stayed calm.
Don't let the ticking clock fluster you during the exam.
etymology: Probably of Scandinavian origin.

definition: Continuous change or flow.
examples: The industry is in a state of flux.
Plans are in flux until the budget is approved.
etymology: From Latin fluxus, from fluere 'to flow'.

definition: Central or most important; relating to a focus.
examples: The fireplace is the focal point of the living room.
Climate policy became a focal issue in the election.
etymology: From focus, from Latin focus 'hearth'.

definition: Food for livestock, or material used to supply something.
examples: The awkward interview became fodder for late-night comedians.
Farmers stored hay as fodder for the winter.
etymology: From Old English fodor, related to food.

definition: A minor weakness or eccentricity in someone's character.
examples: Her habit of alphabetizing the spice rack is a harmless foible.
Good friends forgive each other's foibles.
etymology: From obsolete French foible, 'weak', the weaker part of a sword blade.

definition: To prevent someone or something from succeeding.
examples: A sharp-eyed cashier helped foil the robbery.
Heavy rain managed to foil our plans for a picnic.
etymology: From Middle English, originally meaning 'to trample', probably from Old French.

definition: To impose something unwanted on someone.
examples: Don't foist your chores on your little brother.
The vendor tried to foist a cheap copy on us.
etymology: From Dutch dialect vuisten 'to take in the hand', originally used of palming a loaded die.

definition: Foolish talk or nonsense; also a useless trinket.
examples: Skip the folderol and tell me what happened.
The drawer was full of souvenirs and folderol.
etymology: From a meaningless refrain in old songs.

definition: Informal, friendly, and down-to-earth in manner.
examples: The candidate's folksy charm won over rural voters.
The café has a folksy feel with quilts on the walls.
etymology: From folk + -sy, first recorded in American English.

definition: Foolishness, or a foolish action or idea.
examples: It would be folly to hike that trail without water.
The tower was a rich man's folly that served no purpose.
etymology: From Old French folie 'madness', from fol 'fool'.

definition: To stir up trouble, rebellion, or discord.
examples: Agitators tried to foment unrest among the workers.
Rumors can foment distrust in a small town.
etymology: From Late Latin fomentare, from fomentum 'poultice', from fovere 'to warm'.

definition: A great fuss over something trivial; also showy finery.
examples: There was a big foofaraw about who sat at the head table.
The costume was all feathers and foofaraw.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in American English.

definition: Recklessly bold.
examples: It was foolhardy to sail into the storm.
A foolhardy investor bet everything on one stock.
etymology: From Old French fol hardi 'foolishly bold'.

definition: A secure position from which to make further progress.
examples: The brand gained a foothold in Asia with one popular product.
The climber searched the rock for a foothold.
etymology: From foot + hold.

definition: Excessively concerned with fashion and appearance.
examples: The foppish young lord wore lace cuffs to the hunt.
His foppish manners amused the farmhands.
etymology: From fop 'a vain dandy', originally meaning 'fool', + -ish.

definition: To search widely for food or supplies.
examples: Bears forage for berries all summer before hibernating.
We had to forage in the back of the fridge for something to eat.
etymology: From Old French fourrage, from fuerre 'fodder', of Germanic origin.

definition: A brief venture or attempt into a new activity or area.
examples: The novelist's first foray into film was surprisingly successful.
Our foray into the night market ended with too many dumplings.
etymology: From Middle English forrayen, 'to pillage', from Old French forrier, 'forager'.

definition: Patient self-control and restraint, especially in the face of provocation.
examples: The teacher showed great forbearance with the restless class.
The bank offered forbearance on loan payments during the crisis.
etymology: From Old English forberan, 'to bear, endure', + -ance.

definition: A feeling that something bad is going to happen.
examples: She was filled with foreboding as the storm clouds gathered.
A sense of foreboding hung over the empty house.
etymology: From forebode, from fore- + bode 'to portend'.

definition: Most important or leading; first in position.
examples: She is one of the foremost experts on bird migration.
Safety is our foremost concern on the job site.
etymology: From Old English formest 'first'.

definition: Relating to scientific methods used to investigate crimes; also relating to courts or debate.
examples: Forensic experts examined the fingerprints.
The audit was a forensic look at every expense.
etymology: From Latin forensis 'of the forum, public', from forum.

definition: To determine or decree in advance.
examples: No leader can foreordain the outcome of a war.
Some believe fate will foreordain every turn of our lives.
etymology: From fore- + ordain.

definition: A person or thing that comes before and paves the way for another.
examples: The telegraph was a forerunner of the internet.
Those early protests were a forerunner of the larger movement.
etymology: From fore- + runner.

definition: The ability to predict and prepare for what will happen in the future.
examples: Thanks to her foresight, we packed umbrellas before the storm hit.
The city showed foresight by planting shade trees decades ago.
etymology: From fore 'before' + sight.

definition: To prevent or obstruct something by acting ahead of time.
examples: She answered the obvious questions early to forestall any objections.
Regular maintenance can forestall costly repairs.
etymology: From Old English foresteall, 'an ambush, intervention'.

definition: To lose or give up something as a penalty.
examples: If you cancel late, you forfeit your deposit.
The team had to forfeit the game after failing to show up.
etymology: From Old French forfet 'crime', from forfaire 'to transgress'.

definition: To prevent or ward off; used mostly in the phrase 'heaven forfend'.
examples: Heaven forfend that we should arrive late to Grandma's dinner.
He took every precaution to forfend disaster.
etymology: From for- + fend, a shortening of defend.

definition: To choose to go without something.
examples: We'll forgo dessert tonight since we had cake at lunch.
Many students forgo sleep before exams.
etymology: From Old English forgan, 'to pass over', from for- + gan 'to go'.

definition: Sad and lonely, or unlikely to succeed.
examples: A forlorn puppy sat at the shelter's gate.
They made a forlorn attempt to save the factory.
etymology: From Old English forloren, past participle of forleosan 'to lose'.

definition: Having a strong influence on development, especially early in life.
examples: She spent her formative years in Kenya.
That first job was a formative experience.
etymology: From French formatif, from Latin formare 'to form'.

definition: Inspiring respect or fear because of size, power, or skill.
examples: She is a formidable opponent in any debate.
The climbers faced a formidable wall of ice.
etymology: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare 'to fear'.

definition: Following a predictable pattern, lacking originality.
examples: The romance novel was entertaining but formulaic.
Her emails are formulaic and impersonal.
etymology: From formula + -ic.

definition: To abandon or give up someone or something.
examples: He refused to forsake his friends when times got hard.
Few people will forsake comfort for a principle.
etymology: From Old English forsacan 'to renounce, refuse'.

definition: To solemnly give up or renounce something.
examples: He vowed to forswear alcohol for a year.
The rebels agreed to forswear violence.
etymology: From Old English forswerian.

definition: Something a person is especially good at.
examples: Cooking isn't my forte, but I make a decent omelet.
Public speaking was always her forte.
etymology: From French fort, 'strong'.

definition: About to happen or appear; also willing to share information.
examples: Details of the merger will be published in a forthcoming report.
The witness was not very forthcoming about where he had been.
etymology: From forth + coming.

definition: Direct and outspoken; saying plainly what one thinks.
examples: My grandmother was forthright about her opinions on my haircut.
We appreciated the manager's forthright explanation of the layoffs.
etymology: From Old English forthriht 'straight forward'.

definition: Immediately; without delay.
examples: The order takes effect forthwith.
Please return the borrowed keys forthwith.
etymology: From Middle English forth + with.

definition: To strengthen something, especially against attack.
examples: Villagers worked through the night to fortify the riverbank with sandbags.
A big breakfast will fortify you for the long hike.
etymology: From Latin fortis 'strong' + facere 'to make', via French fortifier.

definition: Courage and strength of mind in the face of pain or hardship.
examples: She faced her long recovery with quiet fortitude and never once complained to her nurses.
It took real fortitude to start over in a new country without family nearby.
etymology: From Latin fortitudo, 'strength', from fortis 'strong'.

definition: Happening by lucky chance, usually with a pleasant result.
examples: A fortuitous meeting at the airport led to their business partnership.
It was fortuitous that the plumber lived next door when the pipe burst.
etymology: From Latin fortuitus, 'happening by chance', from fors 'chance'.

definition: To encourage the growth or development of something over time.
examples: Good teachers foster curiosity by welcoming every question.
The festival aims to foster understanding between neighboring communities.
etymology: From Old English fostrian, 'to nourish, bring up', related to foda, 'food'.

definition: To fail or collapse; originally, of a ship, to fill with water and sink.
examples: The talks began to founder over the issue of land.
Small boats founder quickly in heavy seas.
etymology: From Old French fondrer 'to submerge, collapse', from Latin fundus 'bottom'.

definition: A noisy disturbance or quarrel.
examples: Police broke up a fracas outside the stadium.
The fracas in the comment section went on for days.
etymology: From French fracas, from Italian fracasso, from fracassare 'to make an uproar'.

definition: Irritable and quarrelsome; hard to control.
examples: The fractious toddler refused to nap.
A fractious meeting ended without a vote.
etymology: From fraction in the obsolete sense 'discord'.

definition: Weak and delicate, especially from age or illness.
examples: My frail grandfather still insists on walking to the store.
The economy remains frail after the recession.
etymology: From Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis 'fragile'.

definition: Fragile; easily broken.
examples: Pack the frangible ornaments in bubble wrap.
Their frangible truce lasted only a week.
etymology: From medieval Latin frangibilis, from frangere, 'to break'.

definition: Honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: Let me be frank: the proposal needs a lot more work.
They had a frank conversation about money before moving in together.
etymology: From Old French franc 'free', from Latin Francus 'a Frank'.

definition: To associate in a friendly way, especially with people one is expected to avoid.
examples: Officers were told not to fraternize with the enemy.
Managers shouldn't fraternize too closely with their staff.
etymology: From French fraterniser, from Latin frater 'brother'.

definition: Obtained or done by deception, especially criminally.
examples: The bank flagged several fraudulent charges on my card.
He made fraudulent claims about his qualifications.
etymology: From Latin fraudulentus, from fraus 'deceit'.

definition: Filled with something undesirable, or causing anxiety.
examples: The negotiations were fraught with tension.
It was a fraught week, with two deadlines and a sick child.
etymology: From Middle Dutch vrachten, 'to load', from vracht, 'freight'.

definition: A pirate or lawless adventurer who seeks plunder.
examples: The coast was once a haunt for every freebooter in the Caribbean.
Critics called the hedge-fund manager a modern freebooter.
etymology: From Dutch vrijbuiter, from vrij 'free' + buit 'booty'.

definition: Fast, energetic, and uncontrolled.
examples: The kitchen is frenetic during the dinner rush.
The film moves at a frenetic pace.
etymology: From Old French frenetique, from Greek phrenitis 'delirium'.

definition: A state of wild, uncontrolled excitement or activity.
examples: The holiday sale sent shoppers into a frenzy.
Sharks circled in a feeding frenzy around the bait.
etymology: From Old French frenesie, from Greek phrenitis 'delirium', from phren 'mind'.

definition: A sudden rise or flood of a river from heavy rain or melting snow.
examples: The spring freshet swept away the old footbridge.
A freshet of new ideas revived the magazine.
etymology: From fresh, probably via Old French freschete.

definition: A frivolous, trifling person.
examples: He was a fribble who spent his inheritance on hats.
The novel mocks every fribble at court.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to frivol.

definition: Conflict or disagreement between people; also resistance when surfaces rub.
examples: There was some friction between the two departments over the budget.
Friction between the tires and the road keeps the car from sliding.
etymology: From Latin frictio, from fricare 'to rub'.

definition: The outer edge of something, or a group with extreme views.
examples: Those ideas were once on the fringe but are now mainstream.
The lamp had a silk fringe around its shade.
etymology: From Old French frenge, from Latin fimbria 'border'.

definition: Showy, unnecessary ornament or trivial things.
examples: The minimalist apartment had no frippery at all.
She dismissed the gala as expensive frippery.
etymology: From French friperie 'secondhand clothes', from Old French frepe 'rag'.

definition: A sudden thrill of excitement or emotion.
examples: A frisson of anticipation ran through the crowd as the lights dimmed.
She felt a frisson of fear when the door creaked open.
etymology: From French frisson, 'a shiver, thrill'.

definition: Not serious or sensible; silly or of little real value.
examples: He spent his bonus on frivolous gadgets he never used.
The judge dismissed the frivolous lawsuit within minutes, calling it a waste of court time.
etymology: From Latin frivolus, 'silly, worthless'.

definition: A border between countries, or the outer limit of what is known.
examples: Gene editing is a new frontier in medicine.
Guards checked every truck crossing the frontier.
etymology: From Old French frontiere, from front 'front'.

definition: Stubbornly contrary and disobedient.
examples: The froward child refused every meal on principle.
Proverbs warns against the froward heart.
etymology: From Old English fromweard 'turned away'.

definition: Scruffy, neglected, and dingy.
examples: He arrived in a frowzy sweater with holes in the elbows.
The frowzy motel room smelled of old smoke.
etymology: Of unknown origin.

definition: To bear fruit or become productive.
examples: Years of research began to fructify in a series of discoveries.
With rain, the orchard will fructify again.
etymology: From Latin fructificare, from fructus 'fruit'.

definition: Careful about spending money and avoiding waste.
examples: Growing up poor made her frugal, and she still reuses every jar.
A frugal traveler, he packed his own lunches and stayed in hostels.
etymology: From Latin frugalis, 'economical', from frugi 'useful, thrifty'.

definition: Producing good or useful results.
examples: It was a fruitful meeting, and we left with a clear plan.
The partnership proved fruitful for both companies.
etymology: From fruit + -ful.

definition: The realization or fulfillment of a plan or project.
examples: After ten years, her dream of opening a clinic came to fruition.
The garden's design reached full fruition in its third summer.
etymology: From Old French fruition, from Latin frui, 'to enjoy'.

definition: Failing to achieve the desired result; useless.
examples: After a fruitless search, we found the keys in my coat.
Arguing with him about politics is fruitless.
etymology: From fruit + -less.

definition: A warm, stuffy, smoky atmosphere in a closed room.
examples: We stepped out of the fug of the pub into the cold night.
A fug of cigar smoke hung over the card table.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first recorded in the 19th century.

definition: Fleeting; lasting only a short time.
examples: The fugacious bloom of the cactus lasts a single night.
Youth, the poet warns, is fugacious.
etymology: From Latin fugax 'fleeing', from fugere 'to flee'.

definition: The point on which a lever turns; also the central thing on which a situation depends.
examples: The swing state became the fulcrum of the election.
Move the fulcrum closer to the rock to lift it more easily.
etymology: From Latin fulcrum 'bedpost, support', from fulcire 'to prop up'.

definition: Shining brightly; dazzling.
examples: A fulgent moon rose over the bay.
The ballroom was fulgent with chandeliers.
etymology: From Latin fulgent-, from fulgere 'to shine'.

definition: Sooty or dusky in color; murky.
examples: Fuliginous smoke poured from the factory chimneys.
The painter favored a fuliginous palette of browns and grays.
etymology: From Latin fuligo 'soot'.

definition: To protest loudly and angrily.
examples: He would fulminate against slow drivers every morning.
Editorials fulminated about the rise in bus fares.
etymology: From Latin fulminare, from fulmen, 'lightning'.

definition: Excessively flattering or effusive, to the point of seeming insincere.
examples: The senator's fulsome praise for the donors made the whole room cringe.
I distrust fulsome compliments from people who stand to gain something from me.
etymology: From Middle English ful 'full' + -some; it originally meant abundant, later 'excessive' and insincere.

definition: To handle something clumsily or awkwardly.
examples: I watched him fumble with his keys in the rain.
Don't fumble the handoff on the last play of the game.
etymology: Probably from Low German or Dutch.

definition: A tightrope walker.
examples: A funambulist crossed the gorge on a single cable.
In politics she was a funambulist, balancing every faction.
etymology: From Latin funis 'rope' + ambulare 'to walk'.

definition: Gloomy and solemn, as at a funeral.
examples: The office had a funereal mood after the layoffs.
He spoke in a funereal tone about the election results.
etymology: From Latin funereus, from funus 'funeral'.

definition: Interchangeable with another thing of the same kind.
examples: Money is fungible, so it doesn't matter which bill you spend.
Workers are not fungible parts in a machine.
etymology: From Medieval Latin fungibilis, from Latin fungi 'to perform', in the sense 'to serve in place of'.

definition: A showy ruffle or ornament on clothing; any fussy decoration.
examples: The gown had a furbelow of lace at every hem.
Her prose is free of every unnecessary furbelow.
etymology: An alteration of French falbala 'flounce'.

definition: A temporary leave of absence, especially unpaid leave from work or leave from military duty.
examples: Thousands of workers were placed on furlough during the shutdown.
The soldier came home on furlough.
etymology: From Dutch verlof 'leave, permission'.

definition: To provide something needed, or to supply a room with furniture.
examples: Please furnish a copy of your ID with the application.
It cost a fortune to furnish the new apartment.
etymology: From Old French furnir 'to provide', of Germanic origin.

definition: An outbreak of public anger or excitement.
examples: The new logo caused a furor among longtime fans.
The furor over the tax hike faded after a few weeks.
etymology: From Latin furor 'madness', from furere 'to rage'.

definition: Attempting to avoid notice, typically because of guilt.
examples: He cast a furtive glance at his phone during the meeting.
The kids made furtive trips to the cookie jar.
etymology: From Latin furtivus, from furtum, 'theft'.

definition: In a secretive way, trying not to be noticed.
examples: He furtively checked his phone during the meeting.
The squirrel furtively buried an acorn under the porch.
etymology: From Latin furtivus, from furtum 'theft'.

definition: A rapid series of shots, or a rapid outburst of criticism or questions.
examples: The minister faced a fusillade of questions from reporters.
A fusillade of gunfire echoed through the valley.
etymology: From French fusillade, from fusiller 'to shoot', from fusil 'musket'.

definition: Pompous, inflated speech or writing.
examples: Beneath the fustian of his speech, there was hardly an idea at all.
Critics mocked the novel's fustian and its endless adjectives.
etymology: From Old French fustaigne, a coarse cloth, probably named after Fustat near Cairo.

definition: To beat with a stick; to criticize severely.
examples: The columnist loved to fustigate lazy politicians.
Old schoolmasters would fustigate unruly pupils.
etymology: From Late Latin fustigare 'to cudgel', from fustis 'stick'.

definition: Smelling stale and musty; also old-fashioned.
examples: The fusty attic smelled of mothballs.
The museum shed its fusty image with a bold new wing.
etymology: From Old French fust 'wine cask', originally meaning smelling of the cask.

definition: Having no chance of success; pointless.
examples: Their futile attempts to start the old car ended with a dead battery.
It is futile to argue with someone who refuses to listen.
etymology: From Latin futilis, 'leaky, worthless', related to fundere 'to pour'.

definition: The future, or a future event or state.
examples: The novel gazes into a distant futurity of floating cities.
Our choices today echo into futurity.
etymology: From future + -ity.

definition: A person who provokes others into action through persistent criticism.
examples: The local gadfly attends every council meeting with questions.
Socrates called himself the gadfly of Athens.
etymology: From gad 'goad, spike' + fly; originally an insect that bites livestock.

definition: An embarrassing social blunder.
examples: Calling the host by the wrong name was an awkward gaffe.
The speech was full of gaffes, but the crowd laughed along.
etymology: From French gaffe, 'blunder', originally 'boathook'.

definition: A disorderly or noisy group of people, or a flock of geese.
examples: A gaggle of reporters waited outside the courthouse.
We passed a gaggle of geese by the pond.
etymology: From Middle English gagelen 'to cackle', imitative of a goose's cry.

definition: Serving to bring in money; paid.
examples: After graduation, he finally found gainful employment.
The program helps refugees find gainful work.
etymology: From gain, from Old French gaaignier 'to earn', plus -ful.

definition: To deny or contradict.
examples: No one can gainsay her dedication to the team.
The evidence was too strong to gainsay.
etymology: From Middle English gain- 'against' + say.

definition: Confused, meaningless talk; gibberish.
examples: The memo was a galimatias of buzzwords.
I couldn't follow his galimatias about blockchain destiny.
etymology: From French galimatias, of unknown origin.

definition: Bold, impudent behavior; nerve.
examples: He had the gall to ask for a raise on his first day.
I can't believe she had the gall to cut in line.
etymology: From Old English galla 'bile'; the sense of impudence arose in 19th-century American English.

definition: Brave and heroic, or politely attentive and chivalrous.
examples: The underdogs made a gallant effort in the final.
It was a gallant gesture to give up his seat.
etymology: From Old French galant, from galer 'to make merry'.

definition: A confused jumble or medley of things.
examples: The yard sale offered a gallimaufry of lamps, records, and mismatched teacups.
Her novel is a delightful gallimaufry of myth, romance, and satire.
etymology: From French galimafrée, a kind of stew, of uncertain origin.

definition: Relating to the order of heavy ground-feeding birds like chickens and turkeys.
examples: Quail and pheasants are gallinaceous birds.
The gallinaceous chatter from the coop woke us at dawn.
etymology: From Latin gallinaceus, from gallina 'hen'.

definition: To go from place to place seeking pleasure and entertainment.
examples: They gallivant around Europe every summer.
I can't gallivant all weekend; I have a deadline.
etymology: Perhaps a playful alteration of gallant.

definition: In great numbers or abundance, used after the noun it describes.
examples: The flea market had bargains galore.
There were puns galore in his wedding speech.
etymology: From Irish go leór 'to sufficiency, enough'.

definition: Sudden, startling, and energizing, as if from an electric shock.
examples: Her speech had a galvanic effect on the crowd.
The news gave the sleepy office a galvanic jolt.
etymology: From Luigi Galvani, an 18th-century Italian physiologist who studied electricity in animals.

definition: To shock or excite someone into taking action.
examples: The flood galvanized residents to demand better drainage.
Her speech helped galvanize the team before the final.
etymology: From Luigi Galvani, an Italian scientist who studied electricity in muscles.

definition: An opening move or action calculated to gain an advantage.
examples: Offering a free trial was a clever gambit to win new customers.
His opening gambit in the negotiation was to ask for double.
etymology: From Italian gambetto, 'a tripping up', from gamba, 'leg'.

definition: To run or jump about playfully.
examples: Lambs gambol in the spring meadow.
We watched the puppies gambol across the lawn.
etymology: From French gambade 'a leap', from Italian gamba 'leg'.

definition: Playful and merry.
examples: The gamesome puppies tumbled over each other.
She was in a gamesome mood after the exams.
etymology: From game + -some.

definition: A slim, girlish young woman with mischievous, boyish charm.
examples: With her pixie cut, she played the gamine perfectly.
Audrey Hepburn defined the gamine look for a generation.
etymology: From French gamine, feminine of gamin 'street urchin'.

definition: The complete range or scope of something.
examples: Reviews ran the gamut from glowing to brutal.
Her moods covered the whole gamut in one afternoon.
etymology: From Medieval Latin gamma ut, the name of the lowest note in a medieval musical scale.

definition: To stare in wonder with one's mouth open, or to be wide open.
examples: Tourists gape at the canyon from the overlook.
Don't just gape at me; help me lift this.
etymology: From Old Norse gapa 'to open the mouth'.

definition: To distort or confuse a message so it is misleading or unclear.
examples: Bad reception can garble a phone call.
Rumors tend to garble the facts as they spread.
etymology: From Italian garbellare 'to sift', from Arabic ġarbala.

definition: A medieval privy, or a small room for storing clothes and valuables.
examples: The castle's garderobe jutted out over the moat.
Tour guides love to point out the garderobe.
etymology: From French garde 'keep' + robe 'garment'.

definition: Enormous in size, amount, or volume.
examples: The diner is famous for its gargantuan pancakes.
Moving the archive was a gargantuan task.
etymology: From Gargantua, the giant in Rabelais's 16th-century satire.

definition: Unpleasantly bright, flashy, or showy.
examples: The casino's garish lights glowed all night.
She painted over the garish orange walls on day one.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: To gather or collect, especially support or attention.
examples: The video garnered millions of views in a week.
Her proposal managed to garner support from both departments.
etymology: From Old French gernier, 'granary', from Latin granarium.

definition: Talking a great deal, especially about unimportant things.
examples: My garrulous neighbor can turn a quick hello into an hour-long monologue.
The garrulous cab driver told us his entire life story before we reached the airport.
etymology: From Latin garrulus, 'talkative', from garrire 'to chatter'.

definition: Extravagant boasting or bragging.
examples: Beneath the gasconade, he was a timid man.
The campaign speech was pure gasconade.
etymology: From French gasconnade, from Gascon, as the people of Gascony were reputed to be boastful.

definition: Socially awkward and lacking grace or tact.
examples: It felt gauche to talk about money at the dinner.
His gauche compliment made her blush for the wrong reasons.
etymology: From French gauche 'left, awkward'.

definition: Awkward, tactless behavior, or an instance of it.
examples: His gaucherie at the embassy dinner became legendary.
She forgave the gaucherie of the nervous young poet.
etymology: From French gaucherie, from gauche 'left, awkward'.

definition: Extravagantly bright or showy in a tasteless way.
examples: The gaudy jewelry drew stares across the room.
They replaced the gaudy wallpaper with plain white paint.
etymology: Probably from gaud 'showy ornament', perhaps from Old French gaudir 'to rejoice'.

definition: To estimate or judge something, such as a feeling or amount.
examples: It's hard to gauge the mood of a room over video.
We ran a survey to gauge interest in the new class.
etymology: From Old North French gauger, of uncertain origin.

definition: Very thin and haggard, especially from illness, hunger, or worry.
examples: He looked gaunt after weeks in the hospital.
A gaunt stray dog followed us down the street.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in late Middle English.

definition: A series of difficult challenges, or a challenge issued to someone.
examples: New hires must run a gauntlet of interviews.
The rival chef threw down the gauntlet on live TV.
etymology: From Old French gantelet, a diminutive of gant 'glove'.

definition: Relating to or provoking laughter.
examples: The comedian's gelastic powers never failed him.
Doctors described a rare gelastic seizure.
etymology: From Greek gelastikos, from gelan 'to laugh'.

definition: Icy; extremely cold.
examples: We plunged into the gelid lake on New Year's Day.
He fixed the waiter with a gelid stare.
etymology: From Latin gelidus, from gelu 'frost'.

definition: Friendly and cheerful.
examples: Our genial host poured everyone a drink.
He has a genial manner that puts patients at ease.
etymology: From Latin genialis 'of generation or marriage, festive', from genius.

definition: Polite and refined, sometimes in an affected or old-fashioned way.
examples: The genteel tea room seemed frozen in 1950.
Beneath the genteel manners lay a ruthless negotiator.
etymology: From French gentil 'well-born', from Latin gentilis 'of the same clan'.

definition: To renovate a poorer area so that it attracts wealthier residents.
examples: New cafés began to gentrify the old warehouse district.
Investors want to gentrify the block, but tenants are pushing back.
etymology: A back-formation from gentrification, from gentry, coined in the 1960s.

definition: To bend one knee in worship, or to show servile deference.
examples: Worshippers genuflect before entering the pew.
Some executives genuflect to every whim of the founder.
etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin genuflectere, from genu 'knee' + flectere 'to bend'.

definition: Divination from patterns in earth, or the arrangement of sites for luck.
examples: Feng shui is sometimes called Chinese geomancy.
The fortune-teller practiced geomancy with handfuls of sand.
etymology: From Medieval Latin geomantia, from Greek gē 'earth' + manteia 'divination'.

definition: A poem or book dealing with agriculture or rural life.
examples: Her novel reads like a modern georgic about vineyard work.
Virgil's famous georgic praises the farmer's labor.
etymology: From Latin georgicus, from Greek geōrgikos 'agricultural', from geōrgos 'farmer'.

definition: Relevant to the subject being discussed.
examples: Her comments were germane to the question of funding.
Keep your remarks germane, as we only have ten minutes.
etymology: A variant of german, 'closely related', from Latin germanus, 'of the same parents'.

definition: In the earliest stage of development, but with potential for growth.
examples: The essay contains the germinal idea of her later theory.
Their movement was still in a germinal phase.
etymology: From Latin germen 'sprout, seed'.

definition: To begin to grow or develop, as a seed or an idea does.
examples: Tomato seeds germinate in about a week.
Great ideas often germinate in casual conversations.
etymology: From Latin germinare 'to sprout', from germen 'seed, sprout'.

definition: Government by old people, or a society ruled by its elders.
examples: Young voters complain of a gerontocracy in the capital.
The village council was a gentle gerontocracy.
etymology: From Greek gerōn, geront- 'old man' + -cracy 'rule'.

definition: To manipulate electoral district boundaries to favor one party.
examples: Courts ruled that lawmakers tried to gerrymander the state map.
It's harder to gerrymander when an independent panel draws districts.
etymology: From Governor Elbridge Gerry + salamander, after a Massachusetts district shaped like one in 1812.

definition: An organized whole that is perceived as more than the sum of its parts.
examples: The band's gestalt fell apart when the drummer left.
Designers think about the gestalt of a page, not just its parts.
etymology: From German Gestalt 'form, shape'.

definition: The process of carrying young in the womb, or of developing an idea.
examples: An elephant's gestation lasts nearly two years.
The novel had a ten-year gestation.
etymology: From Latin gestatio, from gestare 'to carry'.

definition: To use dramatic gestures while speaking, or in place of speech.
examples: He tends to gesticulate wildly when excited.
Across the noisy room, she began to gesticulate toward the door.
etymology: From Latin gesticulari, from gesticulus 'little gesture'.

definition: A showy but worthless trinket.
examples: The souvenir stand sold every gewgaw imaginable.
She refused to clutter her desk with a single gewgaw.
etymology: From Middle English, of unknown origin.

definition: Causing great horror or fear, or very unpleasant.
examples: The crash scene was ghastly.
What a ghastly color for a kitchen.
etymology: From obsolete gast 'to terrify', from Old English gǣstan, plus -ly.

definition: A lyric poem of rhyming couplets, often on love and loss, from Arabic and Persian tradition.
examples: She recited a ghazal by Hafez.
Each couplet in the ghazal ends with the same refrain.
etymology: From Arabic ġazal 'love poetry'.

definition: Showing a morbid interest in death or disaster.
examples: He has a ghoulish fascination with shipwrecks.
Crowds gathered with ghoulish curiosity at the crash site.
etymology: From ghoul, from Arabic ġūl, a desert spirit said to eat corpses, plus -ish.

definition: To speak rapidly and unintelligibly, especially from fear or shock.
examples: The terrified witness could only gibber.
Don't gibber; tell me slowly what happened.
etymology: Probably imitative; first recorded in the early 17th century.

definition: A gallows, or an upright post where executed bodies were displayed.
examples: A rusted gibbet still stands at the crossroads.
Highwaymen once swung from the gibbet on the hill.
etymology: From Old French gibet 'staff, cudgel, gallows'.

definition: Of the moon, more than half but less than fully illuminated.
examples: A gibbous moon rose over the harbor.
Tonight the moon is gibbous and nearly full.
etymology: From Late Latin gibbosus, from Latin gibbus 'hump'.

definition: An insulting or mocking remark.
examples: He ignored the gibe about his haircut.
Her closing gibe drew laughs from the audience.
etymology: Perhaps from Old French giber 'to handle roughly'.

definition: Dizzy, or excitedly light-hearted and frivolous.
examples: The kids were giddy on the last day of school.
I felt giddy looking down from the observation deck.
etymology: From Old English gidig 'insane', literally 'possessed by a god'.

definition: To cover with a thin layer of gold, or to make something seem better than it is.
examples: Artisans gild the dome every few decades.
Don't gild the truth in your report.
etymology: From Old English gyldan, related to gold.

definition: Showy but flimsy and poorly made.
examples: The gimcrack furniture fell apart within a year.
Tourists crowded the gimcrack stalls near the pier.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in Middle English.

definition: A trick or device meant to attract attention rather than to be truly useful.
examples: The folding screen felt like a gimmick to most reviewers.
Free pizza was a gimmick to get people to the open house.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in early 20th-century American slang.

definition: In a careful, cautious way.
examples: She gingerly stepped onto the frozen pond.
He gingerly lifted the bandage to check the cut.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: The measurement around the middle of something.
examples: The redwood's girth was over thirty feet.
He loosened his belt to accommodate his growing girth.
etymology: From Old Norse gjǫrð 'belt'.

definition: The main point or general meaning of something.
examples: I didn't catch every word, but I got the gist of the lecture.
The gist of her email was that the meeting moved to Friday.
etymology: From Anglo-French gist, 'lies', from a legal phrase meaning 'this action lies'.

definition: Free from hair or down; smooth.
examples: The plant has glabrous leaves that shine in the sun.
His glabrous head gleamed under the stage lights.
etymology: From Latin glaber 'hairless, smooth'.

definition: Extremely slow, or cold and unfriendly in manner.
examples: The project moved at a glacial pace.
She gave him a glacial stare across the table.
etymology: From Latin glacialis 'icy', from glacies 'ice'.

definition: Of a pale gray-green or blue-gray color, often with a powdery bloom.
examples: The succulent's glaucous leaves look almost frosted.
A glaucous sea stretched out under the fog.
etymology: From Latin glaucus, from Greek glaukos 'bluish green, gray'.

definition: To gather information gradually from various sources.
examples: I gleaned a few useful tips from the online reviews.
What can we glean from last year's sales numbers?
etymology: From Old French glener, originally to gather leftover grain after a harvest.

definition: A piece of land serving as part of a clergyman's benefice; poetically, soil.
examples: The vicar grew potatoes on the glebe behind the church.
The poem praises the humble glebe and those who till it.
etymology: From Latin gleba 'clod, land, soil'.

definition: Exuberantly or triumphantly joyful, sometimes at another's misfortune.
examples: The kids let out a gleeful shout when school was canceled.
His gleeful grin told me he'd beaten my score.
etymology: From glee, from Old English glēo 'entertainment, mirth', plus -ful.

definition: Fluent and easy but insincere or shallow.
examples: His glib answer didn't reassure the worried parents.
It's too glib to say they should just move.
etymology: Perhaps from Dutch glibberig 'slippery'.

definition: A faint, wavering light, or a faint sign of something.
examples: There's finally a glimmer of hope for the project.
We saw a glimmer of light at the end of the tunnel.
etymology: From Middle English glimeren, probably of Scandinavian origin.

definition: To sparkle or glitter.
examples: Frost began to glister on the windowpanes.
Watch the river glister in the late sun.
etymology: From Middle English glistren, probably related to Middle Low German glisteren.

definition: The time of evening twilight; dusk.
examples: We walked home through the gloaming as fireflies began to blink.
In the gloaming, the old barn looked almost ghostly.
etymology: From Old English glōmung, from glōm, 'twilight'.

definition: To dwell on one's own success or another's misfortune with smug pleasure.
examples: Try not to gloat when your team wins the office pool.
He couldn't resist the chance to gloat about being right.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Old Norse glotta 'to grin'.

definition: Speech in an unknown or invented language, often in religious ecstasy.
examples: The revival meeting erupted in glossolalia.
Linguists have studied glossolalia for its sound patterns.
etymology: From Greek glōssa 'tongue, language' + lalia 'speech'.

definition: To have an angry or sullen look on one's face; to scowl.
examples: The goalie began to glower at the referee.
