examples: Grandpa's jeremiad about modern music lasted the whole car ride.
The essay is a jeremiad against wasteful packaging.
etymology: From French jérémiade, after the prophet Jeremiah and the Book of Lamentations.

definition: A joke or playful remark.
examples: He said it in jest, but she took it seriously.
Many a true word is spoken in jest.
etymology: From Middle English geste, 'a tale of exploits', from Latin gesta 'deeds'.

definition: To throw away or abandon something no longer wanted.
examples: We jettisoned half our furniture before the move.
The team decided to jettison the old design and start over.
etymology: From Old French getaison, 'a throwing', from Latin jactare, 'to throw'.

definition: To be in agreement or consistent with something.
examples: His story doesn't jibe with what the security camera recorded.
Make sure the totals jibe before you send the invoice.
etymology: An American usage of unknown origin, first recorded in the early 1800s.

definition: To abruptly reject or abandon a lover.
examples: In the novel, she will jilt the duke at the altar.
He never expected her to jilt him by text.
etymology: From an earlier noun jilt, 'a deceitful woman', of uncertain origin.

definition: Aggressive, boastful patriotism, especially favoring war with other countries.
examples: The newspaper's jingoism whipped the public into a frenzy before the war.
Politicians often resort to jingoism when they want to distract from problems at home.
etymology: From the 1870s British music-hall song containing the oath 'by jingo', supporting war with Russia.

definition: A person or thing believed to bring bad luck.
examples: Don't say the game is won yet, or you'll put a jinx on us.
The old car seemed to carry a jinx on every road trip.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly from jynx, the wryneck bird once used in charms.

definition: Nervous and unable to relax.
examples: Three espressos left me jittery all afternoon.
Investors were jittery ahead of the earnings report.
etymology: From jitter, American slang of the 1920s and of unknown origin.

definition: Corrupt use of public office for private gain.
examples: The scandal exposed years of municipal jobbery.
Jobbery decided which firm built the bridge.
etymology: From job, in an old sense of public business turned to private profit.

definition: To maneuver or compete skillfully for advantage.
examples: Candidates jockey for position before the debate.
Cars jockey for space at the merge.
etymology: From Jockey, a Scottish pet form of the name Jock (John).

definition: Playful and humorous.
examples: His jocose letters always made her laugh.
The speech struck a jocose tone.
etymology: From Latin jocosus, from jocus 'joke'.

definition: Fond of joking; humorous in tone.
examples: His jocular toast had the whole room laughing.
She kept a jocular tone even during bad news.
etymology: From Latin jocularis, from jocus 'joke'.

definition: Cheerful and lighthearted.
examples: A jocund crowd filled the square for the festival.
Wordsworth wrote of daffodils in jocund company.
etymology: From late Latin jocundus, from Latin jucundus 'pleasant', influenced by jocus 'joke'.

definition: A sudden rough movement, or a sudden shock or surprise.
examples: The train stopped with a jolt that spilled my tea.
The bad news gave the whole office a jolt.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: A traveling medieval minstrel or entertainer.
examples: A jongleur sang ballads in the castle courtyard.
The street performer was a modern jongleur.
etymology: From French, from Old French jogleor, from Latin joculator 'joker'.

definition: To push and bump against others in a crowd, or to compete for position.
examples: Shoppers jostle for the last discounted televisions.
Reporters jostle at the door whenever the senator appears.
etymology: From joust, the mounted combat of knights.

definition: A reliable but unremarkable worker; a trained craftsman working for an employer.
examples: He was a journeyman pitcher who played for nine teams.
A journeyman electrician wired the whole house.
etymology: From journey in its old sense 'a day's work', from French journée 'day'.

definition: Cheerful, friendly, and full of good humor.
examples: The jovial innkeeper greeted us with a booming laugh and a warm meal.
Grandpa was in a jovial mood and told jokes all through dinner.
etymology: From French jovial, 'under the influence of Jupiter', associated with happiness in astrology.

definition: Feeling or showing great joy and triumph.
examples: Jubilant fans poured into the streets after the final whistle.
She was jubilant when the acceptance letter arrived.
etymology: From Latin jubilare, 'to shout for joy'.

definition: Having or showing good judgment.
examples: A judicious use of color makes the design pop.
She made a judicious decision to wait for more data.
etymology: From French judicieux, from Latin judicium, 'judgment'.

definition: A huge, powerful force or organization that seems unstoppable.
examples: The streaming juggernaut crushed its rivals.
The team was a juggernaut, undefeated for two seasons.
etymology: From Hindi Jagannāth, 'lord of the world', a form of Vishnu whose huge temple car is pulled in procession.

definition: An untidy, confused mixture of things.
examples: The drawer was a jumble of cables, batteries and takeout menus.
My notes from the lecture are a jumble of half-sentences.
etymology: Probably imitative in origin.

definition: A particular point in time or events, especially a critical one.
examples: At this juncture, we need to decide whether to continue the project.
The negotiations have reached a delicate juncture.
etymology: From Latin junctura, 'a joining', from jungere, 'to join'.

definition: A pleasure trip taken by officials at public or company expense.
examples: Taxpayers paid for the mayor's junket to Hawaii.
The press junket included free spa treatments.
etymology: From Middle English jonket, a rush basket, from Latin juncus 'rush'.

definition: The official power to make legal decisions, or the area where that power applies.
examples: The case falls outside the county's jurisdiction.
Parking tickets are not within my jurisdiction, the clerk said.
etymology: From Latin iurisdictio, from ius 'law' + dicere 'to say'.

definition: The theory and philosophy of law, or a body of legal decisions.
examples: She teaches jurisprudence at the law school.
Privacy jurisprudence has changed dramatically since the internet.
etymology: From Latin iurisprudentia, 'knowledge of law'.

definition: Relating to young people, or childish and immature.
examples: The prank was juvenile, but we laughed anyway.
A juvenile hawk circled clumsily over the field.
etymology: From Latin juvenilis, from juvenis 'young'.

definition: Works produced by an author or artist while young.
examples: The archive holds Austen's juvenilia.
He winces when critics quote his juvenilia.
etymology: From Latin juvenilia, neuter plural of juvenilis 'youthful'.

definition: To place two things side by side to highlight their contrast.
examples: The exhibit will juxtapose old photographs with modern street scenes.
Poets often juxtapose joy and grief to make each feel sharper.
etymology: From French juxtaposer, from Latin juxta 'next to' + French poser 'to place'.

definition: The opportune or decisive moment for action.
examples: Good speakers sense the kairos for a joke.
The protest seized its kairos.
etymology: From Greek kairos, 'the right moment'.

definition: Government by the least qualified or worst people.
examples: Critics called the cabinet a kakistocracy.
The satire imagines a kakistocracy run by influencers.
etymology: From Greek kakistos 'worst' + -kratia 'rule'.

definition: A constantly changing pattern or mix of elements.
examples: The market was a kaleidoscope of color and noise.
Her memoir is a kaleidoscope of cities and lovers.
etymology: Coined by Scottish physicist David Brewster in 1817 from Greek kalos 'beautiful' + eidos 'form' + -scope.

definition: A hangover, or a loud discordant uproar.
examples: He woke with a katzenjammer after the wedding.
The rehearsal was a katzenjammer of tuning violins.
etymology: From German Katzenjammer, literally 'cats' wailing'.

definition: Eager and enthusiastic, or sharp and quick.
examples: She's keen to start the new job.
Owls have a keen sense of hearing.
etymology: From Old English cene, 'bold, brave'.

definition: A small object kept in memory of a person or event.
examples: She kept the ticket stub as a keepsake from their first date.
Every guest left with a little jar of honey as a keepsake.
etymology: From keep + sake, meaning something kept for the sake of its giver.

definition: One's range of knowledge or understanding.
examples: Quantum physics is beyond my ken.
Such cruelty was outside her ken.
etymology: From Old English cennan, 'to make known'.

definition: A compound metaphor used in Old English or Norse poetry, like 'whale-road' for sea.
examples: 'Bone-house' is a kenning for the body.
Each kenning in Beowulf rewards a slow reading.
etymology: From Old Norse kenning, from kenna 'to know, name'.

definition: Self-emptying, especially the renunciation of one's own will.
examples: Monastic life aims at kenosis.
The poem describes love as a kind of kenosis.
etymology: From Greek kenōsis, 'emptying'.

definition: A commotion or fuss, especially over a minor matter.
examples: There was a kerfuffle at the checkout when two shoppers reached for the last cake.
The kerfuffle over the parking spaces lasted all week.
etymology: From Scots curfuffle, from fuffle, 'to disorder'.

definition: The central or most important part of something; also a seed or grain.
examples: There's a kernel of truth in every rumor.
A single kernel of popcorn was stuck in my tooth.
etymology: From Old English cyrnel, a diminutive of corn 'seed'.

definition: The main speech at a conference, or the central idea of something.
examples: The astronaut gave the keynote at the science fair.
Simplicity is the keynote of her designs.
etymology: Originally the note on which a musical key is based, which sets the tone for the rest.

definition: An onlooker who offers unwanted advice.
examples: A kibitzer hovered over our chess game.
Every home renovation attracts a kibitzer.
etymology: From Yiddish, from German kiebitzen, from Kiebitz 'lapwing', a noisy bird.

definition: Something that puts an end to a plan, used in 'put the kibosh on'.
examples: The rain put the kibosh on our picnic.
Legal put the kibosh on the prank ad.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first recorded in the 1830s.

definition: An illegal payment given in return for a favor or contract.
examples: The inspector was fired for taking a kickback from the builder.
Investigators traced every kickback to an offshore account.
etymology: Formed from kick + back.

definition: To light a fire, or to stir up a feeling or interest.
examples: A great teacher can kindle a lifelong love of math.
Use dry pine needles to kindle the campfire.
etymology: From Old Norse kynda, 'to set on fire'.

definition: Sharing a similar nature, spirit, or close relationship.
examples: At the conference she found kindred spirits who loved obscure poetry as much as she did.
The two novels have a kindred theme of loneliness in big cities.
etymology: From Old English cynn 'kin, family' + ræden 'condition'.

definition: Relating to motion, or full of lively energy.
examples: The dancer's kinetic style kept the audience on edge.
A rolling boulder has a lot of kinetic energy.
etymology: From Greek kinētikos, from kinein 'to move'.

definition: A family relationship, or a feeling of close connection with others.
examples: I felt an instant kinship with the other night-shift nurses.
Kinship ties shape inheritance in many cultures.
etymology: From kin, Old English cynn 'family, race', + -ship.

definition: Destiny or fate.
examples: Meeting again in Lisbon felt like kismet.
Was it kismet or just coincidence?
etymology: From Turkish kısmet, from Arabic qisma 'portion, lot'.

definition: One's friends and acquaintances, usually in 'kith and kin'.
examples: All his kith and kin came to the wedding.
She invited kith from every chapter of her life.
etymology: From Old English cȳth, 'knowledge, native land'.

definition: Art or objects considered tasteless or overly sentimental, often enjoyed ironically.
examples: The diner is full of fifties kitsch.
Lawn flamingos are pure kitsch, and I love them.
etymology: From German Kitsch, 'gaudy trash'.

definition: A government whose leaders steal from the country they rule.
examples: The regime was a kleptocracy dressed up as a democracy.
Journalists traced the kleptocracy's money to London.
etymology: From Greek kleptēs 'thief' + -kratia 'rule'.

definition: A clumsy but workable fix, especially in computing.
examples: The code is a kludge, but it ships tonight.
Duct tape on the mirror was a kludge that lasted years.
etymology: Tech slang from the 1960s, of uncertain origin.

definition: A natural skill or talent for doing something.
examples: He has a knack for making strangers feel welcome.
She's got a knack for finding the best deals at thrift stores.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 14th century.

definition: A dishonest, unscrupulous man; a rogue.
examples: The knave pocketed the reward and fled.
Only a knave would cheat a widow.
etymology: From Old English cnafa, 'boy, servant'.

definition: The sound of a bell rung for a death; a sign that something is ending.
examples: The new mall sounded the death knell for downtown shops.
A distant church bell tolled a slow knell.
etymology: From Old English cnyll, the sound of a bell.

definition: A paradoxical riddle used in Zen to provoke insight.
examples: 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' is a famous koan.
The error message read like a koan.
etymology: From Japanese kōan, 'public case'.

definition: To act in an excessively submissive way toward someone.
examples: She refused to kowtow to the network executives.
Why kowtow to a boss who doesn't respect you?
etymology: From Chinese kòutóu, 'knock the head', a deep bow touching the forehead to the ground.

definition: Praise and honor given for an achievement.
examples: Kudos to the kitchen staff for feeding three hundred guests.
The young coder earned plenty of kudos for fixing the bug.
etymology: From Greek kudos, 'glory, renown'.

definition: To beam with pride and pleasure, especially about a family member.
examples: Grandparents kvell over every drawing.
Watch his mother kvell when he plays the piano.
etymology: From Yiddish kveln, 'to be delighted'.

definition: To complain persistently.
examples: My uncle loves to kvetch about the weather.
Customers kvetch about the parking, then come back every week.
etymology: From Yiddish kvetshn, 'to squeeze, pinch'.

definition: Requiring a lot of time and effort.
examples: Sorting the old photos was a laborious task.
He wrote in a slow, laborious hand.
etymology: From Latin laboriosus, from labor 'work'.

definition: Extremely complicated and confusing, like a maze.
examples: Getting a permit meant navigating a labyrinthine bureaucracy.
The old town's labyrinthine streets confused every tourist.
etymology: From labyrinth, from Greek labyrinthos, the maze that held the Minotaur in Greek myth.

definition: To tear or deeply cut flesh; also to wound someone's feelings.
examples: Broken glass can lacerate bare feet.
Critics will lacerate the film for its weak script.
etymology: From Latin lacerare 'to tear', from lacer 'torn'.

definition: In law, unreasonable delay in asserting a right, which can bar a claim.
examples: The court dismissed the claim under the doctrine of laches.
Waiting twenty years to sue invited a defense of laches.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman laches 'slackness', from Old French lasche 'loose, lax'.

definition: Tearful, or tending to cause tears and sadness.
examples: The lachrymose ballad had half the audience dabbing their eyes.
He grew lachrymose after a second glass of wine and began recalling old loves.
etymology: From Latin lacrimosus, from lacrima 'tear'.

definition: Lacking enthusiasm and determination; carelessly lazy.
examples: The team's lackadaisical defense cost them the game.
He took a lackadaisical approach to studying and paid for it.
etymology: From archaic lackaday, 'alas the day', an expression of regret.

definition: A servile follower who does whatever a powerful person wants.
examples: The CEO surrounded himself with every lackey willing to agree.
She refused to be a lackey for anyone.
etymology: From French laquais 'footman', of uncertain earlier origin.

definition: Lacking energy, brightness, or excitement.
examples: The team gave a lackluster performance in the first half.
Sales were lackluster this quarter.
etymology: From lack + luster.

definition: Using very few words, often in a blunt way.
examples: His laconic reply to the long email was simply 'Fine'.
The laconic cowboy answered every question with a single nod.
etymology: From Greek Lakonikos, 'Spartan', as the Spartans were known for brief speech.

definition: A gap or missing part, especially in a text or body of knowledge.
examples: The historian noted a lacuna in the records covering the winter of 1347.
There is a glaring lacuna in the report: it never mentions the costs.
etymology: From Latin lacuna, 'pit, gap', related to lacus 'lake'.

definition: Relating to or living in lakes.
examples: Lacustrine fossils show the valley was once underwater.
The region has a rich lacustrine ecosystem.
etymology: From Latin lacus 'lake'.

definition: Heavily loaded or weighed down.
examples: The table was laden with holiday dishes.
Trucks laden with fruit lined up at the border.
etymology: The past participle of lade 'to load', from Old English hladan.

definition: To fall behind or move more slowly than others.
examples: Our town continues to lag behind in internet speeds.
Don't lag too far back on the trail.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: A person or thing that falls behind the others.
examples: The country is a laggard in renewable energy.
Every group project has a laggard who misses deadlines.
etymology: From lag + -ard.

definition: A small gift given as a bonus, especially to a customer.
examples: The baker tossed in an extra cookie as lagniappe.
As a little lagniappe, the concert ended with a surprise encore.
etymology: From Louisiana French, from Spanish la ñapa, 'the gift', from Quechua yapa.

definition: Relating to laypeople rather than clergy; secular.
examples: The school maintains a strictly laic curriculum.
Laic leaders took over the charity from the monks.
etymology: From Greek laikos 'of the people', via Late Latin.

definition: Allowing things to take their own course without interfering.
examples: The manager has a laissez-faire style and rarely checks in.
The government took a laissez-faire approach to the markets.
etymology: From French laissez faire 'let do, leave alone'.

definition: To criticize someone harshly.
examples: Fans were quick to lambaste the team for its lackluster performance.
The review lambastes the restaurant's overpriced menu.
etymology: Probably from lam 'to beat' + baste 'to thrash'.

definition: Softly glowing or flickering, or lightly brilliant.
examples: Lambent candlelight played across the dinner table.
Her lambent wit lit up the conversation.
etymology: From Latin lambere, 'to lick'.

definition: To express deep sadness or regret about something.
examples: Fans lament the closing of the old theater on Main Street.
She would often lament the days when neighbors knew each other well.
etymology: From Latin lamentari, 'to wail', from lamentum 'a weeping'.

definition: Deplorable or regrettable; deserving disappointment.
examples: The bridge is in a lamentable state of repair.
His lamentable performance cost the team the game.
etymology: From Latin lamentabilis, from lamentari 'to lament'.

definition: To mock or ridicule someone publicly, especially through satire.
examples: Late-night hosts love to lampoon the president.
The play aims to lampoon the excesses of the art world.
etymology: From French lampon, perhaps from lampons 'let us drink', a refrain in drinking songs.

definition: A huge victory in an election, or a collapse of earth down a slope.
examples: She won the election in a landslide.
A landslide blocked the canyon road.
etymology: From land + slide.

definition: Slow, relaxed, and lacking energy, often in a pleasant way.
examples: They spent a languid afternoon drifting down the slow river with nothing to do.
She gave a languid wave and went back to her book.
etymology: From Latin languidus, from languere 'to be faint'.

definition: To lose strength or be forced to remain in an unpleasant situation.
examples: The proposal languished on the manager's desk for months.
Plants languish without enough sunlight.
etymology: From Old French languir, from Latin languere, 'to be faint'.

definition: A pleasant tiredness or lack of energy; also a heavy stillness.
examples: The languor of a summer afternoon settled over the porch.
After the big meal, a happy languor came over us.
etymology: From Latin languor, from languere 'to be weak, languish'.

definition: Tall and thin in an awkward way.
examples: A lanky teenager unfolded himself from the back seat.
The puppy has lanky legs it hasn't grown into yet.
etymology: From lank 'thin', from Old English hlanc.

definition: Lukewarm or indifferent, especially about religion or politics.
examples: His laodicean support for the campaign worried the organizers.
Voters were laodicean about both candidates.
etymology: From Laodicea, whose church is rebuked in the Book of Revelation for being lukewarm.

definition: A person who is completely under someone else's control; also a small pet dog.
examples: Critics called the senator the president's lapdog.
Her Pomeranian is a pampered lapdog.
etymology: From lap + dog.

definition: Elegant and concise, as if engraved in stone.
examples: The poet's lapidary lines are often quoted.
Her lapidary summary fit on a single index card.
etymology: From Latin lapidarius, from lapis, 'stone'.

definition: A brief failure of concentration or judgment, or a period of time passing.
examples: A momentary lapse in focus cost him the match.
After a lapse of ten years, the band is touring again.
etymology: From Latin lapsus 'a slip', from labi 'to slip'.

definition: The crime of theft of personal property.
examples: He was charged with petty larceny for stealing a bike.
Grand larceny carries a much stiffer sentence.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman larcin, from Latin latrocinium, from latro 'robber'.

definition: Generous giving of money or gifts, often by someone wealthy.
examples: The museum owes its new wing to the largesse of a local donor.
Students benefited from the largesse of an alumnus who funded scholarships.
etymology: From Old French largesse, from large 'generous'.

definition: In Australia, a boisterous, irreverent young person, often admired for mischief.
examples: The prime minister played up his image as a lovable larrikin.
Every football club has a larrikin who pranks the coach.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in Australia in the 1860s.

definition: Showing open or offensive sexual desire.
examples: The critic complained about the lascivious lyrics.
He gave her a lascivious wink, and she walked away.
etymology: From Late Latin lasciviosus, from Latin lascivia 'playfulness, wantonness'.

definition: A state of physical or mental weariness and lack of energy.
examples: A heavy lassitude settled over the office after the long holiday lunch.
The summer heat brought on a pleasant lassitude.
etymology: From Latin lassitudo, from lassus, 'weary'.

definition: Existing but not yet visible, active, or developed.
examples: The coach saw latent talent in the shy new player.
The virus can stay latent in the body for years.
etymology: From Latin latens, 'lying hidden', from latere 'to lie hidden'.

definition: Large landed estates, especially those worked by laborers or slaves.
examples: Roman latifundia relied heavily on slave labor.
Land reform broke up the old latifundia of the region.
etymology: From Latin latus 'broad' + fundus 'estate'.

definition: Freedom to act or think as one chooses; also distance north or south of the equator.
examples: Our manager gives us a lot of latitude in how we work.
The city sits at the same latitude as Rome.
etymology: From Latin latitudo 'breadth', from latus 'broad'.

definition: A person who is tolerant of differing views, especially in religion.
examples: The bishop was a latitudinarian who welcomed doubters.
As a latitudinarian, she cared more about kindness than doctrine.
etymology: From Latin latitudo 'breadth'.

definition: Recently; in the later stages of a period.
examples: He worked as a lawyer and, latterly, as a novelist.
Latterly, the band has focused on acoustic music.
etymology: From latter + -ly.

definition: Deserving praise and admiration, even if the result is imperfect.
examples: Her goal of cutting waste in the office is laudable.
It is laudable that so many neighbors volunteered after the storm.
etymology: From Latin laudabilis, from laudare 'to praise'.

definition: Expressing praise.
examples: The book received laudatory reviews in every major paper.
Her speech was full of laudatory remarks about the volunteers.
etymology: From Latin laudatorius, from laudare 'to praise'.

definition: A person honored for outstanding achievement, especially with a major prize.
examples: The Nobel laureate spoke to students about her research.
The city named a poet laureate for the first time.
etymology: From Latin laureatus 'crowned with laurel'.

definition: Extravagant, rich, and given in great and generous abundance.
examples: They threw a lavish party with live music and a five-course dinner.
The hotel's lavish lobby has marble floors and a giant crystal chandelier.
etymology: From Old French lavasse, 'downpour of rain', from laver 'to wash'.

definition: Not strict, careful, or firm enough.
examples: Security at the event was surprisingly lax.
The teacher is lax about late homework.
etymology: From Latin laxus 'loose'.

definition: A lazy person who avoids work.
examples: Her uncle was a charming layabout who never held a job.
Don't be a layabout; help with the dishes.
etymology: From the phrase lay about.

definition: A person without professional or specialized knowledge of a subject.
examples: Can you explain the diagnosis in terms a layman can understand?
To a layman, the two paintings look identical.
etymology: From lay 'not of the clergy', from Greek laikos 'of the people', + man.

definition: A hospital or building for quarantine, especially for leprosy or plague.
examples: Ships from infected ports had to unload at the lazaretto.
The old lazaretto on the island is now a museum.
etymology: From Italian lazzaretto, from lazzaro 'leper', after the biblical Lazarus.

definition: Dull, heavy, or gray, like lead.
examples: The sky was leaden all week.
His leaden prose made the history book hard to finish.
etymology: From Old English leaden, from lead 'the metal'.

definition: To lighten or enliven something with a contrasting element.
examples: A few jokes helped leaven the serious lecture.
She knows how to leaven bad news with kindness.
etymology: From Old French levain, from Latin levamen, from levare 'to raise'.

definition: A person who exploits or lives off others; also a bloodsucking worm.
examples: Her roommate was a leech who never paid rent.
The doctor used a leech to drain the bruise.
etymology: From Old English læce, a word for both the worm and a physician.

definition: Cautious or suspicious about something.
examples: I'm leery of any deal that sounds too good to be true.
The cat stayed leery of the new dog for weeks.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly related to leer.

definition: Freedom or room to act, decide, or change.
examples: The teacher gave us some leeway on the deadline because of the storm.
Leave yourself some leeway in the budget for surprises.
etymology: From nautical lee + way, the sideways drift of a ship pushed by the wind.

definition: Something handed down or remembered from someone in the past.
examples: Her legacy as a coach lives on in the players she mentored.
The park is the legacy of a neighbor who donated the land.
etymology: From Old French legacie, from Medieval Latin legatia, from Latin legare 'to bequeath'.

definition: The confusing technical language of legal documents.
examples: The contract was twenty pages of dense legalese.
Can you translate this legalese into plain English?
etymology: From legal + -ese.

definition: Skillful trickery or sleight of hand, used to deceive or impress.
examples: The magician's legerdemain made the coin vanish from his open palm.
Through accounting legerdemain, the company hid its losses for years.
etymology: From Old French leger de main, 'light of hand'.

definition: Quickness and lightness of movement or mind.
examples: The pianist played the scherzo with astonishing legerity.
She answered with the legerity of a born debater.
etymology: From French légèreté, from léger 'light'.

definition: Clear enough to be read.
examples: Please make your handwriting legible on the form.
The old gravestone was barely legible.
etymology: From Late Latin legibilis, from legere 'to read'.

definition: Very numerous.
examples: The problems with the new software are legion.
Her fans are legion, and they follow her on every tour.
etymology: From Latin legio, a unit of the Roman army; the sense 'numerous' echoes the biblical phrase 'my name is Legion: for we are many'.

definition: The tiring, practical work of gathering information or getting things done.
examples: The interns did the legwork for the investigation.
She did all the legwork of finding a venue.
etymology: From leg + work, originally of work involving walking around.

definition: A recurring theme or melody associated with a person, idea, or situation.
examples: The hero's leitmotif swells every time he appears on screen.
Loneliness is the leitmotif running through all her short stories.
etymology: From German Leitmotiv, 'leading motive'.

definition: A statement proved as a step toward proving another; also a dictionary headword.
examples: The proof begins with a simple lemma about prime numbers.
Each lemma in the dictionary lists its inflected forms.
etymology: From Greek lemma 'something assumed'.

definition: Gentle and merciful in punishment or in applying rules.
examples: The judge was lenient and gave the first-time offender a warning.
Our lenient teacher accepts late homework if you explain what happened.
etymology: From Latin leniens, 'soothing', from lenis 'soft, mild'.

definition: Soothing or easing pain or distress.
examples: The balm had a lenitive effect on the burn.
Her lenitive words calmed the angry crowd.
etymology: From Medieval Latin lenitivus, from Latin lenire 'to soften'.

definition: Mercy or gentleness, especially in punishment.
examples: The judge showed lenity to the first-time offender.
Critics said the treaty's lenity encouraged further aggression.
etymology: From Latin lenitas, from lenis 'gentle'.

definition: Like a lion in appearance or nature.
examples: The conductor shook his leonine mane of white hair.
He had a leonine courage that inspired his troops.
etymology: From Latin leo 'lion'.

definition: The crime of insulting a monarch; any insult to someone's dignity.
examples: He was jailed for lese-majesty after mocking the king online.
Questioning the founder's ideas is treated as lese-majesty in that company.
etymology: From French lèse-majesté, from Latin laesa majestas 'injured sovereignty'.

definition: Sluggish and drowsy, with very little energy or desire to move.
examples: After the enormous lunch, the whole office felt lethargic and a little sleepy.
The patient seemed lethargic and slept through most of the day.
etymology: From Greek lethargos, 'forgetful', from lethe 'forgetfulness'.

definition: Causing forgetfulness or oblivion.
examples: He sank into a lethean sleep after the long journey.
The music had a lethean effect, erasing her worries.
etymology: From Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld.

definition: The inability to recall a particular word.
examples: A bout of lethologica left her pointing and saying 'the thingy'.
Lethologica strikes everyone, especially when tired.
etymology: From Greek lethe 'forgetfulness' + logos 'word'.

definition: Power or influence used to get a desired result.
examples: Having another job offer gave her leverage in salary talks.
A longer handle gives you more leverage on the bolt.
etymology: From lever, from Old French levier, from lever 'to raise'.

definition: Humor or light-heartedness, especially when a situation is serious.
examples: A moment of levity eased the tension in the boardroom.
He rarely showed levity at work, which made his jokes surprising.
etymology: From Latin levitas, 'lightness', from levis 'light'.

definition: To officially impose and collect a tax, fee, or fine.
examples: The city plans to levy a tax on sugary drinks.
The league can levy fines on players who skip interviews.
etymology: From Old French levee, from lever 'to raise', from Latin levare.

definition: The vocabulary of a language, person, or field; also a dictionary.
examples: 'Doomscrolling' has entered the everyday lexicon.
Every profession has its own lexicon of jargon.
etymology: From Greek lexikon 'of words', from lexis 'word'.

definition: Legal responsibility for something, or a person or thing that causes problems.
examples: The company accepted liability for the damage.
His temper became a liability on the team.
etymology: From liable + -ity.

definition: Legally responsible for something, or likely to do something.
examples: The landlord is liable for repairs to the roof.
That old ladder is liable to collapse.
etymology: Probably from Anglo-Norman, from French lier 'to bind', from Latin ligare.

definition: A person who helps two groups communicate, or the communication itself.
examples: She serves as the liaison between the school and parents.
Close liaison with local police helped the event run smoothly.
etymology: From French liaison, from lier 'to bind', from Latin ligare.

definition: A drink poured as an offering to a god; humorously, an alcoholic drink.
examples: The priest poured a libation of wine on the altar.
After the long week, we enjoyed a libation on the terrace.
etymology: From Latin libatio, from libare 'to pour as an offering'.

definition: A false written statement that damages someone's reputation.
examples: The actor sued the magazine for libel.
Publishing that rumor could expose the paper to a libel suit.
etymology: From Latin libellus 'little book', a diminutive of liber 'book'.

definition: A person who lives with no moral restraint, especially in sexual matters.
examples: The novel's hero is a charming libertine who ruins everyone he meets.
In his youth he was a libertine; in old age, a preacher.
etymology: From Latin libertinus 'freedman'.

definition: The text or words of an opera or musical.
examples: Mozart worked with Da Ponte on the libretto.
She wrote both the music and the libretto.
etymology: From Italian libretto 'little book', a diminutive of libro.

definition: Disregarding accepted rules, especially of sexual behavior.
examples: Puritan critics condemned the licentious plays of the era.
The court was known for its licentious parties.
etymology: From Latin licentiosus, from licentia 'freedom, license'.

definition: Permitted by law; lawful.
examples: The trade in certain antiques is licit only with a permit.
They debated what counts as licit evidence.
etymology: From Latin licitus 'lawful', from licere 'to be allowed'.

definition: A person who flatters and obeys powerful people to win favor.
examples: The king surrounded himself with every lickspittle at court.
She refused to play the lickspittle to her new boss.
etymology: From lick + spittle.

definition: A feudal lord, or a vassal bound to serve one.
examples: The knight knelt before his liege.
Every liege could demand military service from his vassals.
etymology: From Old French lige, of uncertain earlier origin.

definition: The essential element that keeps something alive or working.
examples: Tourism is the lifeblood of the island's economy.
Volunteers are the lifeblood of the food bank.
etymology: From life + blood.

definition: Something that provides essential help or support.
examples: The bus route is a lifeline for elderly residents.
The small loan was a lifeline for the struggling bakery.
etymology: Originally a rope used to rescue people or to keep sailors safe on deck.

definition: Something used to tie or bind; also two letters joined as one character.
examples: The surgeon tied a ligature around the artery.
The 'æ' in 'encyclopædia' is a ligature.
etymology: From Late Latin ligatura, from ligare 'to bind'.

definition: To point out a resemblance between two things.
examples: Critics liken her voice to Billie Holiday's.
Some liken the startup to a young Google.
etymology: From like + -en.

definition: Very small; trivial.
examples: The apartment had a lilliputian kitchen with one burner.
Their lilliputian squabbles bored everyone.
etymology: From Lilliput, the island of tiny people in Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726).

definition: A pleasant, gentle rise and fall in the voice or in music.
examples: She spoke with an Irish lilt.
The song has a cheerful lilt.
etymology: From Middle English, of uncertain origin.

definition: Flexible and supple.
examples: Yoga keeps her limber at seventy.
Stretch first to get limber before the run.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly related to limb.

definition: An uncertain state of waiting, with no decision made.
examples: The project has been in limbo since the funding dried up.
Refugees can spend years in legal limbo.
etymology: From Latin in limbo, from limbus 'edge', in theology the region on the border of hell.

definition: The focus of public attention.
examples: After the scandal, he tried to stay out of the limelight.
She never wanted the limelight; she just loved to sing.
etymology: From limelight, a bright stage light made by heating quicklime.

definition: A threshold, especially the point at which a stimulus becomes perceptible.
examples: The sound was just below the limen of hearing.
She paused at the limen of a new career.
etymology: From Latin limen 'threshold'.

definition: The intense, obsessive state of being infatuated with another person.
examples: In the grip of limerence, he checked his phone every minute.
Limerence often fades into a calmer kind of love.
etymology: Coined by the American psychologist Dorothy Tennov in the 1970s.

definition: Relating to a transitional state or threshold between two stages.
examples: The weeks after graduation feel like a liminal time.
Airports are liminal spaces, neither here nor there.
etymology: From Latin limen 'threshold'.

definition: To depict or describe in painting or words.
examples: The novelist limns the small town with affectionate detail.
In a few strokes, the artist could limn a sleeping fox.
etymology: From obsolete lumine, 'to illuminate a manuscript', from Old French luminer.

definition: Clear and transparent, or easily understood.
examples: We swam in a limpid mountain pool.
Her prose is limpid and precise.
etymology: From Latin limpidus, 'clear'.

definition: A person or thing that is vital to holding something together.
examples: The office manager is the linchpin of the entire team.
Cheap shipping is the linchpin of their business model.
etymology: From Old English lynis 'axle pin' + pin.

definition: A person's line of descent from ancestors.
examples: She can trace her lineage back to Norway.
The breed's lineage goes back centuries.
etymology: From Old French lignage, from Latin linea 'line'.

definition: A distinctive feature or characteristic, especially of the face.
examples: The portrait captured every lineament of her grandmother's face.
Each lineament of the old city told a story.
etymology: From Latin lineamentum, from linea 'line'.

definition: To stay longer than necessary, or to last a long time.
examples: Guests like to linger over coffee long after dinner ends.
The smell of smoke lingered for days.
etymology: From Middle English lengeren, 'to dwell', from Old English lengan 'to lengthen'.

definition: Very brave.
examples: The lionhearted firefighter went back in for the dog.
It was a lionhearted defense against a far stronger team.
etymology: From lion + hearted, echoing the nickname of Richard I of England, the Lionheart.

definition: To treat someone as a celebrity or hero.
examples: The town lionized the young swimmer after her Olympic medal.
The press tends to lionize tech founders.
etymology: From lion, in the sense 'a celebrated person'.

definition: A text written without using a particular letter.
examples: Georges Perec wrote a whole novel as a lipogram, never using the letter e.
Try writing a short lipogram without the letter a.
etymology: From Greek lipogrammatos 'lacking a letter', from leipein 'to leave' + gramma 'letter'.

definition: To close a business and sell its assets; also to convert into cash or to eliminate.
examples: The company had to liquidate after years of losses.
They plan to liquidate their stocks to buy the house.
etymology: From Medieval Latin liquidare 'to make clear', from Latin liquidus 'liquid'.

definition: Thin, supple, and graceful.
examples: A lissome dancer leapt across the stage.
The willow bent its lissome branches in the wind.
etymology: An alteration of lithesome, from lithe + -some.

definition: Lacking energy or interest.
examples: The heat left everyone feeling listless.
The team played a listless first half.
etymology: From the obsolete noun list 'desire' + -less.

definition: A long, repetitive list, often of complaints; originally a series of prayers.
examples: He recited a litany of complaints about the hotel.
The report lists a litany of safety failures.
etymology: From Greek litaneia 'prayer, entreaty', via Latin.

definition: Taking words in their most basic, exact sense.
examples: The literal meaning of the phrase is quite different from how it's used.
He gave a literal translation that sounded stiff.
etymology: From Latin litteralis, from littera 'letter'.

definition: Well-educated people who are interested in literature.
examples: The café was a favorite haunt of the city's literati.
Her debut novel was the talk of the literati.
etymology: From Latin literati, plural of literatus 'learned'.

definition: Slim, supple, and graceful.
examples: A lithe cat leaped onto the fence.
The dancer's lithe movements drew applause.
etymology: From Old English lithe 'gentle, soft'.

definition: Too ready to take legal action.
examples: We live in a litigious society where everyone sues.
The litigious neighbor took them to court over a tree.
etymology: From Latin litigiosus, from lis 'lawsuit'.

definition: A dye that changes color with acidity, used figuratively in 'litmus test' for a decisive test.
examples: How a company treats its interns is a litmus test of its values.
Blue litmus paper turns red in acid.
etymology: From Old Norse litmosi 'dye moss', since the dye comes from lichens.

definition: Understatement that expresses an idea by denying its opposite, as in 'not bad'.
examples: Calling a hurricane 'a bit breezy' is a classic litotes.
British humor relies heavily on litotes.
etymology: From Greek litotes 'plainness', from litos 'simple'.

definition: Relating to the shore of a sea or lake.
examples: Littoral zones teem with crabs and snails.
The navy ordered new ships for littoral combat.
etymology: From Latin litoralis, from litus 'shore'.

definition: A special uniform worn by servants or staff; also a company's distinctive color scheme.
examples: The doorman wore a green livery with brass buttons.
The airline unveiled a new livery for its jets.
etymology: From Old French livree 'delivered', originally the clothing allowance given to servants.

definition: Furiously angry; also dark bluish in color, like a bruise.
examples: Mom was livid when she saw the dent in the car.
A livid bruise spread across his knee.
etymology: From Latin lividus 'bluish', from livere 'to be bluish'.

definition: Unwilling or reluctant to do something.
examples: I was loath to leave the party so early.
Banks are loath to lend to companies with no history.
etymology: From Old English lath 'hostile, hateful'.

definition: To feel intense dislike or disgust for something.
examples: I loathe getting up before sunrise.
Many people loathe the sound of nails on a chalkboard.
etymology: From Old English lathian 'to be hateful', related to loath.

definition: Causing hatred or disgust.
examples: The villain was a truly loathsome character.
Cleaning the grease trap is a loathsome job.
etymology: From Middle English, from loath + -some.

definition: To try to influence lawmakers or officials on an issue.
examples: Farmers came to the capital to lobby for drought relief.
Parents plan to lobby the school board for later start times.
etymology: From the noun lobby, from Medieval Latin lobia 'covered walk', after people approaching legislators in the lobby.

definition: A place where something happens or is set.
examples: The film's locale shifts from Paris to Cairo.
The quiet locale made it perfect for a writing retreat.
etymology: From French local 'local', respelled to show the stress.

definition: Close, rigid conformity, as when everyone moves together.
examples: The two parties voted in lockstep on the bill.
Prices rose in lockstep with demand.
etymology: Originally a style of marching in which each person follows the one ahead as closely as possible.

definition: The central point or place where something happens.
examples: The kitchen was the locus of family life.
The city became the locus of the protest movement.
etymology: From Latin locus 'place'.

definition: A particular word or phrase, or a style of speaking.
examples: 'Y'all' is a locution typical of the South.
Her careful locution marked her as a lawyer.
etymology: From Latin locutio, from loqui 'to speak'.

definition: A guiding principle or example; originally a star used for navigation.
examples: Fairness has been the lodestar of her entire legal career.
For young climbers, his memoir became a lodestar.
etymology: From Middle English lode, 'way, course', + star.

definition: Very high, or noble and ambitious, sometimes to the point of arrogance.
examples: The startup has lofty goals of ending food waste.
They lived in a lofty apartment with twenty-foot ceilings.
etymology: From loft, from Old Norse lopt 'air, upper room'.

definition: The detailed planning and organization of a complex operation.
examples: The logistics of moving a whole office are a nightmare.
She handles logistics for music festivals.
etymology: From French logistique, from loger 'to lodge', originally the quartering and supply of troops.

definition: A deadlock or blockage that stops progress.
examples: The new budget broke a months-long logjam in Congress.
There's a logjam of cases waiting for trial.
etymology: Originally a mass of logs blocking a river, from log + jam.

definition: An argument about words or their meanings.
examples: The debate degenerated into a logomachy over the word 'freedom'.
Academic feuds often become pure logomachy.
etymology: From Greek logomakhia, from logos 'word' + makhe 'fight'.

definition: A lover of words.
examples: Any logophile will enjoy this dictionary of forgotten words.
As a logophile, she collects odd words like stamps.
etymology: From Greek logos 'word' + philos 'loving'.

definition: Excessive and often incoherent talkativeness.
examples: The panelist's logorrhea left no time for questions.
After three coffees, my roommate is prone to logorrhea.
etymology: From Greek logos, 'word', + rhoia, 'flow'.

definition: To stand or wait around without a clear purpose.
examples: Teenagers like to loiter outside the corner store.
Signs warn people not to loiter near the entrance.
etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch loteren 'to wag about'.

definition: To sit or lie in a relaxed, lazy way; also to hang loosely.
examples: We spent the lazy afternoon content to loll in hammocks by the lake.
On hot days the dog will loll on the cool tiles.
etymology: From Middle English lollen, probably imitative.

definition: Patient endurance of hardship or offense.
examples: She bore her neighbor's insults with remarkable longanimity.
The monks were known for their longanimity.
etymology: From Late Latin longanimitas, from longus 'long' + animus 'mind'.

definition: A long life or a long duration of something.
examples: Regular exercise is linked to longevity.
The show's longevity surprised even its creators.
etymology: From Late Latin longaevitas, from longus 'long' + aevum 'age'.

definition: A tedious, dull stretch in a book, film, or piece of music.
examples: Despite a longueur or two in the middle, the documentary is gripping.
The novel's longueurs are redeemed by its breathtaking final chapter.
etymology: From French longueur, 'length'.

definition: A gap in rules or laws that lets someone avoid them.
examples: The accountant found a loophole that saved them thousands.
Lawmakers promised to close the loophole next year.
etymology: Originally a narrow slit in a castle wall for shooting through, from obsolete loop 'opening' + hole.

definition: To run with long, relaxed, bounding strides.
examples: We watched the wolf lope across the snowfield.
He likes to lope along the beach each morning.
etymology: From Old Norse hlaupa 'to leap'.

definition: Uneven, with one side larger or lower than the other.
examples: My first homemade cake came out lopsided.
The game ended with a lopsided score of 48 to 3.
etymology: From lop 'to droop' + sided.

definition: Very talkative, often to the point of rambling.
examples: The loquacious taxi driver told us his entire life story in ten minutes.
She grew loquacious after her second cup of coffee and chatted with everyone nearby.
etymology: From Latin loquax, 'talkative', from loqui 'to speak'.

definition: Grand and dignified, or arrogant and haughty.
examples: He waved us away with a lordly gesture.
The house stood on a lordly hill above the town.
etymology: From lord + -ly.

definition: A body of traditional knowledge, stories, or beliefs about a subject.
examples: Local lore says the lake has no bottom.
Fans love the deep lore of the fantasy series.
etymology: From Old English lar 'teaching, learning'.

definition: A person who lives in idle, dreamy indulgence, forgetting their duties.
examples: After his windfall he became a lotus-eater on a Greek island.
Don't turn into a lotus-eater just because summer is here.
etymology: From the Lotophagi in Homer's Odyssey, who ate the lotus and forgot their homes.

definition: Disreputable or sleazy, but often in an attractive way.
examples: The bar had a louche charm, with velvet booths and dim lights.
He played a louche aristocrat in the film.
etymology: From French louche 'squinting', from Latin luscus 'one-eyed'.

definition: A rude, aggressive, or uncouth man.
examples: Some lout spilled beer on my jacket.
He was a lout at school but became a gentle father.
etymology: Possibly from Old Norse lutr 'stooping'.

definition: Not intellectual or refined in taste.
examples: I love lowbrow comedies about talking animals.
Critics sneered at the lowbrow humor of the show.
etymology: From low + brow, formed as the opposite of highbrow.

definition: Low in status or importance.
examples: He started as a lowly mailroom clerk and became CEO.
Even the lowly potato can be a gourmet dish.
etymology: From low + -ly.

definition: Clumsy and awkward, especially like an inexperienced sailor.
examples: The lubberly recruit tripped over every rope on deck.
He gave a lubberly bow and knocked over a vase.
etymology: From lubber 'clumsy fellow' + -ly.

definition: Lewd or lustful; also smooth and slippery.
examples: Censors objected to the novel's lubricious passages.
He gave a lubricious grin that made her uneasy.
etymology: From Latin lubricus 'slippery'.

definition: Glowing with light; translucent.
examples: The lucent moon hung above the harbor.
Morning light made the paper lanterns lucent.
etymology: From Latin lucent-, from lucere 'to shine'.

definition: Clear and easy to understand, or thinking in a clear and sane way.
examples: The professor gave a lucid explanation of a very difficult theory.
Though very ill, he remained lucid and chatted with his visitors.
etymology: From Latin lucidus, 'shining, clear', from lucere 'to shine'.

definition: Having bad luck; unsuccessful.
examples: The luckless fisherman went home empty-handed.
A luckless team lost its fifth straight game.
etymology: From luck + -less.

definition: Producing a lot of money or profit.
examples: She left a lucrative job in finance to open a bakery.
Selling lemonade at the parade turned out to be lucrative.
etymology: From Latin lucrativus, from lucrum 'profit'.

definition: Money, especially when gained in a dishonorable way.
examples: He sold out his friends for filthy lucre.
The band claimed they weren't in it for the lucre.
etymology: From Latin lucrum 'gain, profit'.

definition: Laborious study late at night, or the overly elaborate writing it produces.
examples: The professor's latest lucubration ran to nine hundred pages.
Her midnight lucubrations finally produced a finished thesis.
etymology: From Latin lucubratio, 'work by lamplight', from lux 'light'.

definition: Clearly expressed; easy to understand.
examples: Her luculent explanation made quantum physics seem simple.
The judge wrote a luculent opinion.
etymology: From Latin luculentus 'bright', from lux 'light'.

definition: Showing spontaneous playfulness.
examples: The museum's ludic exhibits invite visitors to touch everything.
There's a ludic quality to her architecture.
etymology: From French ludique, from Latin ludus, 'play'.

definition: So unreasonable or silly that it is laughable.
examples: Paying fifteen dollars for popcorn is ludicrous.
The plot of the movie was completely ludicrous.
etymology: From Latin ludicrus, from ludus 'play, sport'.

definition: Looking or sounding sad, gloomy, and dismal, often in an exaggerated way.
examples: The lugubrious clerk greeted every customer as if announcing a funeral.
A lugubrious tune drifted from the cellar, matching the gray afternoon.
etymology: From Latin lugubris, 'mournful', from lugere 'to mourn'.

definition: Only slightly warm, or showing little enthusiasm.
examples: The coffee had gone lukewarm by the time I drank it.
The movie got a lukewarm response from critics.
etymology: From Middle English luke 'tepid' + warm.

definition: A temporary period of quiet or reduced activity.
examples: There's usually a lull in customers right after lunch.
During a lull in the storm, we ran to the car.
etymology: From Middle English lullen, 'to soothe', imitating a soothing sound.

definition: To move in a slow, heavy, awkward way.
examples: We watched the elephants lumber toward the water hole.
Old trucks lumber up the steep mountain road.
etymology: From Middle English lomeren, perhaps imitative.

definition: A person who inspires others or is famous in a field.
examples: The conference drew every luminary in the world of physics.
She was a luminary of the jazz scene.
etymology: From Latin luminare 'lamp', from lumen 'light'.

definition: Giving off light; bright or glowing.
examples: The watch has luminous hands you can read in the dark.
Her luminous smile lit up the room.
etymology: From Latin luminosus, from lumen 'light'.

definition: Uneducated and unthinking; belonging to the lowest social class.
examples: The film sneers at the lumpen masses glued to television.
Critics called his supporters a lumpen mob.
etymology: From German Lumpen 'rags', from Marx's term Lumpenproletariat.

definition: To make a sudden forward thrust with the body.
examples: The goalkeeper had to lunge to his left to make the save.
Watch the dog lunge at every squirrel it sees.
etymology: From earlier longe, shortened from French allonger 'to lengthen', originally a fencing term.

definition: Like a wolf, especially fierce or ravenous.
examples: He flashed a lupine grin across the poker table.
The dog had a lupine look in the moonlight.
etymology: From Latin lupus 'wolf'.

definition: To make a sudden, unsteady, uncontrolled movement.
examples: Passengers began to lurch forward when the bus braked.
The economy seems to lurch from one crisis to the next.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; originally a nautical term for a sudden roll of a ship.

definition: To tempt someone or something to go somewhere or do something.
examples: Free pizza is a good way to lure students to a meeting.
Anglers use shiny bait to lure fish.
etymology: From Old French luere, a device for recalling a trained hawk, of Germanic origin.

definition: Shocking and sensational, or unnaturally bright in color.
examples: Tabloids printed lurid details of the trial.
The motel was painted a lurid shade of green.
etymology: From Latin luridus 'pale yellow, wan'.

definition: To wait hidden, often with bad intent, or to read online without posting.
examples: Danger can lurk in the most ordinary places.
Plenty of people lurk in forums without ever commenting.
etymology: From Middle English, possibly of Scandinavian origin.

definition: Growing thickly and healthily, or rich and luxurious.
examples: The valley turns lush and green after the spring rains.
The hotel lobby was lush with velvet and gold.
etymology: From Middle English, possibly from Old French lasche 'loose, slack'.

definition: A gentle shine, or glory and distinction.
examples: Polish the silver to bring back its luster.
The scandal took some of the luster off his reputation.
etymology: From French lustre, from Italian lustro, from Latin lustrare 'to illuminate'.

definition: To purify by ritual; also to remove compromised officials from public office.
examples: Priests would lustrate the city after a plague.
The new government moved to lustrate former secret-police officers.
etymology: From Latin lustrare 'to purify by sacrifice'.

definition: Shining with a soft glow.
examples: She had long, lustrous black hair.
The pearl had a lustrous sheen.
etymology: From luster + -ous.

definition: A period of five years.
examples: The club celebrates every lustrum with a grand reunion.
A lustrum has passed since we last met.
etymology: From Latin lustrum, a purification ceremony held every five years after the Roman census.

definition: Healthy, strong, and full of energy.
examples: The choir gave a lusty rendition of the anthem.
A lusty cry came from the newborn.
etymology: From lust in its older sense 'pleasure, vigor' + -y.

definition: A maker or repairer of stringed instruments.
examples: The violinist trusted only one luthier with her Stradivarius.
A local luthier rebuilt the cracked guitar.
etymology: From French luthier, from luth 'lute'.

definition: Growing thickly and richly.
examples: The garden was luxuriant with ferns and vines.
He was proud of his luxuriant beard.
etymology: From Latin luxuriant-, from luxuriare 'to grow rankly'.

definition: To enjoy something as a great pleasure or luxury.
examples: I plan to luxuriate in a hot bath tonight.
On vacation we will luxuriate in doing nothing.
etymology: From Latin luxuriare 'to grow rankly, indulge'.

definition: The supposed magical transformation of a person into a wolf; werewolf legend.
examples: Medieval tales of lycanthropy terrified villagers.
The horror film treats lycanthropy as a curse passed by bite.
etymology: From Greek lykos 'wolf' + anthropos 'human being'.

definition: Sluggish and pale; also relating to the body's lymph system.
examples: The hot afternoon left everyone lymphatic and dull.
The lymphatic system helps fight infection.
etymology: From Latin lympha 'water'; the sense 'sluggish' comes from an old belief that excess lymph caused dullness.

definition: Expressing emotion in a beautiful, poetic way.
examples: The author writes lyrical descriptions of the Irish coast.
He grew lyrical about his grandmother's cooking.
etymology: From lyric, from Greek lyrikos, from lyra 'lyre'.

definition: Disturbing and horrifying because it involves death or injury.
examples: The museum has a macabre collection of Victorian mourning jewelry.
He has a macabre sense of humor that unsettles new coworkers.
etymology: From French danse macabre, 'dance of death'; the further origin is uncertain.

definition: Mixing words or phrases from two or more languages, especially comically.
examples: The poet's macaronic verse jumps between Latin and slang.
Their family texts are a macaronic blend of Spanish and English.
etymology: From Italian dialect macaronico, from maccarone, 'macaroni'; coined for burlesque verse mixing Latin with vernacular.

definition: To soften food by soaking it in liquid.
examples: Macerate the strawberries in sugar for an hour before serving.
Chefs macerate onions in lime juice to tame their bite.
etymology: From Latin macerare, 'to soften by soaking'.

definition: Cunning, scheming, and unscrupulous, especially in politics.
examples: Her Machiavellian maneuvering won her the corner office.
The show's Machiavellian villain never makes a move without three backups.
etymology: From Niccolò Machiavelli, the Florentine author of The Prince (1532).

definition: A secret, cunning plot or scheme, usually to gain power or harm someone.
examples: He fell victim to the machinations of a rival who wanted his job.
Behind the polite smiles, the machination of the board was already underway.
etymology: From Latin machinatio, from machinari 'to contrive', from machina 'device'.

definition: Strong or aggressive pride in being masculine.
examples: The locker room was thick with machismo before the game.
Refusing to ask for directions is pure machismo.
etymology: From Mexican Spanish machismo, from macho, 'male'.

definition: The whole of a complex structure, especially the universe, seen as a unity.
examples: Medieval thinkers saw the human body as a mirror of the macrocosm.
The novel moves from a single family to the macrocosm of the nation.
etymology: From Medieval Latin macrocosmus, from Greek makros, 'great', + kosmos, 'world'.

definition: A situation of violent turmoil, or a powerful whirlpool.
examples: The senator was swept into a maelstrom of scandal.
Our kitchen becomes a maelstrom an hour before guests arrive.
etymology: From early modern Dutch maelstroom, from malen, 'to grind', + stroom, 'stream'.

definition: A frenzied woman, originally a female follower of the god Dionysus.
examples: She danced like a maenad at the festival's final set.
Greek vases show a maenad whirling with a thyrsus.
etymology: From Greek mainas, 'raving woman', from mainesthai, 'to rave'.

definition: To celebrate boisterously in public.
examples: Fans began to maffick in the streets after the cup final.
Whole cities would maffick when a war ended.
etymology: A back-formation from Mafeking, whose relief in 1900 sparked wild celebrations in London.

definition: Having or showing great authority and command of a subject.
examples: The historian wrote a magisterial account of the war.
She spoke in a calm, magisterial tone.
etymology: From Medieval Latin magisterialis, from magister, 'master'.

definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
examples: The magnanimous winner praised her opponent's effort and shook his hand warmly.
It was magnanimous of him to share the credit with the whole team.
etymology: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus 'great' + animus 'soul'.

definition: A wealthy and influential person in business or industry.
examples: A shipping magnate bought the crumbling mansion.
The film follows a media magnate whose empire collapses.
etymology: From Late Latin magnas, 'great person', from magnus, 'great'.

definition: To make something appear larger or more important than it is.
examples: A good lens can magnify the tiniest insect.
Stress tends to magnify small problems.
etymology: From Latin magnificare, from magnus, 'great'.

definition: Using high-flown, pompous language.
examples: The magniloquent toast went on for twenty minutes.
His magniloquent prose buries a simple idea.
etymology: From Latin magniloquus, from magnus, 'great', + loqui, 'to speak'.

definition: A sorcerer or wise man, originally a Zoroastrian priest.
examples: The novel's aging magus hides his spells in plain sight.
Fans treat the tech founder like a magus of the future.
etymology: From Latin magus, from Greek magos, from Old Persian maguš, a member of a priestly caste.

definition: Drawing out latent ideas through questioning, as in the Socratic method.
examples: Her maieutic teaching style made students discover answers themselves.
The coach used a maieutic approach, answering every question with another.
etymology: From Greek maieutikos, 'of midwifery'; Socrates compared his method to midwifery.

definition: A person or thing on which something else chiefly depends.
examples: Rice is the mainstay of the local diet.
She has been a mainstay of the volunteer fire department for twenty years.
etymology: From nautical mainstay, the rope supporting a ship's mainmast.

definition: Having impressive beauty, dignity, or grandeur.
examples: We hiked toward the majestic peaks at sunrise.
A majestic oak shades the whole courtyard.
etymology: From majesty + -ic, ultimately from Latin majestas, 'greatness'.

definition: A large or capital letter.
examples: Each chapter opens with an illuminated majuscule.
Medieval scribes wrote whole gospels in majuscule script.
etymology: From Latin majuscula (littera), 'somewhat larger (letter)'.

definition: Serving as a temporary, improvised substitute when nothing better is available.
examples: We rigged a makeshift desk from two crates and an old door.
After the flood, volunteers set up a makeshift clinic in the school gym.
etymology: From make + shift, in the old sense of 'a means of getting by'.

definition: Clumsy or awkward, especially in handling situations.
examples: His maladroit apology only made her angrier.
The rollout was maladroit from start to finish.
etymology: From French maladroit, from mal, 'badly', + adroit, 'skillful'.

definition: A disease or ailment, or a deep-rooted problem.
examples: Loneliness is a quiet malady of modern cities.
The doctor could not name the malady.
etymology: From Old French maladie, from malade, 'sick'.

definition: A general feeling of discomfort, unease, or low energy.
examples: A sense of malaise settled over the office after the layoffs.
He felt a vague malaise all winter and finally saw a doctor.
etymology: From French malaise, from mal 'bad' + aise 'ease'.

definition: Boldly disrespectful; impudent.
examples: The malapert page boy mocked the duke behind his back.
A malapert reply to the judge earned him a fine.
etymology: From Old French mal apert, 'ill-skilled, impudent', from mal, 'badly', + apert, 'open, bold'.

definition: The comic misuse of a word in place of one that sounds similar.
examples: Saying someone is 'the pineapple of politeness' is a classic malapropism.
The sitcom character is famous for his malapropisms.
etymology: From Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Sheridan's 1775 play The Rivals.

definition: A person who is chronically dissatisfied and rebellious.
examples: Every office has a malcontent who complains about the coffee.
The king feared a malcontent in his own court.
etymology: From Old French malcontent, from mal, 'badly', + content, 'pleased'.

definition: A curse; a spoken wish for harm to befall someone.
examples: The witch uttered a malediction over the cradle.
He muttered a malediction at the parking meter.
etymology: From Latin maledictio, from male, 'badly', + dicere, 'to speak'.

definition: Having or showing a wish to do harm to others.
examples: The villain flashed a malevolent smile.
Not every mistake is malevolent; most are just careless.
etymology: From Latin malevolent-, from male, 'ill', + velle, 'to wish'.

definition: Wrongdoing, especially by a public official.
examples: The mayor resigned amid allegations of malfeasance.
Auditors found no evidence of malfeasance, just sloppy records.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman malfaisance, from mal, 'evil', + faisance, 'doing'.

definition: To speak about someone in a spitefully critical way.
examples: Tabloids love to malign celebrities who fall from grace.
It is unfair to malign the whole department for one mistake.
etymology: From Old French malignier, from Latin malignus, 'evil-natured'.

definition: To pretend to be ill in order to avoid work or duty.
examples: He was accused of trying to malinger through exam week.
Soldiers who malinger risk serious punishment.
etymology: From French malingre, 'sickly', of uncertain further origin.

definition: Easily shaped, bent, or influenced without breaking or resisting.
examples: Gold is so malleable that it can be hammered into sheets thinner than paper.
Young minds are malleable and absorb new ideas quickly when they feel safe and curious.
etymology: From Latin malleare, 'to hammer', from malleus 'hammer'.

definition: Smelling very unpleasant.
examples: A malodorous fridge is a sure sign of forgotten leftovers.
The malodorous swamp kept tourists away.
etymology: From mal- 'badly' + odorous, from Latin odor, 'smell'.

definition: Corrupt conduct in public office, especially misuse of public funds.
examples: The treasurer was charged with malversation of relief money.
Historians document the malversation of colonial administrators.
etymology: From French malversation, from malverser, from Latin male, 'badly', + versari, 'to behave'.

definition: Wealth regarded as an evil influence or false object of worship.
examples: The preacher warned against serving mammon over neighbor.
The city's skyline is a cathedral to mammon.
etymology: From Late Latin mammona, from Greek mamōnas, from Aramaic māmōnā, 'riches'.

definition: A metal band or chain fastened around a prisoner's wrist; a restraint.
examples: The museum displays a rusty iron manacle from the old jail.
Debt can feel like a manacle on your future.
etymology: From Old French manicle, from Latin manicula, diminutive of manus, 'hand'.

definition: A powerful official, especially a senior bureaucrat seen as remote.
examples: Some Treasury mandarin killed the proposal in committee.
The museum's old mandarin resisted every change.
etymology: From Portuguese mandarim, from Malay menteri, ultimately from Sanskrit mantrin, 'counselor'.

definition: An official order or the authority given to carry out a task.
examples: The new committee has a mandate to improve city parks.
Voters gave the mayor a clear mandate for change.
etymology: From Latin mandatum, 'something commanded', from mandare 'to command'.

definition: To move skillfully or carefully, or to steer a situation cleverly.
examples: It took ten minutes to maneuver the couch up the stairs.
She knows how to maneuver around office politics.
etymology: From French manœuvre, from Medieval Latin manuopera, 'work by hand'.

definition: Seeing the world as a stark struggle between good and evil.
examples: The film's Manichean plot leaves no room for gray areas.
Political debate has grown dangerously Manichean.
etymology: From Manichaeism, a dualistic religion founded by the Persian prophet Mani in the 3rd century.

definition: Clearly apparent to the eye or mind; obvious.
examples: Her delight was manifest the moment she opened the letter.
The flaws in the plan became manifest within a week.
etymology: From Latin manifestus, 'clear, evident'.

definition: A public declaration of a group's or person's aims and beliefs.
examples: The band's first album reads like a manifesto for young rebels.
The party released its manifesto a month before the vote.
etymology: From Italian manifesto, from manifestare, from Latin manifestus, 'clear'.

definition: Many and of several different kinds.
examples: The benefits of walking are manifold.
Her talents are manifold, though cooking is not one of them.
etymology: From Old English manigfeald, 'many-fold'.

definition: Gentleness or mildness of manner.
examples: She handled the furious customer with remarkable mansuetude.
The old priest was known for his mansuetude.
etymology: From Latin mansuetudo, from mansuetus, 'tame', literally 'accustomed to the hand'.

definition: Relating to divination or prophecy.
examples: The fortune teller claimed mantic powers.
Ancient mantic rituals read the future in birds' flight.
etymology: From Greek mantikos, from mantis, 'prophet'.

definition: A phrase that is repeated often as a guiding belief or for focus.
examples: 'Progress, not perfection' became her mantra during training.
The startup's mantra was to ship fast and learn from users.
etymology: From Sanskrit mantra, 'instrument of thought, sacred text'.

definition: The formal release of a person from slavery.
examples: The archive holds a deed of manumission from 1792.
Her ancestor purchased his own manumission.
etymology: From Latin manumissio, from manus, 'hand', + mittere, 'to send, release'.

definition: Severe wasting of the body from malnutrition; figuratively, decline.
examples: Aid workers treated children suffering from marasmus.
The essay diagnoses a cultural marasmus in the old city.
etymology: From Greek marasmos, 'withering', from marainein, 'to wither'.

definition: A person or animal that roams in search of things to steal or attack.
examples: A raccoon marauder raided the campsite at midnight.
Medieval villages built walls against every marauder.
etymology: From French maraudeur, from marauder, 'to prowl'.

definition: Withering but remaining attached to the plant, as some dead leaves do in winter.
examples: Marcescent oak leaves rattle in the January wind.
The beech hedge stays marcescent until spring.
etymology: From Latin marcescere, 'to begin to wither'.

definition: Small in importance or effect; close to a lower limit.
examples: The new update made only a marginal difference to battery life.
Profits were marginal, so the shop closed after a year.
etymology: From Medieval Latin marginalis, from Latin margo, 'edge'.

definition: Notes written in the margins of a book or manuscript.
examples: The secondhand copy was full of a previous owner's witty marginalia.
Scholars study the marginalia of medieval monks for clues about daily life.
etymology: From medieval Latin marginalia, from Latin margo, 'edge'.

definition: In a clearly noticeable way.
examples: Her mood improved markedly after a good night's sleep.
The new model is markedly quieter than the old one.
etymology: From marked + -ly; the medial -ed- is pronounced as a full syllable.

definition: Made of or resembling marble; cold, smooth, and white.
examples: The actress had a marmoreal beauty that cameras loved.
His marmoreal composure never cracked during the trial.
etymology: From Latin marmoreus, from marmor, 'marble'.

definition: A person who spoils a plan by meddling.
examples: My little brother played marplot and blurted out the surprise.
Every heist film needs a marplot who trips the alarm.
etymology: From mar + plot; popularized by Marplot, a character in Susanna Centlivre's 1709 play The Busy Body.

definition: A strict disciplinarian who insists on rigid obedience to rules.
examples: The new editor is a martinet about comma placement.
Her piano teacher was a martinet who timed every scale.
etymology: Named after Jean Martinet, a 17th-century French army officer known for strict drill.

definition: To be filled with wonder or astonishment.
examples: Visitors marvel at the size of the redwoods.
I still marvel that the old car made it across the country.
etymology: From Old French merveille, from Latin mirabilia, 'wonderful things'.

definition: To pretend to be someone or something one is not.
examples: Spam emails often masquerade as messages from your bank.
He likes to masquerade as an expert on wine.
etymology: From French mascarade, from Italian maschera, 'mask'.

definition: A person who plans and directs a complex scheme or project.
examples: The quiet intern turned out to be the mastermind behind the viral campaign.
Police are still searching for the mastermind of the heist.
etymology: From master + mind, first recorded in the early 18th century.

definition: To chew food thoroughly.
examples: Cows masticate their cud for hours.
Please masticate with your mouth closed.
etymology: From Late Latin masticare, 'to chew', from Greek mastikhan, 'to gnash the teeth'.

definition: A woman who is the powerful head of a family or group.
examples: Grandma is the undisputed matriarch at holiday dinners.
The elephant herd follows its oldest matriarch to water.
etymology: From Latin mater, 'mother', on the pattern of patriarch.

definition: Of, relating to, or occurring in the morning.
examples: My matutinal ritual involves coffee and a crossword.
The matutinal chorus of birds woke the campers.
etymology: From Late Latin matutinalis, from Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn.

definition: Excessively and tearfully sentimental, often as a result of drinking.
examples: Late in the evening he turned maudlin and began toasting long-lost friends.
The movie's maudlin ending felt like an obvious attempt to force tears.
etymology: From Middle English Maudelen, Mary Magdalene, who was often painted weeping.

definition: To talk or move in a rambling, aimless way.
examples: He would maunder on about his vacation while the meeting dragged.
We maundered through the market with no plan at all.
etymology: Of uncertain origin.

definition: An independent person who refuses to follow the usual rules or group.
examples: The maverick filmmaker ignored every studio rule and succeeded anyway.
As a maverick in the party, she often voted against its leaders.
etymology: From Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher who left his calves unbranded.

definition: Overly sentimental in a way that feels false or sickly.
examples: The movie's ending was mawkish and predictable.
He avoided mawkish speeches at the retirement party.
etymology: From obsolete mawk, 'maggot', originally 'nauseated'.

definition: A short statement expressing a general truth or rule of conduct.
examples: His favorite maxim is that you should never shop hungry.
The old maxim about measuring twice saved my bookshelf.
etymology: From Medieval Latin maxima (propositio), 'greatest (proposition)'.

definition: Violent or extreme disorder; chaos.
examples: Black Friday brought total mayhem to the mall.
Two toddlers and a birthday cake can create instant mayhem.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman mahaym, related to maim; originally a legal term for maiming.

definition: Winding and intricate, like a maze.
examples: Coleridge's river ran with a mazy motion through the wood.
We got lost in the mazy lanes of the old town.
etymology: From maze + -y.

definition: Lacking in quantity or quality; small.
examples: He survived on a meager diet of rice and beans.
The meager crowd made the stadium feel empty.
etymology: From Old French maigre, from Latin macer 'thin'.

definition: Afraid to speak frankly or directly; evasive.
examples: The company issued a mealy-mouthed apology.
I want a straight answer, not a mealy-mouthed excuse.
etymology: From mealy, 'soft like meal', + mouthed.

definition: To follow a winding path or wander without a clear purpose.
examples: The creek will meander through the meadow before reaching the lake.
We let the afternoon meander, strolling wherever the streets led.
