etymology: From Greek Maiandros, a winding river in Asia Minor.

definition: Large enough to be noticed or able to be counted and assessed.
examples: Set measurable goals so you know when you have succeeded.
The new policy had a measurable effect on wait times.
etymology: From Old French mesurable, from Latin mensurabilis.

definition: A process or system by which something works or is brought about.
examples: Humor is his favorite defense mechanism.
The app has no mechanism for reporting bugs.
etymology: From Modern Latin mechanismus, from Greek mēkhanē, 'machine'.

definition: To interfere in something that is not one's concern.
examples: Please do not meddle in your sister's wedding plans.
Politicians should not meddle with the court's decisions.
etymology: From Old French medler, 'to mix', from Latin miscere.

definition: Fond of interfering in other people's affairs.
examples: A meddlesome aunt kept rearranging the seating chart.
The meddlesome neighbor reported our shed to the city.
etymology: From meddle + -some.

definition: To help people involved in a disagreement reach an agreement.
examples: A counselor mediated the dispute between the roommates.
The teacher stepped in to mediate between the two groups.
etymology: From Late Latin mediare, 'to be in the middle', from medius.

definition: Of only average quality, neither good nor bad, and unimpressive.
examples: The food was mediocre, so we do not plan to return.
Years of mediocre results finally convinced the owners to hire a new coach.
etymology: From Latin mediocris, 'of middle height', from medius 'middle' + ocris 'rugged mountain'.

definition: A deserved share or reward.
examples: The volunteers received their meed of praise at the gala.
Every soldier earned a meed of honor.
etymology: From Old English mēd, 'reward, wages'.

definition: An obsession with power and an inflated sense of one's own importance.
examples: The tech founder's megalomania alarmed his investors.
Building a statue of yourself suggests a touch of megalomania.
etymology: From Greek megas, 'great', + mania, 'madness'.

definition: Originally a migraine; now chiefly a fit of low spirits or a passing whim.
examples: A gray Sunday always brings on a fit of megrim.
She dismissed his latest scheme as another megrim.
etymology: From Old French migraine, from Greek hēmikrania, 'pain in half the head'.

definition: Deliberate understatement used for effect; also, a kind of cell division.
examples: Calling the hurricane 'a bit of weather' is pure British meiosis.
His meiosis about his injury fooled no one.
etymology: From Greek meiōsis, 'lessening', from meioun, 'to lessen'.

definition: A deep, lingering, often pensive sadness.
examples: A gentle melancholy settles over the beach town in October.
The song captures the melancholy of leaving home.
etymology: From Greek melankholia, 'black bile', once thought to cause sadness.

definition: A mixture of varied elements.
examples: The soup was a melange of roasted vegetables and spices.
The city's architecture is a melange of colonial and modern styles.
etymology: From French mélange, from mêler, 'to mix'.

definition: A confused, noisy fight or scramble involving many people.
examples: A melee broke out over the last discounted television.
The bouquet toss turned into a full melee.
etymology: From French mêlée, 'mixture, scuffle', from mêler, 'to mix'.

definition: The belief that the world can be made better through human effort.
examples: Her meliorism shows in every volunteer shift she works.
The essay argues for a practical meliorism between hope and despair.
etymology: From Latin melior, 'better', + -ism; popularized in the 19th century.

definition: A group of several notes sung on a single syllable.
examples: The soul singer stretched the word 'love' into a dazzling melisma.
Gregorian chant is rich in melisma.
etymology: From Greek melisma, 'song, melody'.

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
examples: The narrator's mellifluous voice made the audiobook a joy.
Italian sounds mellifluous to many ears.
etymology: From late Latin mellifluus, from mel 'honey' + fluere 'to flow'.

definition: A sudden collapse, whether emotional, financial, or of a system.
examples: The toddler had a meltdown in the cereal aisle.
Analysts warned of a market meltdown if rates kept rising.
etymology: From melt + down, originally describing the overheating of a nuclear reactor core.

definition: An object kept as a reminder of a person, place, or event.
examples: She kept a seashell as a memento of the trip.
The ticket stub is my only memento from that concert.
etymology: From Latin memento, 'remember!', imperative of meminisse.

definition: A written account of one's own life and experiences.
examples: The chef's memoir is full of kitchen disasters.
She is writing a memoir about growing up on a farm.
etymology: From French mémoire, 'memory'.

definition: A person or thing likely to cause harm; a threat.
examples: Distracted drivers are a menace on these narrow roads.
The raccoon has become a menace to every trash can on the block.
etymology: From Old French menace, from Latin minacia, from minax, 'threatening'.

definition: A collection of wild animals, or a diverse group of people or things.
examples: Their farmhouse holds a menagerie of rescued goats and geese.
The comedy club drew a menagerie of oddballs.
etymology: From French ménagerie, originally the management of a household or livestock.

definition: Not telling the truth; habitually lying or deceitful.
examples: The mendacious witness changed his story three times in one afternoon.
Voters grew tired of the mendacious claims in the candidate's ads.
etymology: From Latin mendax, 'lying', related to mendum 'fault'.

definition: The quality of being untruthful; habitual lying.
examples: The memoir was exposed as a work of staggering mendacity.
Voters grew weary of the campaign's mendacity.
etymology: From Late Latin mendacitas, from mendax, 'lying'.

definition: A beggar, or a member of a religious order that lives on alms.
examples: The novel opens with a mendicant knocking at the monastery gate.
Each morning the mendicant sat beside the temple steps.
etymology: From Latin mendicant-, from mendicare, 'to beg'.

definition: A tall, upright prehistoric standing stone.
examples: A lone menhir towers over the Breton field.
Hikers rest against the menhir at the trail's summit.
etymology: From Breton men, 'stone', + hir, 'long'.

definition: Requiring little skill and lacking prestige.
examples: Interns are often stuck with menial tasks like filing.
No job is too menial for a founder in the early days.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman meinial, 'domestic', from meinee, 'household'.

definition: A characteristic way of thinking shared by a person or group.
examples: The team has a winning mentality this season.
A scarcity mentality can make people hoard things they never use.
etymology: From mental + -ity, from Latin mens, 'mind'.

definition: Fiendishly clever and cunning, like a devil.
examples: He flashed a Mephistophelean grin across the poker table.
The lawyer's Mephistophelean bargain left his client ruined.
etymology: From Mephistopheles, the devil to whom Faust sells his soul in German legend.

definition: Foul-smelling and noxious.
examples: A mephitic odor rose from the drain.
The mephitic swamp air made the explorers gag.
etymology: From Late Latin mephiticus, from mephitis, 'noxious vapor'.

definition: Relating to trade or merchants.
examples: Venice grew rich as a mercantile republic.
The old mercantile district is now full of galleries.
etymology: From Italian mercantile, from mercante, 'merchant'.

definition: Motivated chiefly by money rather than principle.
examples: His mercenary approach to friendship left him lonely.
Critics called the sequel a mercenary cash grab.
etymology: From Latin mercenarius, 'hired', from merces, 'wages'.

definition: Changing mood or mind quickly and unpredictably.
examples: The mercurial director could be charming at noon and absolutely furious by three.
Her mercurial temper kept the entire staff on edge from the moment she arrived.
etymology: From Mercury, the Roman god, and the planet associated with a quick, changeable temperament.

definition: Attractive in a showy way but actually false or without real value.
examples: The hotel's meretricious decor hid cheap fixtures and thin walls.
Critics dismissed the novel as a meretricious blend of glitter and cliché.
etymology: From Latin meretricius, 'of a prostitute', from meretrix, from mereri 'to earn'.

definition: The quality of being good or deserving praise or reward.
examples: Each proposal will be judged on its merit alone.
There is some merit in waiting until prices drop.
etymology: From Latin meritum, 'something earned', from merere, 'to earn'.

definition: A system in which people advance based on ability and achievement.
examples: The firm claims to be a meritocracy, but connections still matter.
True meritocracy requires equal access to education.
etymology: From merit + -cracy, 'rule'; popularized by Michael Young's 1958 book The Rise of the Meritocracy.

definition: To hold someone's attention so completely that they seem spellbound.
examples: The northern lights can mesmerize even jaded travelers.
A spinning washing machine can mesmerize a toddler for ages.
etymology: Named after Franz Anton Mesmer, an 18th-century physician who practiced a form of hypnotism.

definition: A complete change of form, character, or nature.
examples: The old warehouse underwent a metamorphosis into a bright food hall.
A caterpillar's metamorphosis still amazes me.
etymology: From Greek metamorphōsis, from meta-, 'change', + morphē, 'form'.

definition: A profound change of mind or heart; a transformative shift in outlook.
examples: Her year abroad sparked a metanoia that changed her career plans entirely.
The story traces a miser's metanoia into a generous neighbor.
etymology: From Greek metanoia, 'change of mind, repentance'.

definition: The supposed passing of a soul into a new body after death.
examples: Pythagoras reportedly believed in metempsychosis.
In Joyce's Ulysses, Molly puzzles over the word metempsychosis.
etymology: From Greek metempsukhōsis, from meta-, 'change', + en, 'in', + psukhē, 'soul'.

definition: Extremely rapid in development or success, like a meteor.
examples: Her meteoric rise took her from intern to director in three years.
The app's meteoric growth surprised even its founders.
etymology: From meteor + -ic, from Greek meteōros, 'raised up, lofty'.

definition: Done in an orderly, systematic, step-by-step way.
examples: She is methodical about backing up her photos every Sunday.
A methodical search of the apartment turned up the missing keys.
etymology: From Greek methodikos, from methodos, 'pursuit of knowledge'.

definition: Showing extreme care and attention to every small detail.
examples: The meticulous accountant checked every figure twice before filing the report.
She kept meticulous notes of each experiment in a leather notebook.
etymology: From Latin meticulosus, 'fearful', from metus 'fear'; the sense shifted to 'overly careful'.

definition: A figure of speech in which something is named by a closely associated thing.
examples: Calling the king 'the crown' is a classic metonymy.
When reporters say 'Hollywood', that metonymy stands for the film industry.
etymology: From Greek metōnumia, 'change of name', from meta- + onoma, 'name'.

definition: A standard of measurement used to judge performance or progress.
examples: Sales are not the only metric that matters.
The team tracks one key metric: how many users come back each week.
etymology: From Greek metrikos, from metron, 'measure'.

definition: The ability to handle difficulties with spirit and resilience.
examples: The tough final round really tested the players' mettle.
She proved her mettle by finishing the project alone.
etymology: A variant spelling of metal, used figuratively.

definition: A heavy, unpleasant atmosphere or vapor, physical or emotional.
examples: A miasma of gloom hung over the office after the bad news.
The swamp gave off a miasma that made our eyes water.
etymology: From Greek miasma, 'pollution', from miainein, 'to pollute'.

definition: Something small that represents a much larger whole.
examples: The tiny village is a microcosm of the whole country.
A school cafeteria is a microcosm of society.
etymology: From Greek mikros kosmos, 'little world'.

definition: A person's look or manner, especially as revealing character or mood.
examples: The judge had a stern mien that silenced the courtroom.
Despite his gentle mien, he was a fierce competitor.
etymology: Probably from obsolete demean, 'bearing', influenced by French mine, 'expression'.

definition: To move from one place, region, or system to another.
examples: Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles each fall.
We plan to migrate all our files to the new server this weekend.
etymology: From Latin migrare, 'to move from one place to another'.

definition: An important event or stage in development or progress.
examples: Learning to walk is a big milestone for a toddler.
The app hit a milestone of one million users.
etymology: From mile + stone, a roadside stone marking distance in miles.

definition: A person's social environment or setting.
examples: He thrived in the fast-paced milieu of the newsroom.
The novel captures the artistic milieu of 1920s Paris.
etymology: From French milieu, 'middle', from mi, 'mid', + lieu, 'place'.

definition: To be a powerful factor working against something.
examples: The steep cost militates against buying a new car this year.
Several factors militate against holding the event outdoors.
etymology: From Latin militare, 'to serve as a soldier'.

definition: A timid, submissive person who is easily dominated.
examples: He is no milquetoast; he will push back if the deal is unfair.
The film's hero starts as a milquetoast and ends as a leader.
etymology: From Caspar Milquetoast, a timid comic-strip character created by H. T. Webster in the 1920s.

definition: The representation or imitation of the real world in art and literature.
examples: Realist novels strive for faithful mimesis of everyday life.
Aristotle saw tragedy as a mimesis of action.
etymology: From Greek mimēsis, 'imitation', from mimeisthai, 'to imitate'.

definition: Relating to imitation, especially in art or biology.
examples: The painting's mimetic detail fools the eye.
Some butterflies have mimetic wings that copy toxic species.
etymology: From Greek mimētikos, from mimeisthai, 'to imitate'.

definition: To imitate someone's voice, gestures, or behavior, often to amuse.
examples: My nephew can mimic every teacher at his school.
Some insects mimic twigs to hide from birds.
etymology: From Greek mimikos, from mimos, 'actor, mime'.

definition: Menacing; threatening.
examples: Minacious clouds gathered over the harbor.
He sent a minacious letter to the editor.
etymology: From Latin minax, 'threatening', + -ious.

definition: Expressing a threat; menacing.
examples: The sky took on a minatory shade of green.
The principal sent a minatory email about tardiness.
etymology: From late Latin minatorius, from minari, 'to threaten'.

definition: Aware of and attentive to something; consciously present.
examples: Be mindful of the neighbors when you come home late.
She tries to stay mindful instead of scrolling through every meal.
etymology: From mind + -ful, attested since Middle English.

definition: To mix with others, especially to move around and chat at a gathering.
examples: Grab a drink and mingle before dinner starts.
In the market, the scents of spice and smoke mingle in the air.
etymology: From Middle English menglen, frequentative of mengen, 'to mix'.

definition: A servile follower of a powerful person.
examples: The boss sent a minion to deliver the bad news.
Each villain needs at least one loyal minion.
etymology: From French mignon, 'darling, favorite'.

definition: Extremely small; tiny.
examples: The chance of winning the lottery is minuscule.
She wrote her notes in minuscule handwriting along the margin.
etymology: From French minuscule, from Latin minuscula (littera), 'somewhat smaller (letter)'.

definition: Small, precise, or trivial details of something.
examples: Let's agree on the big picture before we debate the minutiae.
She loves the minutiae of tax law that bore everyone else.
etymology: From Latin minutiae, 'trifles', from minutus, 'small'.

definition: An optical illusion caused by heat, or a hope that proves illusory.
examples: The shimmering lake turned out to be a mirage.
For many renters, owning a home feels like a mirage.
etymology: From French mirage, from se mirer, 'to be reflected'.

definition: A stretch of swampy ground, or a difficult situation one cannot escape.
examples: The truck sank axle-deep in the mire.
The company is stuck in a mire of debt.
etymology: From Old Norse mýrr, 'bog'.

definition: Amusement expressed in laughter.
examples: His dance moves were a source of great mirth at the wedding.
She could barely contain her mirth during the solemn speech.
etymology: From Old English myrgth, related to merry.

definition: An unfortunate incident or mishap.
examples: Our road trip was one misadventure after another.
Losing our passports in Rome was a misadventure we still laugh about.
etymology: From Old French mesaventure, from mes- 'badly' + aventure, 'chance'.

definition: A person who dislikes and avoids other people.
examples: The misanthrope moved to a remote cabin to escape human company.
Though he played the misanthrope, he secretly enjoyed the neighbors' visits.
etymology: From Greek misanthropos, from misein 'to hate' + anthropos 'human being'.

definition: Badly conceived, planned, or designed.
examples: The misbegotten rebrand confused loyal customers.
They abandoned their misbegotten scheme to sell ice in Alaska.
etymology: From mis- + begotten, past participle of beget.

definition: A mixture of various things, or a collection of assorted writings.
examples: The drawer holds a miscellany of cables, coins, and keys.
She published a miscellany of essays and recipes.
etymology: From Latin miscellanea, from miscellus, 'mixed'.

definition: Playful misbehavior or trouble, especially by children.
examples: The puppy gets into mischief whenever we leave the room.
There was a glint of mischief in her eyes as she shuffled the cards.
etymology: From Old French meschief, 'misfortune', from meschever, 'to come to grief'.

definition: Playfully causing minor trouble or annoyance.
examples: The mischievous cat knocked every pen off my desk.
He gave a mischievous grin before pulling the prank.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman meschevous, from meschief, 'misfortune'.

definition: A mistaken view or belief based on faulty understanding.
examples: It is a common misconception that goldfish have three-second memories.
The video cleared up a misconception I had held since school.
etymology: From mis- 'wrongly' + conception.

definition: To interpret someone's words or actions wrongly.
examples: Please do not misconstrue my silence as agreement.
Short texts are easy to misconstrue.
etymology: From mis- + construe, from Latin construere, 'to build'.

definition: A person who behaves badly or breaks the law.
examples: Some miscreant keeps stealing our garden gnomes.
The teacher glared at the miscreant who had hidden the chalk.
etymology: From Old French mescreant, 'unbeliever', from mes- + creant, 'believing'.

definition: A wicked or illegal act.
examples: Every misdeed of the old regime came to light.
He confessed to a childhood misdeed involving his sister's bike.
etymology: From Old English misdǣd, from mis- + dǣd, 'deed'.

definition: To suspect, distrust, or have doubts about something.
examples: I misdoubt his story about the lost homework.
Never misdoubt your instinct about a bad deal.
etymology: From mis- + doubt.

definition: A ledge under a folding choir seat that supports a person standing.
examples: Each misericord in the cathedral is carved with a different beast.
The guide lifted a seat to reveal the misericord beneath.
etymology: From Latin misericordia, 'compassion', as the seat was a mercy to those standing through long services.

definition: A feeling of doubt or worry about whether something is right.
examples: I signed the lease, but not without some misgiving.
Her only misgiving was leaving the dog with strangers.
etymology: From mis- + giving, from the old verb misgive, 'to fill with doubt'.

definition: A minor accident or piece of bad luck.
examples: Apart from one mishap with the tent, the camping trip went smoothly.
A kitchen mishap left the ceiling covered in flour.
etymology: From mis- + hap, 'luck', from Old Norse happ.

definition: A confused mixture of unrelated things.
examples: The menu is a mishmash of tacos, sushi, and pasta.
His speech was a mishmash of quotes and clichés.
etymology: A reduplication of mash.

definition: A name or label that is wrong or misleading.
examples: Calling it a 'quick fix' is a misnomer; it took three weeks.
The term 'koala bear' is a misnomer, since koalas are marsupials.
etymology: From Old French mesnommer, 'to misname', from mes-, 'wrongly', + nommer, 'to name'.

definition: Hatred of marriage.
examples: Her uncle's misogamy was a running joke at weddings.
The poet's misogamy shows up in every sonnet.
etymology: From Greek misein, 'to hate', + gamos, 'marriage'.

definition: A hatred or distrust of reasoning and argument.
examples: Plato warned that disappointment in debate can breed misology.
The forum descended into misology and name-calling.
etymology: From Greek misologia, from misein, 'to hate', + logos, 'reason'.

definition: Hatred or fear of anything new or changed.
examples: His misoneism kept him clinging to a flip phone.
Institutional misoneism blocked every reform.
etymology: From Italian misoneismo, from Greek misein, 'to hate', + neos, 'new'.

definition: Concealment of a crime, or a mistaken interpretation.
examples: He was charged with misprision for failing to report the plot.
The critic's misprision of the poem became famous in its own right.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman mesprision, 'error', from mesprendre, 'to make a mistake'.

definition: A letter or message, especially a long or official one.
examples: The landlord sent a stern missive about recycling.
Her weekly missive to the team doubles as a newsletter.
etymology: From Medieval Latin missivus, from mittere, 'to send'.

definition: A clumsy or badly judged action; a mistake.
examples: One misstep on the icy trail could be dangerous.
The ad campaign was a rare misstep for the brand.
etymology: From mis- + step.

definition: A lack of trust; suspicion.
examples: Years of broken promises bred deep mistrust between the neighbors.
There is widespread mistrust of online reviews.
etymology: From mis- + trust.

definition: Immunity to a poison gained by taking gradually increasing doses of it.
examples: The assassin's mithridatism let him drink from the poisoned cup unharmed.
Years of bad coffee have given me a kind of mithridatism.
etymology: Named after Mithridates VI of Pontus, who reputedly dosed himself with poisons to gain immunity.

definition: To make something bad less severe, harsh, or painful.
examples: Planting more trees along streets can mitigate the effects of heat in crowded cities.
The company took steps to mitigate the damage from the data leak.
etymology: From Latin mitigare, 'to soften', from mitis 'mild' + agere 'to do'.

definition: A light, misty drizzle.
examples: We walked the cliffs in a cold mizzle.
A gray mizzle hung over the harbor all morning.
etymology: Probably from Low German dialect miseln, 'to drizzle'.

definition: A pattern of letters, words, or ideas that helps someone remember something.
examples: I still use a mnemonic to remember the order of the planets.
A good mnemonic can turn a dull list into a silly story.
etymology: From Greek mnēmonikos, from mnēmōn, 'mindful'.

definition: To organize people or resources for action toward a goal.
examples: The neighborhood managed to mobilize two hundred volunteers overnight.
It takes time to mobilize support for a new law.
etymology: From French mobiliser, from mobile, from Latin mobilis, 'movable'.

definition: Average in amount or degree; not extreme.
examples: Bake the bread in a moderate oven for forty minutes.
She holds moderate views and dislikes shouting matches.
etymology: From Latin moderatus, 'kept within bounds', from moderari.

definition: Unassuming about one's abilities, or moderate in size and amount.
examples: She is modest about her award and rarely mentions it.
They live in a modest house at the end of the street.
etymology: From Latin modestus, 'keeping due measure'.

definition: A small quantity of something, especially something desirable.
examples: With a modicum of planning, the trip could have been much easier.
He finally achieved a modicum of fame with his third album.
etymology: From Latin modicum, 'a little', from modicus, 'moderate'.

definition: Fashionable, sometimes in a fleeting or superficial way.
examples: The café has a modish menu of oat-milk everything.
Modish jargon fills every slide of the presentation.
etymology: From mode, 'fashion', + -ish.

definition: To adjust or vary the strength, tone, or pitch of something.
examples: Good speakers modulate their voices to keep listeners engaged.
Learn to modulate your reactions during tense meetings.
etymology: From Latin modulari, 'to measure, make melody', from modus, 'measure'.

definition: An important or powerful person, especially in business or media.
examples: The real estate mogul owns half of downtown.
She went from blogger to media mogul in a decade.
etymology: From Mughal, the Muslim dynasty that ruled much of India, via Persian mughul, 'Mongol'.

definition: Each of two parts into which something is divided; a portion.
examples: Each heir received a moiety of the estate.
Only a moiety of the budget reached the schools.
etymology: From Old French moitie, from Latin medietas, 'middle, half'.

definition: To slowly decay or crumble.
examples: Old letters molder in a box in the attic.
Do not let good ideas molder in a forgotten folder.
etymology: Probably from mold, 'loose earth', + -er.

definition: To calm someone's anger or anxiety by making them feel less upset.
examples: The manager offered a refund to mollify the furious customer.
Nothing I said could mollify her after the missed anniversary dinner.
etymology: From Latin mollificare, from mollis 'soft' + facere 'to make'.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time; brief.
examples: There was a momentary silence before everyone laughed.
It was just a momentary lapse in concentration.
etymology: From Latin momentarius, from momentum, 'moment'.

definition: Of great importance, especially for the future.
examples: Moving abroad was a momentous decision for the whole family.
The vote marked a momentous shift in public opinion.
etymology: From moment in its older sense of 'importance' + -ous.

definition: The force or energy that keeps something moving or growing.
examples: After two quick wins, the team had real momentum.
Don't lose momentum by taking a long break halfway through.
etymology: From Latin momentum, 'movement', from movere 'to move'.

definition: Relating to monks or monastic life.
examples: The library has a hushed, monachal calm.
Her monachal routine left no room for parties.
etymology: From Late Latin monachalis, from monachus, 'monk'.

definition: A single indivisible unit, especially in philosophy.
examples: Leibniz pictured each soul as a monad, a tiny world sealed off from all others.
For the mystic, the soul is a monad reflecting the whole.
etymology: From Greek monas, 'unit', from monos, 'alone'.

definition: Resembling the simple, secluded life of monks.
examples: During exam week he lives a monastic life of rice and textbooks.
The cabin has a monastic simplicity: a bed, a desk, a lamp.
etymology: From Greek monastikos, from monazein, 'to live alone'.

definition: A misheard word or phrase, especially in a song lyric.
examples: For years I sang a mondegreen, convinced the lyric was about a bathroom on the right.
Every family has a favorite mondegreen from a holiday carol.
etymology: Coined in 1954 by Sylvia Wright from her mishearing of 'laid him on the green' as 'Lady Mondegreen'.

definition: A name or nickname.
examples: The rapper adopted a new moniker for his second album.
Her moniker at work is 'the fixer'.
etymology: Originally slang, of uncertain origin; possibly from Shelta munnik, 'name'.

definition: A warning of impending danger, or a formal admonition.
examples: The rising wind was a monition of the coming squall.
The bishop issued a monition to the wayward priest.
etymology: From Latin monitio, from monere, 'to warn'.

definition: A poem lamenting someone's death, or a song for a single voice.
examples: Milton wrote 'Lycidas' as a monody for a drowned friend.
A lone cellist played a monody at the memorial.
etymology: From Greek monōidia, from monos, 'single', + ōidē, 'song'.

definition: Massive, uniform, and resistant to change.
examples: Voters are not a monolithic bloc.
The startup replaced its monolithic software with small services.
etymology: From monolith, from Greek monolithos, 'made of a single stone'.

definition: An exaggerated obsession with a single subject or idea.
examples: Ahab's monomania drives him across the oceans after the whale.
Her monomania for productivity apps baffles her friends.
etymology: From Greek monos, 'single', + mania, 'madness', via French monomanie.

definition: Exclusive control of a market, product, or thing by one party.
examples: The company held a monopoly on the town's internet service.
My brother thinks he has a monopoly on good taste.
etymology: From Greek monopōlion, from monos, 'single', + pōlein, 'to sell'.

definition: Dull and tedious because unchanging and repetitive.
examples: Data entry is monotonous, so I listen to podcasts while I work.
The drive across the plains was flat and monotonous.
etymology: From Greek monotonos, 'of one tone'.

definition: Great in importance, size, or extent.
examples: Cleaning out the garage was a monumental task.
Forgetting the rings was a monumental blunder.
etymology: From Latin monumentum, 'memorial', from monere, 'to remind'.

definition: A foolish, absent-minded person who daydreams.
examples: He mooned around the office like a lovesick mooncalf.
Stop gazing out the window like a mooncalf and help me.
etymology: From moon + calf, once used of a misshapen birth blamed on the moon's influence.

definition: Open to debate, or no longer relevant in practice.
examples: Since the concert sold out, the question of seats is moot.
Whether he meant it is a moot point now.
etymology: From Old English mōt, 'assembly', where matters were debated.

definition: The confidence and enthusiasm of a person or group.
examples: Free lunches on Fridays did wonders for staff morale.
Morale was low after the team's fifth straight loss.
etymology: From French moral, 'good conduct, spirit', spelled morale to keep the stress on the last syllable.

definition: To comment on right and wrong, typically in a self-righteous way.
examples: I asked for help, not for you to moralize about my spending.
The film never stops to moralize; it lets the story speak.
etymology: From French moraliser, from moral, from Latin moralis.

definition: A complicated situation that is hard to escape; also, a swamp.
examples: The project sank into a morass of paperwork.
Lawmakers are stuck in a morass of competing demands.
etymology: From Dutch moeras, 'marsh', from Old French marais.

definition: A temporary ban or suspension of an activity.
examples: The city declared a moratorium on new hotel construction.
I have placed a moratorium on discussing politics at dinner.
etymology: From Late Latin moratorius, 'delaying', from morari, 'to delay'.

definition: Having an unhealthy interest in disturbing subjects such as death.
examples: She has a morbid fascination with true-crime podcasts.
Sorry for the morbid question, but have you written a will?
etymology: From Latin morbidus, from morbus, 'disease'.

definition: Sharply sarcastic or biting, especially in humor.
examples: Her mordant wit made the panel discussion memorable.
The cartoon offers mordant commentary on office life.
etymology: From French mordre, from Latin mordere, 'to bite'.

definition: As a further matter; besides.
examples: The plan is cheap; moreover, it can start right away.
The hotel was noisy and, moreover, far from the beach.
etymology: From Middle English more over, 'further beyond'.

definition: The essential customs and conventions of a community.
examples: The novel skewers the social mores of 1950s suburbia.
Office mores have changed a lot since remote work took off.
etymology: From Latin mores, plural of mos, 'custom'.

definition: Of a marriage between royalty and a commoner, whose spouse and children gain no rank.
examples: The archduke's morganatic marriage barred his children from the throne.
Royal advisers proposed a morganatic union to settle the crisis.
etymology: From Medieval Latin matrimonium ad morganaticam, from a Germanic word for 'morning gift'.

definition: Near death, or in terminal decline and lacking vitality.
examples: The new owners revived a moribund newspaper.
Downtown felt moribund until the farmers' market arrived.
etymology: From Latin moribundus, from mori, 'to die'.

definition: Gloomy, sullen, and unwilling to be cheerful.
examples: He sat morose in the corner while everyone else laughed and danced around him.
The rainy week left the whole household feeling morose and strangely quiet at dinner.
etymology: From Latin morosus, 'peevish, fussy', from mos 'manner, habit'.

definition: A small piece of food, or a small amount of something.
examples: The dog waited under the table for every fallen morsel.
He offered not a morsel of information about the deal.
etymology: From Old French morsel, diminutive of mors, 'a bite'.

definition: To cause someone to feel deeply embarrassed or humiliated.
examples: My dad loves to mortify me by dancing in public.
Nothing could mortify him more than a typo in his own wedding speech.
etymology: From Latin mortificare, 'to put to death', from mors, 'death'.

definition: The lasting control of the present by the dead or the past.
examples: The founder's will imposed a mortmain on the charity's every decision.
Old traditions hold the town in a kind of mortmain.
etymology: From Old French mortemain, from Medieval Latin mortua manus, 'dead hand'.

definition: A witty remark.
examples: She closed the debate with a perfectly timed mot.
His best mot ended up on a T-shirt.
etymology: From French mot, 'word', from Latin muttum, 'grunt'.

definition: A recurring idea, image, or pattern in a work of art or design.
examples: Water is a recurring motif in all of her paintings.
The wallpaper has a delicate leaf motif.
etymology: From French motif, 'motive, pattern'.

definition: Made up of a varied, mismatched mixture of people or things.
examples: A motley crew of retirees and students ran the community garden.
The shelf held a motley assortment of mugs.
etymology: From Middle English motlei, possibly from mote, 'speck'; once the parti-colored dress of a jester.

definition: A small pouting grimace.
examples: She made a moue of distaste at the instant coffee.
The model's practiced moue sold a million lipsticks.
etymology: From French moue, 'pout', of Germanic origin.

definition: A swindler or charlatan who deceives people.
examples: The traveling mountebank sold bottles of colored water as a cure-all.
Critics called the self-proclaimed expert a mountebank.
etymology: From Italian montambanco, 'one who climbs on a bench', from monta in banco.

definition: Courage, determination, and energy; nerve.
examples: It took real moxie to pitch her idea to the CEO in the elevator.
The underdog team showed plenty of moxie in the final.
etymology: From Moxie, the brand name of an American soft drink sold since the 1880s.

definition: Sticky and slimy, like a plant gum.
examples: Okra releases a mucilaginous liquid when cooked.
Chia seeds turn mucilaginous after soaking.
etymology: From Late Latin mucilago, 'musty juice', from mucus.

definition: A journalist who searches out and exposes scandal and corruption.
examples: Upton Sinclair was a famous muckraker of the early 1900s.
The senator dismissed the reporter as a muckraker.
etymology: From muckrake; popularized by Theodore Roosevelt in a 1906 speech.

definition: A confused or disorganized state.
examples: My tax receipts are in a complete muddle.
The schedule change left everyone in a muddle.
etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch moddelen, 'to make water muddy'.

definition: A person who scavenges riverbank mud for objects of value.
examples: A mudlark found a Roman coin on the Thames foreshore.
At low tide the mudlark heads out with a trowel and bucket.
etymology: From mud + lark, the bird; used in Victorian London for children who scavenged the river.

definition: To wrap or cover something to deaden its sound.
examples: Thick curtains help muffle the traffic noise.
She tried to muffle her laughter with a pillow.
etymology: Probably from Old French moufle, 'mitten'.

definition: Plain clothes worn by someone who usually wears a uniform.
examples: The colonel looked oddly ordinary in mufti.
Fridays at the bank are mufti days.
etymology: Probably from mufti, a Muslim legal scholar, whose robes suggested off-duty dress to British officers.

definition: A person who remains independent or neutral, especially in politics.
examples: As a lifelong mugwump, he refuses to join either party.
The mugwump on the committee cast the deciding vote.
etymology: From Massachusett mugquomp, 'great chief'; applied in 1884 to Republicans who refused to back their party's nominee.

definition: To extract money from someone by fine, taxation, or fraud.
examples: Scammers mulct retirees with fake tech-support calls.
The court did not mulct the company as heavily as expected.
etymology: From Latin mulcta, 'a fine'.

definition: Womanly qualities; womanhood.
examples: The sculptor sought to capture muliebrity in bronze.
Victorian critics praised the heroine's gentle muliebrity.
etymology: From Late Latin muliebritas, from mulier, 'woman'.

definition: To think about something carefully over time.
examples: Let me mull it over before I give you an answer.
She mulled the job offer for a week.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 19th century.

definition: A state of gloomy sulkiness; low spirits.
examples: A rainy Monday gives me the mulligrubs.
He sat in the corner with a bad case of the mulligrubs.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; a fanciful word first recorded in the late 16th century.

definition: Having many different aspects or features.
examples: Homelessness is a multifaceted problem with no single fix.
She is a multifaceted artist who paints, sings, and codes.
etymology: From multi- 'many' + faceted, from facet.

definition: Having great variety; of many kinds.
examples: Her multifarious interests range from beekeeping to opera.
The city's multifarious food scene keeps critics busy.
etymology: From Latin multifarius, 'manifold'.

definition: A very large number of people or things.
examples: The app offers a multitude of ways to customize your feed.
A multitude of fans waited outside the stadium.
etymology: From Latin multitudo, from multus, 'many'.

definition: Language or ritual that is meaningless or deliberately confusing.
examples: The contract was full of legal mumbo-jumbo.
He dismissed astrology as mumbo-jumbo.
etymology: From Mumbo Jumbo, described by 18th-century European travelers as a West African masked figure; the exact source is uncertain.

definition: Ridiculous, pretentious ceremony or ritual.
examples: The award show was three hours of empty mummery.
He dismissed the corporate retreat as mummery.
etymology: From Old French mommerie, from momer, 'to act in a mime'.

definition: A stubborn clinging to an error or outdated custom, or a person who does so.
examples: Insisting on the wrong name after being corrected is a true mumpsimus.
The office mumpsimus still prints every email.
etymology: From a story about a priest who misread Latin sumpsimus as 'mumpsimus' and refused correction.

definition: Ordinary and dull, lacking excitement or interest.
examples: He escaped the mundane routine of office life by traveling every summer.
Even mundane chores like washing dishes can be calming with some music.
etymology: From Latin mundanus, 'of the world', from mundus 'world'.

definition: Remarkably generous, especially in giving gifts or money.
examples: A munificent donor funded the entire new wing of the library.
The company's munificent bonuses made it the most envied employer in town.
etymology: From Latin munificus, from munus 'gift, duty' + facere 'to make'.

definition: Dark and dirty, or unclear and suspicious.
examples: We could not see the bottom of the murky pond.
The company's finances remain murky.
etymology: From murk, 'darkness', of Scandinavian origin, + -y.

definition: An infectious disease of cattle; archaically, a plague.
examples: A murrain swept through the valley's herds that winter.
The chronicles record a murrain that killed half the sheep.
etymology: From Old French morine, 'pestilence', from Latin mori, 'to die'.

definition: To gather or summon something, such as courage or support.
examples: He finally managed to muster the courage to ask her to dance.
The team mustered enough votes to pass the proposal.
etymology: From Old French moustrer, from Latin monstrare 'to show'.

definition: Liable to change; changeable.
examples: Fashion is mutable, but good tailoring lasts.
Our plans for the weekend are highly mutable.
etymology: From Latin mutabilis, from mutare, 'to change'.

definition: Rebellious, or refusing to obey those in authority.
examples: The crew grew mutinous after weeks of short rations.
My kids turn mutinous when bedtime is announced.
etymology: From mutiny, from obsolete French mutin, 'rebellious'.

definition: To speak quietly and indistinctly, often in complaint.
examples: I heard him mutter something about the price.
Commuters mutter whenever the train stalls in the tunnel.
etymology: From Middle English moteren, probably imitative of the sound.

definition: To prevent a person or group from speaking freely.
examples: The regime tried to muzzle independent newspapers.
You cannot muzzle employees who report safety problems.
etymology: From Old French musel, diminutive of muse, 'snout'.

definition: Lacking foresight or broad thinking; also, nearsighted.
examples: Cutting the research budget is a myopic way to save money.
His myopic focus on quarterly numbers hurt the brand.
etymology: From myopia, from Greek muōps, from muein, 'to shut', + ōps, 'eye'.

definition: Too many to count; extremely large in number or variety.
examples: The city offers myriad options for dinner, from simple street food to fine dining.
Scientists face myriad challenges when they try to study the deepest parts of the ocean.
etymology: From Greek myrias, meaning 'ten thousand'.

definition: A follower who carries out orders unquestioningly, often brutally.
examples: The dictator's every myrmidon was ready to crush dissent.
She arrived with a myrmidon from legal in tow.
etymology: From the Myrmidons, the warriors who followed Achilles in Homer's Iliad.

definition: A person who initiates others into mystical beliefs or obscure knowledge.
examples: The yoga retreat was led by a self-styled mystagogue.
In the seminar, the professor played mystagogue to Heidegger's texts.
etymology: From Greek mustagōgos, from mustēs, 'initiate', + agōgos, 'leading'.

definition: To utterly bewilder or puzzle someone.
examples: His sudden resignation continues to mystify his coworkers.
Magic tricks still mystify me, even when I know the secret exists.
etymology: From French mystifier, from mystère, 'mystery'.

definition: An air of mystery and glamour surrounding someone or something.
examples: The chef's refusal to give interviews only added to her mystique.
Vinyl records have a mystique that streaming lacks.
etymology: From French mystique, 'mystic'.

definition: An abnormal tendency to exaggerate or tell lies.
examples: His mythomania spun a minor fender bender into a car chase.
The documentary explores the mythomania of a con artist.
etymology: From Greek muthos, 'story', + mania, 'madness', via French mythomanie.

definition: Relating to the making of myths; creating new mythology.
examples: Tolkien's mythopoeic ambition produced a whole invented history.
The band's albums have a mythopoeic grandeur.
etymology: From Greek muthopoios, 'myth-maker', from muthos, 'story', + poiein, 'to make'.

definition: Having the iridescent sheen of mother-of-pearl.
examples: The shell's nacreous interior shimmered pink and silver.
Nacreous clouds glow in the polar winter sky.
etymology: From nacre, 'mother-of-pearl', via French, ultimately from Arabic.

definition: The lowest point of a situation, fortune, or period.
examples: Losing his job and his apartment in one week was the nadir of his year.
The team's morale hit its nadir after the fifth straight loss.
etymology: From Arabic nazir as-samt, 'opposite the zenith', via Medieval Latin.

definition: To keep criticizing or reminding someone in an annoying way.
examples: I hate to nag, but the rent is due tomorrow.
Doubts about the decision continued to nag at her.
etymology: Probably of Scandinavian or Low German origin, originally meaning 'to gnaw'.

definition: A water nymph of rivers, springs, and lakes in Greek myth.
examples: Legend says a naiad guards the spring at the top of the hill.
She swam like a naiad, barely rippling the water.
etymology: From Greek Naias, related to naein 'to flow'.

definition: A birth or origin, especially of an idea or movement.
examples: The exhibit traces the naissance of hip-hop in the Bronx.
Few noticed the naissance of the idea in a late-night chat.
etymology: From French naissance 'birth', from Latin nasci 'to be born'.

definition: A person or thing with the same name as another, especially one named after it.
examples: The ship's namesake attended its launch.
My son met his namesake, my grandfather, only once.
etymology: From name + sake, probably from the phrase 'for the name's sake'.

definition: Excessive interest in or admiration of oneself.
examples: His narcissism showed in the forty selfies he posted from one dinner.
Psychologists distinguish healthy self-esteem from narcissism.
etymology: From Narcissus, the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection.

definition: To tell a story or give a spoken account of events.
examples: A famous actor will narrate the nature documentary.
My dad likes to narrate everything the dog does.
etymology: From Latin narrare 'to relate', from gnarus 'knowing'.

definition: A story or account of connected events, or a way of explaining them.
examples: The campaign tried to control the narrative after the debate.
Her novel weaves three lives into a single narrative.
etymology: From Latin narrativus 'telling a story', from narrare 'to relate'.

definition: Not a single one; used in phrases like 'nary a'.
examples: We waited all day and saw nary a whale.
The speech had nary a mention of the budget.
etymology: A dialect variant of ne'er a, 'never a'.

definition: Just beginning to exist and showing signs of future growth.
examples: The nascent startup has only three employees, a tiny office, and one big idea.
Scientists across the country are studying the nascent field of quantum biology with great excitement.
etymology: From Latin nascens, 'being born', from nasci 'to be born'.

definition: Swimming or floating.
examples: Natant shrimp darted among the mangrove roots.
Water lilies spread their natant leaves across the pond.
etymology: From Latin natare 'to swim'.

definition: An indoor swimming pool or the building that houses it.
examples: The swim meet was held at the university natatorium.
The old natatorium smelled permanently of chlorine.
etymology: From Late Latin natatorium 'swimming place', from natare 'to swim'.

definition: A policy or attitude favoring native-born inhabitants over immigrants.
examples: The candidate's speeches leaned heavily on nativism.
Historians trace waves of nativism in American politics.
etymology: From native, from Latin nativus 'innate', + -ism.

definition: To chat casually and at length about unimportant things.
examples: The two neighbors natter over the fence every morning.
We could natter for hours about nothing at all.
etymology: Originally a dialect word meaning 'to grumble', probably imitative.

definition: Smart, neat, and fashionable in dress.
examples: He showed up in a natty tweed suit and a bow tie.
The natty doorman tipped his hat to every guest.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; possibly related to neat.

definition: An artistic or literary style that depicts life realistically and in detail.
examples: The film's naturalism makes the family's struggles painfully real.
Nineteenth-century naturalism portrayed workers' lives without romance.
etymology: From natural, from Latin naturalis, + -ism.

definition: Nothing at all; zero or no result.
examples: All our planning came to naught when the venue canceled.
Her warnings went for naught.
etymology: From Old English nawiht, from na 'no' + wiht 'thing'.

definition: To make someone feel sick or disgusted.
examples: Long bus rides nauseate me.
Hypocrisy like that would nauseate anyone.
etymology: From Latin nauseare 'to be seasick', from Greek naus 'ship'.

definition: Relating to ships, sailors, or navigation.
examples: The bar had a nautical theme, with ropes and anchors everywhere.
A nautical mile is slightly longer than a land mile.
etymology: From Greek nautikos, from nautes 'sailor'.

definition: Excessive self-absorption or contemplation of oneself or a single issue.
examples: Less navel-gazing and more action, please.
The memoir drifts into navel-gazing in its middle chapters.
etymology: From navel + gazing, alluding to contemplating one's own navel.

definition: Able to be traveled through or found one's way around.
examples: The river is navigable only in spring.
The redesigned website is far more navigable.
etymology: From Latin navigabilis, from navigare 'to sail'.

definition: A person who habitually criticizes or expresses doubt about plans.
examples: Every bold idea has at least one naysayer in the room.
She proved the naysayer wrong by finishing the marathon.
etymology: From nay 'no', from Old Norse nei, + sayer.

definition: A timid, meek, and ineffectual person.
examples: In the film, a mild nebbish discovers he has superpowers.
He played the nebbish so well that audiences forgot he was a heartthrob.
etymology: From Yiddish nebekh 'poor thing'.

definition: Vague, unclear, and lacking definite form.
examples: The manager gave only a nebulous idea of what the new project would require.
Her memories of that long summer were nebulous and dreamlike, more feeling than fact.
etymology: From Latin nebulosus, 'cloudy', from nebula 'mist, cloud'.

definition: To make something necessary as a result or consequence.
examples: The leak will necessitate replacing the whole pipe.
Budget cuts may necessitate layoffs.
etymology: From Medieval Latin necessitare, from necessitas 'necessity'.

definition: A list of people who have died recently, or an obituary.
examples: The alumni magazine's necrology grows longer every year.
He wrote a tender necrology for his mentor.
etymology: From Greek nekros 'dead person' + -logy.

definition: Supposed communication with the dead, or black magic generally.
examples: The villain of the fantasy series dabbles in necromancy.
Reviving that failed TV show would take actual necromancy.
etymology: From Greek nekromanteia, from nekros 'corpse' + manteia 'divination'.

definition: Unnecessary, especially in a way that could have been avoided.
examples: The meeting caused needless confusion about the deadline.
Needless to say, we never went back to that restaurant.
etymology: From need, from Old English nied, plus the suffix -less.

definition: Too wicked or abominable to be spoken of.
examples: The tyrant's nefandous crimes were only revealed decades later.
Horror writers love a nefandous ritual in a crumbling crypt.
etymology: From Latin nefandus 'unspeakable', from ne- 'not' + fari 'to speak'.

definition: Wicked or criminal in a deliberate, scheming way.
examples: The villain's nefarious plan involved poisoning the city's water supply.
Investigators uncovered a nefarious network behind the stolen identities.
etymology: From Latin nefarius, 'wicked', from nefas 'a crime against divine law'.

definition: To cancel out the effect of something.
examples: A late-night pizza can negate a whole day of healthy eating.
One rude comment can negate a dozen compliments.
etymology: From Latin negare 'to deny'.

definition: To fail to give proper care or attention to something.
examples: Don't neglect your sleep during exam season.
Owners who neglect their houseplants end up with crispy leaves.
etymology: From Latin neglegere 'to disregard'.

definition: Failing to take proper care in doing something.
examples: The court found the driver negligent for texting at the wheel.
A negligent landlord ignored the leaking roof for months.
etymology: From Latin neglegere 'to disregard', from neg- 'not' + legere 'to choose'.

definition: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.
examples: The price difference between the two brands is negligible.
Side effects from the vaccine were negligible.
etymology: From French négligible, from Latin neglegere 'to disregard'.

definition: A long-standing rival or something that a person cannot overcome.
examples: Parallel parking remains my nemesis.
The detective finally faced his old nemesis.
etymology: From Greek Nemesis, the goddess of retribution, from nemein 'to give what is due'.

definition: A newly coined word or expression.
examples: 'Doomscrolling' was a neologism that quickly went mainstream.
Shakespeare is credited with many a neologism.
etymology: From French néologisme, from Greek neos 'new' + logos 'word'.

definition: A strong attraction to novelty and new things.
examples: Her neophilia means she owns every new gadget on launch day.
Tech culture runs on neophilia.
etymology: From Greek neos 'new' + -philia 'love of'.

definition: A beginner or newcomer to a subject, skill, or activity.
examples: As a neophyte climber, she hired a guide for her first mountain.
The forum is friendly to every neophyte who asks a question.
etymology: From Greek neophytos, 'newly planted', from neos 'new' + phyein 'to plant'.

definition: The retention of juvenile features into adulthood.
examples: The axolotl is a famous case of neoteny, staying larval all its life.
Some scientists link dogs' puppyish faces to neoteny.
etymology: From German Neotenie, from Greek neos 'young' + teinein 'to extend'.

definition: Recent, new, or modern.
examples: The museum mixes classical sculpture with neoteric installations.
His neoteric slang baffled his grandparents.
etymology: From Greek neoterikos 'youthful', from neoteros 'younger'.

definition: Something that brings forgetfulness of grief or pain.
examples: For him, music was a nepenthe after the funeral.
Binge-watching has become my nepenthe for bad weeks.
etymology: From Greek nepenthes 'banishing pain', a drug mentioned in Homer's Odyssey.

definition: The scientific study of clouds.
examples: Her love of watching the sky turned into a career in nephology.
Nephology helps meteorologists predict storms.
etymology: From Greek nephos 'cloud' + -logy.

definition: The practice of favoring relatives or friends, especially with jobs.
examples: Hiring his unqualified nephew was blatant nepotism.
Hollywood is often accused of nepotism.
etymology: From Italian nepotismo, from nipote 'nephew', referring to popes who favored relatives.

definition: Courage or boldness, sometimes to the point of rudeness.
examples: It took a lot of nerve to ask for a raise in her first month.
He had the nerve to cut in line and then complain about the wait.
etymology: From Latin nervus 'sinew, tendon'.

definition: Bold or impudent, or in British use, nervous and jumpy.
examples: It was nervy of him to ask the CEO for a ride home.
She made a nervy move by quitting before she had another offer.
etymology: From nerve, from Latin nervus 'sinew', + -y.

definition: Lacking knowledge; ignorant.
examples: The nescient tourist asked where the Eiffel Tower was while standing beneath it.
We are all nescient of what tomorrow holds.
etymology: From Latin nescire 'to not know', from ne- 'not' + scire 'to know'.

definition: A wise old man, especially a respected senior figure in a field.
examples: At ninety, he was the nestor of American jazz critics.
Young reporters sought out the newsroom's nestor for advice.
etymology: From Nestor, the aged and wise king of Pylos in Homer's Iliad.

definition: The underworld of the dead, or a hidden, shadowy realm.
examples: The novel explores the netherworld of underground gambling.
In the myth, the hero descends into the netherworld.
etymology: From nether 'lower', from Old English neothera, + world.

definition: To irritate or annoy someone.
examples: Comments about her age always nettle her.
His smug tone seemed designed to nettle the panel.
etymology: From Old English netele, the stinging plant, whose sting suggested irritation.

definition: A dated diagnosis of chronic fatigue, anxiety, and irritability.
examples: Victorian doctors blamed neurasthenia on the pace of modern life.
The heroine retreats to the country to cure her neurasthenia.
etymology: From Greek neuron 'nerve' + astheneia 'weakness'.

definition: A persistent anxiety or obsessive pattern of thought.
examples: Checking the stove five times is my particular neurosis.
Woody Allen built a career on comic neurosis.
etymology: Coined in the 18th century from Greek neuron 'nerve' + -osis.

definition: Excessively anxious, sensitive, or obsessive.
examples: I get a bit neurotic about locking the front door.
The sitcom's neurotic hero worries about everything.
etymology: From neurosis, from Greek neuron 'nerve'.

definition: A person who has recently arrived or started an activity.
examples: The newcomer won the chess tournament on her first try.
Every newcomer gets a welcome basket from the neighbors.
etymology: From new + comer, from Old English cuman 'to come'.

definition: Newly invented and, in the speaker's view, unnecessarily complicated.
examples: Grandpa refuses to use any newfangled payment app.
This newfangled coffee maker needs a firmware update.
etymology: From Middle English newefangel 'eager for novelty', from new + an element related to Old English fon 'to take'.

definition: Deliberately ambiguous and misleading language, especially in politics or business.
examples: Calling layoffs 'rightsizing' is pure corporate newspeak.
The memo was written in bureaucratic newspeak.
etymology: Coined by George Orwell in his novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).

definition: A connection or central point linking multiple things.
examples: The café became a nexus for the town's artists and writers.
Researchers are studying the nexus between sleep and memory.
etymology: From Latin nexus, 'a binding together', from nectere, 'to bind'.

definition: A fine detail or distinction, or a small point of etiquette.
examples: He skipped every social nicety and got straight to business.
The lawyers argued over a legal nicety.
etymology: From Old French niceté 'foolishness', from nice, which once meant 'silly'.

definition: A specialized area or role that suits someone or something well.
examples: She found her niche writing guides for beginner gardeners.
The shop serves a small niche of vintage camera fans.
etymology: From French niche, 'recess in a wall', from nicher 'to nest'.

definition: To blink or wink.
examples: Owls nictitate with a clear inner eyelid.
Under the bright lights the witness began to nictitate nervously.
etymology: From Medieval Latin nictitare, frequentative of Latin nictare 'to blink'.

definition: A place where something originates, develops, or is fostered.
examples: The stagnant pond became a nidus for mosquitoes.
The café was the nidus of the city's first punk bands.
etymology: From Latin nidus 'nest'.

definition: Clever, skillful, or particularly useful.
examples: She showed me a nifty trick for peeling garlic.
This nifty gadget folds flat for travel.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in American English in the 1860s.

definition: Near or nearly.
examples: The end of the semester is nigh.
Finding parking downtown is well nigh impossible.
etymology: From Old English neah 'near'.

definition: The belief that life is meaningless or that traditional values have no basis.
examples: The novel's teenage narrator flirts with nihilism.
Their nihilism was mostly a pose to seem edgy.
etymology: From Latin nihil 'nothing' + -ism.

definition: Quick and light in movement or thought.
examples: The nimble goat leapt from rock to rock.
Small companies can be more nimble than large ones.
etymology: From Old English næmel, 'quick to take', from niman 'to take'.

definition: A luminous cloud or halo surrounding a figure or object.
examples: In the painting, a golden nimbus surrounds the saint's head.
The streetlight wore a nimbus of fog.
etymology: From Latin nimbus 'cloud, aureole'.

definition: Excess or overabundance.
examples: The menu suffered from a nimiety of truffle oil.
A nimiety of choices can paralyze shoppers.
etymology: From Late Latin nimietas, from Latin nimis 'too much'.

definition: A state of perfect happiness, or in Buddhism, release from suffering.
examples: A hot shower after camping is pure nirvana.
Buddhist monks meditate in pursuit of nirvana.
etymology: From Sanskrit nirvana 'extinction, blowing out'.

definition: A mental or physical effort to attain a goal; a striving.
examples: The novel traces one woman's nisus toward independence.
Every living thing shows some nisus to survive.
etymology: From Latin nisus 'effort', from niti 'to strive'.

definition: To find fault with trivial details.
examples: Editors nitpick so readers don't have to.
Please don't nitpick my grammar in the group chat.
etymology: From nit, the egg of a louse, + pick, from the tedious work of removing lice.

definition: Having fine personal qualities or high moral principles.
examples: Giving the reward to charity was a noble gesture.
It's a noble goal, but is it realistic?
etymology: From Latin nobilis 'noted, high-born', from noscere 'to know'.

definition: A harmless treatment that causes ill effects because the patient expects them.
examples: Reading the side-effects list can trigger a nocebo response.
The sugar pill acted as a nocebo, giving her headaches.
etymology: From Latin nocebo 'I shall harm', on the model of placebo 'I shall please'.

definition: A sleepwalker, or a person who roams at night.
examples: A lifelong noctambulist, she wandered the city's streets after midnight.
Our cat is a noctambulist who patrols the house at 3 a.m.
etymology: From Latin nox 'night' + ambulare 'to walk'.

definition: Shining at night, especially of high, thin clouds lit by the sun after dusk.
examples: We spotted noctilucent clouds glowing blue long after sunset.
The bay sparkled with noctilucent plankton.
etymology: From Latin nox 'night' + lucere 'to shine'.

definition: Active or happening at night.
examples: Owls and bats are nocturnal hunters.
My roommate keeps nocturnal hours during finals.
etymology: From Late Latin nocturnalis, from nox 'night'.

definition: A dreamy musical piece or painting inspired by the night.
examples: She played a Chopin nocturne as the guests arrived.
Whistler painted a moody nocturne of the Thames.
etymology: From French nocturne, from Latin nocturnus 'of the night'.

definition: A difficult or complicated point; the knot of a problem.
examples: The nodus of the plot is a forged letter.
Lawyers argued for hours over the nodus of the case.
etymology: From Latin nodus 'knot'.

definition: Relating to the mind or intellect.
examples: The retreat promised noetic insight along with yoga.
Philosophers distinguish noetic knowledge from mere sensation.
etymology: From Greek noetikos, from noein 'to perceive, think'.

definition: A genre of crime fiction or film marked by cynicism, menace, and moral ambiguity.
examples: The novel is a rain-soaked noir set in 1940s Los Angeles.
He loves classic noir with trench coats and femme fatales.
etymology: From French film noir 'black film'.

definition: Having an extremely unpleasant smell, or harmful and offensive.
examples: A noisome odor drifted from the dumpster behind the restaurant.
The swamp released noisome gases in the heat.
etymology: From Middle English noy, a shortening of annoy, + -some; it is unrelated to noise.

definition: A person who moves from place to place rather than living in one spot.
examples: She lived as a digital nomad, working from a different city each month.
The desert nomad moved his herds with the seasons.
etymology: From Greek nomas 'roaming in search of pasture', from nemein 'to pasture'.

definition: A system of names used in a particular field.
examples: Botanists use Latin nomenclature to avoid confusion.
The company's product nomenclature confuses even its own staff.
etymology: From Latin nomenclatura, from nomen 'name' + calare 'to call'.

definition: Existing in name only, or very small in amount.
examples: The museum charges a nominal fee of two dollars.
He is the nominal head of the company, but his daughter runs it.
etymology: From Latin nominalis, from nomen 'name'.

definition: The view that general ideas are only names, with no real existence.
examples: Medieval nominalism challenged the reality of universals like 'redness'.
Her nominalism made her suspicious of grand abstractions.
etymology: From French nominalisme, from Latin nominalis 'relating to names'.

definition: To formally propose someone for a role, office, or award.
examples: I'd like to nominate Priya for team captain.
Critics are expected to nominate the film for best picture.
etymology: From Latin nominare 'to name'.

definition: A person who has been formally proposed for an office or award.
examples: Each nominee gave a short speech before the vote.
She was a first-time Oscar nominee.
etymology: From nominate + -ee, from Latin nominare 'to name'.

definition: Seeking general laws rather than studying individual cases.
examples: Physics is nomothetic, while biography studies one life in depth.
The study took a nomothetic approach, surveying ten thousand people.
etymology: From Greek nomothetes 'lawgiver', from nomos 'law'.

definition: The period of legal minority, or any period of immaturity.
examples: During her nonage, the estate was managed by trustees.
The internet was still in its nonage in 1995.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman nonage, from non- 'not' + age.

definition: A person between ninety and ninety-nine years old.
examples: The spry nonagenarian still swims every morning.
Our oldest volunteer is a nonagenarian who never misses a shift.
etymology: From Latin nonagenarius 'containing ninety'.

definition: The present occasion or purpose, as in 'for the nonce'.
examples: For the nonce, we'll camp in the living room.
He coined the word for the nonce, never expecting it to stick.
etymology: From Middle English for than anes 'for the one (occasion)', misdivided as for the nanes.

definition: Calm and casual, appearing not to care or worry.
examples: He gave a nonchalant shrug and strolled past the angry crowd.
She tried to look nonchalant as she opened her exam results.
etymology: From French nonchalant, 'being indifferent', from nonchaloir 'to have no concern'.

definition: Not expressing or revealing a clear opinion or decision.
examples: She gave a noncommittal shrug when I asked about the job.
The senator's noncommittal answer satisfied no one.
etymology: From non- 'not' + committal, from commit, from Latin committere 'to entrust'.

definition: A person whose behavior or views differ from accepted norms.
examples: As a lifelong nonconformist, she wore sneakers to her own wedding.
Every artistic movement starts with a nonconformist or two.
etymology: From non- 'not' + conformist; originally used of English Protestants outside the Church of England.

definition: Lacking distinctive or interesting features.
examples: The best taco shop in town is in a nondescript strip mall.
He wore a nondescript gray jacket so no one would notice him.
etymology: From non- 'not' + Latin descriptus 'described'.

definition: A person or thing of no importance.
examples: He went from political nonentity to governor in four years.
At the party, she felt like a complete nonentity.
etymology: From non- 'not' + entity, from Late Latin entitas 'being'.

definition: A person or thing without equal; a paragon.
examples: In her grandfather's eyes, she was a nonesuch.
The orchard's pride was an apple called the nonesuch.
etymology: From none + such, meaning 'there is none such'.

definition: In spite of that; even so.
examples: The movie was long; nonetheless, I enjoyed every minute.
It was raining, but the parade went ahead nonetheless.
etymology: From none + the + less.

definition: The failure to perform a duty one is required to do.
examples: The officials were charged with nonfeasance for ignoring the warnings.
Nonfeasance can be as costly as wrongdoing.
etymology: From non- 'not' + Anglo-Norman faisance 'doing'.

definition: Having no equal; unrivaled.
examples: She was a nonpareil storyteller who could hush any room.
The bakery's croissants are nonpareil.
etymology: From French nonpareil, from non 'not' + pareil 'equal'.

definition: Not biased toward or supporting any political party.
examples: A nonpartisan group will host the debate.
The budget office is meant to be strictly nonpartisan.
etymology: From non- 'not' + partisan, from Italian partigiano, from parte 'part'.

definition: So surprised or confused that one does not know how to react.
examples: The teacher was nonplussed when the class actually did the reading.
He looked nonplussed by the question about his middle name.
etymology: From nonplus, from Latin non plus 'not more', a state where nothing more can be said or done.

definition: An organization that uses its income for a cause rather than for owners' profit.
examples: She left banking to run a nonprofit that teaches kids to code.
The nonprofit depends on volunteers and small donations.
etymology: From non- 'not' + profit, from Latin profectus 'progress, profit'.

definition: Not affiliated with or restricted to any particular religious group.
examples: The hospital is nonsectarian and welcomes patients of any faith.
They sent their kids to a nonsectarian summer camp.
etymology: From non- 'not' + sectarian, from sect, from Latin secta 'following'.

definition: Having no meaning or making no sense; absurd.
examples: The new parking rules are completely nonsensical.
Lewis Carroll filled his poems with nonsensical words.
etymology: From nonsense, from non- 'not' + sense, from Latin sensus 'feeling'.

definition: An idea or plan that has no chance of succeeding.
examples: A four-hour commute is a nonstarter for me.
The proposal was a nonstarter with the board.
etymology: From non- 'not' + starter, originally a racehorse that failed to start.

definition: Not involving words or speech.
examples: Crossed arms are a classic nonverbal signal of defensiveness.
Much of a toddler's communication is nonverbal.
etymology: From non- 'not' + verbal, from Latin verbum 'word'.

definition: Something that is usual, typical, or expected.
examples: Working from home has become the norm for many tech jobs.
In this office, eating lunch at your desk is the norm.
etymology: From Latin norma 'carpenter's square, rule'.

definition: The condition of being normal or usual.
examples: After the storm, the town slowly returned to normalcy.
The kids craved some normalcy after the move.
etymology: From normal + -cy; popularized in American politics in 1920.

definition: To make something seem normal or bring it back to a usual state.
examples: We need to normalize asking for help at work.
Doctors waited for her heart rate to normalize.
etymology: From normal, from Latin normalis 'made according to a carpenter's square'.

definition: Establishing or relating to a standard of how things should be.
examples: The study is descriptive, not normative; it shows what people do, not what they should do.
Normative ideas about gender shape children's toys.
etymology: From French normatif, from norme 'norm', from Latin norma 'rule'.

definition: A small bunch of flowers, especially sweet-scented ones.
examples: The flower girl carried a nosegay of violets.
He brought her a nosegay picked from the roadside.
etymology: From nose + gay in the obsolete sense 'ornament', a pretty thing to smell.

definition: The use of 'we' to refer to oneself.
examples: The editor's nosism was a newspaper tradition.
Royal nosism, the 'we' of monarchs, sounds odd from a manager.
etymology: From Latin nos 'we' + -ism.

definition: The branch of medicine dealing with the classification of diseases.
examples: Psychiatric nosology changes with each edition of the manual.
His nosology of office ailments included 'meeting fatigue'.
etymology: From Greek nosos 'disease' + -logy.

definition: A wistful longing for the past.
examples: The old cartoon filled him with nostalgia for Saturday mornings.
Vinyl records sell partly on nostalgia.
etymology: From Greek nostos 'return home' + algos 'pain'.

definition: A favorite remedy or scheme, especially an ineffective one.
examples: Cutting the art program was the board's nostrum for every budget problem.
The old almanac is full of nostrums for colds and gout.
etymology: From Latin nostrum, 'our own (remedy)'.

definition: Worthy of attention or notice because important or interesting.
examples: The report has one notable omission: the actual costs.
The town's most notable resident is a retired astronaut.
etymology: From Latin notabilis, from notare 'to note'.

definition: Especially; in a way worth noticing.
examples: Several cities, notably Denver, saw record snowfall.
The kitchen was notably cleaner after the new rules.
etymology: From notable, from Latin notabilis, from notare 'to mark'.

definition: Interesting or significant enough to deserve attention.
examples: Nothing noteworthy happened at the meeting.
The museum's most noteworthy piece is a tiny gold bird.
etymology: From note + worthy, from Old English weorthig.

definition: A belief, idea, or vague understanding of something.
examples: I have no notion of how to fix a carburetor.
The notion that we only use ten percent of our brain is a myth.
etymology: From Latin notio 'idea, conception', from noscere 'to know'.

definition: Fame for something bad or scandalous.
examples: The restaurant gained notoriety for its rude waiters.
He enjoyed his brief notoriety as the man who crashed the parade.
etymology: From Medieval Latin notorietas, from notorius 'well known'.

definition: Famous for something bad.
examples: This intersection is notorious for accidents.
He's notorious for showing up late.
etymology: From Medieval Latin notorius, 'well known', from notus.

definition: In spite of that; nevertheless.
examples: The reviews were harsh; the film was a hit notwithstanding.
She knew the risks and went notwithstanding.
etymology: From not + withstanding, a translation of Latin non obstante.

definition: In Kant's philosophy, a thing as it is in itself, beyond perception.
examples: Kant argued we can never know the noumenon, only its appearances.
Behind each sensation, he imagined an unreachable noumenon.
etymology: From Greek nooumenon 'thing being perceived', from noein 'to think'.

definition: To provide what is needed for growth and health, or to keep a feeling alive.
examples: Soups like this nourish you on cold nights.
Good friends nourish your confidence when it runs low.
etymology: From Old French norir, from Latin nutrire 'to feed'.

definition: Practical intelligence and common sense, or in philosophy, the mind or intellect.
examples: She had the business nous to buy before prices soared.
In Greek philosophy, nous is the faculty that grasps first principles.
etymology: From Greek nous 'mind'.

definition: New, original, or unlike anything seen before.
examples: The researchers took a novel approach to recycling plastic.
Using drones to deliver pizza was a novel idea in 2015.
etymology: From Latin novellus, diminutive of novus 'new'.

definition: A short novel or long short story.
examples: She finished the novella in a single afternoon.
Steinbeck's novella packs a lot into a hundred pages.
etymology: From Italian novella 'new story', from Latin novellus 'new'.

definition: The quality of being new and unusual, or a new and unusual thing.
examples: The novelty of working from home wore off after a few months.
For a city kid, seeing cows up close was a novelty.
etymology: From Old French novelte, from Latin novellus 'new'.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of a stepmother.
examples: Fairy tales rarely show novercal kindness.
She resisted every novercal cliché and became the kids' favorite adult.
etymology: From Latin novercalis, from noverca 'stepmother'.

definition: A person who is new to a skill or activity and still learning.
examples: As a novice cook, he burned the rice on his first attempt.
The race has separate categories for experts and novices, so everyone can compete fairly.
etymology: From Old French novice, from Latin novicius 'newly imported', from novus 'new'.

definition: The period of being a novice, especially in a religious order.
examples: She spent her novitiate in a convent in the Alps.
My first year at the firm felt like a long novitiate.
etymology: From Medieval Latin novitiatus, from Latin novicius 'new, inexperienced'.

definition: Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant.
examples: Noxious fumes forced the evacuation of the factory.
The comment section had become a noxious place.
etymology: From Latin noxius, from noxa 'harm'.

definition: A slight, subtle difference in meaning, tone, or expression.
examples: Translators must capture every nuance of the original poem.
The debate lacked nuance, reducing a complex issue to two slogans.
etymology: From French nuance, 'shade, subtle difference', from nuer, 'to shade', from Latin nubes, 'cloud'.

definition: The central point or core of a matter, or a small lump.
examples: The nub of the problem is that nobody owns the project.
Only a nub of pencil was left in the drawer.
etymology: A variant of knub, from Middle Low German knubbe 'knob'.

definition: Cloudy or foggy, or vague and obscure.
examples: A nubilous sky threatened rain all afternoon.
His nubilous explanation left us more confused.
etymology: From Latin nubilus 'cloudy', from nubes 'cloud'.

definition: The central and most important part around which others gather.
examples: Five veteran players form the nucleus of the team.
The old library became the nucleus of the new campus.
etymology: From Latin nucleus 'kernel', from nux 'nut'.

definition: To push gently, or to gently encourage someone toward an action.
examples: The app tries to nudge you to drink more water.
Could you nudge your brother awake?
etymology: Probably of Scandinavian origin; compare Norwegian dialect nugga 'to push'.
