Her perfunctory apology convinced no one that she regretted what she had said.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius, 'done carelessly', from Latin perfungi, 'to get through with'.

definition: A short passage extracted from a text, especially for reading aloud.
examples: The priest read a pericope from the Gospel of Luke.
Each lesson centered on a single pericope.
etymology: From Greek perikope 'section', from peri- 'around' + koptein 'to cut'.

definition: The point in an orbit where a planet or comet is closest to the sun.
examples: Earth reaches perihelion in early January.
The comet will glow brightest near perihelion.
etymology: From Greek peri- 'near' + helios 'sun'.

definition: Serious and immediate danger.
examples: The hikers ignored the warning signs at their peril.
Rising seas put the coastal town in real peril.
etymology: From Old French peril, from Latin periculum 'danger, trial'.

definition: The continuous outer boundary of an area.
examples: Guards patrolled the perimeter of the base all night.
We planted lavender along the perimeter of the garden.
etymology: From Greek perimetros, from peri- 'around' + metron 'measure'.

definition: Happening at intervals, either regular or occasional.
examples: The software makes periodic backups throughout the day.
She suffers from periodic bouts of insomnia.
etymology: From Greek periodikos, from periodos 'cycle, circuit'.

definition: Traveling from place to place; itinerant.
examples: Her peripatetic childhood included schools in six countries.
A peripatetic chef, he cooked at pop-ups across the country.
etymology: From Greek peripatētikos, from peripatein, 'to walk up and down', after Aristotle's habit of teaching while walking.

definition: A sudden reversal of fortune, especially in a drama.
examples: The hero's arrest is the play's central peripeteia.
Her career had its peripeteia when the scandal broke.
etymology: From Greek peripeteia 'sudden change', a term used by Aristotle in the Poetics.

definition: The outer edge of an area, or a position of minor importance within a group.
examples: New housing developments are spreading along the periphery of the city.
For years she worked on the periphery of the industry before landing a major role.
etymology: From Greek periphereia 'circumference', from peri- 'around' + pherein 'to carry'.

definition: Using more words than necessary to express something; roundabout speech.
examples: 'Vertically challenged' is periphrasis for 'short'.
The memo was a masterpiece of bureaucratic periphrasis.
etymology: From Greek periphrasis, from peri- 'around' + phrazein 'to declare'.

definition: To die or be destroyed, especially suddenly or violently.
examples: Without water, the seedlings will perish within days.
Without a rescue boat, the stranded sailors would perish in the storm.
etymology: From Old French periss-, stem of perir, from Latin perire 'to pass away'.

definition: The crime of lying under oath.
examples: The witness was charged with perjury.
Lying to the grand jury could amount to perjury.
etymology: From Latin perjurium 'false oath', from perjurare 'to swear falsely'.

definition: An extra benefit that comes with a job or situation.
examples: Free gym access is one of the best perks of the job.
One perk of living downtown is walking to work.
etymology: Short for perquisite, from Latin perquisitum 'thing acquired'.

definition: Allowing liquids, gases, or influences to pass through.
examples: Sandy soil is more permeable than clay.
The border between fiction and memoir has grown permeable.
etymology: From Late Latin permeabilis, from Latin permeare 'to pass through'.

definition: To spread throughout something completely.
examples: The smell of fresh bread began to permeate the whole apartment.
A spirit of optimism seemed to permeate the team after the win.
etymology: From Latin permeare 'to pass through', from per- 'through' + meare 'to pass'.

definition: Allowing great freedom of behavior, often more than is thought wise.
examples: Some blame permissive parenting for the kids' behavior.
The city has permissive rules on outdoor dining.
etymology: From Medieval Latin permissivus, from Latin permittere 'to allow'.

definition: Each of several possible ways in which things can be arranged or ordered.
examples: We tried every permutation of the lock's code.
The show is the latest permutation of a classic format.
etymology: From Latin permutatio, from permutare 'to change completely'.

definition: Causing serious harm in a gradual or hidden way.
examples: The pernicious rumor slowly destroyed the small company's reputation over several months.
Experts warn about the pernicious effects of constant sleep loss on the heart.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus, 'destructive', from pernicies, 'ruin'.

definition: Overly fussy about small details.
examples: My pernickety uncle irons his socks.
The pernickety editor flagged every comma.
etymology: Originally Scots, of unknown origin; American English often uses persnickety.

definition: To speak at great length, or to conclude a speech.
examples: The senator perorated for an hour about local history.
He likes to perorate at family dinners.
etymology: From Latin perorare, 'to speak to the end'.

definition: A person who carries out a harmful, illegal, or immoral act.
examples: Police are still searching for the perpetrator of the robbery.
The prank's perpetrator finally confessed.
etymology: From Latin perpetrator, from perpetrare 'to perform', from per- + patrare 'to bring about'.

definition: Never ending or changing, or occurring so often it seems endless.
examples: The office lives in a state of perpetual chaos.
He wore a perpetual grin that annoyed his coworkers.
etymology: From Latin perpetualis, from perpetuus 'continuing throughout'.

definition: To make something, especially something undesirable, continue indefinitely.
examples: Old cartoons can perpetuate silly stereotypes.
Retelling the myth only perpetuates the confusion.
etymology: From Latin perpetuare, 'to make perpetual', from perpetuus 'continuous'.

definition: The state of lasting forever.
examples: The land was donated to the city in perpetuity.
The trust will pay for the scholarship in perpetuity.
etymology: From Latin perpetuitas, from perpetuus 'continuous'.

definition: To make someone confused and unsure, especially by being hard to understand.
examples: The new tax rules perplex even seasoned accountants.
Her sudden silence continued to perplex her friends.
etymology: From Latin perplexus 'entangled', from per- + plexus 'interwoven'.

definition: A benefit that comes with a job or position beyond the salary.
examples: A company car was one perquisite of the role.
Free travel is a perquisite that airline staff enjoy.
etymology: From Medieval Latin perquisitum 'acquisition', from Latin perquirere 'to search diligently'.

definition: To repeat a thought or action compulsively beyond what is needed.
examples: Anxious people often perseverate on small mistakes.
The child would perseverate on one question for hours.
etymology: A back-formation from perseveration, from Latin perseverare 'to persist'.

definition: To keep trying to do something despite difficulty or delay.
examples: If you persevere through the hard first month, the work gets much easier.
She chose to persevere with her training even after the knee injury.
etymology: From Latin perseverare, 'to continue steadfastly', from perseverus 'very strict'.

definition: Light, teasing banter.
examples: The dinner party sparkled with persiflage between old friends.
Beneath the persiflage, his question was entirely serious.
etymology: From French persifler, 'to banter', from siffler, 'to whistle'.

definition: Continuing firmly despite difficulty, or lasting longer than expected.
examples: A persistent cough kept him home all week.
Her persistent emails finally got a response from the manager.
etymology: From Latin persistere 'to continue steadfastly', from per- + sistere 'to stand'.

definition: The image or character a person presents to others, often different from their private self.
examples: On stage he adopts a brash persona that is nothing like his quiet real self.
Her online persona is far more confident than she is in person.
etymology: From Latin persona 'mask used by an actor, character'.

definition: Pleasant in manner and appearance, and easy to like.
examples: The new manager is personable and remembers everyone's name.
A personable waiter can make a mediocre meal enjoyable.
etymology: From person + -able, ultimately from Latin persona.

definition: Having keen insight and quick understanding of people or situations.
examples: A perspicacious investor, she sold before the market turned.
The perspicacious editor spotted the plot hole on the first read.
etymology: From Latin perspicax, from perspicere 'to see through'.

definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand.
examples: Her perspicuous explanation cleared up the confusion.
The manual is admirably perspicuous.
etymology: From Latin perspicuus 'transparent', from perspicere 'to look through'.

definition: To relate to or be relevant to something.
examples: Please ask only questions that pertain to today's agenda.
These rules pertain to all employees, including managers.
etymology: From Old French partenir, from Latin pertinere 'to extend to, relate to'.

definition: Holding firmly to a purpose or opinion; stubbornly persistent.
examples: A pertinacious reporter finally uncovered the truth.
The pertinacious weeds returned every spring.
etymology: From Latin pertinax 'holding fast', from per- + tenax 'tenacious'.

definition: Directly relevant to the matter being considered.
examples: The lawyer asked only pertinent questions and ignored anything off topic.
Please include all pertinent details when you describe the problem to support.
etymology: From Latin pertinens, 'relating to', from pertinere 'to concern', from per- + tenere 'to hold'.

definition: To make someone anxious or unsettled.
examples: Nothing seems to perturb her, even a canceled flight.
The odd noises began to perturb the campers.
etymology: From Latin perturbare 'to throw into confusion', from per- + turbare 'to disturb'.

definition: To read or examine something carefully and thoroughly.
examples: Take time to peruse the contract before signing.
She likes to peruse the shelves of used bookstores.
etymology: Probably from per- 'thoroughly' + use; the earliest sense was 'to use up'.

definition: To spread through and be present in every part of something.
examples: A sense of nostalgia seems to pervade the whole album.
The smell of smoke would pervade the house for weeks.
etymology: From Latin pervadere, from per- 'through' + vadere 'to go'.

definition: Spreading widely through every part of a place or group.
examples: Smartphones have become a pervasive part of daily life.
There was a pervasive sense of unease in the office before the layoffs.
etymology: From Latin pervas-, past participle stem of pervadere 'to go through'.

definition: Deliberately contrary or unreasonable, often against what is expected.
examples: He took a perverse pleasure in spoiling movie endings.
The subsidy had the perverse effect of raising prices.
etymology: From Latin perversus 'turned away', from pervertere 'to overturn'.

definition: A person who tends to expect the worst outcome.
examples: Call me a pessimist, but I doubt the train will be on time.
Even the biggest pessimist on the team admitted the launch went well.
etymology: From Latin pessimus 'worst' + -ist.

definition: To annoy someone with persistent requests or interruptions.
examples: The kids pester me for a puppy every single day.
Please don't pester the staff while they're working.
etymology: From French empestrer 'to hobble an animal', influenced by pest.

definition: A small bomb once used to blow open gates; famous in 'hoist with his own petard'.
examples: The scheming senator was hoist with his own petard.
Engineers fixed a petard to the castle gate.
etymology: From French pétard, from péter 'to break wind'.

definition: A formal written request, often signed by many people, appealing to an authority.
examples: Over ten thousand residents signed a petition to save the park.
The students delivered their petition to the principal's office.
etymology: From Latin petitio, from petere 'to aim at, seek'.

definition: The pleasant earthy smell that follows rain after dry weather.
examples: After the summer storm, the garden filled with petrichor.
She opened the window to breathe in the petrichor.
etymology: Coined in 1964 from Greek petra 'stone' + ikhōr, the fluid in the veins of the gods.

definition: An inferior lawyer who uses petty, dubious tricks, or anyone who quibbles over trivia.
examples: The pettifogger dragged out the case over a missing comma.
Don't be a pettifogger about the restaurant bill.
etymology: From petty + obsolete fogger 'underhand dealer', perhaps from the Fugger banking family.

definition: Of little importance, or showing small-minded concern with trivial things.
examples: Let's not fight over something so petty.
It was petty of him to unfollow her after the argument.
etymology: From Old French petit 'small'.

definition: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered over small annoyances.
examples: He gave a petulant shrug and refused to join the game.
The petulant tone of her reply made it clear she was still angry.
etymology: From Latin petulans, 'impudent', from petere 'to attack, seek'.

definition: A tightly packed body of people or soldiers moving together.
examples: A phalanx of reporters waited outside the courthouse.
The bodyguards formed a phalanx around the singer.
etymology: From Greek phalanx 'line of battle', via Latin.

definition: A shifting series of real or imagined images, as in a dream.
examples: The festival was a phantasmagoria of lights and costumes.
His fever dreams became a vivid phantasmagoria.
etymology: From French fantasmagorie, the name of a 1790s magic-lantern show, from Greek phantasma 'image'.

definition: Hypocritically self-righteous, emphasizing outward forms of virtue.
examples: His pharisaical outrage ignored his own faults.
The memo's pharisaical tone irritated the staff.
etymology: From Pharisee, an ancient Jewish sect portrayed in the Gospels as legalistic.

definition: A lighthouse or beacon guiding sailors.
examples: The old pharos still guides ships into the harbor.
Her book became a pharos for young writers.
etymology: From Pharos, the island off Alexandria with a famous ancient lighthouse.

definition: Used for social contact rather than to convey information.
examples: 'Nice weather today' is phatic small talk.
Much office chatter is phatic, meant only to keep things friendly.
etymology: From Greek phatos 'spoken'; the term was coined by anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski in 1923.

definition: To have casual affairs with women, typically while committed to someone else.
examples: The character continues to philander despite his marriage.
He was known to philander at every company retreat.
etymology: From Greek philandros 'fond of men', later used as a lover's name in stories and plays.

definition: The practice of giving money or time to help others and promote the public good.
examples: After selling her company, she devoted herself to philanthropy.
Local philanthropy funded the new children's library.
etymology: From Greek philanthropia, from philein 'to love' + anthropos 'human being'.

definition: A bitter verbal attack or denunciation.
examples: The coach delivered a philippic against the team's lazy defense.
Her op-ed was a philippic against single-use plastics.
etymology: From Greek philippikos, the name of Demosthenes' speeches against Philip II of Macedon.

definition: A person hostile or indifferent to art and culture.
examples: Only a philistine would paint over that mural.
He called himself a philistine who preferred action movies to opera.
etymology: From the Philistines of the Bible; the cultural sense came from German student slang.

definition: A lover of learning, especially of mathematics and science.
examples: A true philomath, she reads textbooks for fun.
The library was a haven for every young philomath in town.
etymology: From Greek philomathes 'fond of learning', from philein 'to love' + manthanein 'to learn'.

definition: A magic potion, especially one meant to arouse love.
examples: In the opera, a philter makes Tristan fall for Isolde.
She joked that her soup was a love philter.
etymology: From Greek philtron 'love charm', from philein 'to love'.

definition: The vertical groove between the nose and the upper lip.
examples: A drop of sweat ran down his philtrum.
The doctor examined the infant's philtrum.
etymology: From Greek philtron 'love charm', the groove once seen as a feature of beauty.

definition: Calm and unemotional, not easily excited or upset.
examples: The phlegmatic pilot calmly announced the engine failure as if reading a menu.
Her phlegmatic nature kept the team steady through every crisis.
etymology: From Greek phlegmatikos, 'abounding in phlegm', one of the four humors linked to a sluggish temperament.

definition: A substance once thought to be released by burning; now any discredited theory.
examples: Chemists abandoned phlogiston after Lavoisier's experiments.
Some economists treat that idea as the phlogiston of their field.
etymology: From Greek phlogistos 'burned', from phlogizein 'to set on fire'.

definition: A small leather box containing scripture worn in Jewish prayer, or an amulet.
examples: He wrapped a phylactery around his arm before morning prayers.
The sorcerer kept his soul hidden in a phylactery.
etymology: From Greek phulakterion 'safeguard, amulet', from phulassein 'to guard'.

definition: A person's facial features, or the general outward character of something.
examples: The portrait captured his stern physiognomy.
Highways have changed the physiognomy of the countryside.
etymology: From Greek phusiognomonia, from phusis 'nature' + gnomon 'judge, interpreter'.

definition: Relating to an episodic story of a likable rogue's adventures.
examples: Don Quixote is often read as a picaresque novel.
His picaresque road trip involved three flat tires and a runaway llama.
etymology: From Spanish picaresco, from pícaro, 'rogue'.

definition: A rogue, thief, or pirate.
examples: The picaroon talked his way out of every jail.
A picaroon ship lurked off the coast.
etymology: From Spanish picarón, from pícaro 'rogue'.

definition: Petty and of little value or importance.
examples: Let's not argue over such picayune details.
His complaints seemed picayune next to the real problems.
etymology: From Louisiana French picaillon, a small coin, from Provençal picaioun.

definition: Having irregular patches of two colors, typically black and white.
examples: A piebald pony grazed in the meadow.
The town was a piebald mix of old and new buildings.
etymology: From pie 'magpie', for its black and white plumage, + bald in the old sense 'streaked with white'.

definition: Gradually, one part at a time.
examples: They renovated the house piecemeal over several years.
The data was released piecemeal, making it hard to analyze.
etymology: From Middle English pece, 'piece', + -mele, 'measure'.

definition: Deep religious devotion, or a conventional belief held with reverence.
examples: Her piety showed in her daily prayers and charity work.
He spoke of the cathedral with quiet piety.
etymology: From Old French piete, from Latin pietas 'dutifulness'.

definition: To steal small things, typically in petty amounts.
examples: The raccoons pilfer food from our trash every night.
Employees who pilfer supplies can be fired.
etymology: From Old French pelfrer 'to pillage', from pelfre 'spoils'.

definition: To rob a place violently, especially in wartime.
examples: Raiders came ashore to pillage the coastal villages.
Developers seemed ready to pillage the old neighborhood.
etymology: From Old French piller 'to plunder'.

definition: To attack or ridicule someone publicly.
examples: Columnists were quick to pillory the minister for the gaffe.
Fans began to pillory the referee online.
etymology: From Old French pilori, a wooden frame used for public punishment; origin uncertain.

definition: Cheap, sham, or counterfeit; looking valuable but worthless.
examples: The pinchbeck jewelry turned his wrist green.
Critics dismissed the remake as pinchbeck glamour.
etymology: From Christopher Pinchbeck, an 18th-century London watchmaker who invented a gold-like alloy.

definition: To restrain someone by holding or binding their arms.
examples: Guards rushed to pinion the intruder.
Two officers managed to pinion his arms behind his back.
etymology: From Old French pignon 'wing feather', ultimately from Latin pinna 'feather'.

definition: The highest point of achievement or success.
examples: Winning the championship was the pinnacle of her career.
Many consider this album the pinnacle of the band's work.
etymology: From Old French pinacle, from Late Latin pinnaculum 'small wing, peak'.

definition: To find or identify something with great precision.
examples: Mechanics couldn't pinpoint the source of the rattle.
Can you pinpoint the moment things went wrong?
etymology: From pin + point, originally the point of a pin.

definition: A person who is among the first to explore or develop a new area, idea, or method.
examples: She was a pioneer in the field of computer graphics.
Every pioneer of the electric car faced skeptics at first.
etymology: From French pionnier 'foot soldier, digger', from Old French peon 'foot soldier'.

definition: Devoutly religious, or making a hypocritical show of virtue.
examples: Her pious grandmother attended mass daily.
Spare me the pious lecture about saving money.
etymology: From Latin pius 'dutiful, devout'.

definition: Pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste, or stimulating to the mind.
examples: The piquant sauce had hints of lime and chili.
She added a piquant detail that made the story memorable.
etymology: From French piquant 'stinging', from piquer 'to prick'.

definition: To stir up interest or curiosity.
examples: A good trailer can pique my interest in a whole series.
A strange noise from the attic piqued the kids' curiosity.
etymology: From French piquer, 'to prick, irritate'.

definition: Relating to or resembling fish.
examples: The aquarium's piscine residents swam in lazy circles.
He had a cold, piscine stare.
etymology: From Latin piscis 'fish'.

definition: A hidden danger or common mistake.
examples: The guide warns about common pitfalls for first-time home buyers.
One pitfall of working from home is never logging off.
etymology: From pit + fall, originally a covered pit used as a trap.

definition: Concise and forcefully meaningful in expression.
examples: Her pithy reply summed up the debate in a single line.
I love his pithy advice: show up, work hard, be kind.
etymology: From pith, Old English pitha, meaning the core of a plant stem, hence the essential part.

definition: A very small or inadequate amount of money.
examples: He worked long hours for a pittance at his first job.
The old painting sold for a pittance, then turned out to be valuable.
etymology: From Old French pitance, 'pious gift, allowance', related to pity.

definition: To turn on a central point, or to change strategy or direction.
examples: The startup had to pivot when its first product failed.
Watch the dancer pivot on one foot without losing balance.
etymology: From French pivot, of uncertain origin.

definition: Of crucial importance because other things depend on it.
examples: The goal in the final minute was the pivotal moment of the match.
Her research played a pivotal role in finding the cure.
etymology: From pivot, from Old French pivot, 'hinge pin', of uncertain earlier origin.

definition: Slightly eccentric or bewildered, as if led astray by pixies; also tipsy.
examples: The pixilated professor wore mismatched shoes.
After two glasses of punch, he was slightly pixilated.
etymology: From pixie, in the sense of being led astray by pixies; first recorded in 19th-century American English.

definition: Easily calmed or forgiving.
examples: Luckily, the landlord was a placable man.
A placable temper serves a diplomat well.
etymology: From Latin placabilis, from placare 'to appease'.

definition: A sign carried or posted in public, often at a protest.
examples: Each protester carried a hand-painted placard.
A placard by the door listed the rules.
etymology: From Old French placquart, from plaquier 'to lay flat'.

definition: To calm someone's anger or upset by giving them something or making concessions.
examples: The airline offered free vouchers to placate passengers stranded overnight by the storm.
Nothing I said could placate her after she found out about the cancelled trip.
etymology: From Latin placare, 'to soothe, appease'.

definition: An inactive substance given for psychological effect or as a control in a drug trial.
examples: Half the volunteers received a placebo instead of the drug.
For some people, a sugar pill works as a placebo.
etymology: From Latin placebo 'I shall please', from placere 'to please'.

definition: Calm and peaceful, with little movement or excitement.
examples: The lake was placid at dawn, reflecting the mountains perfectly.
Even during the crisis, the pilot kept a placid tone.
etymology: From Latin placidus 'gentle, quiet', from placere 'to please'.

definition: To take someone else's work or ideas and pass them off as one's own.
examples: The software flags essays that plagiarize published articles.
It is never acceptable to plagiarize another designer's work.
etymology: From plagiary, from Latin plagiarius 'kidnapper'.

definition: A person who brings a case against another in a court of law.
examples: The plaintiff claimed the ladder was defective.
The judge ruled in favor of the plaintiff.
etymology: From Old French plaintif 'complaining', from plainte 'complaint'.

definition: Sounding sad and mournful.
examples: We heard the plaintive cry of a loon across the lake.
The song's plaintive melody stayed with me all day.
etymology: From Old French plaintif, from plainte, 'lament'.

definition: Loud and resonant with a mournful tone.
examples: The plangent notes of a bagpipe drifted over the hills.
Her plangent ballad brought the audience to tears.
etymology: From Latin plangere, 'to lament, beat the breast'.

definition: A period when progress levels off after a time of growth or improvement.
examples: After losing ten pounds, he hit a frustrating plateau.
Sales reached a plateau in the third quarter.
etymology: From French plateau, from Old French platel 'flat piece', from plat 'flat'.

definition: A dull, overused remark presented as if it were fresh and meaningful.
examples: His speech was a string of platitude after platitude about hard work and dreams.
Offering a platitude like 'everything happens for a reason' rarely comforts someone who is grieving.
etymology: From French platitude, 'flatness', from plat, 'flat'.

definition: Affectionate or intimate but not romantic or sexual.
examples: Their friendship has always been platonic.
He insisted the trip was purely platonic.
etymology: From the Greek philosopher Plato, whose writings discuss love of ideal beauty.

definition: An expression of praise or approval.
examples: The young director's debut earned plaudit after plaudit from critics.
Each plaudit she received only made her work harder.
etymology: From Latin plaudite 'applaud!', said by Roman actors at the end of a play.

definition: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true.
examples: His excuse sounded plausible, but the manager still checked the facts.
Scientists have proposed a plausible explanation for the strange lights.
etymology: From Latin plausibilis, 'deserving applause', from plaudere 'to applaud'.

definition: An urgent, emotional request, or a formal answer to a criminal charge.
examples: The mayor made a plea for calm after the protest.
The defendant entered a plea of not guilty.
etymology: From Old French plait 'agreement, lawsuit', from Latin placitum 'something pleasing, a decision'.

definition: To interweave branches to form a hedge or arbor.
examples: The gardeners pleach the lime trees into a living wall.
It takes years to pleach a proper hedge.
etymology: From Old French plaissier, from Latin plectere 'to plait'.

definition: Of the common people, or lacking refinement.
examples: He mocked her plebeian taste in music.
The restaurant's plebeian roots show in its hearty menu.
etymology: From Latin plebeius, from plebs 'the common people'.

definition: A direct vote by all the people on an important public question.
examples: The region held a plebiscite on independence.
Critics called the election a plebiscite on the president.
etymology: From Latin plebiscitum, from plebs 'common people' + scitum 'decree'.

definition: To make a solemn promise to do or give something.
examples: Donors pledge money each spring to keep the radio station running.
The leaders will pledge to cut emissions by half.
etymology: From Old French plege, from Medieval Latin plebium 'security', probably of Germanic origin.

definition: Attended by all members, or unqualified and absolute.
examples: The vote will take place at the plenary session.
The commission was granted plenary powers.
etymology: From Late Latin plenarius 'complete', from plenus 'full'.

definition: A diplomat given full power to act for a government.
examples: The king sent a plenipotentiary to sign the treaty.
As plenipotentiary, she could make binding decisions.
etymology: From Medieval Latin plenipotentiarius, from plenus 'full' + potentia 'power'.

definition: An abundance, or the condition of being full or complete.
examples: The market offered a plenitude of fresh fruit.
She felt a sense of plenitude watching her grandchildren play.
etymology: From Late Latin plenitudo, from plenus 'full'.

definition: The use of more words than necessary to express a meaning, as in the phrase 'free gift'.
examples: 'Past history' is a common pleonasm that editors love to cut.
Her speech was riddled with pleonasm, from 'end result' to 'added bonus.'
etymology: From Greek pleonasmos, from pleonazein, 'to be superfluous'.

definition: Insatiable greed or desire for more than one's share.
examples: Plato saw pleonexia as a root of injustice.
The banker's pleonexia was never satisfied.
etymology: From Greek pleonexia, from pleon 'more' + ekhein 'to have'.

definition: A large or excessive amount of something.
examples: The new phone offers a plethora of features that most people will never use.
A plethora of streaming options left us scrolling for an hour without picking anything.
etymology: From Greek plethore, 'fullness', from plethein, 'to be full'.

definition: Excessive or overabundant; also ruddy-faced.
examples: The report was plethoric with charts no one read.
The plethoric squire had a face like a beet.
etymology: From Greek plethorikos, from plethore 'fullness'.

definition: Easily bent, or easily influenced by others.
examples: Warm the clay to make it more pliable.
The committee hoped for a more pliable candidate.
etymology: From French pliable, from plier 'to bend'.

definition: Flexible, or easily influenced and yielding to others.
examples: Willow branches are pliant enough to weave into baskets.
The dictator surrounded himself with pliant advisers.
etymology: From Old French pliant 'bending', from plier 'to bend'.

definition: A dangerous, difficult, or unfortunate situation.
examples: The documentary drew attention to the plight of refugees.
News of the stranded hikers' plight spread quickly.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman plit 'condition', with spelling influenced by an older English word plight 'peril'.

definition: A heavy base supporting a statue, column, or vase.
examples: The bronze lion sits on a granite plinth.
Protesters climbed onto the empty plinth.
etymology: From Greek plinthos 'tile, brick', via Latin plinthus.

definition: Slow, steady, and dull, without imagination or excitement.
examples: The plodding pace of the film tested my patience.
He was a plodding but reliable worker.
etymology: From plod, probably imitative of the sound of heavy steps.

definition: A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage.
examples: The free trial is just a ploy to get your credit card number.
Her tears were a ploy to avoid doing the dishes.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; originally Scots and northern English.

definition: Showing determined courage in difficult circumstances.
examples: The plucky underdog team made it to the finals.
A plucky kitten faced down the neighbor's dog.
etymology: From pluck in the sense 'courage', originally the heart and innards of an animal.

definition: To explore or understand something fully, often its depths.
examples: The memoir tries to plumb the depths of grief.
Scientists still cannot plumb the full mystery of sleep.
etymology: From Latin plumbum 'lead', from the lead weight used to measure depth.

definition: To fall or drop straight down very quickly.
examples: Temperatures can plummet after sunset in the desert.
Investors watched the share price plummet after the announcement.
etymology: From Old French plommet 'small sounding lead', from plomb 'lead'.

definition: To fall or move suddenly and steeply, or to throw oneself into something.
examples: Stock prices could plunge if the deal falls through.
He likes to plunge into the cold lake every morning.
etymology: From Old French plungier, from Latin plumbum 'lead'.

definition: Government by the wealthy, or a society ruled by the rich.
examples: Critics warn that campaign donations are turning democracy into plutocracy.
The novel imagines a plutocracy run by tech billionaires.
etymology: From Greek ploutokratia, from ploutos 'wealth' + kratos 'power'.

definition: Relating to or characterized by rain.
examples: The region has a long pluvial season.
Geologists studied ancient pluvial lakes in the desert.
etymology: From Latin pluvialis, from pluvia 'rain'.

definition: To illegally hunt game, or to lure away employees or customers from a rival.
examples: Rivals tried to poach their best engineer with a huge salary.
It is illegal to poach elephants for ivory.
etymology: From Old French pochier 'to poke, put in a bag', of Germanic origin.

definition: Indifferent or nonchalant; caring little.
examples: His pococurante shrug infuriated his mother.
The pococurante clerk barely looked up from his phone.
etymology: From Italian poco curante 'caring little'; Voltaire's Candide features a senator named Pococurante.

definition: Poetry, or the art of writing it.
examples: The old textbook was steeped in Romantic poesy.
She spoke of love with youthful poesy.
etymology: From Old French poesie, from Greek poiesis 'creation, poetry'.

definition: A writer of trivial or inferior poetry.
examples: The salon was crowded with every poetaster in the city.
He dismissed his rival as a mere poetaster.
etymology: From Modern Latin, from Latin poeta 'poet' + -aster, a disparaging suffix.

definition: The growing and grooming of a beard.
examples: November inspires a nationwide wave of pogonotrophy.
His dedication to pogonotrophy involved three kinds of oil.
etymology: From Greek pogon 'beard' + -trophia 'nourishment'.

definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or deep emotion.
examples: The film ends with a poignant scene of the family saying goodbye.
It was poignant to see him return to the village where he grew up.
etymology: From Old French poignant, 'pricking', from Latin pungere 'to prick'.

definition: Graceful composure and calm self-confidence.
examples: She answered the tough questions with remarkable poise.
The young pianist played with the poise of a seasoned professional.
etymology: From Old French pois, 'weight', from Latin pensum.

definition: To divide people into two sharply opposing groups.
examples: Issues like this tend to polarize voters.
The film's ending is sure to polarize audiences.
etymology: From French polariser, from Latin polaris 'of the poles'.

definition: A strongly worded verbal or written attack on a belief or person.
examples: Her book is a fierce polemic against fast fashion.
What began as a review turned into a polemic.
etymology: From Greek polemikos 'warlike', from polemos 'war'.

definition: Wise and shrewd in a given situation; tactful.
examples: It seemed politic to stay quiet until the boss calmed down.
A politic answer kept both families happy.
etymology: From Greek politikos 'civic', from polites 'citizen'.

definition: An organized society such as a state, or its form of government.
examples: Ancient Athens was a small but influential polity.
Corruption weakens the entire polity.
etymology: From Greek politeia 'citizenship, government', from polites 'citizen'.

definition: To cut a tree back to the trunk to promote dense new growth.
examples: The council will pollard the plane trees this winter.
Farmers used to pollard willows for basket weaving.
etymology: From poll 'head' + -ard; the noun first meant a hornless animal.

definition: Excessively or blindly optimistic.
examples: His pollyannaish view of the economy ignored rising debt.
It sounds pollyannaish, but I think this will work out.
etymology: From Pollyanna, the cheerful heroine of a 1913 novel by Eleanor H. Porter.

definition: An utter coward.
examples: Only a poltroon would abandon his friends in danger.
The general branded the deserter a poltroon.
etymology: From French poltron, from Italian poltrone 'sluggard'.

definition: A person who knows and uses several languages.
examples: A true polyglot, she switched between five languages at dinner.
The hotel hired a polyglot to work the front desk.
etymology: From Greek poluglottos, from polu- 'many' + glotta 'tongue'.

definition: A person of very wide learning across many fields.
examples: Leibniz was a polyhistor at home in law, math, and theology.
The museum curator was a genial polyhistor.
etymology: From Greek poluistor 'very learned', from polu- 'much' + histor 'knowing'.

definition: A person of wide-ranging knowledge or learning.
examples: Leonardo da Vinci was the archetypal polymath.
Our neighbor is a polymath who restores clocks and writes poetry.
etymology: From Greek polumathēs, 'having learned much'.

definition: Music combining several independent melodies, or a blend of many voices.
examples: Renaissance choirs excelled at polyphony.
The novel's polyphony gives each character a voice.
etymology: From Greek poluphonia, from polu- 'many' + phone 'voice, sound'.

definition: The existence of several related meanings for a single word.
examples: The word 'run' is a striking case of polysemy.
Polysemy makes machine translation surprisingly hard.
etymology: From Greek polu- 'many' + sema 'sign'.

definition: A ball of fragrant substances, or an orange studded with cloves, used to scent a room.
examples: She made a pomander from an orange and a handful of cloves.
Tudor nobles carried a pomander to mask street smells.
etymology: From Old French pome d'embre, from Medieval Latin pomum de ambra 'apple of amber'.

definition: Showing an inflated sense of one's own importance in a self-satisfied, solemn way.
examples: The pompous speaker quoted himself three times.
His pompous emails made everyone roll their eyes.
etymology: From Late Latin pomposus, from Latin pompa 'procession, display'.

definition: To think about something carefully.
examples: She pondered the question for a long time before answering.
We sat on the porch to ponder our next move.
etymology: From Latin ponderare, 'to weigh'.

definition: Slow and clumsy because of great weight, or dull and labored.
examples: The elephant moved with ponderous steps.
The report was ponderous and full of jargon.
etymology: From Latin ponderosus, from pondus, 'weight'.

definition: Relating to a pope, or pompously dogmatic.
examples: The cardinal read the pontifical decree aloud.
His pontifical manner made every opinion sound like law.
etymology: From Latin pontificalis, from pontifex 'high priest'.

definition: To express opinions in a pompous, dogmatic way.
examples: He likes to pontificate about wine at every dinner party.
Pundits pontificate on topics they barely understand.
etymology: From Medieval Latin pontificare 'to officiate as bishop', from Latin pontifex 'high priest'.

definition: A vain, conceited person who chatters and dresses showily.
examples: The popinjay strutted through the ballroom in a velvet coat.
She had no patience for that popinjay and his compliments.
etymology: From Old French papingay 'parrot', perhaps from Arabic babagha.

definition: The ordinary people living in a country or area, considered as a whole.
examples: The new law was unpopular with the general populace.
The king rarely spoke directly to the populace.
etymology: From French populace, from Italian popolaccio 'common people', from popolo 'people'.

definition: Claiming to represent ordinary people against a privileged elite.
examples: He ran a populist campaign against big banks.
The party's populist message resonated with rural voters.
etymology: From Latin populus 'people' + -ist, first used of a US political party in the 1890s.

definition: Relating to or resembling pigs.
examples: The villain had small, porcine eyes.
Researchers studied a porcine virus.
etymology: From Latin porcinus, from porcus 'pig'.

definition: A sign or warning that something important or bad is about to happen.
examples: The sudden silence of the birds felt like a portent.
Some saw the market dip as a portent of recession.
etymology: From Latin portentum 'omen', from portendere 'to foretell'.

definition: Ominously significant, or overly solemn and self-important.
examples: The portentous music warned us something was coming.
His portentous speech dragged on far too long.
etymology: From Latin portentosus, from portentum 'omen'.

definition: A collection of a person's work samples, or a range of investments held together.
examples: Bring your portfolio to the interview so we can see your designs.
Her investment portfolio includes stocks, bonds, and real estate.
etymology: From Italian portafogli, from portare 'to carry' + foglio 'sheet of paper'.

definition: Somewhat stout and heavy, often with a dignified air.
examples: A portly gentleman in a waistcoat greeted us.
The portly cat could barely fit through the door.
etymology: From port 'bearing, deportment' + -ly; the sense 'stout' developed later.

definition: A word blending the sounds and meanings of two others.
examples: 'Brunch' is a portmanteau of breakfast and lunch.
Lewis Carroll invented the portmanteau 'chortle'.
etymology: From French portemanteau 'cloak carrier', a traveling bag; Lewis Carroll gave it its linguistic sense.

definition: To depict or describe someone or something in a particular way.
examples: The film tries to portray the inventor as a lonely genius.
Actors often struggle to portray real people convincingly.
etymology: From Old French portraire, from por- 'forth' + traire 'to draw'.

definition: A person who behaves affectedly to impress others.
examples: He's a poseur who carries novels he never reads.
The scene was full of every kind of poseur.
etymology: From French poseur, from poser 'to place, to pose'.

definition: To put forward something as a fact or basis for argument.
examples: Some scientists posit that comets carried water to Earth.
Few historians would posit a single cause for the war.
etymology: From Latin posit-, past participle stem of ponere 'to place'.

definition: A hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale; today, a set lemon cream dessert.
examples: Lady Macbeth drugs the guards' posset.
For dessert, the chef served a lemon posset.
etymology: From late Middle English possot, of unknown origin.

definition: All future generations of people.
examples: The letters were preserved for posterity.
She photographed the old house for posterity before it was torn down.
etymology: From Latin posteritas, from posterus 'following'.

definition: With great speed; immediately.
examples: When she heard the news, she drove to the hospital posthaste.
The broken water main needs to be fixed posthaste.
etymology: From the old instruction 'post, haste' written on urgent letters.

definition: Occurring, awarded, or published after a person's death.
examples: The soldier received a posthumous medal for bravery.
Her posthumous novel became a bestseller.
etymology: From Latin postumus 'last', with spelling influenced by humus 'earth' or humare 'to bury'.

definition: Relating to the time after the Fall of Man; flawed and fallen.
examples: The novel portrays a postlapsarian world of toil and doubt.
We live in a postlapsarian age of spam calls.
etymology: From post- 'after' + Latin lapsus 'a fall'.

definition: Happening after a meal, especially dinner.
examples: Grandpa takes a postprandial nap every Sunday.
They enjoyed a postprandial stroll along the river.
etymology: From post- 'after' + Latin prandium 'late breakfast, lunch'.

definition: To assume something as a basis for reasoning or argument.
examples: Einstein chose to postulate that the speed of light is constant.
Economists postulate rational buyers, but real people differ.
etymology: From Latin postulare 'to ask, demand'.

definition: The way a person holds their body, or a stance adopted toward an issue.
examples: Working at a laptop all day ruined my posture.
The government took an aggressive posture in the trade talks.
etymology: From French posture, from Italian postura, from Latin positura 'position'.

definition: Behavior meant to impress or mislead rather than reflect real intent.
examples: The threats were mostly political posturing.
Behind all the posturing, both sides wanted a deal.
etymology: From posture, from Latin positura 'position'.

definition: Safe to drink.
examples: After the flood, the town had no potable water.
Is the tap water potable here?
etymology: From Late Latin potabilis, from Latin potare 'to drink'.

definition: Having great power, influence, or effect.
examples: This coffee is so potent that one cup keeps me up all night.
Fear is a potent motivator in politics.
etymology: From Latin potent-, present participle stem of posse 'to be able'.

definition: A ruler or very powerful person, especially an autocratic one.
examples: The media mogul behaved like a medieval potentate.
Each potentate at the summit arrived with a huge entourage.
etymology: From Latin potentatus 'dominion', from potent- 'powerful'.

definition: A commotion or fuss over something trivial.
examples: Why all this pother over a missing spoon?
The new parking rules caused quite a pother in the village.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first recorded in the late 16th century.

definition: A mixture of dried scented petals, or a varied mixture of things.
examples: A bowl of lavender potpourri sat on the shelf.
The album is a potpourri of jazz, folk, and pop.
etymology: From French pot pourri 'rotten pot', a translation of Spanish olla podrida, a stew.

definition: A broken piece of pottery, especially one found at a dig.
examples: Every potsherd from the site was carefully labeled.
She found a painted potsherd in the riverbank.
etymology: From pot + sherd, from Old English sceard 'fragment'.

definition: A person actively engaged in a profession or skill, especially medicine or law.
examples: Each practitioner at the clinic sees about twenty patients a day.
She is a longtime practitioner of meditation.
etymology: From obsolete practitian, from Old French practicien, ultimately from Greek praktikos 'practical'.

definition: Dealing with problems in a sensible, practical way rather than ideally.
examples: She took a pragmatic approach and chose the cheaper option that still worked.
A pragmatic leader focuses on what is achievable, not what sounds impressive.
etymology: From Greek pragmatikos, 'skilled in affairs', from pragma 'deed, act'.

definition: To talk foolishly or at tedious length.
examples: He would prate about his golf swing for hours.
Let fools prate; we have work to do.
etymology: From Middle Dutch or Middle Low German praten, probably imitative.

definition: To talk at length in a foolish or trivial way.
examples: Toddlers prattle happily to their stuffed animals.
He tends to prattle on about his fantasy football team.
etymology: From Middle Low German pratelen, from prate 'to chatter'.

definition: Practice as distinguished from theory; the application of an idea.
examples: The course bridges educational theory and classroom praxis.
For the activists, praxis mattered more than slogans.
etymology: From Greek praxis 'doing, action', from prattein 'to do'.

definition: An introductory statement, often explaining the purpose of what follows.
examples: Without preamble, she announced her resignation.
The preamble to the constitution states its goals.
etymology: From Medieval Latin praeambulus 'going before', from Latin praeambulare.

definition: Not safe or stable; likely to fall, fail, or collapse.
examples: The hikers inched across the precarious rope bridge, gripping the rails tightly.
Her finances were precarious after losing her job and her main client in the same month.
etymology: From Latin precarius, 'obtained by asking', hence 'uncertain, dependent on another's will'.

definition: Expressing a wish or request rather than a binding command.
examples: The will's precatory language merely hoped the house would stay in the family.
Shareholders passed a precatory resolution the board could ignore.
etymology: From Late Latin precatorius, from precari 'to pray'.

definition: An action taken in advance to prevent something bad from happening.
examples: As a precaution, we backed up all the files before the update.
Wearing a helmet is a simple precaution that saves lives.
etymology: From Late Latin praecautio, from Latin praecavere 'to guard against beforehand'.

definition: To come before something in time, order, or position.
examples: A short speech will precede the awards ceremony.
Dark clouds usually precede a summer thunderstorm.
etymology: From Latin praecedere, from prae- 'before' + cedere 'to go'.

definition: The condition of being considered more important than something else and coming first.
examples: Safety takes precedence over speed.
Family obligations took precedence over the conference.
etymology: From precedent, from Latin praecedere 'to go before'.

definition: An earlier event or decision used as an example for later ones.
examples: Letting one employee work remotely could set a precedent for everyone.
The court's ruling set an important precedent.
etymology: From Latin praecedere, 'to go before'.

definition: A general rule meant to guide behavior or thought.
examples: Kindness was the guiding precept of her life.
The basic precept of the diet is simple: eat less sugar.
etymology: From Latin praeceptum 'maxim, order', from praecipere 'to warn, instruct'.

definition: A very steep cliff, or a situation of great danger.
examples: The trail runs along the edge of a precipice.
The economy stood on the precipice of a recession.
etymology: From Latin praecipitium 'abrupt descent', from praeceps 'headlong'.

definition: To cause something, usually bad, to happen suddenly or sooner.
examples: One careless remark could precipitate a crisis.
Rising rates may precipitate a housing slowdown.
etymology: From Latin praecipitare 'to throw headlong', from praeceps 'headlong'.

definition: Dangerously steep, or done suddenly and without careful thought.
examples: The road made a precipitous drop toward the sea.
The company saw a precipitous fall in profits.
etymology: From obsolete French précipiteux, from Latin praeceps 'headlong'.

definition: A person who insists on rigid observance of rules or forms.
examples: The editor was a precisian about citation style.
Only a precisian would object to rounding the number.
etymology: From precise + -ian, first used of 16th-century Puritans.

definition: To prevent something from happening or make it impossible.
examples: A knee injury precluded him from running the marathon.
Their busy schedules preclude a long vacation this year.
etymology: From Latin praecludere, 'to shut off', from prae-, 'before', + claudere, 'to shut'.

definition: Showing unusually early development or maturity, especially in a child.
examples: The precocious seven-year-old was already reading novels meant for teenagers.
Her precocious talent for chess stunned the adults who had come to play her.
etymology: From Latin praecox, 'ripening early', from prae- 'before' + coquere 'to cook, ripen'.

definition: Something that comes before and leads to the development of something else.
examples: The telegraph was a precursor to the telephone.
Chest pain can be a precursor of a heart attack.
etymology: From Latin praecursor 'forerunner', from praecurrere 'to run before'.

definition: Living by preying on other animals; predatory.
examples: Predacious beetles keep aphids in check.
The company had a predacious appetite for smaller rivals.
etymology: From Latin praeda 'booty, prey' + -acious.

definition: Exploiting or preying on others, especially the weak.
examples: The bank was fined for predatory lending.
Hawks are predatory birds with keen eyesight.
etymology: From Latin praedatorius, from praedari 'to plunder', from praeda 'booty'.

definition: A person who held a position before someone else, or a thing replaced by another.
examples: The new CEO undid many of her predecessor's decisions.
This phone is lighter than its predecessor.
etymology: From Late Latin praedecessor, from prae- 'before' + decessor 'one who departs'.

definition: A difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation that is hard to escape.
examples: Locked out without his phone, he was in quite a predicament.
The company's predicament worsened when its main supplier closed.
etymology: From Late Latin praedicamentum 'something predicated', from praedicare 'to declare'.

definition: A preference or special liking for something.
examples: She has a predilection for old jazz records.
His predilection for long meetings frustrated the team.
etymology: From French prédilection, from Medieval Latin praediligere, 'to prefer'.

definition: To make someone likely or inclined to do or suffer something.
examples: Genetics may predispose some people to heart disease.
A warm welcome will predispose the judges in your favor.
etymology: From pre- 'before' + dispose, from Latin disponere 'to arrange'.

definition: Present as the strongest or most common element.
examples: Blue is the predominant color in her paintings.
Spanish is the predominant language in the neighborhood.
etymology: From Medieval Latin praedominari 'to predominate', from prae- 'before' + dominari 'to rule'.

definition: Surpassing all others; most distinguished in a field.
examples: She is the preeminent expert on medieval maps.
The preeminent concern for travelers is safety.
etymology: From Latin praeeminent-, from praeeminere 'to project, excel'.

definition: To act in advance to prevent something from happening or to forestall someone.
examples: The company cut prices to preempt a competitor's launch.
She tried to preempt criticism by admitting the flaws first.
etymology: A back-formation from preemption, from Medieval Latin praeemere 'to buy in advance'.

definition: To groom oneself fussily, or to show self-satisfaction.
examples: Swans preen their feathers on the riverbank.
Actors preen for the cameras on the red carpet.
etymology: Probably an alteration of obsolete prune 'to trim the feathers', influenced by Middle English preen 'to pierce'.

definition: Serving as an introduction.
examples: After a few prefatory remarks, the lecture began.
The prefatory note explains how the book was written.
etymology: From Latin praefat-, past participle stem of praefari 'to speak beforehand'.

definition: To be an early sign or version of something that comes later.
examples: His early sketches prefigure his later masterpieces.
These small protests may prefigure a larger movement.
etymology: From Late Latin praefigurare, from prae- 'before' + figurare 'to form'.

definition: Relating to an innocent, unspoiled time before a fall from grace.
examples: The film paints a prelapsarian picture of small-town summers.
Before smartphones, our childhood seemed almost prelapsarian.
etymology: From pre- + Latin lapsus, 'fall'.

definition: Coming before and preparing for the main part of something.
examples: The preliminary results look promising, but we need more data.
After some preliminary small talk, they got down to business.
etymology: From Modern Latin praeliminaris, from prae- 'before' + limen 'threshold'.

definition: An action or event that serves as an introduction to something larger.
examples: The skirmish was a prelude to a much larger war.
Light rain was a prelude to the storm.
etymology: From French prélude, from Medieval Latin praeludium, from Latin praeludere 'to play beforehand'.

definition: Thought out or planned in advance.
examples: Prosecutors argued that the attack was premeditated.
Her premeditated silence spoke louder than words.
etymology: From Latin praemeditari 'to think over beforehand'.

definition: An idea or statement on which an argument or story is based.
examples: The movie's premise is simple: a dog finds its way home across the country.
Your conclusion rests on a false premise.
etymology: From Medieval Latin praemissa, 'things put before', from praemittere 'to send before'.

definition: An extra amount paid above the normal price, or a regular payment for insurance.
examples: Customers pay a premium for organic produce.
My insurance premium went up again this year.
etymology: From Latin praemium 'reward, booty'.

definition: A strong feeling that something, especially something bad, is about to happen.
examples: She had a premonition that the flight would be canceled.
A premonition of trouble kept him awake.
etymology: From Late Latin praemonitio, from Latin praemonere 'to forewarn'.

definition: So absorbed in one's thoughts that one pays little attention to anything else.
examples: He seemed preoccupied during dinner and barely spoke.
She was too preoccupied with the deadline to notice the fire alarm test.
etymology: From preoccupy, from Latin praeoccupare 'to seize beforehand'.

definition: Decided or determined in advance, as if by fate.
examples: Their victory felt preordained from the opening kickoff.
She refused to believe her future was preordained.
etymology: From pre- 'before' + ordain, from Latin ordinare 'to put in order'.

definition: The quality of being greater in number, weight, or importance.
examples: A preponderance of evidence pointed to the landlord.
The preponderance of young voters surprised pollsters.
etymology: From Latin praeponderare 'to outweigh', from prae- + ponderare 'to weigh'.

definition: Attractive or making a good first impression.
examples: The hotel's lobby was hardly prepossessing, but the rooms were lovely.
He was a prepossessing young man with an easy smile.
etymology: From prepossess 'to influence beforehand', from pre- + possess.

definition: Completely absurd or ridiculous.
examples: The idea that he stole the cake is preposterous.
They charged a preposterous price for a bottle of water.
etymology: From Latin praeposterus 'reversed, absurd', from prae 'before' + posterus 'coming after'.

definition: Greater than others in power, influence, or effect.
examples: Fear proved the prepotent motive in the crowd.
A prepotent stallion passes his traits to most of his foals.
etymology: From Latin praepotent-, from prae- 'before' + potens 'powerful'.

definition: Something that must exist or be done before something else can happen.
examples: Basic algebra is a prerequisite for this course.
Trust is a prerequisite for any good partnership.
etymology: From pre- 'before' + requisite, from Latin requirere 'to require'.

definition: A right or privilege that belongs to a particular person or group.
examples: It's your prerogative to change your mind.
Setting the dinner menu is the host's prerogative.
etymology: From Latin praerogativa, the voting group asked to vote first, from praerogare 'to ask first'.

definition: To be a sign or warning of something about to happen.
examples: Falling sales often presage layoffs.
Those dark clouds presage a stormy afternoon.
etymology: From Latin praesagium 'presentiment', from praesagire 'to perceive beforehand'.

definition: Having or showing knowledge of events before they happen.
examples: Her prescient warning about the housing market proved right.
The novel seems prescient in its view of social media.
etymology: From Latin praescire, 'to know beforehand'.

definition: To set aside or leave out of consideration for the moment.
examples: Let us prescind from the question of cost and consider design.
Philosophers prescind certain details to isolate a principle.
etymology: From Latin praescindere 'to cut off in front'.

definition: To recommend a medicine or treatment officially, or to set down a rule to be followed.
examples: The doctor may prescribe antibiotics if the fever continues.
The guidelines prescribe a strict format for every report.
etymology: From Latin praescribere 'to write before, direct', from prae- + scribere 'to write'.

definition: A vague feeling that something, usually bad, is going to happen.
examples: A presentiment of disaster hung over the voyage.
She had a presentiment that the letter carried bad news.
etymology: From obsolete French présentiment, from pré- 'before' + sentiment 'feeling'.

definition: Requiring quick or immediate attention.
examples: Housing is the most pressing issue for the city council.
Sorry to leave early, but I have a pressing appointment.
etymology: From press, from Old French presser, from Latin pressare 'to press'.

definition: Sleight of hand performed as entertainment.
examples: The magician's prestidigitation left the children gasping.
The accountant's prestidigitation made the losses vanish.
etymology: From French prestidigitateur, from preste 'nimble' + Latin digitus 'finger'.

definition: Widespread respect and admiration earned through achievement or quality.
examples: The award carries enormous prestige in the publishing world.
Some students choose a college for its prestige rather than its programs.
etymology: From French prestige 'illusion, glamour', from Latin praestigiae 'conjuring tricks'.

definition: Used to say that something is likely to be true.
examples: The package is presumably stuck at the post office.
Presumably, the store will restock by Monday.
etymology: From presume, from Latin praesumere 'to take beforehand'.

definition: To suppose something is true without proof, or to act too boldly.
examples: I presume you've already read the report.
Don't presume to tell me how to raise my kids.
etymology: From Old French presumer, from Latin praesumere 'to take beforehand'.

definition: Assumed to be true or likely, based on available evidence.
examples: She is the presumptive nominee after winning the primaries.
The heir presumptive could be displaced by a later birth.
etymology: From Late Latin praesumptivus, from praesumere 'to take beforehand'.

definition: Overstepping proper limits by acting too confidently or boldly.
examples: It would be presumptuous to book the venue before she says yes.
His presumptuous request for a promotion surprised his boss.
etymology: From Late Latin praesumptuosus, from praesumptio 'presumption'.

definition: Trying to seem more important, cultured, or intelligent than one really is.
examples: The menu was so pretentious that no one knew what to order.
He avoids sounding pretentious when he talks about wine.
etymology: From French prétentieux, from prétention 'claim'.

definition: A verb tense expressing a past action or completed state.
examples: 'Sang' is the preterite of 'sing'.
Spanish learners often confuse the preterite with the imperfect.
etymology: From Latin praeteritus 'gone by', from praeterire 'to pass by'.

definition: The act of passing over something, or mentioning it by saying it will be omitted.
examples: 'I won't dwell on his arrest' is a sly preterition.
The eulogy used preterition to hint at old quarrels.
etymology: From Late Latin praeteritio, from praeterire 'to pass by'.

definition: Beyond what is normal or natural; extraordinary.
examples: She had a preternatural calm in emergencies.
The goalkeeper's reflexes seemed almost preternatural.
etymology: From Medieval Latin praeternaturalis, from Latin praeter naturam 'beyond nature'.

definition: A false reason given to hide the real reason for an action.
examples: He called on the pretext of returning a book, but really wanted to talk.
The inspection was a pretext for searching the office.
etymology: From Latin praetextus 'outward display', from praetexere 'to weave in front, disguise'.

definition: To prove more powerful or win out, or to be widespread.
examples: I trust that common sense will prevail.
Cooler temperatures will prevail through the weekend.
etymology: From Latin praevalere 'to have greater power', from prae- + valere 'to be strong'.

definition: Widespread and common at a particular time or place.
examples: Flu is most prevalent during the cold winter months, when people stay indoors.
Smartphones are so prevalent that many children use them before learning to read.
etymology: From Latin praevalens, 'very powerful', from praevalere 'to prevail'.

definition: To speak evasively to avoid telling the truth.
examples: When asked where the cookies went, my brother began to prevaricate.
The spokesperson prevaricated for several minutes.
etymology: From Latin praevaricari, 'to walk crookedly'.

definition: Coming before or in anticipation of something.
examples: Theologians speak of prevenient grace that precedes faith.
A prevenient warning saved the crew from disaster.
etymology: From Latin praevenient-, present participle stem of praevenire 'to come before'.

definition: Stiffly formal, proper, and easily shocked by anything improper.
examples: She gave a prim little smile and folded her hands.
His prim manner made the rowdy party feel awkward.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the late 17th century.

definition: The state of being most important or first in rank.
examples: The court affirmed the primacy of federal law.
Our team stresses the primacy of the user experience.
etymology: From Medieval Latin primatia, from Latin primas 'of the first rank'.

definition: Basic and instinctive, as if from the earliest stage of human life.
examples: She let out a primal scream at the summit.
Hunger is a primal need.
etymology: From Medieval Latin primalis, from Latin primus 'first'.

definition: Belonging to the earliest ages of the world; ancient and untouched.
examples: They hiked through a primeval forest of giant ferns.
A primeval fear gripped him in the dark cave.
etymology: From Latin primaevus, from primus 'first' + aevum 'age'.

definition: The right of the firstborn child, often the eldest son, to inherit everything.
examples: Under primogeniture, the younger brothers received nothing.
The novel critiques the cruelty of primogeniture.
etymology: From Medieval Latin primogenitura, from Latin primo 'first' + genitura 'birth'.

definition: Existing from the very beginning of time, or basic and fundamental.
examples: Life may have begun in a primordial soup of chemicals.
Fear of the dark is a primordial instinct.
etymology: From Late Latin primordialis, from primordium 'origin', from primus 'first' + ordiri 'to begin'.

definition: To dress up or adjust one's appearance fussily.
examples: He would prink in front of the mirror for half an hour.
The guests stopped to prink before entering the ballroom.
etymology: Probably related to prank in the obsolete sense 'to adorn'.

definition: In original condition; clean and unspoiled.
examples: The used bike was in pristine condition.
We swam in a pristine mountain lake.
etymology: From Latin pristinus, 'former'.

definition: A state of hardship caused by lacking basic necessities.
examples: The settlers endured years of privation.
Wartime privation shaped her frugal habits.
etymology: From Latin privatio, from privare 'to deprive'.

definition: Marked by the absence of a quality, or expressing negation, as the prefix un-.
examples: The 'a-' in 'amoral' is a privative prefix.
Darkness was once described as a privative state, the absence of light.
etymology: From Latin privativus, from privare 'to deprive'.

definition: Sharing in knowledge of something secret or private.
examples: Only a few executives were privy to the merger talks.
I wasn't privy to their conversation.
etymology: From Old French prive 'private', from Latin privatus.

definition: Taking action to control a situation in advance rather than reacting to it.
examples: Be proactive and ask for feedback before the review.
The city took a proactive approach to flood prevention.
etymology: From pro- 'before' + active, coined in the 20th century on the model of reactive.

definition: Having the quality of proving something, especially in law.
examples: The judge ruled the photos had little probative value.
Only probative evidence should go before the jury.
etymology: From Latin probativus, from probare 'to test, prove'.

definition: To investigate or examine something thoroughly.
examples: Journalists began to probe the senator's finances.
The dentist used a tool to probe the sore tooth.
etymology: From Late Latin proba 'proof', from Latin probare 'to test'.

definition: Strong moral principles; honesty and decency.
examples: The judge was known for her probity and fairness.
Questions about his financial probity ended his campaign.
etymology: From Latin probitas, from probus 'good, honest'.

definition: A long, flexible snout or feeding tube, as of an elephant or insect.
examples: The butterfly uncurled its proboscis to sip nectar.
An elephant's proboscis can lift a log.
etymology: From Greek proboskis, from pro 'before' + boskein 'to feed'.

definition: To announce something officially or publicly.
examples: The banners proclaim the town the barbecue capital of Texas.
The mayor will proclaim Friday a city holiday after the big win.
etymology: From Latin proclamare 'to cry out', from pro- 'forth' + clamare 'to shout'.

definition: A natural tendency to choose or do something regularly.
examples: He has a proclivity for procrastination that shows up every time a deadline nears.
Their shared proclivity for bad puns made them instant friends at the office.
etymology: From Latin proclivitas, 'a tendency', from proclivis, 'sloping downward'.

definition: To delay doing something that should be done.
examples: I tend to procrastinate when a task feels overwhelming.
If you procrastinate on your taxes, April will be stressful.
etymology: From Latin procrastinare, from pro- 'forward' + crastinus 'of tomorrow'.

definition: Forcing strict conformity regardless of individual differences.
examples: The school's procrustean rules ignored students' needs.
Critics called the budget formula procrustean.
etymology: From Procrustes, a mythical Greek robber who stretched or cut victims to fit his bed.

definition: To obtain something, especially with care or effort.
examples: The hospital struggled to procure enough ventilators.
Can you procure tickets for the sold-out show?
etymology: From Old French procurer, from Latin procurare 'to take care of'.

definition: Wastefully extravagant with money or resources.
examples: His prodigal spending left the estate in debt.
Her prodigal habits meant each paycheck vanished within a week.
etymology: From Late Latin prodigalis, from Latin prodigus 'lavish'.

definition: Remarkably or impressively large in extent, size, or degree.
examples: She has a prodigious memory for faces.
The young chef showed prodigious talent.
etymology: From Latin prodigiosus, from prodigium 'portent'.

definition: A young person with exceptional talent or ability.
examples: The chess prodigy beat a grandmaster at age twelve.
She was hailed as a musical prodigy before she could read.
etymology: From Latin prodigium 'portent, wonder'.

definition: Relating to early symptoms that signal the onset of a disease.
examples: A headache is often a prodromal sign of migraine.
Doctors watched for prodromal symptoms of measles.
etymology: From Greek prodromos 'running before', from pro- + dromos 'running'.

definition: A preface or preamble to a book or speech.
examples: The epic opens with a proem invoking the Muse.
His brief proem set the tone for the lecture.
etymology: From Greek prooimion 'prelude', from pro 'before' + oime 'song'.

definition: Showing disrespect for sacred things, or secular rather than religious.
examples: His profane outburst shocked the congregation.
The museum displays both sacred and profane art.
etymology: From Latin profanus 'outside the temple', from pro 'before' + fanum 'temple'.

definition: To claim openly that something is true, often falsely, or to declare one's faith.
examples: Many people profess to love reading but rarely open a book.
I don't profess to be an expert on wine.
etymology: From Latin professus, past participle of profiteri 'to declare publicly'.

definition: To hold out or offer something for someone to accept.
examples: The host will proffer a tray of drinks as guests arrive.
He was quick to proffer advice nobody wanted.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman proffrir, from Latin pro- 'forth' + offerre 'to offer'.

definition: Competent and skilled at doing something.
examples: Applicants must be proficient in spreadsheets.
After a year abroad, he became proficient in Japanese.
etymology: From Latin proficient-, present participle stem of proficere 'to advance'.

definition: Recklessly wasteful, or shamelessly given to indulgence.
examples: The governor was accused of profligate spending.
He regretted the profligate years of his youth.
etymology: From Latin profligatus 'ruined, dissolute', from profligare 'to overthrow'.

definition: Very deep, intense, or showing great insight.
examples: The book had a profound effect on the way she saw the world.
He felt a profound sadness when the old house was sold.
etymology: From Latin profundus, 'deep', from pro- 'forth' + fundus 'bottom'.

definition: In large amounts; abundantly.
examples: He apologized profusely for missing the party.
The runner was sweating profusely after the race.
etymology: From Latin profusus, 'poured out', from profundere.

definition: An ancestor, or a person who originated an idea or movement.
examples: He is considered the progenitor of modern jazz guitar.
The family's progenitor was a Scottish weaver who emigrated in 1820.
etymology: From Latin progenitor, from progignere 'to beget'.

definition: A person's or animal's offspring or descendants.
examples: The prize stallion's progeny sell for huge sums.
The billionaire left his fortune to his progeny.
etymology: From Latin progenies 'descendants', from progignere 'to beget'.

definition: Having a jaw that projects forward.
examples: The Habsburg family was known for its prognathous jaw.
The fossil skull was strongly prognathous.
etymology: From pro- 'forward' + Greek gnathos 'jaw'.

definition: A forecast of the likely course of a disease or situation.
examples: The doctor gave a hopeful prognosis.
The prognosis for the economy is grim.
etymology: From Greek prognosis 'foreknowledge', from pro- 'before' + gignoskein 'to know'.

definition: To foretell or predict a future event.
examples: Analysts love to prognosticate about interest rates.
Nobody can prognosticate the weather a month ahead.
etymology: From Medieval Latin prognosticare, from Greek prognostikos 'foreknowing'.

definition: So high or severe as to prevent something from being done.
examples: The cost of housing downtown is prohibitive for most families.
Shipping fees were prohibitive, so we bought locally.
etymology: From French prohibitif, from Latin prohibere 'to prevent'.

definition: Elongated along the polar axis, like a football.
examples: A rugby ball has a prolate shape.
Some galaxies are prolate rather than flattened.
etymology: From Latin prolatus 'extended', past participle of proferre 'to bring forward'.

definition: A critical introduction to a longer work or field of study.
examples: The first chapter serves as a prolegomenon to the theory.
Her lecture was a prolegomenon to a much larger book.
etymology: From Greek prolegomenon 'something said beforehand', from prolegein.

definition: Representing a future event as if it had already happened; a flash-forward.
examples: The novel opens with a prolepsis showing the hero's funeral.
'He was a dead man' is a prolepsis when said of the living.
etymology: From Greek prolepsis 'anticipation', from prolambanein 'to anticipate'.

definition: Working-class people regarded collectively, especially in Marxist theory.
examples: Marx predicted that the proletariat would rise up.
The novel portrays the urban proletariat of 1900s London.
etymology: From French prolétariat, from Latin proletarius 'citizen of the lowest class'.

definition: To increase rapidly in number; to multiply.
examples: Food trucks began to proliferate across the city.
Rumors proliferate whenever leaders stay silent.
etymology: A back-formation from proliferation, from French prolifère 'producing offspring'.

definition: Producing a great deal of work, offspring, or results.
examples: The prolific author wrote more than sixty novels in her lifetime.
Rabbits are prolific breeders and can quickly overrun a meadow.
etymology: From Medieval Latin prolificus, from Latin proles 'offspring' + -ficus 'making'.

definition: Using too many words; tediously lengthy.
examples: The prolix report could have been a single page.
His prolix emails require a second cup of coffee.
etymology: From Latin prolixus, 'extended'.

definition: To make something last longer.
examples: Regular oil changes prolong the life of your engine.
Let's not prolong this meeting any further.
etymology: From Late Latin prolongare, from pro- 'forward' + longus 'long'.

definition: A preliminary essay or performance; a warm-up exercise.
examples: Milton's student prolusion was delivered in Latin.
The skirmish was a mere prolusion to the battle.
etymology: From Latin prolusio, from proludere 'to practice beforehand'.

definition: A paved public walk, especially by the sea, or a leisurely stroll.
examples: We bought ice cream on the seaside promenade.
An evening promenade through the park was their ritual.
etymology: From French promenade, from se promener 'to take a walk'.

definition: Important and well known, or standing out so as to be easily seen.
examples: A prominent lawyer agreed to take the case for free.
The logo should be more prominent on the homepage.
etymology: From Latin prominent-, present participle stem of prominere 'to jut out'.

definition: Showing signs of future success or excellence.
examples: The early test results are promising.
She's a promising young chef with her own ideas.
etymology: From promise, from Latin promissum 'something promised'.

definition: A high point of land jutting out into the sea.
examples: A lighthouse stands on the rocky promontory.
From the promontory we watched whales pass below.
etymology: From Latin promunturium, perhaps related to prominere 'to jut out'.

definition: Done or acting quickly and without delay.
examples: Thank you for your prompt reply.
Prompt treatment can prevent the infection from spreading.
etymology: From Latin promptus 'brought forth, ready', from promere 'to bring out'.

definition: Quickness and readiness of action.
examples: The firefighters responded with admirable promptitude.
She answered every letter with promptitude.
