etymology: From Late Latin promptitudo, from Latin promptus 'ready'.

definition: To make an idea or law widely known or officially announce it.
examples: The agency will promulgate new safety rules next month.
Early teachers of the method worked hard to promulgate it.
etymology: From Latin promulgare, 'to make public'.

definition: Likely to suffer from or do something, usually something undesirable.
examples: This old car is prone to breaking down in the cold.
He is prone to exaggeration when he tells stories.
etymology: From Latin pronus 'leaning forward'.

definition: Serving as preliminary instruction or an introduction to further study.
examples: Logic was once a propaedeutic subject for all university students.
The propaedeutic course prepares students for advanced chemistry.
etymology: From Greek propaideuein 'to teach beforehand', from pro- + paideuein 'to teach'.

definition: Biased or misleading information spread to promote a political cause or point of view.
examples: The posters were wartime propaganda designed to stir up fear.
Learn to tell journalism from propaganda.
etymology: From Modern Latin congregatio de propaganda fide 'congregation for propagating the faith', a Catholic committee founded in 1622.

definition: To spread an idea widely, or to grow new plants from a parent.
examples: Social media can propagate false claims in minutes.
You can propagate mint from a single cutting.
etymology: From Latin propagare 'to multiply from layers', from propago 'young shoot'.

definition: To drive or push something forward.
examples: Strong reviews helped propel the book onto the bestseller list.
Two engines propel the boat across the bay.
etymology: From Latin propellere, from pro- 'forward' + pellere 'to drive'.

definition: A natural tendency to behave in a certain way.
examples: My cat has a propensity for knocking things off tables.
He has a propensity to overpack for short trips.
etymology: From Latin propensus, 'inclined', from propendere 'to hang forward'.

definition: A prediction of what will happen in the future, sometimes believed to be divinely inspired.
examples: The fantasy novel centers on an ancient prophecy.
His gloomy prophecy about the market came true.
etymology: From Greek propheteia, from prophetes 'spokesman, interpreter'.

definition: Nearness in place, time, or relationship.
examples: Propinquity, not shared interests, explained most of their college friendships.
The propinquity of the two houses made privacy difficult.
etymology: From Latin propinquitas, from propinquus, 'near'.

definition: To win or regain someone's favor by pleasing them.
examples: I brought flowers to propitiate my annoyed neighbor.
Ancient sailors offered gifts to propitiate the gods of the sea.
etymology: From Latin propitiare, from propitius, 'favorable'.

definition: Indicating a good chance of success; favorable.
examples: It wasn't a propitious moment to ask for a raise.
Clear skies made for propitious sailing conditions.
etymology: From Latin propitius 'favorable, gracious'.

definition: A person who argues for or supports an idea or plan.
examples: She is a vocal proponent of the four-day work week.
Each proponent of the bill spoke for five minutes.
etymology: From Latin proponent-, present participle stem of proponere 'to set forth'.

definition: A suggested plan or offer, or a statement expressing a judgment or opinion.
examples: Opening a café downtown is an expensive proposition.
The proposition that money buys happiness is hotly debated.
etymology: From Latin propositio, from proponere 'to set forth'.

definition: To put forward an idea or theory for others to consider.
examples: Darwin went on to propound the theory of natural selection.
She likes to propound bold theories at dinner.
etymology: From Latin proponere 'to set forth', via an earlier English form propone.

definition: Owned privately, especially protected by a trademark or patent.
examples: The company guards its proprietary software closely.
The sauce is made from a proprietary blend of spices.
etymology: From Late Latin proprietarius, from proprietas 'ownership'.

definition: Correct behavior that conforms to accepted moral or social standards.
examples: Critics questioned the propriety of the senator's gifts.
She always behaved with perfect propriety at formal dinners.
etymology: From Old French propriete 'ownership, peculiarity', from Latin proprietas.

definition: The body's sense of its own position and movement.
examples: Proprioception lets you touch your nose with your eyes closed.
Balance training improves proprioception in older adults.
etymology: From Latin proprius 'one's own' + reception.

definition: To suspend a session of a parliament without dissolving it.
examples: The prime minister asked the monarch to prorogue Parliament.
Courts ruled that it was unlawful to prorogue the assembly.
etymology: From Latin prorogare 'to prolong', from pro- 'in front of' + rogare 'to ask'.

definition: Ordinary and unimaginative; lacking poetry or excitement.
examples: The prosaic reality of the job was mostly filling out forms and answering emails.
He described the glittering city's origins in surprisingly prosaic terms, as a mere trading post.
etymology: From Late Latin prosaicus, from Latin prosa, 'straightforward discourse'.

definition: To forbid, especially by law or rule.
examples: The pool rules proscribe running on the deck.
The school proscribes phones during exams.
etymology: From Latin proscribere, 'to publish in writing'.

definition: To try to convert people to one's beliefs or opinions.
examples: My uncle loves to proselytize about the joys of sourdough baking.
She proselytizes for cycling to anyone who will listen.
etymology: From proselyte, from Greek proselytos 'one who has come over'.

definition: The patterns of rhythm and sound in poetry or in speech intonation.
examples: The seminar focused on the prosody of Milton.
Speech therapists study prosody to help with flat-sounding voices.
etymology: From Greek prosoidia 'song sung to music, accent', from pros 'toward' + oide 'song'.

definition: An inability to recognize familiar faces.
examples: Because of prosopagnosia, she recognizes friends by their voices.
The neurologist diagnosed him with prosopagnosia after the stroke.
etymology: From Greek prosopon 'face' + agnosia 'ignorance'.

definition: The study of a group's shared traits through collective biographies.
examples: Her prosopography traced the careers of Roman senators.
The project is a prosopography of medieval merchants.
etymology: From Greek prosopon 'face, person' + -graphy 'writing'.

definition: A figure of speech in which an absent or imaginary person, or a thing, is made to speak.
examples: The poem uses prosopopoeia to let the old house tell its story.
In prosopopoeia, the dead may address the living.
etymology: From Greek prosopopoiia, from prosopon 'face, person' + poiein 'to make'.

definition: The possibility or likelihood of something happening in the future.
examples: The prospect of a long winter made her book a beach trip.
There's little prospect of the bridge reopening this year.
etymology: From Latin prospectus 'view', from prospicere 'to look forward'.

definition: To succeed and do well, especially financially.
examples: Small businesses tend to prosper when tourism is strong.
He moved to the city hoping to prosper.
etymology: From Latin prosperare, from prosperus 'doing well'.

definition: Lying stretched out face down, or completely overcome.
examples: The pilgrims lay prostrate before the altar.
She was prostrate with grief after the loss.
etymology: From Latin prostratus, past participle of prosternere 'to throw down'.

definition: The main character in a story, or a leading figure in a cause or event.
examples: The protagonist of the novel is a retired detective.
She was a key protagonist in the fight for voting rights.
etymology: From Greek protagonistes, from protos 'first' + agonistes 'actor, contestant'.

definition: The 'if' clause of a conditional sentence.
examples: In 'If it rains, we stay home,' the protasis is 'If it rains'.
Each protasis in the contract sets out a condition.
etymology: From Greek protasis 'proposition', from proteinein 'to put forward'.

definition: Able to change frequently or easily take many different forms.
examples: Her protean talent spans painting, music, and film.
Viruses are protean enemies that constantly mutate.
etymology: From Proteus, a Greek sea god who could change his shape at will.

definition: An official set of rules or procedures for how something should be done.
examples: Hospital staff followed strict protocol during the outbreak.
Royal protocol dictates who enters the room first.
etymology: From Greek protokollon 'first leaf glued to a manuscript', via Medieval Latin and French.

definition: Lasting much longer than expected or usual.
examples: After protracted negotiations, the strike finally ended.
The protracted heat wave strained the power grid.
etymology: From Latin protract-, past participle stem of protrahere 'to prolong'.

definition: Intended to persuade or urge someone toward a course, especially study.
examples: Aristotle wrote a protreptic work urging readers toward philosophy.
Her protreptic speech persuaded many to enroll.
etymology: From Greek protreptikos 'exhortative', from protrepein 'to urge on'.

definition: To stick out beyond a surface or edge.
examples: Rusty nails protrude from the old fence.
Make sure no wires protrude from the casing.
etymology: From Latin protrudere, from pro- 'forward' + trudere 'to thrust'.

definition: The place of origin or history of ownership of something.
examples: The museum carefully checked the provenance of the sculpture.
Shoppers increasingly care about the provenance of their coffee.
etymology: From French provenance, from provenir, 'to come forth'.

definition: Animal fodder, or food and provisions in general.
examples: The stable kept a winter's worth of provender.
Our picnic basket held ample provender for the hike.
etymology: From Old French provendre, from Latin praebenda 'things to be supplied'.

definition: Referred to in a well-known saying, or so well known as to be typical.
examples: Finding him in that crowd was like finding the proverbial needle in a haystack.
His proverbial stinginess was a family joke.
etymology: From Latin proverbialis, from proverbium 'proverb'.

definition: Careful in planning and saving for the future.
examples: A provident farmer stores grain for lean years.
Being provident, she kept six months of savings.
etymology: From Latin provident-, present participle stem of providere 'to foresee'.

definition: Unsophisticated or narrow-minded, as associated with life outside the capital.
examples: City critics dismissed the play as provincial.
His provincial outlook began to change once he traveled.
etymology: From Latin provincialis, from provincia 'province'.

definition: The act of supplying something, or a condition included in an agreement.
examples: The contract includes a provision for remote work.
The provision of clean water is the charity's main goal.
etymology: From Latin provisio 'foresight', from providere 'to foresee'.

definition: Arranged for the present, with the possibility of being changed later.
examples: The dates are provisional until the venue confirms.
A provisional government took over after the election collapsed.
etymology: From provision, from Latin provisio 'foresight', from providere 'to foresee'.

definition: A condition attached to an agreement.
examples: She accepted the job with the proviso that she could work remotely.
The grant came with one proviso: publish the results.
etymology: From Medieval Latin proviso quod 'it being provided that', from providere 'to provide'.

definition: A person who deliberately provokes controversy or trouble.
examples: The comedian enjoys his role as a provocateur.
Police suspected a provocateur had started the riot.
etymology: From French provocateur, from Latin provocare 'to challenge'.

definition: To deliberately cause a strong reaction, especially anger.
examples: Don't provoke the dog by waving that stick.
The article was written to provoke debate.
etymology: From Latin provocare 'to challenge', from pro- 'forth' + vocare 'to call'.

definition: Great skill or ability in a particular activity.
examples: Her prowess on the basketball court earned her a scholarship.
The chef's prowess with knives was fun to watch.
etymology: From Old French prouesse, 'valor', from prou 'brave'.

definition: To move about stealthily, as if hunting.
examples: Coyotes prowl the neighborhood at night.
Shoppers prowl the outlet mall for bargains.
etymology: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin.

definition: Nearness in space, time, or relationship.
examples: They chose the apartment for its proximity to the subway.
The proximity of the two deadlines made the week stressful.
etymology: From Latin proximitas, from proximus 'nearest'.

definition: A person authorized to act for another, or something used to represent something else.
examples: She voted by proxy because she was traveling.
Test scores are a poor proxy for intelligence.
etymology: From Middle English procracie, a contraction of procuracy 'stewardship'.

definition: Careful and sensible, especially in planning for the future.
examples: It is prudent to save some money for unexpected repairs.
The prudent hiker checked the forecast and packed an extra jacket.
etymology: From Latin prudens, a contraction of providens 'foreseeing'.

definition: Easily shocked by matters relating to sex or nudity.
examples: The film seems tame now, but prudish critics once condemned it.
She isn't prudish, just private.
etymology: From prude, from French prude, from prudefemme 'virtuous woman'.

definition: To trim a plant by cutting away branches, or to cut away what is unnecessary.
examples: Prune the roses in late winter for better blooms.
The editor asked me to prune the article by a third.
etymology: From Old French proignier, of uncertain origin.

definition: Having or encouraging an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters.
examples: The tabloid fed readers' prurient curiosity about the divorce.
Critics accused the film of prurient sensationalism.
etymology: From Latin prurient-, present participle stem of prurire 'to itch, long for'.

definition: The statistical study of elections and voting trends.
examples: Psephology became a popular hobby during the election.
Her degree in psephology landed her a job with a pollster.
etymology: From Greek psephos 'pebble', used by Athenians for voting, + -logy.

definition: A fictitious name used by an author or other person to hide their identity.
examples: She published her first mystery under a pseudonym.
Mark Twain was the pseudonym of Samuel Clemens.
etymology: From French pseudonyme, from Greek pseudonymos, from pseudes 'false' + onoma 'name'.

definition: A conflict of the soul, especially between virtues and vices.
examples: The novel stages a psychomachia between duty and desire.
Every diet is a small psychomachia over dessert.
etymology: From the title of a Latin poem by Prudentius, from Greek psukhe 'soul' + makhe 'battle'.

definition: A guide who leads souls of the dead to the afterlife.
examples: Hermes served as a psychopomp in Greek myth.
In the novel, a black dog acts as a psychopomp.
etymology: From Greek psukhopompos, from psukhe 'soul' + pompos 'guide'.

definition: Playful and mischievous.
examples: With a puckish grin, he hid his sister's shoes.
The comedian's puckish humor delighted kids and adults alike.
etymology: From Puck, the mischievous sprite of English folklore and Shakespeare.

definition: Childishly silly and immature.
examples: The comments section was full of puerile jokes.
His puerile behavior embarrassed his colleagues.
etymology: From Latin puerilis, from puer 'boy'.

definition: A boxer, especially a professional one.
examples: The old pugilist still trains at the gym every morning.
He had the flattened nose of a pugilist.
etymology: From Latin pugil 'boxer'.

definition: Eager and quick to argue or fight.
examples: The pugnacious senator picked a fight with every reporter at the briefing.
Pugnacious as ever, he challenged the referee's call before the whistle stopped.
etymology: From Latin pugnax, from pugnare 'to fight', related to pugnus 'fist'.

definition: Great power, might, or influence.
examples: The empire was at the height of its puissance.
The general's puissance on the battlefield was legendary.
etymology: From Old French puissance, from puissant 'powerful', from Latin posse 'to be able'.

definition: Genuine, excellent, or properly done.
examples: That's a pukka curry, just like my grandmother's.
He spoke with a pukka accent.
etymology: From Hindi pakka 'cooked, ripe, substantial'.

definition: Physical beauty, especially of a striking kind.
examples: Critics praised the film's pulchritude more than its thin plot.
The statue's pulchritude drew visitors from across the continent.
etymology: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher 'beautiful'.

definition: To multiply rapidly, or to teem and swarm with life.
examples: Mosquitoes pullulate in the summer marshes.
Ideas seem to pullulate whenever she starts a new project.
etymology: From Latin pullulare 'to sprout', from pullulus 'young animal'.

definition: To crush into fine powder, or to defeat utterly.
examples: Use a mortar to pulverize the spices.
The champion expects to pulverize her opponent.
etymology: From Late Latin pulverizare, from Latin pulvis 'dust'.

definition: A fine point of etiquette, or great attention to formality.
examples: The ambassador observed every punctilio of court ceremony.
He followed the rules with absurd punctilio.
etymology: From Italian puntiglio 'small point', influenced by Latin punctum 'point'.

definition: Showing great attention to detail and correct behavior.
examples: The punctilious accountant checked every figure twice before signing.
She was punctilious about thanking every guest with a handwritten note.
etymology: From Italian puntiglio, 'small point', from Latin punctum 'point'.

definition: Arriving or doing something at the agreed time.
examples: Swiss trains are famously punctual.
Please be punctual; the tour leaves at nine sharp.
etymology: From Medieval Latin punctualis, from Latin punctum 'point'.

definition: An expert who frequently gives opinions to the public, especially in the media.
examples: Every cable news pundit predicted the wrong winner.
A sports pundit criticized the coach's decision.
etymology: From Hindi pandit 'learned man', from Sanskrit pandita.

definition: Having a sharp, strong smell or taste; also sharply critical.
examples: A pungent smell of garlic filled the kitchen.
Her pungent review of the play went viral.
etymology: From Latin pungent-, present participle stem of pungere 'to prick'.

definition: Intended as punishment, or harshly severe.
examples: The jury awarded punitive damages against the company.
Critics called the new tax punitive for small farmers.
etymology: From Medieval Latin punitivus, from Latin punire 'to punish'.

definition: Small and weak, or pitifully inadequate.
examples: The puny fan did nothing against the summer heat.
His excuse seemed puny compared to the damage done.
etymology: From Old French puisne 'born later, younger', from puis 'afterward' + ne 'born'.

definition: Having impaired vision, or lacking insight and understanding.
examples: The purblind old dog bumped into the furniture.
The board was purblind to the coming crisis.
etymology: From Middle English pur blind 'completely blind', from pure + blind.

definition: The practice of secluding women from public view, or any state of seclusion.
examples: The novel depicts a household where women lived in purdah.
Before the budget, ministers enter a kind of purdah.
etymology: From Urdu and Persian parda 'veil, curtain'.

definition: A place or state of temporary suffering, often while waiting.
examples: Sitting in airport purgatory for nine hours was miserable.
In Catholic teaching, purgatory purifies souls before heaven.
etymology: From Medieval Latin purgatorium, from Latin purgare 'to purify'.

definition: To rid something of unwanted people or things, often abruptly.
examples: Every January I purge my closet of clothes I never wear.
The new leader moved to purge the party of rivals.
etymology: From Old French purgier, from Latin purgare 'to purify'.

definition: A person who insists on strict adherence to traditional rules or standards.
examples: A coffee purist will never add sugar.
Any grammar purist would wince at that sign.
etymology: From French puriste, from pur 'pure'.

definition: The area near or surrounding a place, or one's usual haunt.
examples: Artists flocked to the shabby purlieu of the harbor.
The café was his favorite purlieu.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman puralee 'a walk around', influenced by French lieu 'place'.

definition: To steal something, often something small.
examples: Someone managed to purloin the office stapler again.
Spies tried to purloin the secret plans.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman purloigner 'to put away', from pur- + loign 'far'.

definition: To appear or claim to be or do something, especially falsely.
examples: These pills purport to cure baldness.
The documents purport to show secret payments.
etymology: From Old French purporter, from pur- 'forth' + porter 'to carry'.

definition: In accordance with a law, rule, or agreement.
examples: Pursuant to the contract, payment is due in thirty days.
The files were released pursuant to a court order.
etymology: From Old French poursuiant 'pursuing', from poursuivre 'to pursue'.

definition: Containing or discharging pus.
examples: The nurse cleaned the purulent wound.
A purulent infection required antibiotics.
etymology: From Latin purulentus, from pus 'pus'.

definition: To supply goods or information as one's business.
examples: The shop continues to purvey fine cheeses.
Tabloids purvey gossip to millions of readers.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman purveier, from Latin providere 'to foresee, provide'.

definition: The range of authority, responsibility, or concern of someone.
examples: Hiring decisions fall within the purview of the department head.
That question is outside my purview; ask the legal team.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman French purveu, 'provided', a word that began legal clauses.

definition: Lacking courage; timid and fearful of taking risks.
examples: The pusillanimous board refused to back the bold plan.
He called critics pusillanimous for hiding behind anonymous accounts.
etymology: From Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus 'very small' + animus 'spirit'.

definition: Generally considered or reputed to be, though not proven.
examples: The putative father demanded a DNA test.
Investors waited for the putative merger to be confirmed.
etymology: From Late Latin putativus, from Latin putare 'to think'.

definition: To decay and rot, producing a foul smell.
examples: Fruit left in the sun will soon putrefy.
Unused leftovers putrefy at the back of the fridge.
etymology: From Latin putrefacere, from puter 'rotten' + facere 'to make'.

definition: Rotting and giving off a foul smell; also very unpleasant.
examples: A putrid smell rose from the forgotten lunchbox.
The water in the pond had turned putrid.
etymology: From Latin putridus, from putrere 'to rot'.

definition: A sudden, violent attempt to overthrow a government.
examples: The army launched a putsch while the president was abroad.
The failed putsch landed its leaders in prison.
etymology: From Swiss German Putsch 'knock, thrust'.

definition: A heap of wood for burning, especially a body at a funeral.
examples: The villagers gathered around the funeral pyre.
He built a pyre of old furniture in the yard.
etymology: From Greek pura, from pur 'fire', via Latin.

definition: Relating to or producing fever.
examples: The infection caused a pyretic reaction within hours.
Doctors monitored the pyretic patient through the night.
etymology: From Modern Latin pyreticus, from Greek puretos 'fever', from pur 'fire'.

definition: A fireworks display, or a brilliant showy display of skill.
examples: The concert ended with dazzling pyrotechnics.
Her verbal pyrotechnics won the debate.
etymology: From Greek pur 'fire' + tekhne 'art'.

definition: Won at such great cost that the victory is hardly worth it.
examples: Winning the argument was a pyrrhic victory, since she lost the friendship.
The team's pyrrhic win left three starters injured.
etymology: From Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, whose victories over Rome cost him heavily.

definition: Radical philosophical skepticism that suspends judgment on all claims.
examples: His pyrrhonism made him doubt even the existence of the table.
Pyrrhonism teaches that peace comes from suspending judgment.
etymology: From Pyrrho of Elis, a Greek philosopher of about 300 BC who founded the school.

definition: A person who falsely claims medical skill or expertise.
examples: The so-called healer turned out to be a quack.
Don't trust a quack who sells cures online.
etymology: Short for quacksalver, from early modern Dutch, literally one who 'chatters' about his salves.

definition: The four medieval university subjects of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music.
examples: After grammar and logic, students moved on to the quadrivium.
The quadrivium treated music as a branch of mathematics.
etymology: From Latin quadrivium 'place where four roads meet'.

definition: To drink something heartily in large swallows.
examples: After the hike we stopped to quaff cold cider.
Pirates in the movie quaff rum from tin mugs.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the early 16th century.

definition: A soft, boggy area, or a complicated and hard-to-escape situation.
examples: The project became a quagmire of conflicting requirements.
Heavy rain turned the festival field into a quagmire.
etymology: From quag, 'bog', + mire, 'swampy ground'.

definition: To shrink back in fear or lose courage.
examples: Even veteran climbers quail at the sight of that ridge.
She did not quail when the board challenged her.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in late Middle English.

definition: Attractively old-fashioned or charmingly unusual.
examples: We stayed in a quaint cottage with a thatched roof and a tiny garden.
The quaint village has cobbled streets and a bakery that has not changed in decades.
etymology: From Old French cointe, 'clever, pretty', from Latin cognitus 'known'.

definition: The subjective qualities of experience, such as how red looks or pain feels.
examples: Can a machine ever have qualia, or only process data?
Philosophers argue about whether qualia can be explained by physics.
etymology: Plural of Latin quale 'of what kind'.

definition: Relating to the qualities or nature of something rather than its amount.
examples: The survey mixes numbers with qualitative interviews.
There's a qualitative difference between fresh and canned peas.
etymology: From Late Latin qualitativus, from Latin qualitas 'quality'.

definition: An uneasy feeling of doubt, especially about whether something is right.
examples: He had no qualms about asking for help.
I had one small qualm about leaving the dog alone overnight.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in the 16th century meaning 'a sudden feeling of sickness'.

definition: A state of uncertainty about what to do in a difficult situation.
examples: She was in a quandary over whether to take the better salary or stay near family.
The team faced a quandary when both candidates proved equally qualified.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in English in the late 16th century.

definition: To measure or express something as a number or amount.
examples: It's hard to quantify how much the mentoring helped.
Can you quantify the savings from the new process?
etymology: From Medieval Latin quantificare, from Latin quantus 'how much'.

definition: Relating to amounts or numbers that can be measured.
examples: She has strong quantitative skills from her economics degree.
We need quantitative evidence, not just anecdotes.
etymology: From Medieval Latin quantitativus, from Latin quantitas 'quantity'.

definition: An angry argument or disagreement.
examples: The quarrel started over who forgot to buy milk.
I have no quarrel with your plan; I just want more time.
etymology: From Old French querele 'complaint', from Latin querela, from queri 'to complain'.

definition: An animal or person being hunted or pursued.
examples: The hawk circled, searching for its quarry.
The reporter finally cornered her quarry outside the courthouse.
etymology: From Old French cuiree, the parts of a deer given to the hounds, influenced by cuir 'hide'.

definition: To put an end to something firmly, or to officially reject a legal decision.
examples: The CEO moved quickly to quash rumors of a merger.
An appeals court may quash the conviction.
etymology: From Old French quasser 'to annul', from Late Latin cassare, influenced by Latin quassare 'to shatter'.

definition: A stanza or poem of four lines.
examples: Each quatrain of the poem ends with a rhyming couplet.
She scribbled a quatrain on the birthday card.
etymology: From French quatrain, from quatre 'four'.

definition: An ornamental design of four rounded lobes, like a four-leaf clover.
examples: A stone quatrefoil frames the chapel window.
The tiles repeat a simple quatrefoil.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman quatre 'four' + foil 'leaf'.

definition: Of a voice, to shake or tremble, usually from emotion.
examples: His voice began to quaver as he thanked his late father.
I heard her voice quaver over the phone.
etymology: From Middle English quaveren, from quaven 'to tremble'.

definition: Feeling sick to your stomach, or uneasy about something.
examples: The winding mountain road made me queasy.
I feel queasy about lending him that much money.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in late Middle English.

definition: To calm or put an end to something, such as fear or unrest.
examples: The coach's speech helped quell the players' nerves.
Police worked to quell the disturbance outside the stadium.
etymology: From Old English cwellan, 'to kill'.

definition: To satisfy thirst, or to put out a fire or desire.
examples: Nothing can quench my thirst like ice water after a run.
Firefighters worked all night to quench the blaze.
etymology: From Old English -cwencan 'to put out, extinguish'.

definition: A person who asks a question, especially of an astrologer or tarot reader.
examples: The tarot reader asked the querent to shuffle the deck.
Each querent left with a cryptic answer.
etymology: From Latin quaerens 'seeking', from quaerere 'to seek'.

definition: Given to complaining; peevish.
examples: The querimonious passenger griped about every bump.
His letters grew querimonious in old age.
etymology: From Latin querimonia 'complaint', from queri 'to complain'.

definition: Complaining in a whining, irritable way.
examples: The querulous customer complained about the music, the lighting, and the temperature all in one visit.
His querulous tone made even a simple request sound like an accusation.
etymology: From Latin querulus, 'full of complaints', from queri, 'to complain'.

definition: A question, especially one asking for information or expressing doubt.
examples: If you have a query about your bill, call this number.
Type your query into the search box.
etymology: From Latin quaere 'ask!', imperative of quaerere 'to seek'.

definition: To argue or complain about a trivial matter.
examples: Let's not quibble over a few dollars.
Critics may quibble with the ending, but the film is superb.
etymology: Probably a diminutive of obsolete quib 'a petty objection'.

definition: Able to think and respond quickly and cleverly.
examples: A quick-witted host can rescue an awkward interview.
She was quick-witted enough to turn the heckle into a joke.
etymology: From quick + witted, from wit 'mind, intelligence'.

definition: To make or become faster, or to stir into life.
examples: I felt my pulse quicken as the results were announced.
The new coach will quicken the team's tempo.
etymology: From quick, from Old English cwic 'alive'.

definition: The essential nature of a thing; also, a trivial quibble.
examples: The poem captures the quiddity of a lazy summer afternoon.
The lawyers argued over every quiddity in the contract.
etymology: From medieval Latin quidditas, from quid, 'what'.

definition: A nosy person who loves gossip and news.
examples: The village quidnunc knew about the engagement before the bride's parents did.
Every office has a quidnunc who lingers near the coffee machine.
etymology: From Latin quid nunc?, 'what now?'.

definition: In a state of quiet inactivity or dormancy.
examples: The volcano had been quiescent for centuries before the tremors began.
Markets stayed quiescent over the holiday, with barely any trades.
etymology: From Latin quiescere, 'to rest', from quies 'quiet'.

definition: Passive acceptance of things as they are, avoiding action or protest.
examples: Activists criticized the church's political quietism.
His quietism in the face of injustice frustrated his friends.
etymology: From Italian quietismo, the name of a 17th-century mystical movement.

definition: A state of stillness, calm, and peace.
examples: She craved the quietude of the mountain cabin.
The library offered welcome quietude after the noisy café.
etymology: From Late Latin quietudo, from Latin quietus 'quiet'.

definition: Death, or something that puts a final end to an activity.
examples: The new highway delivered the quietus to the old diner.
In Hamlet, the hero muses on making his own quietus.
etymology: From Medieval Latin quietus est 'he is quit', used for settling a debt.

definition: An arrangement of five things with four at the corners and one in the center.
examples: The orchard was planted in a quincunx pattern.
The five on a die is a perfect quincunx.
etymology: From Latin quincunx 'five-twelfths', from quinque 'five' + uncia 'twelfth'.

definition: Happening once every five years, or lasting five years.
examples: The museum hosts a quinquennial survey of national art.
Planners released a quinquennial budget.
etymology: From Latin quinquennis, from quinque 'five' + annus 'year'.

definition: Representing the most perfect or typical example of something.
examples: Pizza on a paper plate is the quintessential New York lunch.
He was the quintessential absent-minded professor.
etymology: From quintessence, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia 'fifth essence'.

definition: A short, clever, funny remark.
examples: He answered every hard question with a quip.
Her closing quip got the biggest laugh of the night.
etymology: Perhaps from Latin quippe 'indeed, forsooth', used ironically.

definition: A peculiar habit or feature.
examples: One quirk of his is eating pizza with a fork.
The old house has its quirks, like a door that only opens halfway.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 16th century.

definition: Unusual in an interesting or charming way.
examples: The café is full of quirky furniture from flea markets.
Her quirky sense of humor won the audience over.
etymology: From quirk 'a peculiar trait', of uncertain origin.

definition: A traitor who collaborates with an occupying enemy.
examples: The resistance branded the mayor a quisling.
No quisling would be welcome after the liberation.
etymology: From Vidkun Quisling, the Norwegian politician who collaborated with Nazi Germany.

definition: To tremble or shake with a slight rapid motion.
examples: Her lip began to quiver as she read the letter.
Watch the aspen leaves quiver in the breeze.
etymology: From Middle English, related to Old English cwifer 'nimble'.

definition: Extremely idealistic and impractical, often in a noble but unrealistic way.
examples: Her quixotic plan to plant a million trees by herself inspired and worried her friends.
Critics called the campaign quixotic, but supporters admired its stubborn hope.
etymology: From Don Quixote, the hero of Cervantes's 1605 novel, with the English suffix -ic.

definition: Showing mild puzzlement or amusement.
examples: The dog tilted its head with a quizzical look.
She raised a quizzical eyebrow at my outfit.
etymology: From quiz, a word of uncertain origin first recorded in the 18th century.

definition: A subtle point for debate, or a playful musical medley of familiar tunes.
examples: Medieval scholars sparred over each quodlibet for hours.
The band closed with a quodlibet of holiday songs.
etymology: From Latin quodlibet 'whatever pleases'.

definition: Former; having once been.
examples: He met his quondam business partner at the reunion.
The quondam mill is now a brewery.
etymology: From Latin quondam 'formerly'.

definition: The minimum number of members needed for a meeting to make valid decisions.
examples: The board couldn't vote because it lacked a quorum.
We finally reached a quorum when two latecomers arrived.
etymology: From Latin quorum, 'of whom', from the wording of commissions.

definition: A fixed share or limit of something that is allowed or required.
examples: The sales team must hit its quota by the end of the quarter.
I've used up my social quota for the week.
etymology: From Medieval Latin quota (pars) 'how great (a part)', from Latin quotus 'how many'.

definition: Ordinary and occurring every day; commonplace.
examples: The poet found beauty in quotidian chores like folding laundry.
Between meetings and emails, her quotidian routine left little room for surprise.
etymology: From Latin quotidianus, from quotidie 'every day'.

definition: The result of dividing one number by another, or a degree of a particular quality.
examples: The new mall has a high fun quotient for kids.
Divide 12 by 4 and the quotient is 3.
etymology: From Latin quotiens 'how many times'.

definition: Marked by earthy, exuberant, and often coarse humor.
examples: The wedding speech was rabelaisian in its bawdiness.
His novels have a rabelaisian appetite for food and life.
etymology: From François Rabelais, the sixteenth-century French author of Gargantua and Pantagruel.

definition: A person skilled at telling stories and anecdotes entertainingly.
examples: The raconteur held the dinner table spellbound with tales of his travels.
Every family gathering needs a raconteur to keep the stories alive.
etymology: From French raconter, 'to recount'.

definition: Worn out and haggard, or crudely made up with rouge.
examples: The raddled rock star looked older than his years.
A raddled old showgirl sang at the piano bar.
etymology: From raddle 'red ochre', a variant of ruddle.

definition: Affecting the basic nature of something in a thorough, far-reaching way.
examples: The new manager made a radical change to how the team planned its weeks.
Switching to a four-day week was a radical idea that actually worked.
etymology: From Late Latin radicalis, from Latin radix 'root'.

definition: Unconventional and slightly disreputable in an appealing way.
examples: He had a raffish charm that made the dull party bearable.
The bar drew a raffish crowd of artists and gamblers.
etymology: Formed from raff 'rubbish, riffraff' plus -ish.

definition: To complain or protest bitterly and at length.
examples: Fans rail against ticket prices every season.
It's pointless to rail at the weather.
etymology: From French railler 'to mock'.

definition: Good-humored teasing or banter.
examples: The old friends traded raillery over dinner.
His raillery never crossed into cruelty.
etymology: From French raillerie, from railler 'to tease, mock'.

definition: Dashingly jaunty or slightly disreputable in style.
examples: He wore his hat at a rakish angle.
The rakish hero charmed everyone in the ballroom.
etymology: From rake 'a dissolute man', short for rakehell, plus -ish.

definition: Uncontrollably energetic and noisy.
examples: The rambunctious puppy knocked over the plant.
A rambunctious crowd filled the stadium.
etymology: An American alteration of rumbustious, of uncertain origin.

definition: A complex or unwelcome consequence of an action or event.
examples: Nobody considered every ramification of the policy.
Each ramification of the merger took months to sort out.
etymology: From French, from Medieval Latin ramificare, from Latin ramus 'branch'.

definition: Spreading or growing quickly and uncontrollably.
examples: Weeds grew rampant in the abandoned lot.
Rumors were rampant before the official announcement.
etymology: From Old French rampant, 'climbing', from ramper 'to climb, crawl'.

definition: In a state of severe disrepair and looking likely to collapse.
examples: They turned a ramshackle farmhouse into a cozy home.
A ramshackle fence was all that kept the goats in.
etymology: An alteration of earlier ramshackled, a variant of ransackled 'ransacked'.

definition: Deep, long-lasting bitterness and resentment toward someone.
examples: Years after the lawsuit, a quiet rancor still lingered between the two brothers.
She spoke without rancor, though she had every reason to be bitter.
etymology: From Old French rancor, from Late Latin rancor, 'rancidness, bitterness'.

definition: To cause lasting annoyance or resentment.
examples: Being passed over for the promotion still rankles her.
Unfair calls can rankle fans for weeks.
etymology: From Old French rancler, 'to fester', from draoncle, 'ulcer'.

definition: Aggressively greedy, especially for money or possessions.
examples: Rapacious landlords hiked rents across the city.
The film is a satire of rapacious bankers.
etymology: From Latin rapax, rapacis 'grasping', from rapere 'to seize'.

definition: The violent seizure of property; plunder.
examples: The chronicles describe years of war and rapine.
The invaders lived by rapine.
etymology: From Latin rapina, from rapere 'to seize'.

definition: A close, harmonious relationship in which people understand each other well.
examples: The teacher quickly built rapport with her new class by learning everyone's name.
Good rapport between doctor and patient makes honest conversation much easier.
etymology: From French rapport, 'a bringing back', from rapporter 'to bring back'.

definition: The re-establishment of friendly relations between two parties.
examples: The two former business partners reached a cautious rapprochement.
The summit marked a rapprochement between the neighboring countries.
etymology: From French rapprochement, from rapprocher, 'to bring together'.

definition: A mischievous rascal or scamp.
examples: Some rapscallion swapped the salt and sugar.
The old rapscallion still flirts with every waitress.
etymology: An alteration of earlier rascallion, from rascal.

definition: Completely absorbed and fascinated by something.
examples: The kids listened in rapt silence to the ghost story.
She watched the eclipse with rapt attention.
etymology: From Latin raptus 'seized, carried off', past participle of rapere.

definition: Predatory, or adapted for seizing prey.
examples: The mantis folds its raptorial forelegs as if praying.
Wall Street's raptorial instincts were on full display.
etymology: From Latin raptor 'plunderer', from rapere 'to seize'.

definition: Expressing great joy or enthusiasm.
examples: The pianist received rapturous applause.
Critics gave the debut a rapturous welcome.
etymology: From rapture, from Medieval Latin raptura 'seizure', from rapere 'to seize'.

definition: To make thinner or less dense, or to make more refined.
examples: Great heights rarefy the air, making every step harder.
Over the years his taste seemed to rarefy until only obscure films satisfied him.
etymology: From Latin rarefacere, from rarus 'rare' + facere 'to make'.

definition: Acting or done too hastily, without enough thought.
examples: Don't make a rash decision while you're angry.
Quitting by text message was a rash move.
etymology: Middle English, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch rasch 'quick'.

definition: To formally approve an agreement and make it valid.
examples: Union members will vote to ratify the contract.
Enough states must ratify an amendment before it takes effect.
etymology: From Medieval Latin ratificare, from Latin ratus 'fixed, settled'.

definition: The process of exact, methodical reasoning.
examples: The detective solves the case through pure ratiocination.
Behind his jokes lay careful ratiocination.
etymology: From Latin ratiocinatio, from ratiocinari 'to calculate, reason'.

definition: Based on clear reasoning and logic rather than feeling or impulse.
examples: Try to make a rational decision before you sign the lease.
She stayed rational even when the meeting turned into a shouting match.
etymology: From Latin rationalis, from ratio 'reckoning, reason'.

definition: The reasons behind a decision or belief.
examples: The manager explained the rationale for the new schedule.
What's the rationale behind closing the library on weekends?
etymology: From Latin rationalis, 'reasonable', from ratio 'reason'.

definition: Making a harsh, loud, disorderly noise.
examples: Raucous laughter came from the back of the bus.
The crows made a raucous racket at dawn.
etymology: From Latin raucus 'hoarse'.

definition: To cause severe and widespread damage.
examples: Wildfires continue to ravage the hillsides.
Pests can ravage a tomato crop overnight.
etymology: From French ravager, from ravine 'a violent rush of water'.

definition: To tangle or complicate, or paradoxically to untangle.
examples: Cats love to ravel a ball of yarn.
It took weeks to ravel out the accounting mess.
etymology: From Dutch ravelen 'to tangle, fray'.

definition: Extremely hungry, or intensely eager for something.
examples: After the hike we were ravenous.
She has a ravenous appetite for mystery novels.
etymology: From Old French ravineus, from raviner 'to ravage'.

definition: To completely destroy a building or town.
examples: The developer wants to raze the old mill.
Invaders threatened to raze the city.
etymology: From Old French raser 'to shave close'.

definition: Without hesitation, or without difficulty.
examples: She readily agreed to help with the move.
Spare parts are readily available online.
etymology: Formed from ready plus -ly; ready comes from Old English.

definition: A field of activity or interest, or a kingdom.
examples: Time travel remains firmly in the realm of fiction.
The knight swore to defend the realm.
etymology: From Old French reaume, from Latin regimen 'government', influenced by real 'royal'.

definition: To rob or plunder by force.
examples: Raiders came each summer to reave the coast.
War would reave them of everything they owned.
etymology: From Old English rēafian.

definition: Unattractive and objectionable; off-putting.
examples: The building's rebarbative concrete facade drove tourists away.
His rebarbative manner made group projects miserable.
etymology: From French rébarbatif, from barbe, 'beard'.

definition: A partial refund of money already paid.
examples: We got a rebate for installing solar panels.
Mail in the form to claim your rebate.
etymology: From Old French rabattre 'to beat down again, deduct'.

definition: To reject an offer or approach abruptly or ungraciously.
examples: She chose to rebuff every attempt at reconciliation.
Don't rebuff help when you need it.
etymology: From obsolete French rebuffer, from Italian ribuffare 'to scold'.

definition: To criticize someone sharply for doing something wrong.
examples: The coach will rebuke any player who mocks an opponent after the game.
She did not rebuke the child, but gently explained why it was wrong.
etymology: From Old French rebuker, 'to beat back', of uncertain earlier origin.

definition: A puzzle in which pictures or symbols stand for words or syllables.
examples: The wedding invitation was written as a rebus.
A picture of an eye and a saw formed a rebus for 'I saw'.
etymology: From Latin rebus 'by things', a form of res 'thing'.

definition: A response that tries to prove an argument or claim false.
examples: She drafted a point-by-point rebuttal to the article.
Each team gets two minutes for rebuttal.
etymology: From rebut, from Old French rebuter 'to push back'.

definition: Stubbornly resisting authority or refusing to follow rules or orders.
examples: The recalcitrant student refused to hand in homework no matter what the teacher tried.
Negotiators struggled to persuade the recalcitrant side to return to the table.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare, 'to kick back', from re- 'back' + calx 'heel'.

definition: To formally withdraw a statement or belief.
examples: The witness later recanted his testimony.
Under pressure, the scientist refused to recant her findings.
etymology: From Latin recantare, 'to revoke', from re- + cantare, 'to sing'.

definition: To summarize the main points again.
examples: Let me recapitulate before we vote.
The final chapter tries to recapitulate the whole argument.
etymology: From Late Latin recapitulare 'to go through heading by heading', from capitulum 'chapter'.

definition: To move back or gradually diminish.
examples: We waited for the floodwaters to recede.
The pain began to recede after an hour.
etymology: From Latin recedere, from re- 'back' plus cedere 'to go'.

definition: A revised version of a text, or the act of revising one.
examples: Scholars compared each recension of the ancient epic.
This recension restores several lost verses.
etymology: From Latin recensio 'review', from recensere 'to revise'.

definition: Willing to consider new ideas or suggestions.
examples: The board was receptive to the proposal for remote work.
Kids are most receptive to learning when they feel safe.
etymology: From Medieval Latin receptivus, from Latin recipere 'to receive'.

definition: A period of temporary economic decline.
examples: Many small shops closed during the recession.
Economists worry that a recession is coming.
etymology: From Latin recessio, from recedere 'to go back'.

definition: The tendency of a convicted offender to commit another crime.
examples: Job training lowers recidivism among former inmates.
The study tracked recidivism over five years.
etymology: From French récidiviste, from Latin recidivus 'falling back'.

definition: To respond to a gesture or action by doing something similar in return.
examples: They invited us to dinner, so we'd like to reciprocate next month.
He hoped she would reciprocate his feelings.
etymology: From Latin reciprocare, 'to move back and forth'.

definition: To get back something lost or taken, or make land usable again.
examples: She went to the airport office to reclaim her lost bag.
The town plans to reclaim the old rail yard as a park.
etymology: From Old French reclamer, from Latin reclamare 'to cry out against'.

definition: Avoiding the company of other people; solitary.
examples: The reclusive author hasn't given an interview in decades.
He grew reclusive after retiring.
etymology: From recluse, from Late Latin reclusus 'shut up', from recludere.

definition: To spring back or flinch in fear, disgust, or shock.
examples: I saw him recoil at the smell from the fridge.
Many readers recoil from such graphic scenes.
etymology: From Old French reculer 'to move back'.

definition: Compensation given for loss, harm, or effort.
examples: The families received little recompense for their land.
She asked for no recompense for her help.
etymology: From Old French recompenser, from Late Latin recompensare.

definition: To restore friendly relations, or to make two things agree.
examples: The brothers reconciled after years of not speaking.
I couldn't reconcile my bank statement with my receipts.
etymology: From Latin reconciliare, 'to bring together again'.

definition: Little known and difficult for ordinary people to understand.
examples: The professor's recondite lecture on medieval tax law lost most of the class.
He collects recondite facts that rarely come up in conversation.
etymology: From Latin reconditus, 'hidden away', from recondere 'to put away'.

definition: To survey an area to gather information, often before acting.
examples: We went early to reconnoiter the parking situation.
Scouts were sent to reconnoiter the ridge.
etymology: From obsolete French reconnoître 'to recognize, explore'.

definition: To regain money or losses that were spent or lost.
examples: It took three years to recoup the cost of the solar panels.
The studio hopes to recoup its investment overseas.
etymology: From French recouper 'to cut back', from re- plus couper 'to cut'.

definition: A source of help or a way out in a difficult situation.
examples: If the seller won't refund you, your only recourse may be small claims court.
Without insurance, they had little recourse after the flood.
etymology: From Latin recursus, 'a running back', from recurrere.

definition: Cowardly, or unfaithful to a duty or cause.
examples: The recreant knight fled before the battle began.
History has not been kind to the recreant officials who abandoned the city.
etymology: From Old French recreant 'yielding', from recroire 'to surrender'.

definition: To respond to an accusation by accusing the accuser in turn.
examples: Rather than recriminate, the partners agreed to move on.
It's tempting to recriminate when someone blames you.
etymology: From Medieval Latin recriminari, from Latin crimen 'accusation'.

definition: A renewed outbreak of something after a period of quiet.
examples: Doctors warned of a recrudescence of the flu this winter.
The band's reunion sparked a recrudescence of nineties nostalgia.
etymology: From Latin recrudescere, 'to become raw again'.

definition: To correct something that is wrong.
examples: The store promised to rectify the billing error.
We need to rectify this mistake before the client notices.
etymology: From Medieval Latin rectificare, from rectus 'right'.

definition: Formed by or moving in straight lines.
examples: The architect favored rectilinear forms and flat roofs.
Manhattan's rectilinear grid makes it easy to navigate.
etymology: From Late Latin rectilineus, from rectus 'straight' plus linea 'line'.

definition: Morally correct behavior or thinking; integrity.
examples: The judge was known for her rectitude.
He lectured us on rectitude while breaking every rule.
etymology: From Late Latin rectitudo, from rectus 'right, straight'.

definition: Lying down or leaning back in a relaxed position.
examples: The tomb shows a recumbent figure of a knight.
He rides a recumbent bicycle to work.
etymology: From Latin recumbere 'to recline'.

definition: Happening again and again.
examples: Loneliness is a recurrent theme in her songs.
He suffers from recurrent headaches.
etymology: From Latin recurrere 'to run back'.

definition: A person who refuses to submit to an authority or rule.
examples: As a lifelong recusant, he ignored every dress code.
Each recusant who skipped Anglican services paid a fine.
etymology: From Latin recusant-, present participle of recusare 'to refuse'.

definition: To withdraw from judging a matter because of a possible conflict of interest.
examples: The judge chose to recuse herself from the case.
Board members should recuse themselves from votes on their own pay.
etymology: From Latin recusare 'to refuse'.

definition: To black out or remove sensitive parts of a document before release.
examples: Lawyers will redact the names before publishing the report.
Please redact my address from the filing.
etymology: From Latin redact-, past participle stem of redigere 'to bring back, reduce'.

definition: To make up for faults, or to exchange a voucher for goods or cash.
examples: He hoped a strong finish would redeem his poor season.
You can redeem the coupon at any store.
etymology: From Old French redimer, from Latin redimere, from re(d)- 'back' plus emere 'to buy'.

definition: Brought back to life or revived, placed after the noun it describes.
examples: Critics hailed the young crooner as Sinatra redivivus.
The movement is a kind of romanticism redivivus.
etymology: From Late Latin redivivus 'living again'.

definition: Strongly suggestive of something, or giving off a distinct smell.
examples: The kitchen was redolent of garlic and fresh basil.
The old photograph was redolent of a childhood she barely remembered.
etymology: From Latin redolere, 'to emit a smell', from re- + olere 'to smell'.

definition: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect.
examples: She faced a redoubtable opponent in the final round.
The redoubtable editor has shaped the magazine for decades.
etymology: From Old French redoutable, from redouter, 'to fear'.

definition: To contribute to someone's credit or discredit, or to come back upon them.
examples: Her kindness to strangers will redound to her credit.
The scandal redounded on everyone who had defended him.
etymology: From Latin redundare, 'to overflow', from re- + unda 'wave'.

definition: Oversimplifying a complex subject in a misleading way.
examples: It's reductive to call the war a simple fight over oil.
The review offered a reductive reading of the novel.
etymology: From Latin reductus, past participle of reducere 'to bring back'.

definition: Unnecessary because it repeats something or is no longer needed.
examples: The phrase 'free gift' is redundant.
We keep a redundant backup of all our photos.
etymology: From Latin redundare, 'to overflow'.

definition: Refreshment with food and drink, or a light meal.
examples: The monks gathered for their evening refection.
After the climb, a little refection was in order.
etymology: From Latin refectio, from reficere 'to remake, restore'.

definition: A direct vote by the public on a single political question.
examples: The city will hold a referendum on the new stadium.
The referendum passed by a narrow margin.
etymology: From Latin, gerund of referre 'to refer, carry back'.

definition: Thoughtful and given to careful consideration.
examples: She grew quiet and reflective on the drive home.
The essay ends on a reflective note about growing older.
etymology: From reflect, from Latin reflectere 'to bend back'.

definition: Stubbornly resistant to control or to treatment.
examples: The refractory mule refused to cross the bridge.
Her doctor called the infection refractory to standard drugs.
etymology: From Latin refractarius 'stubborn', related to refringere 'to break up'.

definition: A place or condition of safety from danger or trouble.
examples: The library was her refuge from a noisy house.
Hikers took refuge in a cave during the storm.
etymology: From Old French, from Latin refugium, from re- 'back' plus fugere 'to flee'.

definition: Shining brightly and radiantly.
examples: The refulgent sunrise lit the whole valley in gold.
She stepped out in a refulgent gown that caught every light.
etymology: From Latin refulgere, 'to shine back', from re- + fulgere 'to shine'.

definition: To renovate and redecorate something.
examples: They plan to refurbish the old train station.
Some shops refurbish used laptops for resale.
etymology: Formed from re- plus furbish 'to polish'.

definition: To prove that a statement or argument is wrong.
examples: The data clearly refute the rumor.
She was ready to refute every claim in the article.
etymology: From Latin refutare 'to repel, rebut'.

definition: Fit for a king or queen; magnificent and dignified.
examples: The cat sat on the windowsill with a regal stare.
Her regal posture made the cheap dress look elegant.
etymology: From Latin regalis, from rex, regis 'king'.

definition: To entertain someone with stories, or to treat them lavishly.
examples: Grandpa loves to regale us with tales of the navy.
They regale their guests with seven courses.
etymology: From French régaler, from Old French gale 'pleasure'.

definition: The killing of a king, or a person who kills one.
examples: Macbeth's regicide haunts him for the rest of the play.
The regicide was hanged in the square.
etymology: From Latin rex, regis 'king' plus -cide 'killing'.

definition: A government, especially an authoritarian one, or a system of rules.
examples: The regime cracked down on independent newspapers.
His new fitness regime starts with a cold shower.
etymology: From French régime, from Latin regimen 'rule'.

definition: A prescribed plan of diet, exercise, or treatment.
examples: Her training regimen includes yoga twice a week.
Stick to the regimen your doctor gave you.
etymology: From Latin regimen 'rule, guidance', from regere 'to rule'.

definition: Reigning, or currently dominant and widespread.
examples: She was a queen regnant, not merely a royal consort.
Minimalism was the regnant style of the decade.
etymology: From Latin regnant-, present participle of regnare 'to reign'.

definition: The layer of loose rock, dust, and soil covering solid bedrock.
examples: Astronauts left bootprints in the lunar regolith.
The probe drilled through regolith to reach bedrock.
etymology: From Greek rhēgos 'blanket' plus lithos 'stone'.

definition: Returning to an earlier, less advanced state, or taking a larger share from those with less.
examples: A sales tax is regressive because it hits poorer households hardest.
Critics called the new policy a regressive step.
etymology: From Latin regressus, from regredi 'to go back'.

definition: To treat an abstract idea as if it were a concrete thing.
examples: Rankings reify a vague notion of quality into a number.
Be careful not to reify the market as a living being.
etymology: From Latin res, rei 'thing' plus -fy.

definition: To strengthen or support something, physically or in principle.
examples: Steel beams reinforce the old bridge.
Praise can reinforce good habits in children.
etymology: Formed from re- plus inforce, an older spelling of enforce.

definition: To restore someone or something to a former position or state.
examples: The court ordered the company to reinstate the fired workers.
The school may reinstate the old schedule.
etymology: Formed from re- plus instate.

definition: To say something again for emphasis or clarity.
examples: Let me reiterate: the deadline is Friday at noon.
The doctor reiterated the importance of rest.
etymology: From Latin reiterare, 'to repeat', from re- + iterum 'again'.

definition: A quick, sharp reply.
examples: Her witty rejoinder ended the debate.
He had no rejoinder to that.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman rejoindre 'to reply', originally a legal term.

definition: To make something look or feel younger, fresher, or more lively.
examples: A week at the beach helped rejuvenate us.
The new owners want to rejuvenate the old theater.
etymology: Formed from re- plus Latin juvenis 'young'.

definition: To assign to a lower or less important position.
examples: We decided to relegate the old sofa to the basement.
The team was relegated to a lower division after a poor season.
etymology: From Latin relegare, 'to send away'.

definition: To finally give in or become less strict.
examples: After hours of pleading, Dad began to relent and let us stay up late.
The rain relented just long enough for the parade.
etymology: From Middle English, perhaps from Latin re- + lentare 'to bend', from lentus 'flexible'.

definition: An object or custom surviving from an earlier time.
examples: That fax machine is a relic of the nineties.
The museum holds a relic from the shipwreck.
etymology: From Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae 'remains'.

definition: To give up something, such as control or a possession.
examples: She relinquished control of the company to her daughter.
It's hard to relinquish the window seat on a long flight.
etymology: From Old French relinquir, from Latin relinquere 'to leave behind'.

definition: A container for holy relics.
examples: Pilgrims knelt before a golden reliquary.
She kept her grandmother's letters in a tin like a reliquary.
etymology: From French reliquaire, from Old French relique 'relic'.

definition: To enjoy something greatly and take pleasure in it.
examples: I relish a quiet morning with coffee and a good book.
He seemed to relish the challenge of fixing the old engine.
etymology: From Old French reles, 'something remaining, aftertaste', from relaisser, 'to leave behind'.

definition: Unwilling and hesitant to do something.
examples: He was reluctant to speak in public, so he asked a friend to go first.
The reluctant witness finally agreed to testify after weeks of persuasion.
etymology: From Latin reluctari, 'to struggle against', from re- 'against' + luctari 'to struggle'.

definition: Intended to correct a problem or improve a deficiency.
examples: He took a remedial math course before starting college.
The city ordered remedial work on the cracked bridge.
etymology: From Late Latin remedialis, from Latin remedium 'cure'.

definition: A treatment or solution for an illness or problem.
examples: Honey and lemon is my favorite remedy for a sore throat.
There is no quick remedy for a housing shortage.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman remedie, from Latin remedium, from re- plus mederi 'to heal'.

definition: To think or talk about pleasant memories of the past.
examples: The old friends sat on the porch and began to reminisce about their school days.
Grandparents love to reminisce when they look through faded family photographs.
etymology: From Latin reminisci, 'to remember', related to mens 'mind'.

definition: Careless in doing one's duty.
examples: I would be remiss if I didn't thank the volunteers.
The landlord was remiss in fixing the heater.
etymology: From Latin remissus 'slackened', past participle of remittere.

definition: A small remaining piece or trace of something.
examples: She sewed a pillow from a remnant of velvet.
The wall is a remnant of the old Roman city.
etymology: From Old French remenant, from remenoir 'to remain'.

definition: To make a forcefully reproachful protest.
examples: Parents went to remonstrate with the board over the cancelled field trip.
She remonstrated that the referee had missed a clear foul.
etymology: From medieval Latin remonstrare, 'to demonstrate'.

definition: Deep regret for a wrong one has done.
examples: He showed real remorse after breaking his friend's guitar.
The apology letter was full of remorse.
etymology: From Medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordere 'to bite again'.

definition: Far away in distance, time, or likelihood.
examples: They rented a remote cabin with no cell service.
The chance of rain today is remote, so leave the umbrella.
etymology: From Latin remotus 'removed, distant', past participle of removere.

definition: To pay someone for services or work.
examples: The firm will remunerate consultants by the hour.
Interns deserve fair pay, and we intend to remunerate them.
etymology: From Latin remunerari, from munus 'gift'.

definition: A revival of interest or vigor in something.
examples: The neighborhood is enjoying a renaissance.
Board games have had a renaissance.
etymology: From French renaissance 'rebirth', from renaître 'to be born again'.

definition: Becoming active or popular again after a period of decline.
examples: The renascent jazz scene filled the old clubs again.
Critics noted a renascent interest in handwritten letters.
etymology: From Latin renascent-, present participle of renasci 'to be born again'.

definition: To tear something apart violently.
examples: The scandal threatened to rend the community.
Mourners in the story rend their clothes in grief.
etymology: From Old English rendan 'to tear'.

definition: To cause to become, or to provide or give.
examples: The update could render your old charger useless.
They were paid well to render their services.
etymology: From Old French rendre 'to give back', from Latin reddere.

definition: A person who deserts or rebels against a group or set of principles.
examples: The chef was a renegade who ignored every culinary rule.
A renegade from the party formed a rival campaign.
etymology: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegare 'to deny'.

definition: To go back on a promise or agreement.
examples: The buyer tried to renege on the deal at the last minute.
Don't renege on your offer to help with the move.
etymology: From Medieval Latin renegare, 'to deny'.

definition: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief.
examples: He chose to renounce his inheritance.
She refused to renounce her principles under pressure.
etymology: From Old French renoncer, from Latin renuntiare 'to announce, protest against'.

definition: Widely known and admired for some quality or achievement.
examples: The bakery is renowned for its sourdough.
A renowned surgeon flew in to consult on the case.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman renoumer 'to make famous', from re- plus nomer 'to name'.

definition: The making of amends for a wrong, often by payment.
examples: The government offered reparation to the displaced families.
He saw volunteering as a kind of reparation.
etymology: From Late Latin reparatio, from reparare 'to restore'.

definition: Quick, witty conversation and replies.
examples: The hosts' easy repartee made the podcast a joy to listen to.
She was known for her sharp repartee at dinner parties.
etymology: From French repartie, 'a reply', from repartir, 'to reply promptly'.

definition: A meal, especially a formal or generous one.
examples: After the service, guests shared a simple repast.
The picnic was a light repast of bread and cheese.
etymology: From Old French repaistre 'to feed', from Late Latin repascere.

definition: The full range of skills, works, or techniques someone can perform.
examples: The band's repertoire includes jazz standards and pop covers.
I'm adding a few quick dinners to my cooking repertoire.
etymology: From French répertoire, from Late Latin repertorium 'inventory'.

definition: To feel or express discontent; to fret.
examples: It does no good to repine over the lost job.
She did not repine but simply started again.
etymology: Formed from re- plus pine, on the pattern of repent.

definition: To fill something up again.
examples: Remember to replenish your water bottle before the hike.
The store replenishes its shelves every night.
etymology: From Old French repleniss-, from re- + plenir 'to fill'.

definition: Well supplied or filled with something.
examples: The memoir is replete with funny stories.
We left the feast replete and sleepy.
etymology: From Latin repletus, past participle of replere 'to fill again'.

definition: To make an exact copy of something or repeat it with the same result.
examples: Other labs could not replicate the findings.
Nobody can replicate my grandmother's pie crust.
etymology: From Latin replicare 'to fold back, repeat'.

definition: According to what people say or what has been reported.
examples: The actor is reportedly in talks for the sequel.
The company reportedly lost millions last year.
etymology: Formed from reported plus -ly; report comes from Latin reportare 'to carry back'.

definition: Deserving strong condemnation.
examples: Lying to patients is reprehensible.
The board called his conduct reprehensible.
etymology: From Late Latin reprehensibilis, from reprehendere 'to rebuke'.

definition: A temporary relief or delay from something unpleasant.
examples: The rain gave us a reprieve from watering the garden.
The library got a reprieve when the council restored its funding.
etymology: From Anglo-French repris, 'taken back', from reprendre.

definition: To scold someone formally for doing something wrong.
examples: The referee had to reprimand both players for arguing.
The officer was reprimanded for being late to his post.
etymology: From French réprimande, from Latin reprimenda, 'things to be held back', from reprimere 'to check'.

definition: An act of retaliation against someone who has caused harm.
examples: Employees feared reprisal if they reported the problem.
The attack was a reprisal for the earlier raid.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman reprisaille, from Medieval Latin reprisalia.

definition: To restore something to its original condition.
examples: Conservators tried to repristinate the faded fresco.
Some reformers hoped to repristinate the early church.
etymology: Formed from re- plus pristine, from Latin pristinus 'former'.

definition: To express disapproval or disappointment to someone.
examples: Don't reproach yourself for an honest mistake.
She didn't reproach him, which somehow felt worse.
etymology: From Old French reprochier, ultimately from Latin prope 'near'.

definition: An unprincipled person, often said with affection.
examples: My uncle is a lovable reprobate who never pays for drinks.
The play's hero is a charming reprobate.
etymology: From Latin reprobatus 'disapproved', from reprobare.

definition: Cold, sly, and unfeeling, as if like a reptile.
examples: The villain flashed a reptilian smile.
His reptilian calm during the crisis unnerved the staff.
etymology: From Late Latin reptilis 'creeping', from repere 'to creep'.

definition: To reject or refuse to accept something as true or valid.
examples: The author was quick to repudiate the claims made in the review.
She repudiated her earlier support for the plan.
etymology: From Latin repudiare, 'to divorce, reject', from repudium, 'divorce'.

definition: Extremely distasteful; causing strong disgust.
examples: She found the idea of cheating repugnant.
The smell of the swamp was repugnant.
etymology: From Latin repugnare 'to fight against'.

definition: Having a good reputation; trustworthy.
examples: Always buy tickets from a reputable seller.
She found a reputable mechanic through a friend.
etymology: From Latin reputare, 'to reckon, consider'.

definition: According to what is generally said or believed.
examples: The inn is reputedly haunted.
He is reputedly the richest man in town.
etymology: From reputed, from Latin reputare 'to think over'.

definition: Required for a particular purpose.
examples: She lacked the requisite experience for the role.
Fill in the requisite forms before your visit.
etymology: From Latin requisitus, past participle of requirere 'to seek, need'.

definition: To return a favor, feeling, or wrong in kind.
examples: He hoped she would someday requite his love.
There's no way to requite such kindness.
etymology: Formed from re- plus quite, an obsolete variant of quit 'to pay off'.

definition: An ornamental screen or panel behind a church altar.
examples: A carved oak reredos rose behind the altar.
Restorers cleaned centuries of soot from the reredos.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman, from Old French areredos, from arere 'behind' plus dos 'back'.

definition: To revoke or cancel a law, order, or agreement.
examples: The school voted to rescind its ban on phones during lunch.
The company rescinded the job offer after a background check.
etymology: From Latin rescindere, 'to cut off'.

definition: Remaining after the greater part has gone or been used.
examples: There was some residual frustration after the long dispute.
The paint left a residual smell in the hallway for days.
etymology: From Latin residuum 'what is left over', from residere 'to remain behind'.

definition: Able to recover quickly after hardship, shock, or change.
examples: Small businesses proved resilient, bouncing back within months of the flood.
Children are often more resilient than their worried parents expect them to be.
etymology: From Latin resilire, 'to leap back', from re- 'back' + salire 'to jump'.

definition: Firmly determined and unwavering in purpose.
examples: She remained resolute in her plan to run the marathon.
The coach gave a resolute speech after the loss.
etymology: From Latin resolutus, past participle of resolvere 'to loosen, release'.

definition: To feel meaningful or familiar to someone, or to echo with sound.
examples: Her story about moving abroad seemed to resonate with many listeners.
The church bells resonated through the valley.
etymology: From Latin resonare, 'to resound'.

definition: Good at finding quick, clever ways to solve problems.
examples: The resourceful campers built a shelter from branches.
She's resourceful enough to fix almost anything with tape.
etymology: From resource + -ful.

definition: A short period of rest or relief from something difficult.
examples: The cool evening brought a welcome respite from the heat.
A weekend away gave the new parents some respite.
etymology: From Old French respit, from Latin respectus 'refuge, consideration'.

definition: Dazzlingly bright and impressive in appearance.
examples: The bride was resplendent in gold silk.
The garden looked resplendent after the spring rain.
etymology: From Latin resplendere 'to shine out'.

definition: Deep, festering resentment, especially toward those seen as superior, that shapes one's values.
examples: The essay traces modern populism to a politics of ressentiment.
Nietzsche saw ressentiment at the root of slave morality.
etymology: From French ressentiment 'resentment', a term made famous in philosophy by Nietzsche.

definition: The return of something lost or stolen, or payment for harm done.
examples: The court ordered restitution to the victims.
The museum made restitution of the looted art.
etymology: From Latin restitutio, from restituere 'to restore'.

definition: Restless and impatient, especially under control or delay.
examples: The crowd grew restive as the concert started late.
Restive shareholders demanded a new CEO.
etymology: From Old French restif 'stubborn, inert', from rester 'to stay'.

definition: A renewed rise in activity, popularity, or occurrence.
examples: Vinyl records are enjoying a resurgence.
Doctors noted a resurgence of measles in the region.
etymology: From Latin resurgere 'to rise again'.

definition: Unwilling to share thoughts or feelings; reserved and quiet about oneself.
examples: He was reticent about his past and rarely mentioned where he had grown up.
The usually chatty actor grew reticent when asked about his upcoming divorce.
etymology: From Latin reticere, 'to keep silent', from re- + tacere 'to be silent'.

definition: Arranged like a net or network of lines.
examples: The leaf has reticulate veins.
A reticulate pattern of canals divides the old city.
etymology: From Latin reticulatus, from reticulum 'little net'.

definition: A group of advisers or attendants accompanying an important person.
examples: The pop star arrived with a retinue of assistants.
The queen's retinue filled three carriages.
etymology: From Old French retenue, from retenir 'to retain'.

definition: Shy and inclined to avoid attention.
examples: Her retiring manner hid a sharp wit.
He was too retiring to give the toast.
etymology: From retire, from French retirer 'to draw back'.

definition: A quick, sharp, or witty reply.
examples: She had a clever retort for every heckler.
His retort silenced the whole table.
etymology: From Latin retort-, from retorquere 'to twist back'.

definition: To withdraw a statement or draw something back in.
examples: The paper had to retract the story after the lawsuit.
Cats retract their claws when they walk.
etymology: From Latin retractus, from retrahere 'to draw back'.

definition: To cut back expenses or scale down operations.
examples: The museum had to retrench after its funding was cut.
Families retrench when prices rise faster than wages.
etymology: From obsolete French retrencher, from trencher 'to cut'.

definition: Punishment inflicted as vengeance for a wrong.
examples: Witnesses feared retribution from the gang.
The novel is a tale of crime and retribution.
etymology: From Late Latin retributio, from retribuere 'to assign again'.

definition: To get something back or bring it from where it was stored.
examples: The dog ran to retrieve the frisbee.
IT was able to retrieve the deleted files.
