etymology: From French spectre, from Latin spectrum 'image, apparition'.

definition: Ghostly, or relating to a spectrum.
examples: Spectral shapes drifted through the fog.
The old film gave her face a spectral glow.
etymology: From specter, from Latin spectrum 'apparition'.

definition: A wide range of related qualities, ideas, or things between two extremes.
examples: The panel included voices from across the political spectrum.
Her moods covered the whole spectrum in a single afternoon.
etymology: From Latin spectrum 'image' or 'apparition', from specere 'to look'.

definition: To form ideas or theories without firm evidence.
examples: Fans love to speculate about the next season's plot.
It's too early to speculate on what caused the outage.
etymology: From Latin speculari 'to observe', from specula 'watchtower'.

definition: A person who spends money recklessly and wastefully.
examples: Her uncle was a spendthrift who died broke.
Don't be a spendthrift with your first paycheck.
etymology: From spend + thrift, in its old sense 'savings, prosperity'.

definition: Spray blown from the crests of waves, or snow swept by the wind.
examples: Spindrift stung our faces on the ferry deck.
Climbers crouched as spindrift poured off the ridge.
etymology: A Scots variant of spoondrift, from spoon 'to run before the wind' + drift.

definition: Wanting to hurt, annoy, or offend someone out of malice.
examples: Leaving a fake review was a spiteful thing to do.
Don't let one spiteful comment ruin your day.
etymology: From spite, shortened from despite, from Latin despectus 'looking down on'.

definition: Magnificent, very impressive, or excellent.
examples: We had a splendid view of the harbor.
What a splendid idea to have a picnic!
etymology: From Latin splendidus, from splendere 'to shine'.

definition: Bad-tempered and spiteful.
examples: The columnist wrote a splenetic attack on cyclists.
He grew splenetic when the waiter forgot his order.
etymology: From Late Latin spleneticus, from the spleen, once thought the seat of bad temper.

definition: To spend money freely on something special.
examples: We splurged on a nice hotel for our anniversary.
I don't usually splurge, but those boots were worth it.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly imitative; first recorded in 19th-century America.

definition: Plundering or destruction, or the deliberate destruction of evidence.
examples: The judge sanctioned the company for spoliation of emails.
The spoliation of the temples lasted centuries.
etymology: From Latin spoliatio, from spoliare 'to strip'.

definition: Done on impulse, without planning or outside prompting.
examples: Their spontaneous road trip turned into the best weekend of the year.
A spontaneous round of applause broke out when the final speaker finished.
etymology: From Latin spontaneus, 'of one's own accord', from sponte, 'willingly'.

definition: An accidental swap of the initial sounds of words, as in 'tease my ears' for 'ease my tears'.
examples: His toast included the spoonerism 'a well-boiled icicle'.
Every spoonerism made the class giggle.
etymology: Named after William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford don famous for such slips.

definition: The track, trail, or droppings of an animal.
examples: The guide pointed to fresh lion spoor in the sand.
Reporters followed the spoor of the money.
etymology: From Afrikaans spoor, from Middle Dutch spor 'track'.

definition: Happening at irregular intervals; occurring here and there, not steadily.
examples: Sporadic showers kept interrupting the outdoor concert throughout the afternoon.
His visits became sporadic once he started the new job overseas.
etymology: From Greek sporadikos, 'scattered', from sporas, 'scattered', related to speirein, 'to sow'.

definition: Intense public attention focused on someone or something.
examples: The young chef suddenly found herself in the spotlight.
The scandal put the spotlight on campaign donations.
etymology: From spot + light, originally a stage lamp casting a narrow beam.

definition: To spread out in an untidy or uncontrolled way.
examples: The kids like to sprawl across the couch after school.
Suburbs continue to sprawl into former farmland.
etymology: From Old English spreawlian 'to move the limbs convulsively'.

definition: Studied carelessness; the art of making difficult things look effortless.
examples: The pianist played the brutal passage with sprezzatura, as if humming in the shower.
His relaxed style has a sprezzatura that hides hours of preparation.
etymology: From Italian sprezzatura, a term popularized by Castiglione's The Book of the Courtier (1528).

definition: Lively and active, especially for an older person.
examples: At ninety, my neighbor is still spry enough to garden daily.
A spry old man led the walking tour.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps dialectal.

definition: Foam or froth, especially on waves.
examples: Spume blew off the breakers onto the rocks.
The beer's spume spilled over the glass.
etymology: From Latin spuma 'foam'.

definition: Not genuine or authentic; based on false reasoning.
examples: The museum discovered the painting was a spurious copy.
Researchers rejected the spurious correlation between ice cream sales and shark attacks.
etymology: From Latin spurius, 'illegitimate, false'.

definition: To reject someone or something with contempt.
examples: Do not spurn advice just because it comes from a rival.
Many voters spurn candidates who never answer questions.
etymology: From Old English spurnan 'to kick, reject'.

definition: A noisy quarrel about something unimportant.
examples: The twins had a squabble over who got the window seat.
Their squabbles about the remote control never lasted long.
etymology: Probably imitative, perhaps of Scandinavian origin.

definition: Extremely dirty and unpleasant, often from poverty or neglect.
examples: The inspector found the kitchen squalid.
Many workers lived in squalid housing near the mines.
etymology: From Latin squalidus, from squalere 'to be rough or dirty'.

definition: Covered with or made of scales.
examples: The lizard's squamous skin glinted in the sun.
Lovecraft loved words like 'squamous' and 'eldritch'.
etymology: From Latin squamosus, from squama 'scale'.

definition: To waste something, such as money, time, or a chance.
examples: Don't squander your vacation days.
The team squandered a ten-point lead.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the late 16th century.

definition: Easily disgusted or made uneasy, especially by unpleasant sights.
examples: Don't watch the surgery video if you're squeamish.
He's too squeamish to clean a fish.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman escoymous, of unknown origin.

definition: To silence or suppress something forcefully.
examples: Management tried to squelch rumors of a merger.
Don't squelch new ideas before you hear them out.
etymology: Imitative in origin, first recorded in the seventeenth century.

definition: A short, witty or satirical piece of writing, or a small firework.
examples: He wrote a squib mocking the city council.
The launch turned out to be a damp squib.
etymology: Probably imitative of a small explosion.

definition: To make or become steady and less likely to change.
examples: Doctors worked to stabilize the patient's breathing.
Prices should stabilize once supply catches up.
etymology: From stable + -ize; stable comes from Latin stabilis 'firm'.

definition: Made up of short, sharp, separate sounds or parts.
examples: The rain beat a staccato rhythm on the roof.
He answered in staccato bursts.
etymology: From Italian staccato 'detached', from staccare.

definition: To walk unsteadily, or to arrange events so they do not happen at the same time.
examples: We stagger lunch breaks so the desk is always covered.
Exhausted runners began to stagger across the finish line.
etymology: From Old Norse stakra 'to push, cause to stumble'.

definition: So great or shocking that it is hard to believe.
examples: The repairs came to a staggering amount.
The film's success was staggering for such a tiny budget.
etymology: From stagger, from Old Norse stakra 'to push'.

definition: Not flowing or moving, and therefore stale or showing no growth.
examples: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water.
Wages have been stagnant for a decade.
etymology: From Latin stagnare 'to form a pool', from stagnum 'pool'.

definition: Sedate, respectable, and unadventurous.
examples: The staid bank surprised everyone with a playful ad.
Our staid neighborhood comes alive during the summer festival.
etymology: Archaic past participle of stay.

definition: An exceptionally hardworking and productive worker.
examples: She's a Stakhanovite who answers emails at midnight.
The factory honored every Stakhanovite with a medal.
etymology: From Alexei Stakhanov, a Soviet miner celebrated in 1935 for record coal output.

definition: A situation in which neither side can make progress or win.
examples: The budget talks ended in a stalemate.
The chess game reached a stalemate after two hours.
etymology: From obsolete stale 'stalemate' (from Anglo-Norman estale 'standstill') + mate, from chess.

definition: To stop making progress, or to delay on purpose.
examples: Talks began to stall over the question of pay.
Try to stall them until the cake is ready.
etymology: From Old English steall 'place for standing'; the delaying sense comes from an old word for a decoy.

definition: A loyal, reliable, and hardworking supporter of an organization.
examples: She has been a stalwart of the community garden since it opened.
Party stalwarts gathered to celebrate the anniversary.
etymology: From Old English stælwierthe, 'serviceable'.

definition: The physical or mental strength to keep going for a long time.
examples: Hiking all day takes more stamina than I expected.
Studying for the bar exam requires mental stamina.
etymology: From Latin stamina, plural of stamen 'thread', referring to the threads of life spun by the Fates.

definition: A publicly stated attitude or position on an issue.
examples: The mayor took a firm stance against the new highway.
What is your stance on homework in elementary school?
etymology: From Italian stanza 'standing place', from Latin stare 'to stand'.

definition: To stop the flow of something, especially blood or losses.
examples: Press firmly to stanch the bleeding.
The company cut prices to stanch the loss of customers.
etymology: From Old French estanchier 'to stop a flow'.

definition: A particular way of looking at or judging a situation.
examples: From a financial standpoint, the merger makes sense.
Try to see the issue from the customer's standpoint.
etymology: A translation of German Standpunkt, 'standing point'.

definition: A situation in which all movement or progress has stopped.
examples: The snowstorm brought the city to a standstill.
Negotiations are at a standstill.
etymology: From stand + still.

definition: A basic item that is used or found regularly and is essential.
examples: Rice is a staple in many households.
Denim jackets have become a wardrobe staple.
etymology: From Old French estaple 'market', from Middle Dutch stapel 'pillar' or 'warehouse'.

definition: Severe or bare in appearance, or sharply clear and unmistakable.
examples: The photo shows a stark contrast between rich and poor neighborhoods.
The desert was stark and beautiful at dawn.
etymology: From Old English stearc 'stiff, strong, severe'.

definition: A state of inactivity or balance in which nothing changes.
examples: The industry has been in stasis for years.
The plot drifts into stasis in the second half.
etymology: From Greek stasis 'standing, stoppage'.

definition: Very loyal and committed.
examples: She's a staunch supporter of the local team.
He has remained a staunch friend through every hard time.
etymology: From Old French estanche, 'watertight'.

definition: Firmly loyal and unwavering in purpose, belief, or commitment.
examples: She remained steadfast in her support for the team through every losing season.
The town's steadfast refusal to sell the park inspired activists elsewhere.
etymology: From Old English stedefæst, from stede 'place' + fæst 'fixed, firm'.

definition: In a quiet, secret way so as not to be noticed.
examples: The cat crept stealthily toward the bird.
He stealthily refilled his plate while no one looked.
etymology: From stealth, from Middle English stelthe, related to steal.

definition: The practice of hiding secret messages inside ordinary-looking content.
examples: Using steganography, he hid the file inside a cat photo.
Spies used steganography long before computers.
etymology: From Greek steganos 'covered' + -graphia 'writing'.

definition: Full of stars.
examples: We lay back under a stelliferous desert sky.
The stelliferous ceiling of the theater delighted kids.
etymology: From Latin stellifer, from stella 'star' + ferre 'to bear'.

definition: Extremely loud and powerful in sound, said of a voice.
examples: The sergeant's stentorian voice carried across the entire parade ground.
A stentorian announcement jolted the sleepy passengers awake.
etymology: From Stentor, a herald in Homer's Iliad with a voice as loud as fifty men.

definition: Serious and strict, especially in demanding obedience.
examples: The coach gave us a stern warning about being late.
Her stern face softened when she laughed.
etymology: From Old English styrne 'severe'.

definition: Noisy and labored, like heavy snoring.
examples: Stertorous breathing came from the hammock.
The old engine gave a stertorous wheeze.
etymology: From Latin stertere 'to snore'.

definition: Dialogue in alternating single lines, typical of Greek drama.
examples: The quarrel scene is a burst of rapid stichomythia.
Screenwriters borrow stichomythia for snappy banter.
etymology: From Greek stikhomythia, from stikhos 'line' + mythos 'speech'.

definition: To hold back or suppress something.
examples: I tried to stifle a laugh during the serious meeting.
Too many rules can stifle creativity.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly from Old French estouffer 'to smother'.

definition: A mark of disgrace or social disapproval attached to something.
examples: Campaigns are working to reduce the stigma around therapy.
There's still a stigma attached to dropping out of college.
etymology: From Greek stigma 'mark made by a pointed instrument', via Latin.

definition: To mark someone out as shameful or unworthy.
examples: Policies like this stigmatize people who need help.
We shouldn't stigmatize asking questions in class.
etymology: From Greek stigmatizein 'to mark', from stigma.

definition: Stiff, formal, and unnatural in manner or speech.
examples: The dialogue in the film felt stilted.
Their stilted small talk was painful to watch.
etymology: From stilt, as if raised up on stilts.

definition: To encourage activity, growth, or interest in something.
examples: Lower interest rates can stimulate the economy.
Good questions stimulate class discussion.
etymology: From Latin stimulare 'to goad', from stimulus 'goad'.

definition: A fixed or limited period spent doing a particular job or activity.
examples: After a stint in the Navy, he went back to school.
She did a two-year stint as a reporter in Tokyo.
etymology: From Old English styntan 'to blunt'; the 'allotted portion' sense developed later.

definition: A fixed regular sum paid as a salary or allowance.
examples: Graduate students receive a modest stipend.
The internship comes with a small stipend for housing.
etymology: From Latin stipendium, from stips 'wages' + pendere 'to pay'.

definition: To mark a surface with many small dots or dabs.
examples: Artists stipple ink to create shading.
Morning light began to stipple the forest floor.
etymology: From Dutch stippelen, from stippen 'to prick'.

definition: To demand or specify something as part of an agreement.
examples: The lease may stipulate that tenants cannot keep pets.
Rules stipulate that players must be under eighteen.
etymology: From Latin stipulari 'to demand a formal promise'.

definition: Involving randomness or probability rather than fixed outcomes.
examples: Weather models rely on stochastic simulations.
Some critics call language models stochastic parrots.
etymology: From Greek stokhastikos 'able to guess', from stokhos 'aim'.

definition: A large supply of something gathered and stored for future use.
examples: The hospital keeps a stockpile of masks.
He has a stockpile of snacks under his desk.
etymology: From stock + pile.

definition: Dull, old-fashioned, and uninspired, or heavy and filling.
examples: The museum shed its stodgy image with a new website.
Winter brings stodgy comfort food.
etymology: From stodge 'heavy food', perhaps imitative.

definition: Enduring pain or hardship calmly, without showing emotion or complaining.
examples: He remained stoic throughout the long recovery, never once complaining about the pain.
Her stoic expression gave nothing away as the verdict was read.
etymology: From Stoic, a follower of the Greek philosophy founded by Zeno, taught at the Stoa, a painted porch in Athens.

definition: To add fuel to a fire, or to encourage a strong feeling.
examples: Headlines like that only stoke public fear.
Stoke the stove before you go to bed.
etymology: A back-formation from stoker, from Dutch stoken 'to feed a fire'.

definition: Calm and unemotional, showing little feeling or excitement.
examples: The stolid guard didn't flinch at the tourists' jokes.
Her stolid expression gave nothing away.
etymology: From Latin stolidus 'dull, stupid'.

definition: To delay or block a request or process by refusing to answer or cooperate.
examples: The agency continued to stonewall reporters' requests.
If you stonewall your partner, the argument never ends.
etymology: From stone wall, originally a cricket term for stubborn defensive batting.

definition: A severe demand on strength, resources, or patience.
examples: The long commute put a strain on their marriage.
Holiday traffic places a heavy strain on the roads.
etymology: From Old French estreindre 'to bind tightly', from Latin stringere.

definition: A clever plan or trick for outwitting an opponent.
examples: Feigning injury was a stratagem to waste time.
Her stratagem for getting a raise worked perfectly.
etymology: From Greek stratēgēma, from stratēgos 'general'.

definition: Planned carefully to achieve a long-term goal or advantage.
examples: Opening a store near the station was a strategic choice.
The company made a strategic decision to focus on its home market.
etymology: From Greek stratēgikos, from stratēgos 'general'.

definition: To arrange or divide into layers or social classes.
examples: Rising rents stratify a city by income.
Researchers stratify the data by age group.
etymology: From Modern Latin stratificare, from stratum 'layer'.

definition: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
examples: The new app helps streamline grocery ordering.
We streamlined the hiring process from six steps to three.
etymology: From stream + line, originally a smooth shape that moves easily through water or air.

definition: Requiring great effort or energy.
examples: Avoid strenuous exercise for a week after surgery.
The hike was strenuous, but the view was worth it.
etymology: From Latin strenuus, 'brisk, active'.

definition: A rule that limits behavior, or a sharp criticism.
examples: The diet comes with one stricture: no sugar.
He ignored every stricture from his critics.
etymology: From Latin strictura, from stringere 'to draw tight'.

definition: Loud and harsh, or forceful and uncompromising in expression.
examples: The strident alarm jolted us awake.
Her strident criticism alienated some supporters.
etymology: From Latin stridere 'to creak, shriek'.

definition: To make a shrill, rasping sound by rubbing body parts together, as insects do.
examples: Crickets stridulate all night in August.
Some beetles stridulate when threatened.
etymology: From Latin stridulus 'creaking', from stridere 'to creak'.

definition: Bitter disagreement or conflict.
examples: Years of civil strife emptied the villages.
The inheritance caused strife among the siblings.
etymology: From Old French estrif, related to estriver 'to strive'.

definition: Strict, precise, and demanding, especially of rules or standards.
examples: The factory must meet stringent safety standards before it can reopen.
Stringent security checks slowed the line at the airport to a crawl.
etymology: From Latin stringens, 'binding tight', from stringere, 'to draw tight'.

definition: To make great efforts to achieve something.
examples: We strive to answer every email within a day.
Athletes strive for improvements of a fraction of a second.
etymology: From Old French estriver 'to quarrel', of Germanic origin.

definition: A section of a poem or ode, originally sung by a Greek chorus while turning.
examples: Each strophe of the ode answers the one before.
The chorus sang the first strophe while circling the stage.
etymology: From Greek strophē 'turning'.

definition: Deliberate and carefully arranged rather than natural.
examples: He looked out the window with studied indifference.
Her outfit had a studied casualness.
etymology: From study, from Latin studium 'zeal'.

definition: To cause to lose enthusiasm and initiative, especially through dull routine.
examples: Endless paperwork can stultify even the most creative workers.
Rigid rules stultify any real discussion in class.
etymology: From late Latin stultificare, from stultus, 'foolish'.

definition: To trip or falter, or to come across something by chance.
examples: You might stumble on a great cafe if you wander the old town.
Speakers often stumble over unfamiliar names.
etymology: From Middle English stumblen, of Scandinavian origin.

definition: To astonish, or to make someone unable to think clearly.
examples: The size of the bill would stupefy anyone.
Hours of meetings stupefy even the sharpest minds.
etymology: From Latin stupefacere, from stupere 'to be amazed' + facere 'to make'.

definition: A state of near-unconsciousness or dazed bewilderment.
examples: After the holiday dinner, we sat in a food stupor.
He wandered out of the exam in a stupor.
etymology: From Latin stupor, from stupere 'to be amazed'.

definition: Extremely dark, gloomy, and forbidding.
examples: We groped through the stygian basement looking for the fuse box.
The cave's stygian depths frightened the younger campers.
etymology: From Greek Stugios, from Styx, the river of the underworld.

definition: An early Christian ascetic who lived atop a pillar.
examples: Simeon the Stylite lived on his pillar for decades.
Working from the tiny loft, she felt like a stylite.
etymology: From Greek stylitēs, from stylos 'pillar'.

definition: To prevent or hinder the progress of something.
examples: A lack of funding could stymie the project.
Thick fog stymied rescue efforts for hours.
etymology: From a golf term for an opponent's ball blocking the line to the hole.

definition: Persuasion, especially by appeal to reason or morality rather than force.
examples: The central bank relied on moral suasion rather than rules.
Gentle suasion worked better than threats.
etymology: From Latin suasio, from suadere 'to urge'.

definition: Charming, confident, and elegant, often in a polished way.
examples: The suave host greeted every guest by name.
He played a suave spy in the film.
etymology: From French suave, from Latin suavis 'agreeable'.

definition: A junior officer, or a person of lower rank or status.
examples: A young subaltern led the patrol.
The memo was written by some anonymous subaltern.
etymology: From Late Latin subalternus, from sub- 'under' + alternus 'every other'.

definition: To bring under control, quiet, or overcome.
examples: Firefighters worked all night to subdue the blaze.
She tried to subdue her laughter during the speech.
etymology: From Old French souduire, from Latin subducere 'to withdraw'; influenced by Latin subdere 'to conquer'.

definition: Dull, dark, and drab in color or character.
examples: He wore a subfusc suit to the gala.
The subfusc little town came alive at the festival.
etymology: From Latin subfuscus, from sub- 'somewhat' + fuscus 'dark brown'.

definition: To bring under domination or control, especially by conquest.
examples: The empire tried to subjugate its neighbors.
Don't let one ambition subjugate everything else in your life.
etymology: From Latin subjugare 'to bring under the yoke', from jugum 'yoke'.

definition: To redirect a strong impulse into a more acceptable or productive activity.
examples: She learned to sublimate her anger into marathon training.
Many artists sublimate grief into their work.
etymology: From Latin sublimare 'to raise up', from sublimis 'lofty'.

definition: Of such great beauty or excellence that it inspires awe.
examples: The view from the summit was sublime.
Her cello solo was simply sublime.
etymology: From Latin sublimis 'uplifted, lofty'.

definition: Affecting the mind without one being consciously aware of it.
examples: The ad seemed to carry a subliminal message.
Background music has a subliminal effect on shoppers.
etymology: From sub- 'below' + Latin limen 'threshold'.

definition: Belonging to this world; earthly and imperfect.
examples: The poet turned from heaven to sublunary matters like rent.
No sublunary pleasure lasts forever.
etymology: From Late Latin sublunaris, 'beneath the moon'.

definition: A person under the authority or control of another, especially at work.
examples: A good boss gives credit to every subordinate.
She treated each subordinate as a future leader.
etymology: From Medieval Latin subordinatus, from sub- 'below' + ordinare 'to arrange'.

definition: To bribe or induce someone to commit wrongdoing, especially perjury.
examples: He tried to suborn a witness with cash.
Agents attempted to suborn officials in the ministry.
etymology: From Latin subornare, from sub- 'secretly' + ornare 'to equip'.

definition: Afterward; later.
examples: He missed the bus and subsequently arrived late to work.
The store closed in March and was subsequently turned into a cafe.
etymology: From Latin subsequi, 'to follow closely'.

definition: Too willing to obey others, or less important than something else.
examples: The new manager didn't want a subservient team.
Profit should be subservient to safety.
etymology: From Latin subservire 'to be subject to', from sub- + servire 'to serve'.

definition: To become less intense, violent, or high.
examples: Wait for the swelling to subside before you run again.
The floodwaters began to subside by Tuesday.
etymology: From Latin subsidere, from sub- 'below' + sidere 'to settle'.

definition: The principle that decisions should be made at the most local level that can handle them.
examples: Under subsidiarity, towns run their own schools.
The EU treaty enshrines subsidiarity.
etymology: From subsidiary, from Latin subsidium 'support'; translating German Subsidiarität.

definition: To support something financially, usually so it can be sold or run more cheaply.
examples: The city will subsidize bus passes for students.
Should governments subsidize electric cars?
etymology: From subsidy, from Latin subsidium 'assistance' or 'reserve troops'.

definition: To stay alive, especially with very limited resources.
examples: They had to subsist on rice and beans that winter.
Few artists can subsist on sales alone.
etymology: From Latin subsistere 'to stand firm'.

definition: Of considerable size, importance, or worth.
examples: They made a substantial donation to the library.
There's substantial evidence that sleep helps memory.
etymology: From Latin substantialis, from substantia 'substance'.

definition: To provide evidence that something is true.
examples: The reporter could not substantiate the rumor, so she didn't publish it.
Lab tests substantiated the doctor's first guess.
etymology: From Medieval Latin substantiare, 'to give substance to', from substantia 'substance'.

definition: Having real importance or meaning, rather than being superficial.
examples: The meeting finally produced substantive progress.
She wants a substantive debate, not slogans.
etymology: From Late Latin substantivus, from substantia 'substance'.

definition: To include or absorb something into a larger group or category.
examples: The national organization agreed to subsume the small charity.
Her personal goals were subsumed by the demands of the job.
etymology: From Medieval Latin subsumere, from sub-, 'under', + sumere, 'to take'.

definition: To extend opposite and define an angle or arc; to underlie.
examples: Each side of a triangle will subtend the angle opposite it.
Shared values subtend the whole agreement.
etymology: From Latin subtendere 'to stretch under'.

definition: Deceit or trickery used to achieve a goal.
examples: They used subterfuge to get the surprise guest inside.
The spy novel is full of subterfuge.
etymology: From Late Latin subterfugium, from subterfugere 'to escape secretly'.

definition: Existing or happening underground, or hidden from view.
examples: The city has a subterranean network of tunnels.
There's a subterranean current of anger in the novel.
etymology: From Latin subterraneus, from sub- 'below' + terra 'earth'.

definition: An underlying meaning that is implied rather than stated directly.
examples: The subtext of his compliment was clearly an insult.
Good actors play the subtext, not just the lines.
etymology: From sub- 'below' + text.

definition: So slight or delicate that it is hard to notice or describe.
examples: There is a subtle difference between confidence and arrogance, and tone often decides it.
The chef added a subtle hint of smoke to the soup.
etymology: From Latin subtilis, 'fine, delicate', possibly from sub- 'under' + tela 'web, woven fabric'.

definition: To undermine the power or authority of an established system or idea.
examples: The film likes to subvert classic horror clichés.
Hackers tried to subvert the voting software.
etymology: From Latin subvertere 'to overturn'.

definition: Expressed briefly and clearly, using few words.
examples: Her succinct summary saved the committee an hour of discussion.
Keep your email succinct, because busy readers rarely finish long messages.
etymology: From Latin succinctus, 'girded up', from sub- 'up' + cingere 'to gird'.

definition: Help and support in a time of hardship.
examples: The shelter offered succor to travelers caught in the blizzard.
Villagers found succor in each other after the flood.
etymology: From Old French socours, from Latin succurrere 'to run to help'.

definition: To give way to a force, pressure, or temptation.
examples: I finally had to succumb to the smell of fresh donuts.
Many small shops succumb to rising rents.
etymology: From Latin succumbere, from sub- 'under' + cumbere 'to lie'.

definition: Tolerance or permission given reluctantly, rather than as a right.
examples: He stayed in the flat on sufferance.
Street vendors operate only on the city's sufferance.
etymology: From Old French souffrance, from Latin sufferre 'to endure'.

definition: To be enough or adequate for a need or purpose.
examples: A quick text will suffice; no need to call.
Two coats of paint should suffice for this wall.
etymology: From Latin sufficere, from sub- 'under' + facere 'to make'.

definition: The right to vote in political elections.
examples: Women won suffrage in the U.S. in 1920.
The movement for universal suffrage took decades.
etymology: From Latin suffragium 'vote, support'.

definition: To gradually spread through or over something, as with light, color, or feeling.
examples: Warm light began to suffuse the room at sunset.
Nostalgia seems to suffuse every song on the album.
etymology: From Latin suffundere 'to pour into'.

definition: To be silent and bad-tempered out of annoyance or disappointment.
examples: Don't sulk just because we picked a different movie.
He went to sulk in his room after the loss.
etymology: A back-formation from sulky.

definition: Gloomy, resentful, and unwilling to be cheerful or talk.
examples: A sullen teenager slouched in the back seat.
The sky stayed sullen and gray all day.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman solein 'solitary', from Latin solus 'alone'.

definition: To damage the purity or reputation of something.
examples: One bad review won't sully a decades-long career.
He refused to sully his name with that deal.
etymology: Perhaps from French souiller 'to soil'.

definition: Without delay or formality.
examples: The intruder was summarily removed from the building.
His proposal was summarily rejected.
etymology: From Medieval Latin summarius, from summa, 'sum', + -ly.

definition: Relating to laws that limit private spending or luxury.
examples: Medieval sumptuary laws banned commoners from wearing silk.
The new dress code felt almost sumptuary.
etymology: From Latin sumptuarius, from sumptus 'expense'.

definition: Splendid and expensive-looking; lavish.
examples: The wedding ended with a sumptuous dessert table.
The hotel lobby was sumptuous, all velvet and brass.
etymology: From Latin sumptuosus, from sumptus 'expense'.

definition: Of various kinds; miscellaneous.
examples: The drawer was full of sundry cables and chargers.
She thanked sundry friends and relatives.
etymology: From Old English syndrig 'separate'.

definition: Too old to be useful, or retired because of age.
examples: The office still runs on superannuated computers.
A superannuated rock star toured one more time.
etymology: From Medieval Latin superannuatus, from super- 'beyond' + annus 'year'.

definition: Behaving as if one is superior to others, in a disdainful way.
examples: The supercilious waiter sneered at our modest wine order.
She gave him a supercilious smile and walked past without speaking.
etymology: From Latin supercilium, 'eyebrow', the raised brow signaling disdain.

definition: Going beyond what duty requires.
examples: Her supererogatory kindness to strangers is legendary.
Thanking the toll collector felt supererogatory, but nice.
etymology: From Late Latin supererogare 'to pay out beyond what is required'.

definition: Existing only on the surface; not deep or thorough.
examples: The scratch was superficial and healed quickly.
Their conversation stayed superficial, mostly about the weather.
etymology: From Late Latin superficialis, from superficies 'surface'.

definition: More than is needed; unnecessary and without useful purpose.
examples: The editor cut every superfluous adjective from the opening paragraph.
Adding a third alarm seemed superfluous when the first two already woke the whole house.
etymology: From Latin superfluus, 'overflowing', from super- 'over' + fluere 'to flow'.

definition: Of the highest quality or degree.
examples: The restaurant earned superlative reviews.
She is a superlative violinist.
etymology: From Late Latin superlativus, from superferre 'to carry beyond'.

definition: Heavenly, celestial, or of exceptional quality.
examples: The choir's supernal harmonies filled the hall.
A supernal light broke through the clouds.
etymology: From Latin supernus 'above'.

definition: Exceeding the normal or required number; extra.
examples: The film hired hundreds of supernumerary actors for the battle scene.
She found herself in a supernumerary role at the meeting.
etymology: From Late Latin supernumerarius, 'soldier added to a full legion'.

definition: To take the place of something older or less effective.
examples: The new policy will supersede all earlier guidelines.
Streaming began to supersede the DVD.
etymology: From Latin supersedere 'to sit above, refrain from'.

definition: To occur later, interrupting or changing a situation.
examples: The patient was recovering well until an infection began to supervene.
Unless complications supervene, he'll be home Friday.
etymology: From Latin supervenire 'to come in addition'.

definition: Lying face upward, or failing to act or resist out of weakness.
examples: The patient lay supine on the table.
Critics called the committee supine in the face of corruption.
etymology: From Latin supinus 'lying on the back'.

definition: To replace something, especially by force or strategy.
examples: Streaming has largely supplanted DVDs.
The new manager hoped to supplant the old way of doing things.
etymology: From Latin supplantare, 'to trip up', from planta, 'sole of the foot'.

definition: Bending and moving easily; flexible.
examples: Yoga keeps her joints supple.
The jacket is made of supple leather.
etymology: From Old French souple, from Latin supplex 'submissive'.

definition: Something added to complete or enhance something else.
examples: He takes a vitamin D supplement in winter.
The tutoring is a supplement to classroom teaching, not a replacement.
etymology: From Latin supplementum, from supplere 'to fill up'.

definition: A person who humbly asks for something.
examples: The suppliant knelt before the throne.
She approached the bank like a suppliant.
etymology: From French suppliant, from supplier, from Latin supplicare 'to beseech'.

definition: To ask or beg humbly and earnestly.
examples: He refused to supplicate before the board for more money.
Pilgrims came to supplicate at the shrine.
etymology: From Latin supplicare 'to kneel down, beseech'.

definition: An idea assumed to be true without proof.
examples: The whole theory rests on a single supposition.
That's pure supposition; we need data.
etymology: From Latin suppositio, from supponere 'to place under'.

definition: Fraudulently substituted or not genuine.
examples: Scholars exposed the letter as supposititious.
The claim rested on a supposititious heir.
etymology: From Latin supposititius, from supponere 'to substitute'.

definition: To forcibly stop or hold back something, such as an activity, feeling, or information.
examples: She tried to suppress a yawn during the lecture.
The regime moved quickly to suppress the protests.
etymology: From Latin supprimere 'to press down'.

definition: To form or discharge pus, or to fester.
examples: Left untreated, the wound will suppurate.
Old grudges tend to suppurate in small towns.
etymology: From Latin suppurare, from sub- + pus 'pus'.

definition: An end or pause, especially relief from something painful.
examples: Sleep brought surcease from the long day's worry.
There was no surcease to the construction noise.
etymology: From Old French sursis, from surseoir 'to refrain', from Latin supersedere.

definition: A person who takes responsibility for another's debt or promise, or a guarantee.
examples: Her father stood surety for the loan.
The deposit serves as surety against damage.
etymology: From Old French seurte, from Latin securitas 'security'.

definition: An excessive amount of something.
examples: A surfeit of streaming options makes choosing hard.
After a surfeit of holiday sweets, I craved salad.
etymology: From Old French sorfait 'excess', from surfaire 'to overdo'.

definition: A sudden, powerful increase or forward rush.
examples: The store saw a surge in sales before the holiday.
A surge of anger rose in her chest.
etymology: From Old French sourgeon 'spring, fountain', from Latin surgere 'to rise'.

definition: Bad-tempered and rude in an unfriendly way.
examples: A surly clerk barely looked up.
He's surly before his first coffee.
etymology: An alteration of obsolete sirly 'lordly, haughty', from sir.

definition: To suppose something is true without solid evidence.
examples: From the mud on his boots, I surmise he took the trail.
We can only surmise what the author intended.
etymology: From Old French surmise 'accused', from surmettre 'to put upon'.

definition: To overcome a difficulty or obstacle.
examples: Together we can surmount almost any setback.
The startup had to surmount strict regulations.
etymology: From Old French surmonter, from sur- 'over' + monter 'to mount'.

definition: To go beyond or be greater than something or someone.
examples: The sequel managed to surpass the original in ticket sales.
Few runners will ever surpass her record.
etymology: From French surpasser, from sur- 'beyond' + passer 'to pass'.

definition: An amount left over after needs have been met.
examples: The bakery gives its surplus to a shelter each night.
The state ended the year with a budget surplus.
etymology: From Old French sorplus, from Medieval Latin superplus, 'more than enough'.

definition: Kept secret, especially because it would not be approved.
examples: She took a surreptitious bite of cake before the party.
He made surreptitious notes during the meeting.
etymology: From Latin surrepticius, 'stolen, secret', from surripere, 'to seize secretly'.

definition: A substitute, especially a person who stands in for another.
examples: The campaign sent a surrogate to the debate.
For years, her older sister acted as a surrogate parent.
etymology: From Latin surrogatus, from surrogare 'to elect as a substitute'.

definition: Close and continuous watching of a person, place, or activity.
examples: The parking lot is under video surveillance.
Critics worry about government surveillance of phone data.
etymology: From French surveiller, from sur- 'over' + veiller 'to watch'.

definition: Likely to be affected or harmed by something.
examples: Young children are more susceptible to the flu.
He is susceptible to flattery, so watch what you promise.
etymology: From Late Latin susceptibilis, from suscipere 'to take up'.

definition: To sigh or breathe deeply.
examples: The old house seemed to suspire in the wind.
She paused to suspire before opening the letter.
etymology: From Latin suspirare, from sub- + spirare 'to breathe'.

definition: To keep something going over time, or to support it physically or emotionally.
examples: It's hard to sustain that pace for a whole marathon.
A good breakfast will sustain you until lunch.
etymology: From Latin sustinere, from sub- 'from below' + tenere 'to hold'.

definition: A soft, whispering or rustling sound.
examples: A susurrus of leaves drifted through the open window.
The susurrus of the crowd faded as the lights went down.
etymology: From Latin susurrus, 'whisper', imitative of the sound.

definition: A state or ruler that controls another's foreign affairs while allowing it internal autonomy.
examples: The empire acted as suzerain over the border kingdoms.
Each tributary prince sent gifts to his suzerain.
etymology: From French suzerain, from sus 'above', modeled on souverain 'sovereign'.

definition: Slender and graceful.
examples: The svelte new laptop weighs under two pounds.
A svelte greyhound trotted past.
etymology: From Italian svelto 'stretched out, quick'.

definition: A very confident and arrogant way of walking or behaving.
examples: The rookie walked onto the court with a swagger.
There's a certain swagger to the band's new album.
etymology: Apparently from swag 'to sway', perhaps of Scandinavian origin.

definition: A young lover or suitor, or a country youth.
examples: A lovesick swain serenaded her from the street.
The pastoral poem features a shepherdess and her swain.
etymology: From Old Norse sveinn 'boy, servant'.

definition: To overwhelm with too much of something.
examples: Holiday orders always swamp the small shop.
Don't swamp new hires with paperwork on day one.
etymology: Probably from a Low German or Dutch source; the noun means a marsh.

definition: An expanse of short grass.
examples: Sheep grazed on the green sward by the river.
We spread our blanket on the sward.
etymology: From Old English sweard 'skin, rind'.

definition: Daring and flamboyantly adventurous.
examples: It's a swashbuckling pirate film for the whole family.
The swashbuckling CEO bet the company on one product.
etymology: From swash 'to strike noisily' + buckler 'small shield'.

definition: A broad strip or area of something.
examples: The fire burned a swathe of forest.
The new law affects a wide swathe of renters.
etymology: From Old English swæth 'track, trace', originally a strip cut by a scythe.

definition: To move gently from side to side, or to influence someone's opinion.
examples: Nothing you say will sway her once she's decided.
The palms sway in the evening breeze.
etymology: Probably from Low German swājen 'to be moved by the wind'.

definition: To change direction suddenly, especially to avoid something.
examples: I had to swerve to miss a deer.
Don't swerve from your plan at the first setback.
etymology: From Old English sweorfan 'to depart, leave'.

definition: Happening or moving quickly and promptly.
examples: The company issued a swift apology.
A swift current carried the kayak downstream.
etymology: From Old English swift, related to swīfan 'to move in a course'.

definition: To cheat someone out of money or property.
examples: Scammers swindle retirees with fake tech-support calls.
He tried to swindle his cousin out of the family farm.
etymology: A back-formation from swindler, from German Schwindler 'extravagant schemer'.

definition: A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
examples: The sybarite spent his weekends in spas and five-star restaurants.
Not quite a sybarite, she nonetheless insisted on silk sheets.
etymology: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in Italy known for its residents' love of luxury.

definition: A person who flatters powerful people to gain favor or advantage.
examples: The CEO surrounded himself with every sycophant who laughed at his jokes and never disagreed.
No honest advisor wants to be seen as a sycophant just to keep their job.
etymology: From Greek sykophantes, originally 'informer', later used for 'flatterer'.

definition: A figure of speech in which one word applies to two others in different senses.
examples: 'She lost her keys and her temper' is a syllepsis.
Dickens loved a well-timed syllepsis.
etymology: From Greek syllēpsis 'taking together'.

definition: A form of reasoning in which a conclusion is drawn from two premises.
examples: 'All cats are mortal; Tom is a cat; so Tom is mortal' is a classic syllogism.
His syllogism had a flawed premise.
etymology: From Greek syllogismos, from syllogizesthai 'to reckon together'.

definition: An imaginary spirit of the air, or a slender, graceful woman or girl.
examples: The ballerina moved like a sylph across the stage.
In Pope's poem, a sylph guards Belinda's beauty.
etymology: From Modern Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus.

definition: Relating to woods; wooded and pleasantly rural.
examples: The cabin sat in a sylvan clearing among the redwoods.
The wedding had a sylvan theme with ferns and moss.
etymology: From Latin silva, 'wood'.

definition: A close relationship between two parties that benefits both.
examples: Clownfish and anemones live in symbiosis.
There's a nice symbiosis between the bakery and the coffee shop next door.
etymology: From Greek symbiōsis 'living together', from syn- + bios 'life'.

definition: Serving as a symbol, or significant for what it represents rather than its practical effect.
examples: The ribbon cutting was mostly symbolic.
Planting a tree together was a symbolic start to their marriage.
etymology: From Late Latin symbolicus, from Greek symbolon 'token'.

definition: Balanced, matching proportions on opposite sides of something.
examples: The architect loved the symmetry of the old courthouse.
There's a pleasing symmetry in how the story begins and ends.
etymology: From Greek symmetria, from syn- 'together' + metron 'measure'.

definition: To make things happen at the same time or rate.
examples: Let's synchronize our watches before the race.
The app will synchronize your notes across devices.
etymology: From Greek synkhronos, from syn- 'together' + khronos 'time'.

definition: The blending of different beliefs, traditions, or cultures into one.
examples: Caribbean religion shows rich syncretism of African and Catholic practice.
The chef's menu is a delicious syncretism.
etymology: From Greek synkrētismos 'union of Cretans', of disputed meaning.

definition: A figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole, or the whole for a part.
examples: Calling a car 'wheels' is a synecdoche.
'Hollywood' works as a synecdoche for the film industry.
etymology: From Greek synekdokhē, from syn- 'together' + ekdekhesthai 'to take up'.

definition: Cooperation that produces a combined result greater than the separate parts.
examples: There's real synergy between the design and marketing teams.
The duo's onstage synergy is obvious.
etymology: From Greek synergos 'working together'.

definition: A condition in which one sense triggers another, such as hearing colors.
examples: With synesthesia, she sees the number five as red.
The composer described his synesthesia in interviews.
etymology: From Greek syn- 'together' + aisthēsis 'sensation'.

definition: A brief summary of the main points of a story or text.
examples: Read the synopsis before choosing a movie.
She sent the publisher a one-page synopsis of her novel.
etymology: From Greek synopsis, from syn- 'together' + opsis 'seeing'.

definition: Giving a general view of the whole.
examples: The report offers a synoptic overview of the last decade.
Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the synoptic gospels.
etymology: From Greek synoptikos, from synopsis 'general view'.

definition: The combination of separate parts or ideas into a coherent whole.
examples: Her essay is a clever synthesis of science and folklore.
The band's sound is a synthesis of jazz and hip-hop.
etymology: From Greek synthesis, from syn- 'together' + tithenai 'to place'.

definition: Done according to a fixed plan or method, thoroughly and in order.
examples: The detectives made a systematic search of the house.
A systematic approach to studying beats cramming.
etymology: From Greek systēmatikos, from systēma 'organized whole'.

definition: Affecting a whole system rather than just one part.
examples: The delays point to a systemic problem, not one bad driver.
The infection became systemic.
etymology: From system, from Greek systēma 'organized whole'.

definition: The alignment of three celestial bodies, or any close pairing of two things.
examples: An eclipse happens during a syzygy of sun, moon, and Earth.
Their partnership was a rare syzygy of talent.
etymology: From Greek syzygia 'yoked together'.

definition: A striking scene or picture, often of people arranged artistically.
examples: The family at the picnic table formed a perfect summer tableau.
The play ends in a frozen tableau as the lights fade.
etymology: From French tableau, 'picture', diminutive of table.

definition: Things that should not be spoken of or made public.
examples: Family money was among the tacenda at holiday dinners.
Every institution has its tacenda.
etymology: From Latin, 'things to be kept silent', from tacere 'to be silent'.

definition: In a way that is understood without being stated.
examples: By not objecting, they tacitly agreed to the plan.
The team tacitly understood that Fridays were for cleanup.
etymology: From Latin tacitus, 'silent', + -ly.

definition: Habitually quiet and saying very little.
examples: The taciturn farmer answered most questions with a nod or a single word.
Her taciturn father rarely spoke at dinner, yet everyone felt his warmth.
etymology: From Latin taciturnus, 'silent', from tacitus, 'silent', from tacere, 'to be silent'.

definition: Careful to speak and act without offending or upsetting other people.
examples: A tactful friend will tell you about the spinach in your teeth privately.
She gave a tactful answer that avoided blaming anyone for the delay.
etymology: From tact, from Latin tactus, 'touch', plus the suffix -ful.

definition: A planned action meant to achieve a particular result.
examples: Stalling is a common tactic in negotiations.
Her tactic of asking questions first worked well.
etymology: From Greek taktikē (technē) 'the art of arrangement', from tassein 'to arrange'.

definition: Planned to achieve a specific short-term goal.
examples: Calling a timeout was a tactical decision.
She made a tactical retreat from the argument.
etymology: From Greek taktikos, from tassein 'to arrange'.

definition: Relating to or perceived by touch.
examples: Toddlers love tactile books with fuzzy pages.
The keyboard gives satisfying tactile feedback.
etymology: From Latin tactilis, from tangere 'to touch'.

definition: An object believed to bring good luck or protection.
examples: He carried his father's watch as a talisman.
The team mascot became a kind of talisman.
etymology: Via French or Spanish from Arabic ṭilsam, from Byzantine Greek telesma 'consecration'.

definition: To count up, or to agree or correspond.
examples: Let's tally the votes before announcing the winner.
Their stories don't tally.
etymology: From Latin talea 'twig, cutting', from the notched sticks once used for counting.

definition: To interfere with something in order to damage or alter it.
examples: Someone tried to tamper with the voting machine.
Never tamper with a smoke detector.
etymology: Originally a variant of temper.

definition: A sudden change of subject to something only loosely related.
examples: Our professor went off on a tangent about his trip to Iceland.
Sorry for the tangent; let's get back to the budget.
etymology: From Latin tangens, 'touching', from tangere 'to touch'.

definition: Only slightly relevant to the main subject.
examples: The discussion drifted into tangential topics.
His comments were tangential to the actual problem.
etymology: From Latin tangent-, 'touching', from tangere, 'to touch'.

definition: Real and able to be seen, touched, or measured.
examples: The new program has produced tangible results.
There was a tangible sense of relief in the room.
etymology: From Late Latin tangibilis, from tangere 'to touch'.

definition: Exciting desire or interest, especially for something just out of reach.
examples: A tantalizing smell drifted from the bakery.
The trailer offers a tantalizing glimpse of the sequel.
etymology: From Tantalus, a king in Greek myth punished with food and water forever just out of reach.

definition: Equivalent in seriousness or effect to something worse.
examples: Ignoring the subpoena would be tantamount to admitting guilt.
His silence was tantamount to a yes.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman tant amunter 'to amount to as much'.

definition: At full gallop; at top speed.
examples: The messenger rode tantivy toward the castle.
The kids ran tantivy down the beach.
etymology: Probably imitative of the sound of galloping hooves.

definition: To become gradually narrower or smaller.
examples: The doctor told him to taper his dose over two weeks.
The trail begins to taper into a footpath.
etymology: From the noun taper 'a slender candle', from Old English.

definition: A microscopic eight-legged animal able to survive extreme conditions; a water bear.
examples: A tardigrade can survive being frozen for decades.
Scientists sent a tardigrade into space to test its toughness.
etymology: From Latin tardigradus 'slow-stepping', from tardus 'slow' plus gradi 'to walk'.

definition: A tax on imported or exported goods.
examples: A new tariff raised the price of steel.
Farmers worried about a tariff on soybeans.
etymology: Via Italian tariffa, ultimately from Arabic taʿrīf 'notification'.

definition: To dull the shine of metal, or to damage a reputation.
examples: One scandal can tarnish a lifetime of good work.
Humid air will tarnish the silverware.
etymology: From French terniss-, stem of ternir 'to dull'.

definition: To linger or delay in leaving a place.
examples: Don't tarry after the movie; the last bus leaves at eleven.
We decided to tarry an extra day by the lake.
etymology: Middle English, of uncertain origin.

definition: Hellish, like the lowest depths of the underworld.
examples: The mine's tartarean heat drove the workers out.
He described the subway at rush hour in tartarean terms.
etymology: From Tartarus, the deepest abyss of the underworld in Greek mythology.

definition: Ragged or shabby in appearance.
examples: A tatterdemalion scarecrow guarded the cornfield.
The band's tatterdemalion costumes were carefully designed.
etymology: From tatter + a fanciful ending, first recorded in the 17th century.

definition: To provoke or insult someone with mocking remarks.
examples: Rival fans began to taunt the goalkeeper.
Don't taunt your brother about the haircut.
etymology: Possibly from French tant pour tant 'tit for tat'.

definition: Like a bull, or relating to bulls.
examples: The wrestler had a taurine neck and shoulders.
He charged through the crowd with taurine force.
etymology: From Latin taurinus, from taurus 'bull'.

definition: Stretched tight, or tense and concise with no slack.
examples: Pull the rope taut before you tie the knot.
The novel is a taut thriller that never drags.
etymology: Middle English, probably related to tough.

definition: Needless repetition of the same idea in different words.
examples: "Free gift" is a tautology, since gifts are free.
The argument collapses into a tautology.
etymology: From Greek tautologia, from tauto 'the same' plus -logia 'saying'.

definition: Showy but cheap and of poor quality, or sordid.
examples: The casino was decorated in tawdry gold plastic.
Tabloids feasted on the tawdry details of the affair.
etymology: From tawdry lace, a shortening of St. Audrey's lace, sold at fairs held in her honor.

definition: Of an orange-brown or yellowish-brown color.
examples: A tawny owl watched from the oak.
The lion's tawny coat blended with the grass.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman tauné, from Old French tané 'tanned'.

definition: Tiresome because it is long, repetitive, or dull.
examples: Entering the survey data by hand was a tedious job that took days.
The movie's tedious middle section nearly put me to sleep.
etymology: From Latin taediosus, from taedium, 'weariness, disgust'.

definition: To be full of or swarming with something.
examples: Coral reefs teem with life.
In summer the beaches teem with tourists.
etymology: From Old English tēman 'to give birth to'.

definition: Never drinking alcohol.
examples: She's been teetotal since college.
The teetotal guests stuck to sparkling cider.
etymology: An emphatic doubling of the first letter of total, popularized by the temperance movement in the 1830s.

definition: Explaining things by their purpose or end goal rather than their cause.
examples: Saying giraffes grew long necks in order to eat leaves is a teleological error.
Her teleological view of history sees progress everywhere.
etymology: From Greek telos 'end, purpose' plus -logy.

definition: In a way that reveals more than intended.
examples: Tellingly, the CEO did not deny the report.
Tellingly, he changed the subject whenever money came up.
etymology: From telling plus -ly; tell comes from Old English tellan.

definition: Of or relating to the earth as a planet.
examples: The aliens in the story found tellurian customs baffling.
Astronauts long for tellurian comforts like rain.
etymology: From Latin tellus, telluris 'earth'.

definition: The ultimate end, aim, or purpose of something.
examples: For Aristotle, the telos of an acorn is the oak.
Profit had become the company's only telos.
etymology: From Greek telos 'end, purpose'.

definition: Excessive boldness or audacity.
examples: He had the temerity to correct the professor's grammar in front of everyone.
Few people had the temerity to question her decisions.
etymology: From Latin temeritas, 'rashness', from temere, 'blindly'.

definition: To moderate or soften something by adding a balancing element.
examples: Try to temper your criticism with praise.
A bit of honey will temper the sourness.
etymology: From Latin temperare 'to mingle, restrain'.

definition: Prone to sudden mood changes, or unreliable in performance.
examples: The old printer is temperamental on cold mornings.
Their temperamental lead singer stormed off stage.
etymology: From temperament, from Latin temperamentum 'correct mixture'.

definition: Full of strong, turbulent emotion or stormy conditions.
examples: The couple had a tempestuous relationship.
Sailors dread the tempestuous seas around the cape.
etymology: From Late Latin tempestuosus, from Latin tempestas 'storm'.

definition: Relating to time, or to worldly rather than spiritual affairs.
examples: The film plays with temporal order, jumping between decades.
Bishops once held temporal as well as religious power.
etymology: From Latin temporalis, from tempus 'time'.

definition: To avoid making a decision in order to gain time.
examples: The landlord temporized for weeks instead of fixing the heater.
Don't temporize; tell them yes or no.
etymology: From French temporiser, 'to bide one's time', from Latin tempus, 'time'.

definition: Able to be maintained or defended against objections.
examples: His argument is no longer tenable given the new evidence.
Is it tenable to keep commuting three hours a day?
etymology: From French tenable, from tenir, 'to hold'.

definition: Holding firmly to a goal or belief and refusing to give up.
examples: A tenacious reporter, she chased the story for three years until the truth emerged.
The vine is tenacious, gripping the wall through storms and frost.
etymology: From Latin tenax, 'holding fast', from tenere, 'to hold'.

definition: A person who rents land or property from a landlord.
examples: The previous tenant left the apartment spotless.
Every tenant received a notice about the rent increase.
etymology: From Old French, present participle of tenir 'to hold'.

definition: Promoting a particular, often controversial, point of view in a biased way.
examples: The documentary was criticized as a tendentious account of the strike.
Her tendentious summary left out every fact that cut against her side.
etymology: From Medieval Latin tendentiosus, from Latin tendere 'to aim, tend'.

definition: A style of painting using dramatic contrasts of deep shadow and bright light.
examples: Caravaggio's tenebrism makes his figures leap from the darkness.
The photographer borrowed the look of tenebrism for her portraits.
etymology: From Italian tenebroso 'dark', from Latin tenebrae 'darkness'.

definition: Dark and shadowy; gloomy.
examples: The tenebrous forest seemed to swallow the path.
His tenebrous moods lasted all winter.
etymology: From Latin tenebrosus, from tenebrae, 'darkness'.

definition: A central principle or belief.
examples: Honesty is a core tenet of the company's culture.
A basic tenet of good cooking is tasting as you go.
etymology: From Latin tenet, 'he holds', from tenere 'to hold'.

definition: The general meaning or character of something.
examples: The tenor of the meeting was surprisingly friendly.
I disagree with the tenor of his remarks.
etymology: From Old French tenour, from Latin tenor 'course', from tenere 'to hold'.

definition: Having tentacles, or spreading and grasping in a far-reaching way.
examples: The conglomerate's tentacular reach extends into every industry.
Tentacular vines covered the ruins.
etymology: From tentacle, from Latin tentare 'to feel, try'.

definition: Not certain or fixed; hesitant.
examples: We have tentative plans to visit in June.
The toddler took a few tentative steps.
etymology: From Medieval Latin tentativus, from tentare 'to try'.

definition: Very weak, thin, or slight, and easily broken or doubted.
examples: The two theories share only a tenuous connection, based on a single old study.
Their friendship hung by a tenuous thread after the argument over money.
etymology: From Latin tenuis, 'thin, slender'.

definition: The period of holding a position, or permanent job status for a professor.
examples: During her tenure as mayor, the city built three parks.
He finally earned tenure after seven years.
etymology: From Old French, from tenir 'to hold'.

definition: Only slightly warm, or lacking enthusiasm.
examples: The coffee had gone tepid by the time I drank it.
The sequel got a tepid response from critics.
etymology: From Latin tepidus, from tepere 'to be warm'.

definition: The scientific study of congenital abnormalities, or a body of lore about monsters.
examples: The drug was tested for risks in teratology studies.
Medieval bestiaries are a rich source of teratology.
etymology: From Greek teras, teratos 'monster, marvel' plus -logy.

definition: Evasive, shifting statements, or the act of changing sides.
examples: After months of tergiversation, the company finally admitted the flaw.
Voters grew tired of the candidate's tergiversation on the issue.
etymology: From Latin tergiversari, 'to turn one's back', from tergum 'back' + vertere 'to turn'.

definition: To bring to an end.
examples: Either party may terminate the contract with notice.
This train will terminate at the next station.
etymology: From Latin terminare 'to limit, end', from terminus 'boundary'.

definition: Relating to dancing.
examples: The wedding guests displayed varying terpsichorean talents.
Her terpsichorean flair made the musical a hit.
etymology: From Terpsichore, the Muse of dance in Greek mythology.

definition: Relating to the earth or to land rather than water or air.
examples: Frogs live both aquatic and terrestrial lives.
Terrestrial radio is losing listeners to podcasts.
etymology: From Latin terrestris, from terra 'earth'.

definition: Using very few words, often in a way that seems curt.
examples: Her reply was a terse "Fine."
The CEO issued a terse statement and took no questions.
etymology: From Latin tersus 'wiped, polished', from tergere 'to wipe'.

definition: To fit shapes together in a repeated pattern with no gaps or overlaps.
examples: Hexagons tessellate perfectly, which is why bees use them.
The artist made birds tessellate across the page.
etymology: From Latin tessella 'small square stone', a diminutive of tessera.

definition: The range within which most notes of a vocal part lie.
examples: The role has a punishingly high tessitura.
Choose songs that suit your natural tessitura.
etymology: From Italian tessitura 'texture'.

definition: Something that serves as clear proof of a fact or quality.
examples: The packed stadium was a testament to the band's popularity.
Her recovery is a testament to her determination.
etymology: From Latin testamentum 'a will', from testari 'to bear witness'.

definition: To give evidence as a witness, or to serve as proof.
examples: She agreed to testify at the trial.
I can testify that the soup is excellent.
etymology: From Latin testificari, from testis 'witness'.

definition: A Roman military formation in which soldiers locked shields overhead and around them.
examples: The legion advanced in a testudo under a hail of arrows.
Riot police formed a modern testudo with their shields.
etymology: From Latin testudo 'tortoise'.

definition: Easily irritated; impatient.
examples: He gets testy when he skips lunch.
The press conference turned testy.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman testif 'headstrong', from Old French teste 'head'.

definition: Bad-tempered and irritable.
examples: The toddler gets tetchy before naptime.
Negotiations turned tetchy late in the day.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the late sixteenth century.

definition: To tie an animal or object with a rope or chain, or to bind closely.
examples: Tether the goat to the post.
Many workers feel they tether their lives to their phones.
etymology: From Old Norse tjóthr.

definition: Relating to the sea, especially smaller or inland seas.
examples: The novel is steeped in thalassic imagery.
Greek culture had a deeply thalassic character.
etymology: From Greek thalassa 'sea'.

definition: A state whose power rests mainly on command of the sea.
examples: Venice was a thalassocracy built on trade.
Ancient Athens grew into a thalassocracy.
etymology: From Greek thalassa 'sea' plus -kratia 'rule'.

definition: A meditation on or view of death.
examples: His final album is a gentle thanatopsis.
The essay begins as a travelogue and ends as a thanatopsis.
etymology: From Greek thanatos 'death' plus opsis 'view'; popularized by William Cullen Bryant's poem 'Thanatopsis'.

definition: Difficult or unpleasant and unlikely to be appreciated.
examples: Refereeing kids' soccer is a thankless job.
She took on the thankless task of organizing the reunion.
etymology: Formed from thank plus -less.

definition: A worker of wonders or miracles; a magician.
examples: The chef is a thaumaturge with leftovers.
Crowds hailed the healer as a thaumaturge.
etymology: From Greek thaumatourgos, from thauma 'marvel' plus -ergos 'working'.

definition: From that place or source, or from that time.
examples: We drove to Denver and thence to the mountains.
He moved to London and thence to Edinburgh.
etymology: From Middle English thennes.

definition: An argument defending the goodness of God despite the existence of evil.
examples: The novel's theodicy failed to convince its grieving hero.
Every theodicy must reckon with natural disasters.
etymology: From French théodicée, coined by Leibniz from Greek theos 'god' plus dikē 'justice'.

definition: A visible appearance of a god to a human.
examples: The burning bush is a classic theophany.
The sunrise over the canyon felt like a theophany.
etymology: From Greek theophaneia, from theos 'god' plus phainein 'to show'.

definition: Having a healing or calming effect.
examples: Gardening is therapeutic for me after a long week.
The spa offers a therapeutic massage.
etymology: From Greek therapeutikos, from therapeuein 'to attend to, treat'.

definition: As a result of that action.
examples: She paid early, thereby avoiding the late fee.
The law cut red tape, thereby speeding up construction.
etymology: From Old English, formed from there plus by.

definition: In that place, document, or respect.
examples: The plan is cheap, and therein lies its appeal.
Read the contract and the terms contained therein.
etymology: From Old English thǣrinne.

definition: Immediately after that, and often as a result of it.
examples: The vote passed; thereupon the crowd erupted.
The witness confessed and was thereupon arrested.
etymology: Formed from there plus upon.

definition: With that, or immediately after that.
examples: She signed the letter and therewith ended the partnership.
He bowed, and therewith left the room.
etymology: From Old English thǣrwith.

definition: An ancient compound medicine believed to cure poison, or any supposed cure-all.
examples: Medieval apothecaries sold theriac in decorated jars.
He treats coffee as a theriac for every ailment.
etymology: From Latin theriaca, from Greek thēriakē, from thērion 'wild animal'.

definition: Having the form of an animal, especially of a deity.
examples: Egyptian art is full of theriomorphic gods.
The museum displayed a theriomorphic vessel shaped like a bull.
etymology: From Greek thērion 'wild beast' plus morphē 'form'.

definition: Rituals meant to invoke divine powers or bring about their intervention.
examples: Late Platonists practiced theurgy alongside philosophy.
The cult mixed astrology with theurgy.
etymology: From Greek theourgia, from theos 'god' plus -ergos 'working'.

definition: To or toward that place.
examples: Shoppers scurried hither and thither.
The road ran thither through the woods.
etymology: From Old English thider.

definition: To endure or put up with something.
examples: There was nothing to do but thole the long winter.
I can't thole his whining any longer.
etymology: From Old English tholian 'to suffer, endure'.

definition: The state of being under someone's or something's power.
examples: The audience was in thrall to the singer.
He lived in thrall to his phone.
etymology: From Old Norse thræll 'slave'.

definition: Bragging and boastful.
examples: His thrasonical speeches about his golf game bored everyone.
The coach's thrasonical predictions looked foolish after the loss.
etymology: From Thraso, a bragging soldier in the Roman playwright Terence's comedy Eunuchus.

definition: Worn thin with use, or tired and overused.
examples: He still wears a threadbare sweater from college.
That excuse is getting a bit threadbare.
etymology: Formed from thread plus bare, describing cloth worn so thin the threads show.

definition: A song, poem, or speech of mourning.
examples: The choir sang a threnody for the town's fallen firefighters.
His last album reads like a threnody for lost friendships.
etymology: From Greek thrēnōidia, from thrēnos 'lament' + ōidē 'song'.

definition: The point at which something begins or changes, or the entrance to a room.
examples: Orders above the fifty-dollar threshold ship for free.
The dog paused at the threshold, unsure whether to come inside.
etymology: From Old English therscold, of uncertain origin.

definition: Careful with money and resources; not wasteful.
examples: My thrifty grandfather reused every glass jar.
Thrift stores are a thrifty way to update your wardrobe.
etymology: From thrift, from Old Norse thrif 'prosperity'.

definition: Intense or violent pain and struggle, especially during a change.
examples: The company is in the throes of a major restructuring.
We were in the throes of moving when the baby arrived.
etymology: From Middle English throwe 'pang, spasm', of uncertain origin.

definition: A large, densely packed crowd of people.
examples: A throng of fans waited outside the hotel.
We pushed through the throng to reach the exit.
etymology: From Old English gethrang 'crowd, tumult'.

definition: A metal censer swung on chains to burn incense.
examples: The priest swung the thurible down the aisle.
Smoke curled from the silver thurible.
etymology: From Latin thuribulum, from thus, thuris 'incense'.

definition: To prevent someone from accomplishing something.
examples: A locked gate thwarted our shortcut through the park.
Security cameras helped thwart the attempted break-in.
etymology: From Old Norse thvert, 'across'.

definition: One of a series of levels or ranks placed one above another.
examples: The wedding cake had a tier for each decade of their marriage.
The premium tier includes offline downloads.
etymology: From French tire 'rank, order'.

definition: A petty quarrel.
examples: They had a tiff over the thermostat.
It was just a tiff, and they made up by dinner.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the eighteenth century.

definition: A light midday meal, especially in India.
examples: Every morning she packed his tiffin in a steel carrier.
Mumbai's delivery runners carry thousands of tiffin boxes a day.
etymology: From obsolete English tiffing 'sipping', from tiff 'to drink'.

definition: Closely united by strong bonds of friendship or loyalty.
examples: It's a tight-knit neighborhood where everyone helps out.
The crew became a tight-knit group during the long shoot.
etymology: Formed from tight plus knit.

definition: The condition of tilled soil, or the cultivation of land.
examples: Compost improved the tilth of the garden beds.
The soil had a fine, crumbly tilth.
etymology: From Old English tilth, from tilian 'to till'.

definition: The distinctive quality or color of a sound or voice.
examples: Her voice has a warm, husky timbre.
The cello's timbre fills the whole hall.
etymology: From French timbre 'bell', ultimately from Greek tumpanon 'drum'.

definition: Happening at a suitable or useful moment.
examples: Thanks for the timely reminder about the meeting.
The documentary is timely given this week's news.
etymology: Formed from time plus -ly.

definition: Damaged or made stale by long use or age.
examples: The steps were timeworn and smooth.
He trotted out a timeworn joke about lawyers.
etymology: Formed from time plus worn.

definition: Lacking courage or confidence; easily frightened.
examples: The timid puppy hid under the couch.
His timid proposal didn't go far enough.
etymology: From Latin timidus, from timere 'to fear'.

definition: Government by those who own property, or rule driven by love of honor.
examples: Plato ranked timocracy just below aristocracy.
Voting by landowners only turned the town into a timocracy.
etymology: From Greek timokratia, from timē 'honor, worth' plus -kratia 'rule'.

definition: Showing nervousness or a lack of confidence.
examples: A timorous knock sounded at the door.
Investors were too timorous to back the idea.
etymology: From Medieval Latin timorosus, from Latin timor 'fear'.

definition: A slight trace of something, or a medicine dissolved in alcohol.
examples: There was a tincture of sarcasm in his praise.
She takes a herbal tincture for sleep.
etymology: From Latin tinctura 'dyeing', from tingere 'to dye'.

definition: Dry material that catches fire easily, or anything that sparks trouble.
examples: Gather dry grass for tinder.
Years of drought turned the forest into tinder.
etymology: From Old English tynder.

definition: To try to repair or improve something casually, by trial and error.
examples: He likes to tinker with old radios on weekends.
Don't tinker with the recipe until you've tried it once.
etymology: From tinker 'a traveling mender of pots', of uncertain origin.

definition: Having a thin, metallic sound, or cheap and flimsy.
examples: Music blared from a tinny speaker.
The car's tinny doors rattled on the highway.
etymology: Formed from tin plus -y.

definition: The ringing or jingling of bells.
examples: The tintinnabulation of sleigh bells drifted across the snowy field.
Poe's poem is filled with the tintinnabulation of silver bells.
etymology: From Latin tintinnabulum 'bell', from tintinnare 'to ring'; popularized by Poe's 'The Bells'.

definition: A long, angry speech of criticism or accusation.
examples: The customer launched into a tirade about the late delivery.
Her online tirade against the referee went viral.
etymology: From French tirade, 'long speech', from Italian tirata, 'volley'.

definition: Working hard with great energy and without stopping.
examples: She is a tireless advocate for clean water.
The rescue crews were tireless through the night.
etymology: Formed from tire plus -less.

definition: Causing boredom or annoyance.
examples: The commute became tiresome after a few months.
His constant bragging is tiresome.
etymology: Formed from tire plus -some.

definition: An herbal tea.
examples: She sipped a chamomile tisane before bed.
The cafe offers a ginger tisane for sore throats.
etymology: From French, from Latin ptisana 'barley water', from Greek ptisanē.

definition: To stimulate or excite someone, often in a mildly provocative way.
examples: The headline was designed to titillate readers.
Gossip columns titillate more than they inform.
etymology: From Latin titillare 'to tickle'.

definition: To make small improvements to one's appearance or to a thing.
examples: She paused to titivate her hair before the interview.
Realtors titivate a house before showing it.
etymology: Perhaps formed from tidy, on the pattern of cultivate.

definition: A tiny amount, or a small written mark such as the dot over an i.
examples: Not one tittle of the contract was changed.
She cares about every jot and tittle of the style guide.
etymology: From Medieval Latin titulus 'title, small stroke'.

definition: Holding a title without real power, or named in a work's title.
examples: The monarch is a titular head of state.
She plays the titular role in a modern remake of Hamlet.
etymology: From Latin titulus 'title'.

definition: The insertion of a word into the middle of another word or phrase.
examples: "Abso-freaking-lutely" is a playful example of tmesis.
The poet used tmesis to split the word for emphasis.
etymology: From Greek tmēsis 'cutting'.

definition: A person who flatters powerful people to win favor.
examples: The boss surrounded himself with every toady in the office.
Nobody likes a toady.
