etymology: Short for toadeater, a charlatan's assistant who pretended to eat toads.

definition: An alarm bell or warning signal.
examples: The report sounded a tocsin about rising seas.
The village tocsin rang when the river breached the levee.
etymology: From French, from Provençal tocasenh, from tocar 'to strike' plus senh 'bell'.

definition: Utter chaos and confusion.
examples: The airport was a tohubohu after the storm grounded every flight.
Out of the tohubohu of the first rehearsal came a decent show.
etymology: From Hebrew tōhū wā-bōhū 'formless and void', from the opening of Genesis.

definition: To work extremely hard for a long time.
examples: Farmhands toil in the fields from dawn to dusk.
Writers toil for years on a first novel.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman toiler 'to strive, dispute'.

definition: A thing that serves as a symbol of a feeling or fact.
examples: Please accept this gift as a token of our thanks.
The arcade gave each kid one token to start.
etymology: From Old English tācn 'sign, symbol'.

definition: To a fairly good or acceptable degree.
examples: He speaks French tolerably well.
The hotel was tolerably clean.
etymology: From tolerable, from Latin tolerare 'to endure'.

definition: A charge for using a road or bridge, or the damage caused by something.
examples: Years of night shifts took a toll on his health.
We paid the toll at the bridge.
etymology: From Old English toll, from Medieval Latin toloneum, from Greek telōnion 'tollhouse'.

definition: A large, heavy, usually scholarly book.
examples: She lugged a tome on Roman law to the library.
His biography is a 900-page tome.
etymology: From French, via Latin from Greek tomos 'slice, volume', from temnein 'to cut'.

definition: Meant ironically or humorously rather than seriously.
examples: The review was tongue-in-cheek, but some readers took it literally.
He gave a tongue-in-cheek speech about the joys of filing taxes.
etymology: From the gesture of pressing the tongue into the cheek to show that one is not serious.

definition: Relating to barbers or hairdressing.
examples: The candidate's tonsorial choices dominated the coverage.
He admired his tonsorial artistry in the mirror.
etymology: From Latin tonsorius, from tonsor 'barber'.

definition: The shaved crown of a monk's or priest's head.
examples: The novice received the tonsure on entering the order.
His bald spot looked like a monk's tonsure.
etymology: From Latin tonsura, from tondere 'to shear'.

definition: A scheme in which investors' shares grow as members die, until the last survivor takes all.
examples: The mystery revolves around a tontine with two survivors left.
A tontine gives investors a grim incentive to outlive each other.
etymology: Named after Lorenzo de Tonti, a Neapolitan banker who proposed such a scheme in seventeenth-century France.

definition: Lacking real power or effectiveness.
examples: Without fines, the new rule is toothless.
Critics called the watchdog agency toothless.
etymology: Formed from tooth plus -less.

definition: Pleasant to eat, or temptingly attractive.
examples: The bakery sells a toothsome rye bread.
The pasta was cooked to a toothsome chewiness.
etymology: Formed from tooth plus -some.

definition: To drink alcohol to excess, especially habitually.
examples: The old poet would tope at the tavern every night.
They sat around the fire to tope and tell stories.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, first recorded in the seventeenth century.

definition: The art of clipping shrubs and trees into ornamental shapes.
examples: The estate is famous for its elephant topiary.
He took up topiary after retiring.
etymology: From Latin topiarius 'ornamental gardener', from topia 'ornamental gardening'.

definition: Relating to current events, or applied directly to the skin.
examples: The comedian's jokes were sharp and topical.
Use a topical cream on the rash twice a day.
etymology: From Greek topikos, from topos 'place'.

definition: Haughty and condescending.
examples: The toplofty sommelier sneered at our wine choice.
Her toplofty tone alienated the volunteers.
etymology: Formed from top plus lofty.

definition: A place name, or a word derived from one.
examples: "Denim" is a toponym, from the French town of Nîmes.
Every toponym on the map tells a story.
etymology: From Greek topos 'place' plus onyma 'name'.

definition: To fall over, or to overthrow someone from power.
examples: One more book will topple the whole stack.
Protesters hoped to topple the government.
etymology: Formed from top plus the frequentative suffix -le.

definition: A state of physical or mental inactivity and sluggishness.
examples: The summer heat sank the town into a lazy torpor.
Some animals fall into torpor to survive the winter on little food.
etymology: From Latin torpor, from torpere 'to be numb'.

definition: A strong, fast stream of water or an overwhelming outpouring.
examples: The creek became a torrent after the storm.
She faced a torrent of criticism online.
etymology: From Latin torrent- 'boiling, roaring', from torrere 'to parch, scorch'.

definition: Very hot and dry, or full of intense passion.
examples: The tourists wilted in the torrid afternoon sun.
The tabloids reported a torrid romance between the stars.
etymology: From Latin torridus, from torrere 'to parch'.

definition: Full of twists and turns, or excessively complicated.
examples: A tortuous road winds up the mountain.
The contract is written in tortuous legal language.
etymology: From Latin tortuosus, from tortus 'twisted', from torquere 'to twist'.

definition: An emblem or symbol held in high regard by a group.
examples: The old stadium became a totem of civic pride.
The car is a totem of suburban success.
etymology: From Ojibwa nindoodem 'my clan'.

definition: To move or stand unsteadily, as if about to fall.
examples: The toddler began to totter across the rug.
Several banks began to totter during the crisis.
etymology: From Middle Dutch touteren 'to swing'.

definition: A standard by which something is judged.
examples: Her first album remains a touchstone for indie bands.
Fairness is the touchstone of good policy.
etymology: Originally a dark stone used to test gold and silver by the streak they left on it.

definition: Easily upset, or requiring careful handling.
examples: He's touchy about his age.
Money is a touchy subject in their family.
etymology: Probably an alteration of tetchy, influenced by touch.

definition: To make hair untidy or rumpled.
examples: He likes to tousle his son's hair.
The wind will tousle your hair on the ferry.
etymology: A frequentative of touse 'to handle roughly'.

definition: To promote or praise something enthusiastically.
examples: Ads tout the new phone as the fastest ever made.
The town touts its beaches as the best on the coast.
etymology: From Middle English tuten, 'to peer, look out', of uncertain origin.

definition: Easy to control, manage, or deal with.
examples: The problem became tractable once we split it up.
The horse was calm and tractable.
etymology: From Latin tractabilis, from tractare 'to handle'.

definition: A balance between two desirable but competing things.
examples: Lower rent was a fair trade-off for the longer commute.
Every design involves a trade-off between cost and speed.
etymology: Formed from trade plus off.

definition: To speak badly of or tell lies about someone, damaging their reputation.
examples: The tabloid traduced the actor with fabricated stories.
It's unfair to traduce a colleague who isn't here to respond.
etymology: From Latin traducere, 'to lead across, to disgrace'.

definition: To walk wearily or reluctantly, often from place to place.
examples: We had to traipse across town to find the right charger.
I don't want to traipse through another mall.
etymology: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the late sixteenth century.

definition: A distinguishing quality or characteristic.
examples: Patience is a trait every teacher needs.
Red hair is a trait that runs in her family.
etymology: From French trait 'line, stroke', from Latin tractus 'a drawing'.

definition: The path followed by a moving object, or the course of development.
examples: The ball's trajectory carried it over the fence.
Her career has followed a steady upward trajectory.
etymology: From Medieval Latin trajectorius, from Latin traicere 'to throw across'.

definition: To restrict or hinder someone's freedom of action.
examples: Don't let old rules trammel new ideas.
Red tape continues to trammel small farms.
etymology: From the noun trammel 'a fishing net', from Late Latin tremaculum, from tri- 'three' plus macula 'mesh'.

definition: Free from noise, disturbance, or worry; calm and peaceful.
examples: We spent a tranquil afternoon reading by the quiet harbor.
After the storm passed, the village returned to its tranquil routine.
etymology: From Latin tranquillus, 'quiet, calm'.

definition: To go beyond the usual limits of something.
examples: Great music can transcend language.
The film manages to transcend its genre.
etymology: From Latin transcendere, from trans- 'across' plus scandere 'to climb'.

definition: To make someone motionless with wonder, horror, or fascination.
examples: The fireworks seemed to transfix the children.
Her performance will transfix any audience.
etymology: From Latin transfigere 'to pierce through'.

definition: To go beyond a moral, legal, or social limit.
examples: Artists often transgress conventions on purpose.
Members who transgress the code are expelled.
etymology: From Latin transgredi 'to step across'.

definition: The seasonal movement of livestock between summer and winter pastures.
examples: Alpine villages still celebrate transhumance each autumn.
Climate change is disrupting traditional transhumance routes.
etymology: From French transhumer, from Latin trans- 'across' plus humus 'ground'.

definition: Lasting only a short time; passing.
examples: The pain was transient and gone by morning.
Beach towns have a large transient population each summer.
etymology: From Latin transire 'to go across'.

definition: Not permanent; lasting only briefly.
examples: Fame on social media is often transitory.
Economists hope the price spike is transitory.
etymology: From Late Latin transitorius, from Latin transire 'to go across'.

definition: Allowing light to pass through but not completely clear.
examples: Light filtered through the translucent curtains.
The jellyfish was nearly translucent.
etymology: From Latin translucere 'to shine through'.

definition: To transform in a surprising or magical way.
examples: The kids transmogrify the living room into a pirate ship every Saturday.
Fresh snow can transmogrify an ugly parking lot into a wonderland.
etymology: A humorous 17th-century coinage of unknown origin.

definition: To change something into a different form or nature.
examples: Alchemists tried to transmute lead into gold.
Great writers transmute pain into art.
etymology: From Latin transmutare, from trans- 'across' plus mutare 'to change'.

definition: To happen, or to come to be known.
examples: Nobody knows what will transpire at the summit.
Let's wait and see what may transpire.
etymology: From French transpirer, from Latin trans- 'through' plus spirare 'to breathe'.

definition: On the far side of a bridge, or cheaply melodramatic in the style of old popular theater.
examples: The film's transpontine plot twists drew laughs from critics.
They moved to a transpontine neighborhood across the river.
etymology: From Latin trans- 'across' plus pons 'bridge'; the theater sense refers to old London playhouses south of the Thames.

definition: To change one substance into another entirely.
examples: Good cooks can transubstantiate leftovers into a feast.
The ritual is believed to transubstantiate bread into something holy.
etymology: From Medieval Latin transsubstantiare, from trans- 'across' plus substantia 'substance'.

definition: Painful or laborious effort.
examples: The book recounts the travail of crossing the desert.
After months of travail, the bridge was finished.
etymology: From Old French travail, from travailler 'to toil'.

definition: To travel across or through an area.
examples: It takes a week to traverse the glacier.
The trail will traverse three canyons.
etymology: From Old French traverser, from Late Latin traversare.

definition: A false, absurd, or distorted version of something.
examples: The rushed trial was a travesty of justice.
Fans called the film adaptation a travesty of the beloved novel.
etymology: From French travesti, 'disguised', from Italian travestire.

definition: Hazardous and unpredictable, or guilty of betrayal.
examples: Ice made the mountain road treacherous.
In the play, a treacherous advisor plots against the king.
etymology: From Old French trecheros, from trecheor 'cheat', from trichier 'to cheat'.

definition: A formal, detailed written work on a subject.
examples: He wrote a treatise on medieval farming.
The treatise runs to three volumes.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman tretis, from Old French traitier 'to treat'.

definition: A formal agreement between countries.
examples: The treaty ended decades of border disputes.
Both nations signed the climate treaty.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman treté, from Latin tractatus 'handling, discussion'.

definition: A medieval siege engine that hurled stones using a heavy counterweight.
examples: The physics class built a trebuchet to launch pumpkins.
A trebuchet could break castle walls from afar.
etymology: From Old French trebuchet, from trebucher 'to overturn'.

definition: A slight shaking movement, such as a small earthquake or a quiver.
examples: We felt a tremor during dinner but nothing fell.
There was a tremor of excitement in her voice.
etymology: From Latin tremor, from tremere 'to tremble'.

definition: Trembling slightly, from fear, nervousness, or weakness.
examples: Her tremulous voice betrayed how nervous she was before the speech.
He gave a tremulous smile as the results were read aloud.
etymology: From Latin tremulus, from tremere 'to tremble'.

definition: Vigorous, incisive, and clear in expression.
examples: Her trenchant analysis cut through the confusion.
The columnist is known for trenchant criticism.
etymology: From Old French trenchant, 'cutting', from trenchier, 'to cut'.

definition: To bore a hole in the skull with a surgical saw.
examples: Neolithic healers would trepan skulls, and some patients survived.
Surgeons had to trepan to relieve the pressure.
etymology: From Medieval Latin trepanum, from Greek trupanon 'borer'.

definition: A feeling of fear or anxiety about something that may happen.
examples: She opened the exam results with trepidation, afraid of what she would see.
He approached the stage with trepidation, his hands trembling around the microphone.
etymology: From Latin trepidatio, 'agitation, alarm', from trepidare, 'to hurry, tremble'.

definition: To enter someone's land or property without permission.
examples: Hikers who trespass on the ranch will be fined.
The sign warned us not to trespass.
etymology: From Old French trespasser 'to pass over'.

definition: A cause of great trouble or suffering.
examples: The memoir describes every tribulation of her childhood.
Each tribulation made them closer.
etymology: From Late Latin tribulatio, from tribulare 'to press', from tribulum 'threshing sledge'.

definition: An act or gift that shows respect, gratitude, or admiration.
examples: The concert was a tribute to the late songwriter.
His speech paid tribute to the nurses.
etymology: From Latin tributum, from tribuere 'to assign, grant'.

definition: Unimportant or trivial.
examples: They argued over a trifling sum of money.
It's a trifling matter, so let it go.
etymology: From trifle, from Old French trufle 'mockery, deceit'.

definition: A difficult choice among three options, often all unfavorable.
examples: Economists describe a trilemma of fixed rates, free capital, and independent policy.
Fast, cheap, or good is the classic project trilemma.
etymology: Formed from tri- 'three' on the model of dilemma.

definition: A work of art in three panels, or a set of three related works.
examples: A gilded triptych hung above the altar.
The novel forms a triptych with her two earlier books.
etymology: From Greek triptukhos 'three-layered', from tri- plus ptux 'fold'.

definition: Overused and lacking originality.
examples: The ending felt trite and predictable.
Avoid trite phrases in your cover letter.
etymology: From Latin tritus 'worn', past participle of terere 'to rub'.

definition: Consisting of three in one.
examples: Theologians debated the triune nature of God.
The festival offers a triune mix of music, food, and film.
etymology: From Latin tri- 'three' plus unus 'one'.

definition: Of little importance or value; not worth serious attention.
examples: Do not let a trivial disagreement about dishes spoil the whole evening.
The error was trivial, and nobody noticed it after the correction.
etymology: From Latin trivialis, 'of the crossroads, commonplace', from trivium, 'place where three roads meet'.

definition: Written in feet of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable.
examples: "Tyger Tyger, burning bright" has a trochaic rhythm.
The chant falls into a steady trochaic beat.
etymology: From Greek trokhaios 'running', from trekhein 'to run'.

definition: A cave dweller, or a person stubbornly out of touch with modern ways.
examples: He calls himself a troglodyte because he has no smartphone.
Ancient troglodyte homes are carved into the cliff.
etymology: From Greek trōglodytēs, from trōglē 'hole' plus dyein 'to enter'.

definition: A common theme, device, or cliché in stories, or a figure of speech.
examples: The chosen-one trope shows up in countless fantasy novels.
The ad leans on a tired trope about clumsy dads.
etymology: From Greek tropos 'turn, way'.

definition: A medieval lyric poet-musician, or any wandering singer of love songs.
examples: A modern troubadour played on the subway platform.
The troubadour sang of courtly love.
etymology: From French, from Occitan trobador, from trobar 'to compose, find'.

definition: To defeat someone decisively.
examples: We expect to trounce them in the rematch.
Polls suggest the challenger will trounce the incumbent.
etymology: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the sixteenth century.

definition: An agreement between enemies or opponents to stop fighting for a time.
examples: The siblings called a truce over the remote.
A holiday truce paused the fighting.
etymology: From Middle English trewes, plural of trewe 'pledge', from Old English trēow 'faith'.

definition: To submit or behave obsequiously toward someone.
examples: He refused to truckle to the demands of wealthy donors.
Some critics truckle to whatever is popular.
etymology: From truckle bed, a low bed that slid under a higher one.

definition: Eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant and hostile.
examples: The truculent customer shouted at the staff until security arrived.
He gave a truculent shrug and refused to answer any more questions.
etymology: From Latin truculentus, 'fierce', from trux, 'wild, harsh'.

definition: To walk slowly and heavily, as if tired.
examples: We had to trudge through the snow to the bus stop.
Students trudge back to class after summer break.
etymology: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the sixteenth century.

definition: A statement so obviously true that it hardly needs saying.
examples: It's a truism that you can't please everyone.
The speech offered one truism after another and few details.
etymology: Formed from true plus -ism.

definition: Showy but worthless things, or nonsense.
examples: The attic was full of Victorian trumpery.
Ignore the marketing trumpery and read the specs.
etymology: From Old French tromperie 'deceit', from tromper 'to deceive'.

definition: To shorten by cutting off a part.
examples: The app will truncate long titles.
They had to truncate the tour because of illness.
etymology: From Latin truncare 'to lop', from truncus 'trunk'.

definition: To move slowly and heavily, typically on wheels.
examples: Delivery carts trundle down the sidewalk each morning.
I watched the old bus trundle up the hill.
etymology: From obsolete trendle 'a wheel', from Old English.

definition: A private romantic meeting between lovers.
examples: They planned a secret tryst in Paris.
The tryst was exposed by a nosy neighbor.
etymology: From Old French triste 'an appointed waiting place in hunting'.

definition: The habit of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread.
examples: My nightstand is a monument to tsundoku.
Book sales feed her tsundoku.
etymology: From Japanese, combining elements meaning 'to pile up' and 'reading'.

definition: Falling to pieces; dilapidated.
examples: They bought a tumbledown cottage by the sea.
A tumbledown shed leaned against the fence.
etymology: Formed from tumble plus down.

definition: An open cart, especially one that carried prisoners to the guillotine.
examples: The tumbrel rattled toward the scaffold.
Critics joked that the executives should be loaded into a tumbrel.
etymology: From Old French tomberel, from tomber 'to fall'.

definition: Swollen or swelling, or pompously inflated in style.
examples: The bee sting left her finger tumescent and red.
The memoir's tumescent prose wore me out.
etymology: From Latin tumescere 'to begin to swell'.

definition: Swollen, or bombastic and overblown in language.
examples: The senator delivered a tumid tribute full of clichés.
The river ran tumid after the snowmelt.
etymology: From Latin tumidus, from tumere 'to swell'.

definition: Loud, excited, and confused, or full of upheaval.
examples: The team returned to a tumultuous welcome.
It was a tumultuous year for the company.
etymology: From Latin tumultuosus, from tumultus 'commotion'.

definition: An ancient burial mound.
examples: Archaeologists excavated a Bronze Age tumulus.
Sheep grazed on the grassy tumulus.
etymology: From Latin tumulus 'mound', from tumere 'to swell'.

definition: Cloudy or muddy from stirred-up sediment, or confused.
examples: The flood left the lake turbid for weeks.
His turbid prose made the argument hard to follow.
etymology: From Latin turbidus, from turba 'disturbance'.

definition: Shaped like a spinning top or spiral, as some shells are.
examples: She collected turbinate shells along the shore.
The turbinate tower twisted toward the sky.
etymology: From Latin turbinatus, from turbo 'spinning top, whirl'.

definition: Marked by conflict, disorder, or violently irregular movement.
examples: The flight was turbulent over the mountains.
The band survived a turbulent decade of lineup changes.
etymology: From Latin turbulentus, from turba 'crowd, disturbance'.

definition: Pompous and overblown in style, or swollen.
examples: The report is written in turgid bureaucratic prose.
After the rain, the river ran turgid and brown.
etymology: From Latin turgidus, from turgere 'to swell'.

definition: A state of great confusion, disturbance, or uncertainty.
examples: The markets were in turmoil after the announcement.
Her mind was in turmoil before the decision.
etymology: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the early sixteenth century.

definition: A person who deserts one side for the opposing one.
examples: Fans called him a turncoat when he joined their rivals.
The turncoat sold secrets to the enemy.
etymology: Formed from turn plus coat, as if switching sides by turning one's coat.

definition: A connoisseur or devoted lover of cheese.
examples: A true turophile, she plans vacations around dairies.
The shop caters to every turophile in town.
etymology: From Greek tyros 'cheese' plus -phile 'lover'.

definition: Deep moral corruption or depravity; vile, shameful conduct.
examples: The judge condemned the moral turpitude of the fraud scheme.
A crime of turpitude can block a person from getting certain licenses.
etymology: From Latin turpitudo, 'ugliness, baseness', from turpis 'foul'.

definition: To struggle or scuffle roughly in a close fight.
examples: The puppies tussle over the same toy.
Two players began to tussle for the ball.
etymology: Originally Scots and northern English, perhaps from touse 'to handle roughly'.

definition: Protection, guidance, or instruction from a mentor.
examples: Under her tutelage, the choir won state.
He learned carpentry under the tutelage of his uncle.
etymology: From Latin tutela 'keeping', from tueri 'to watch over'.

definition: Serving as a protector or guardian.
examples: The Romans honored the tutelary gods of each household.
Her aunt played a tutelary role in her career.
etymology: From Latin tutelarius, from tutela 'keeping, protection'.

definition: A wealthy, powerful person in business or industry.
examples: A tech tycoon bought the struggling newspaper.
He went from paperboy to shipping tycoon.
etymology: From Japanese taikun 'great lord', a title used for the shogun.

definition: Relating to the eardrum, or resonant like a drum.
examples: The nurse used a tympanic thermometer in his ear.
A tympanic boom rolled across the valley.
etymology: From Latin tympanum 'drum', from Greek tumpanon.

definition: To be a typical example or characteristic of something.
examples: Long dinners typify Spanish family life.
These glass towers typify the new skyline.
etymology: Formed from type plus -ify; type comes from Greek typos 'impression'.

definition: Cruel and oppressive rule or control.
examples: The revolution was a revolt against tyranny.
He escaped the tyranny of his inbox for a week.
etymology: From Old French tyrannie, from Greek tyrannos 'absolute ruler'.

definition: A beginner or novice.
examples: Even a tyro can follow this recipe.
The tyro chess player lost in eight moves.
etymology: From Latin tiro 'recruit'.

definition: Present or found everywhere, or seeming to be.
examples: Smartphones have become ubiquitous, appearing in nearly every pocket and purse.
Coffee shops are ubiquitous in the city, with one on almost every corner.
etymology: From Latin ubique, 'everywhere', from ubi, 'where'.

definition: An imagined alternate history in which past events turned out differently.
examples: The novel is a uchronia where Rome never fell.
Fans love the uchronia of a world without the internet.
etymology: Coined in French as uchronie by Charles Renouvier in 1876, from Greek ou 'not' + khronos 'time'.

definition: An arbitrary order or decree issued by an authority.
examples: The CEO's latest ukase banned working from home.
The tsar's ukase took effect immediately.
etymology: From Russian ukaz 'edict'.

definition: Hidden or kept secret, especially a motive behind an action.
examples: I suspect he has an ulterior motive for offering to help.
Her kindness had no ulterior purpose.
etymology: From Latin ulterior 'further, more distant'.

definition: In the end, after everything has been considered.
examples: Ultimately, the decision is yours.
The detour ultimately saved us an hour.
etymology: From ultimate, from Late Latin ultimatus, from Latin ultimus 'last'.

definition: A final demand that comes with a threat if it is not met.
examples: She gave her roommate an ultimatum: clean up or move out.
The union issued an ultimatum to management on Monday.
etymology: From Modern Latin ultimatum, neuter of ultimatus 'final', from Latin ultimus 'last'.

definition: A system of inheritance in which the youngest child inherits.
examples: Under ultimogeniture, the youngest son took over the farm.
Ultimogeniture survived in a few English villages.
etymology: From Latin ultimus 'last' + genitura 'birth'.

definition: Giving opinions beyond one's own knowledge or expertise.
examples: The ultracrepidarian celebrity offered medical advice on social media.
Try not to be ultracrepidarian when the dinner conversation turns to astrophysics.
etymology: From Latin ultra crepidam, 'beyond the sandal', from the saying that a shoemaker should not judge above the sandal.

definition: Strongly supporting the supreme authority of the pope.
examples: The ultramontane bishops opposed any compromise with the state.
His ultramontane views alarmed liberal Catholics.
etymology: From Medieval Latin ultramontanus 'beyond the mountains', meaning beyond the Alps, toward Rome.

definition: To howl or wail, often to express grief or joy.
examples: We heard the wolves ululate from the far side of the ridge.
The crowd ululated in celebration as the bride appeared.
etymology: From Latin ululare 'to howl', of imitative origin.

definition: The darkest central part of a shadow, especially during an eclipse.
examples: Only those inside the moon's umbra see a total eclipse.
The cat napped in the cool umbra of the porch.
etymology: From Latin umbra 'shadow'.

definition: Offense or resentment felt after a slight or insult.
examples: She took umbrage at the suggestion that she had copied the design.
He took umbrage when the waiter corrected his pronunciation.
etymology: From Latin umbraticus 'of shade', from umbra 'shadow'; the sense shifted from shade to suspicion to offense.

definition: Giving shade; also, quick to take offense.
examples: We picnicked beneath an umbrageous oak.
The umbrageous senator bristled at every question.
etymology: From French ombrageux, from Latin umbra 'shadow'.

definition: Not embarrassed or ashamed; open and unrestrained.
examples: He is an unabashed fan of cheesy eighties ballads.
She spoke with unabashed pride about her kids.
etymology: Formed from un- 'not' + abashed, from Old French esbair 'to astound'.

definition: Pure and complete, with nothing mixed in to spoil it.
examples: The win brought the fans unalloyed joy.
It was not an unalloyed success; costs ran high.
etymology: From un- + alloy, from Old French aloi 'combination'.

definition: Impossible to attack, question, or defeat.
examples: With three games left, their lead is unassailable.
She built an unassailable case for the new budget.
etymology: Formed from un- 'not' + assail, from Latin assilire 'to leap upon'.

definition: Not soothed, satisfied, or eased.
examples: His grief remained unassuaged years later.
She left the meeting with her doubts unassuaged.
etymology: From un- + assuage, from Old French assouagier, from Latin suavis 'sweet'.

definition: Modest and not seeking attention.
examples: The unassuming little cafe serves the best soup in town.
Despite her fame, she's warm and unassuming.
etymology: From un- + assuming, 'presumptuous'.

definition: Without warning or noticing; by surprise.
examples: The sudden downpour caught us unawares.
Grief can strike unawares years later.
etymology: From unaware with the adverbial ending -s, as in 'always'.

definition: Not fitting or proper for someone's position, or unflattering.
examples: The officer was disciplined for conduct unbecoming of his rank.
That shade of orange is unbecoming on almost everyone.
etymology: From un- + becoming in its sense of 'suitable, flattering'.

definition: Happening without someone's knowledge.
examples: Unbeknownst to her, the whole office had planned a party.
The leak had been running, unbeknownst to anyone, for months.
etymology: From unbeknown, from un- + obsolete beknown 'known'.

definition: Arriving without being asked or invited.
examples: Tears came unbidden as she read the letter.
An unbidden guest wandered into the wedding.
etymology: From un- + bidden, past participle of bid 'to invite'.

definition: To reveal one's private thoughts or secrets.
examples: Late at night, she would unbosom herself to her diary.
He needed a friend to unbosom his worries to.
etymology: Formed from un- + bosom, the chest as the seat of private feelings.

definition: Not defeated or broken in spirit.
examples: After the loss, the team left the field bloodied but unbowed.
She emerged from the trial unbowed.
etymology: From un- + bowed, from bow 'to bend', from Old English bugan.

definition: Uncontrolled and unrestrained.
examples: The kids ran onto the beach with unbridled joy.
Critics warned against unbridled development along the coast.
etymology: From un- + bridled, from Old English bridel, originally of a horse without a bridle.

definition: Strange in a way that is unsettling or hard to explain.
examples: She bears an uncanny resemblance to my grandmother.
He has an uncanny knack for guessing the ending of movies.
etymology: From un- 'not' + canny, a Scots word meaning 'knowing, careful'.

definition: In an abrupt or rude way, without courtesy.
examples: The rowdy fan was unceremoniously escorted out of the stadium.
My old couch was unceremoniously dumped on the curb.
etymology: From un- + ceremonious, from Latin caerimonia 'sacred rite'.

definition: Not yet mapped or explored; unfamiliar.
examples: With a newborn and a new job, we're in uncharted territory.
Sailors once feared the uncharted waters beyond the cape.
etymology: Formed from un- + charted, from chart, from Latin charta 'paper, map'.

definition: Written in the rounded capital script used in manuscripts from about the 4th to 8th centuries.
examples: The monks copied the gospels in elegant uncial letters.
She studied an uncial manuscript under glass.
etymology: From Latin unciales litterae 'letters an inch high', from uncia 'inch, twelfth'.

definition: Unable to understand what is happening.
examples: The puppy gave me an uncomprehending stare.
Uncomprehending tourists watched the cricket match.
etymology: From un- + comprehend, from Latin comprehendere 'to grasp'.

definition: Morally unacceptable, or excessively unreasonable.
examples: Charging that much for insulin is unconscionable.
We waited an unconscionable length of time for our food.
etymology: From un- + obsolete conscionable 'conscientious', from conscience.

definition: Lacking good manners or refinement.
examples: Talking with your mouth full is considered uncouth.
His uncouth jokes made the dinner guests wince.
etymology: From Old English uncuth 'unknown, strange', from un- + cuth 'known'.

definition: Anointing with oil as a rite; also, an excessively smooth or earnest manner.
examples: The salesman spoke with an oily unction that put me off.
The priest administered unction to the dying man.
etymology: From Latin unctio, from ungere 'to anoint'.

definition: Excessively smooth, flattering, and insincere in manner.
examples: The unctuous salesman called every customer 'my dear friend'.
His unctuous praise made the manager suspicious rather than flattered.
etymology: From Latin unctuosus, 'oily', from unguere 'to anoint'.

definition: Not discouraged or frightened by difficulty or danger.
examples: Undaunted by two failed attempts, she signed up for the bar exam again.
The crew remained undaunted as the storm grew.
etymology: Formed from un- + daunt, from Old French danter, from Latin domitare 'to tame'.

definition: A vaulted underground room, especially a crypt beneath a church.
examples: The tour descends into the cathedral's undercroft.
They stored wine in the cool undercroft.
etymology: From under + Middle English crofte 'crypt', ultimately from Latin crypta.

definition: A person or team expected to lose a contest.
examples: Everyone loves cheering for the underdog.
As the underdog, the tiny startup had nothing to lose.
etymology: From under + dog, originally the dog that loses a fight.

definition: To support or strengthen something from beneath.
examples: Strong data should undergird every claim in the report.
Steel beams undergird the old bridge.
etymology: From under + gird 'to encircle, brace', from Old English gyrdan.

definition: A person of low rank who takes orders from others, said dismissively.
examples: The boss sent an underling to deliver the bad news.
She refused to be treated as anyone's underling.
etymology: From Middle English, under + -ling, a suffix often used for something small or lesser.

definition: Basic and important but not obvious at first.
examples: The rash was a symptom of an underlying allergy.
We need to fix the underlying problem, not just the error message.
etymology: From under + lying, from the verb underlie, Old English underlicgan.

definition: To weaken something gradually, often secretly, by damaging its foundation.
examples: Constant rumors can undermine trust in even the most respected leader.
Skipping sleep will undermine all the effort you put into studying.
etymology: From under + mine, originally meaning to dig beneath a wall to make it collapse.

definition: To support or form the basis of an idea or system.
examples: Solid research should underpin any new policy.
Trust has to underpin every good partnership.
etymology: From under + pin, originally meaning to support a wall from below.

definition: To emphasize or highlight the importance of something.
examples: The outage helps underscore the need for backups.
She paused to underscore her final point.
etymology: Formed in English from under + score 'a line', literally to draw a line beneath.

definition: To describe something as smaller or less important than it really is.
examples: It would understate things to call the storm 'a bit windy'.
Companies sometimes understate the risks of their products.
etymology: Formed in English from under- + state.

definition: To commit yourself to a task or responsibility and begin it.
examples: Few people would undertake a renovation that size alone.
The city agreed to undertake a full review of the program.
etymology: From Middle English undertaken, from under + take.

definition: To accept financial responsibility for something, guaranteeing it against loss.
examples: A local bank agreed to underwrite the festival.
Insurers refused to underwrite homes in the flood zone.
etymology: From under + write, originally signing one's name beneath an insurance policy.

definition: A female water spirit of folklore.
examples: Legend says an undine lives beneath the millpond.
The ballet's heroine is an undine who loves a mortal.
etymology: From Modern Latin undina, a term used by Paracelsus, from Latin unda 'wave'.

definition: Lacking good judgment or taste.
examples: The undiscerning eye might take the copy for the original.
He is an undiscerning eater who likes everything.
etymology: From un- + discern, from Latin discernere 'to separate'.

definition: To move or be shaped with a smooth, wavelike motion.
examples: Fields of wheat undulate in the summer wind.
Watch the eel undulate through the water.
etymology: From Late Latin undulatus 'wavy', from Latin unda 'wave'.

definition: To an excessive or unwarranted degree.
examples: Don't be unduly worried about the test; you've studied hard.
The rules seemed unduly strict for a friendly game.
etymology: From un- + duly, from due, from Old French deu, 'owed'.

definition: Leaving no doubt; clear and absolute in meaning.
examples: After three days of deliberation, the jury delivered an unequivocal verdict of not guilty.
She gave an unequivocal no when reporters asked whether she would run for office again.
etymology: From un- 'not' + equivocal, from Latin aequus 'equal' + vocare 'to call'.

definition: Without any previous example; unparalleled.
examples: The city enjoyed a period of unexampled prosperity.
Her generosity was unexampled in the town's history.
etymology: From un- + example, from Latin exemplum 'sample'.

definition: So satisfactory that no one could object to it.
examples: Her credentials were unexceptionable.
The menu was unexceptionable, if a little dull.
etymology: From un- + exceptionable 'open to objection', from exception.

definition: Complete, with nothing censored or removed.
examples: The unexpurgated diaries were finally published last year.
She read the unexpurgated version of the fairy tales.
etymology: From un- + expurgate, from Latin expurgare 'to cleanse'.

definition: Too deep, vast, or strange to be understood.
examples: The scale of the universe is unfathomable.
For reasons unfathomable to me, he loves pineapple on everything.
etymology: From un- + fathom, from Old English fæthm 'outstretched arms', a unit of depth.

definition: Calm and not bothered, especially by something surprising.
examples: The pilot seemed unfazed by the turbulence.
She was unfazed by the hecklers and kept singing.
etymology: From un- + fazed, from faze, an American variant of dialect feeze 'to drive off'.

definition: Sincere and genuine; not pretended.
examples: Her delight at the gift was unfeigned.
He listened with unfeigned interest.
etymology: From un- + feign, from Old French feindre, from Latin fingere 'to shape'.

definition: Free from restrictions or control.
examples: The artists were given unfettered access to the archive.
Unfettered capitalism has its critics.
etymology: From un- + fetter, from Old English feter 'shackle', related to foot.

definition: Inexperienced and immature, like a bird not yet ready to fly.
examples: The firm hired unfledged graduates and trained them.
An unfledged sparrow fell from the nest.
etymology: From un- + fledge 'to grow feathers', from obsolete fledge 'ready to fly'.

definition: Not showing fear or hesitation in the face of difficulty.
examples: The memoir offers an unflinching account of addiction.
She met his accusations with an unflinching stare.
etymology: From un- + flinch, from Old French flenchir 'to turn aside'.

definition: Having no basis in fact.
examples: The rumors about layoffs turned out to be unfounded.
Her fears of the dentist were unfounded; it didn't hurt at all.
etymology: Formed from un- + founded, from Latin fundare 'to lay a foundation'.

definition: To strip a priest of office, or to expel anyone from a respected position.
examples: The church voted to unfrock the disgraced minister.
Scandal threatened to unfrock the once-celebrated judge.
etymology: From un- + frock, the robe worn by clergy.

definition: Awkward and clumsy in movement or appearance.
examples: The newborn giraffe took a few ungainly steps.
An ungainly sofa blocked half the hallway.
etymology: From un- + obsolete gainly 'graceful', from Old Norse gegn 'straight, convenient'.

definition: Willingly and generously, without resentment.
examples: She ungrudgingly gave up her seat for the elderly man.
The rival coach ungrudgingly praised our defense.
etymology: From un- + grudge, from Old French grouchier 'to grumble'.

definition: A soothing ointment or salve.
examples: The healer rubbed a fragrant unguent into the wound.
Ancient Egyptians prized every precious unguent.
etymology: From Latin unguentum, from ungere 'to anoint'.

definition: A mammal with hooves, such as a horse, deer, or cow.
examples: The bison is the largest ungulate in North America.
Wolves follow every ungulate herd that migrates through the valley.
etymology: From Late Latin ungulatus, from Latin ungula 'hoof'.

definition: Not consecrated as holy; also, wicked or sinful.
examples: Outcasts were buried in unhallowed ground beyond the churchyard.
The villain's unhallowed ambitions knew no limit.
etymology: From un- + hallow 'to make holy', from Old English halgian.

definition: To release someone from your grip, usually said in an old-fashioned or joking way.
examples: 'Unhand me, you brute!' cried the heroine.
'Unhand my sandwich,' he joked as his brother grabbed it.
etymology: Formed in English from un- + hand, first recorded around 1600.

definition: Having a single legislative chamber.
examples: Nebraska has the only unicameral state legislature in the US.
Some reformers want a unicameral parliament.
etymology: From uni- 'one' + Latin camera 'chamber'.

definition: Done by one person or group without the agreement of others.
examples: The manager made a unilateral decision to cancel the project.
A unilateral ceasefire rarely lasts.
etymology: From Modern Latin unilateralis, from uni- 'one' + latus 'side'.

definition: Completely trustworthy and beyond doubt.
examples: The witness had unimpeachable credentials.
Her taste in music is unimpeachable.
etymology: From un- + impeach in its sense of 'to call into question'.

definition: Having only one possible meaning; unambiguous.
examples: Legal terms should be univocal to avoid disputes.
The poem resists any univocal reading.
etymology: From Late Latin univocus, from uni- 'one' + vox 'voice'.

definition: Messy and untidy in appearance.
examples: He showed up to the interview with unkempt hair and a wrinkled shirt.
The unkempt garden was overrun with weeds.
etymology: From un- + kempt, an old past participle of kemb 'to comb'.

definition: To suddenly release a powerful force or feeling.
examples: The new chip could unleash a wave of cheaper gadgets.
Don't unleash your frustration on the customer service rep.
etymology: Formed from un- + leash, originally of freeing a hunting dog.

definition: Poorly educated or unable to read and write.
examples: Her unlettered grandfather was nonetheless a superb storyteller.
The poem was meant to be understood by unlettered listeners.
etymology: From un- + lettered 'educated', from letter.

definition: Unattractive or unpleasant.
examples: The bus station is an unlovely concrete box.
Jealousy is an unlovely emotion.
etymology: Formed in Middle English from un- + lovely.

definition: To deprive someone of courage or composure.
examples: The sight of the cliff was enough to unman the bravest climber.
Grief threatened to unman him at the podium.
etymology: Formed in English from un- + man.

definition: Rude and lacking good manners.
examples: It was unmannerly to leave without thanking the host.
The unmannerly boy grabbed the last cake.
etymology: Formed from un- + mannerly, from manner.

definition: Total and absolute, usually describing something bad.
examples: The product launch was an unmitigated disaster.
What an unmitigated success the bake sale turned out to be!
etymology: From un- + mitigate, from Latin mitigare 'to soften', from mitis 'mild'.

definition: To make someone lose courage or confidence.
examples: The goalie's stare seemed to unnerve the striker.
Sudden silences in a conversation unnerve me.
etymology: Formed in English from un- + nerve, in the old sense of 'strength, courage'.

definition: Different from what is usual or traditional.
examples: Her unorthodox teaching methods got amazing results.
The chef's unorthodox pairing of chocolate and chili worked.
etymology: From un- + orthodox, from Greek orthos 'right' + doxa 'opinion'.

definition: Unpleasant to taste, or hard to accept.
examples: The truth was unpalatable, but they needed to hear it.
Overcooked liver is unpalatable to most kids.
etymology: From un- + palatable, from palate, from Latin palatum 'roof of the mouth'.

definition: Not fully explored or understood; of unknown depth.
examples: The ocean trenches remain largely unplumbed.
Her novels explore the unplumbed depths of grief.
etymology: From un- + plumb, a lead weight for measuring depth, from Latin plumbum 'lead'.

definition: Never having happened or existed before; without any earlier example.
examples: The storm brought unprecedented flooding to a region that had never seen it.
Demand for the new phone was unprecedented, and stores sold out within hours.
etymology: From un- 'not' + precedent, from Latin praecedere, 'to go before'.

definition: Not attractive or impressive at first glance.
examples: The restaurant's unprepossessing exterior hides superb food.
The unprepossessing rookie became the league's best player.
etymology: From un- + prepossessing 'attractive', from prepossess 'to influence beforehand'.

definition: Not favorable; unlikely to lead to success.
examples: The market conditions were unpropitious for a launch.
Rain made it an unpropitious day for the parade.
etymology: From un- + propitious, from Latin propitius 'favorable'.

definition: Restless, uneasy, or disturbed.
examples: She spent an unquiet night waiting for news.
The ballad tells of an unquiet ghost that roams the moors.
etymology: From un- + quiet, from Latin quietus 'at rest'.

definition: To come apart, or to solve or explain something complicated.
examples: The sweater began to unravel at the sleeve.
The detective slowly unraveled the mystery.
etymology: From un- + ravel 'to tangle'.

definition: Irrationality, or a lack of sense or logic.
examples: The mob's anger was pure unreason.
The novel shows a society sliding into unreason.
etymology: Formed in Middle English from un- + reason.

definition: Clinging to old-fashioned views despite changing times.
examples: My uncle is an unreconstructed fan of fax machines.
The novel's hero is an unreconstructed romantic.
etymology: First used of Southerners who rejected Reconstruction after the American Civil War.

definition: Stubbornly unreformed and unwilling to change.
examples: He remains an unregenerate gambler at seventy.
The memoir is the confession of an unregenerate rebel.
etymology: From un- + regenerate, from Latin regenerare 'to bring forth again'.

definition: Never stopping or slackening.
examples: The film is an unremitting portrait of grief.
She faced unremitting pressure from her editor.
etymology: From un- + remit, from Latin remittere 'to send back, slacken'.

definition: Of love, not returned by the person loved.
examples: Half the songs on the album are about unrequited love.
He nursed an unrequited crush all through high school.
etymology: From un- + requite 'to repay', from re- + quit.

definition: Angry dissatisfaction in a population, often leading to protests or disorder.
examples: Rising food prices led to unrest in several cities.
There was unrest among the staff after the layoffs.
etymology: Formed in Middle English from un- + rest.

definition: Calm and composed, even under pressure.
examples: The pilot's voice stayed unruffled during the emergency landing.
She remained unruffled by the tough questions.
etymology: From un- + ruffle, of uncertain origin, first used of smoothing feathers or water.

definition: Disorderly and hard to control.
examples: An unruly passenger forced the plane to turn back.
Her unruly curls refused to stay in a ponytail.
etymology: From un- + Middle English ruly 'orderly', from rule.

definition: Morally offensive or disreputable; also, unpleasant to taste or smell.
examples: The bar attracted an unsavory crowd after midnight.
The scandal revealed some unsavory business practices.
etymology: From un- + savory, from Old French savoure 'tasty', from Latin sapor 'taste'.

definition: Not harmed or damaged at all.
examples: Remarkably, the driver walked away unscathed.
Few companies came through the recession unscathed.
etymology: From un- + scathed, from Old Norse skaða 'to harm'.

definition: Having no moral principles; willing to cheat.
examples: Unscrupulous landlords prey on desperate renters.
An unscrupulous dealer rolled back the car's odometer.
etymology: From un- + scrupulous, from Latin scrupulus 'small sharp stone, uneasiness'.

definition: Not proper or appropriate for the situation.
examples: There was an unseemly scramble for the free samples.
It seemed unseemly to discuss money at the funeral.
etymology: From un- + seemly, from Old Norse sœmr 'fitting'.

definition: To make someone anxious or uneasy, or to disturb something stable.
examples: Loud noises tend to unsettle the horses.
The surprise resignation will unsettle investors.
etymology: Formed in English from un- + settle, from Old English setlan 'to seat, place'.

definition: Not having confessed and received absolution.
examples: The old sailor feared dying unshriven at sea.
In the tale, the knight dies unshriven and haunts the castle.
etymology: From un- + shriven, from shrive, from Old English scrifan 'to hear confession'.

definition: Given or sent without being asked for.
examples: I don't need unsolicited advice about my haircut.
The publisher doesn't accept unsolicited manuscripts.
etymology: From un- + solicit, from Latin sollicitare 'to stir up, urge'.

definition: Merciless or severe; also, given generously.
examples: The review was unsparing in its criticism.
She was unsparing in her praise of the crew.
etymology: From un- + spare, from Old English sparian 'to refrain from harming'.

definition: Given freely and generously.
examples: The volunteers earned unstinting praise from the mayor.
Her unstinting support got me through law school.
etymology: From un- + stint 'to limit', from Old English styntan 'to blunt'.

definition: Natural and unaffected; not forced or rehearsed.
examples: She has an unstudied elegance that cameras love.
His unstudied charm put everyone at ease.
etymology: Formed from un- + studied 'deliberate'.

definition: Not spoiled, stained, or made impure.
examples: The fresh snow lay unsullied across the field.
He retired with his reputation unsullied.
etymology: From un- + sully, possibly from French souiller 'to soil'.

definition: Not celebrated or praised despite deserving it.
examples: Night-shift nurses are the unsung heroes of the hospital.
The bassist is the unsung genius of the band.
etymology: From un- + sung, originally meaning not celebrated in song or poetry.

definition: Constant and unchanging in loyalty or aim.
examples: The dog showed unswerving loyalty to its owner.
She pursued the goal with unswerving focus.
etymology: From un- + swerve, from Old English sweorfan 'to rub, file away'.

definition: Impossible to defend or maintain.
examples: After the scandal, his position became untenable.
The theory is untenable in light of the new data.
etymology: From un- + tenable, from French tenir 'to hold'.

definition: Unexpected and inappropriate or troublesome.
examples: The guard noticed nothing untoward during his shift.
Call me if anything untoward happens while I'm away.
etymology: From un- + toward, which once meant 'promising, willing'.

definition: Free of restrictions or hindrances.
examples: The kids enjoyed a summer of untrammeled freedom.
Her prose is wild and untrammeled.
etymology: From un- + trammel 'net, shackle', from Old French tramail.

definition: Not formally taught or trained.
examples: To the untutored ear, the two pianos sound the same.
He was an untutored but gifted painter.
etymology: From un- + tutor, from Latin tutor 'guardian'.

definition: Plain and straightforward, without softening or decoration.
examples: I want your unvarnished opinion of my draft.
The documentary gives an unvarnished view of prison life.
etymology: From un- + varnish, from French vernis.

definition: To reveal something publicly for the first time.
examples: The company will unveil its new phone on Tuesday.
The mayor is set to unveil the statue at noon.
etymology: Formed from un- + veil, from Latin velum 'covering'.

definition: Not justified or deserved.
examples: The criticism of the young referee was unwarranted.
Police were accused of an unwarranted search.
etymology: From un- + warrant, from Old French warant 'protector, guarantee'.

definition: Steady and firm; not changing or weakening.
examples: Thank you for your unwavering support this year.
Her gaze was unwavering as she answered.
etymology: Formed from un- + waver, from Middle English waveren 'to wander'.

definition: Not mourned or wept for.
examples: The tyrant died unwept and unremembered.
She feared growing old and dying unwept.
etymology: From un- + wept, past participle of weep.

definition: Difficult to carry, handle, or manage because of size or complexity.
examples: The unwieldy suitcase wouldn't fit in the trunk.
The committee grew too unwieldy to make quick decisions.
etymology: From un- + wieldy, 'easy to handle'.

definition: Lack of wisdom; folly.
examples: Critics pointed out the unwisdom of the hasty merger.
He learned the unwisdom of lending to friends.
etymology: From Old English unwisdom, from un- + wisdom.

definition: Without realizing or intending it.
examples: I unwittingly sat in someone else's reserved seat.
She unwittingly gave away the surprise party.
etymology: From un- + witting, from Old English witan 'to know'.

definition: Unusual or not habitual.
examples: The grumpy chef greeted us with unwonted cheer.
An unwonted silence fell over the classroom.
etymology: From un- + wonted 'customary', from wont 'habit'.

definition: A tropical tree with poisonous sap, or a corrupting influence that harms all nearby.
examples: Arrow tips were dipped in sap from the upas tree.
Corruption spread through the city like the shade of a upas.
etymology: From Malay upas 'poison'.

definition: To scold or criticize someone sharply.
examples: The coach had to upbraid the players for missing practice.
She upbraided herself for forgetting her friend's birthday.
etymology: From Old English upbregdan, 'to reproach'.

definition: A sudden, major change that causes disruption.
examples: Moving across the country was a huge upheaval for the kids.
The industry went through a decade of upheaval.
etymology: From upheave, from up + heave, from Old English hebban 'to lift'.

definition: To support or maintain a decision, principle, or law.
examples: The court voted to uphold the original ruling.
Volunteers help uphold the park's rules.
etymology: From up + hold.

definition: The cost or work of keeping something in good condition.
examples: The upkeep on an old sailboat is shockingly expensive.
A lawn needs less upkeep than you might think.
etymology: Formed in English from up + keep.

definition: A loud, angry public outcry or a state of noisy confusion.
examples: The referee's call caused an uproar in the stands.
News of the fee hike sparked an uproar online.
etymology: From Dutch oproer 'uprising'; its English sense was shaped by association with roar.

definition: Expensive and aimed at wealthy customers.
examples: The old warehouse is now an upscale food hall.
They moved to a more upscale neighborhood after the promotion.
etymology: Formed in American English from up + scale, in the sense of a scale of income.

definition: The final result or outcome of something.
examples: The upshot of the meeting was that we need two more weeks.
The upshot is that we'll be moving to a bigger office.
etymology: From up + shot, originally the final shot in an archery match.

definition: To draw attention away from someone else, especially unfairly.
examples: Don't upstage the bride by wearing white.
The puppy managed to upstage the entire school play.
etymology: From the theater: an actor moving upstage forces others to turn away from the audience.

definition: Someone who has risen suddenly to importance and acts arrogantly.
examples: The established brands dismissed the upstart until it stole their customers.
Who does that upstart think he is?
etymology: From up + start, in the old sense of 'to spring up suddenly'.

definition: A rising up of something from below, such as deep ocean water or a strong feeling.
examples: Coastal upwelling brings nutrients that feed the fisheries.
She felt a sudden upwelling of pride.
etymology: From up + well 'to rise, gush', from Old English wellan.

definition: Polished, courteous, and sophisticated in manner.
examples: The urbane host made every guest feel welcome.
He is witty and urbane on screen but shy at home.
etymology: From Latin urbanus 'of the city', from urbs 'city'.

definition: Relating to bears, or resembling a bear.
examples: The coach gave me an ursine hug.
Rangers studied ursine behavior near the campground.
etymology: From Latin ursinus, from ursus 'bear'.

definition: The original version of a text or musical score, or an early model that later works follow.
examples: The pianist insists on playing from the urtext edition.
That 1980s game is the urtext of the open-world genre.
etymology: From German Urtext, from ur- 'original' + Text 'text'.

definition: To guide someone somewhere, or to mark the start of something new.
examples: A volunteer will usher you to your seats.
The invention helped usher in the age of the smartphone.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman usser 'doorkeeper', from Latin ostiarius, from ostium 'door'.

definition: The legal right to use and profit from someone else's property.
examples: The widow kept a usufruct over the farm until her death.
Under the usufruct, he could harvest the orchard but not sell it.
etymology: From Latin usus et fructus 'use and enjoyment'.

definition: To take a position or power illegally or by force.
examples: The general tried to usurp the throne.
Smartphones have usurped the role of alarm clocks.
etymology: From Latin usurpare, 'to seize for use'.

definition: The practice of lending money at unfairly high interest rates.
examples: Critics say payday lending amounts to usury.
Medieval law treated usury as a sin.
etymology: From Medieval Latin usuria, from Latin usura 'use, interest'.

definition: Designed to be useful and practical rather than attractive.
examples: The office has a utilitarian look of gray desks and fluorescent lights.
My first car was utilitarian, not stylish.
etymology: From utility, from Latin utilis 'useful'.

definition: Of the greatest degree or importance.
examples: This matter requires the utmost discretion.
She has the utmost respect for her mentor.
etymology: From Old English utmest 'outermost', from ut 'out'.

definition: An imagined perfect place or society.
examples: For a book lover, the library felt like a utopia.
The commune was meant to be a utopia but fell apart in a year.
etymology: Coined by Thomas More in 1516 from Greek ou 'not' + topos 'place'.

definition: Completely and absolutely.
examples: By midnight we were utterly exhausted.
The sunset was utterly breathtaking.
etymology: From utter 'complete', from Old English uttera 'outer'.

definition: Excessively fond of or submissive to one's wife.
examples: His friends teased the uxorious groom for checking in every hour.
The play mocks an uxorious king ruled by his queen.
etymology: From Latin uxorius, from uxor 'wife'.

definition: To keep switching between choices or opinions, unable to decide.
examples: He continued to vacillate between accepting the job and staying at his old company.
Voters who vacillate until the last day are often decisive in close elections.
etymology: From Latin vacillare, 'to sway, waver'.

definition: Lack of thought, intelligence, or meaning; emptiness.
examples: The speech was striking for its vacuity.
She stared into the vacuity of the blank page.
etymology: From Latin vacuitas, from vacuus 'empty'.

definition: Lacking thought, intelligence, or meaningful content; empty.
examples: The pop star gave a vacuous interview full of cheerful nothings.
Her vacuous stare told me she hadn't heard a word.
etymology: From Latin vacuus, 'empty'.

definition: A person who wanders from place to place without a fixed home.
examples: He lived like a vagabond for a year, hitchhiking through Europe.
The song tells of a carefree vagabond.
etymology: From Latin vagabundus, from vagari 'to wander'.

definition: An unpredictable change or whim.
examples: Every vagary of the weather affects the harvest.
Small shops are exposed to each vagary of the market.
etymology: From Latin vagari 'to wander'.

definition: A person without a settled home or regular work who wanders from place to place.
examples: The novel follows a vagrant crossing the country by train.
An old vagrant slept on the station bench.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman wakerant 'vagabond', influenced by Latin vagari 'to wander'.

definition: Excessively proud and boastful about oneself.
examples: The vainglorious general built statues of himself.
His vainglorious speech annoyed his teammates.
etymology: From vainglory, from Latin vana gloria 'empty glory'.

definition: Serving as a farewell.
examples: The retiring senator gave a valedictory speech.
Her valedictory tour sold out in minutes.
etymology: From Latin valedicere 'to say farewell', from vale 'goodbye' + dicere 'to say'.

definition: A person who is unduly anxious about their health.
examples: The valetudinarian carried three thermometers.
Mr. Woodhouse in Austen's Emma is a classic valetudinarian.
etymology: From Latin valetudinarius 'sickly', from valetudo 'state of health'.

definition: Showing courage and determination, especially against the odds.
examples: The underdogs made a valiant effort in the final quarter.
Despite a valiant attempt, I couldn't finish the giant burrito.
etymology: From Old French vaillant, from Latin valere 'to be strong'.

definition: To confirm that something is correct, or to affirm that someone's feelings are reasonable.
examples: We need more tests to validate the results.
Sometimes friends just want you to validate their frustration.
etymology: From Medieval Latin validare, from Latin validus 'strong'.

definition: Great courage, especially in battle.
examples: The firefighter received a medal for valor.
Stories of valor fill the old war memorial.
etymology: From Latin valor, from valere 'to be strong'.

definition: To give or ascribe value or validity to something.
examples: Hustle culture tends to valorize overwork.
The exhibit aims to valorize women's craft.
etymology: From Latin valor 'value', + -ize.

definition: The leading position in a movement or field, or the people who hold it.
examples: The studio was in the vanguard of digital animation.
Students formed the vanguard of the protest.
etymology: Shortened from avant-garde, French for 'advance guard'.

definition: Excessive pride in one's appearance or achievements.
examples: Out of vanity, he refused to wear his glasses.
His vanity made him check every mirror he passed.
etymology: From Latin vanitas 'emptiness', from vanus 'empty'.

definition: To defeat thoroughly.
examples: The hero must vanquish the dragon to save the town.
She hoped to vanquish her fear of public speaking.
etymology: From Old French vencus, past participle of veintre, from Latin vincere 'to conquer'.

definition: A position that gives a good view or an advantage.
examples: From our vantage point on the hill, we could see the whole valley.
From the vantage of twenty years later, the decision seems obvious.
etymology: From Anglo-French vantage, shortened from avantage 'advantage'.

definition: Lacking interest, energy, or substance; dull.
examples: The interview was full of vapid small talk.
Critics called the song vapid but catchy.
etymology: From Latin vapidus 'flat-tasting', originally of wine.

definition: The amount of difference or disagreement between things.
examples: His actions are at variance with his words.
There's wide variance in test scores across schools.
etymology: From Latin variantia 'difference', from variare.

definition: Marked with patches of different colors, or varied in character.
examples: She grows variegated ivy on the porch.
The city has a variegated mix of cultures.
etymology: From Latin variegare 'to make varied', from varius.

definition: An edition of a text that includes notes by various scholars or variant readings.
examples: She spent years on a variorum of Shakespeare's sonnets.
The variorum lists every change Whitman made to the poem.
etymology: From Latin editio cum notis variorum, 'edition with notes of various people'.

definition: A person or state subordinate to another and owing it loyalty.
examples: The small kingdom became a vassal of the empire.
Critics called the party a vassal of big oil.
etymology: From Medieval Latin vassallus, from vassus 'retainer', of Celtic origin.

definition: Prophetic or oracular.
examples: The poet's vatic pronouncements sounded wise but cryptic.
Fans treat the director's interviews as vatic hints about the next film.
etymology: From Latin vates, 'prophet'.

definition: To foretell or prophesy.
examples: Pundits love to vaticinate about elections.
No one could vaticinate how the pandemic would end.
etymology: From Latin vaticinari, from vates 'prophet'.

definition: A type of variety entertainment with comedy, songs, and acts, popular in the early 1900s.
examples: Her grandfather was a juggler in vaudeville.
The hearing turned into pure vaudeville.
etymology: From French vaudeville, perhaps from Vau de Vire, a valley in Normandy known for songs.

definition: To boast about or praise something excessively.
examples: Ads vaunt the phone's camera above all else.
Politicians love to vaunt their records.
etymology: From Old French vanter, from Late Latin vanitare, from vanus 'vain'.

definition: To change direction suddenly.
examples: The conversation tends to veer toward politics.
Watch the truck; it might veer into our lane.
etymology: From French virer 'to turn'.

definition: Showing strong feeling; forceful and passionate.
examples: He was vehement in his opposition to the new parking rules.
Her vehement denial convinced everyone she was telling the truth.
etymology: From Latin vehemens, 'impetuous, violent'.

definition: A mere wish or inclination too weak to lead to action.
examples: His plan to learn piano remained a velleity for twenty years.
She had a velleity to travel, but never once booked a ticket.
etymology: From medieval Latin velleitas, from Latin velle, 'to wish'.

definition: Fine parchment made from calfskin, or high-quality paper resembling it.
examples: The Book of Kells was written on vellum.
Wedding invitations were printed on cream vellum.
etymology: From Old French velin, from veel 'calf'.

definition: Open to bribery or motivated by money rather than principle.
examples: Voters were tired of venal officials.
The venal judge sold favorable rulings.
etymology: From Latin venalis 'for sale', from venum 'thing for sale'.

definition: Relating to hunting.
examples: The lodge was full of venatic trophies.
Medieval tapestries often depict venatic scenes.
etymology: From Latin venaticus, from venari 'to hunt'.

definition: A prolonged bitter quarrel or campaign against someone.
examples: The columnist seems to have a vendetta against the mayor.
What began as a joke turned into a decade-long vendetta.
etymology: From Italian vendetta 'revenge', from Latin vindicta.

definition: A thin decorative surface layer, or a false outward appearance.
examples: Beneath his veneer of calm, he was panicking.
The table has a walnut veneer over cheap plywood.
etymology: From German furnieren 'to furnish', from French fournir.

definition: Respected because of age, wisdom, or long history.
examples: The venerable newspaper turned 200 this year.
A venerable oak shades the courthouse.
etymology: From Latin venerabilis, from venerari 'to revere'.

definition: To regard someone or something with deep respect and reverence.
examples: Many cultures venerate their elders as keepers of wisdom and tradition.
Fans still venerate the old stadium as a sacred place of the sport.
etymology: From Latin venerari, 'to worship, revere', related to Latin venus, 'love, charm'.

definition: Minor and easily forgiven.
examples: Being late once is a venial offense.
She confessed a few venial sins.
etymology: From Late Latin venialis, from venia 'forgiveness'.

definition: Able to inject poison, or full of malice and spite.
examples: Only a few local snakes are venomous.
She wrote a venomous review of the restaurant.
etymology: From Old French venimeus, from venim 'poison', from Latin venenum.

definition: To express strong feelings, especially anger, freely.
examples: Sometimes you just need to vent to a friend.
Fans went online to vent about the ending.
etymology: From French éventer 'to expose to air', from Latin ventus 'wind'.

definition: To let fresh air into a space, or to air opinions publicly.
examples: Open both windows to ventilate the room.
The town hall gave residents a chance to ventilate their complaints.
etymology: From Latin ventilare 'to fan', from ventus 'wind'.

definition: A risky undertaking, especially a new business.
examples: Her latest venture is a mobile coffee truck.
The joint venture between the two companies collapsed.
etymology: A shortening of adventure, from Latin adventurus 'about to arrive'.

definition: Truthfulness or accuracy.
examples: Reporters questioned the veracity of his story.
The veracity of the data is beyond doubt.
etymology: From Medieval Latin veracitas, from Latin verax 'truthful'.

definition: Relating to or expressed in words, especially spoken rather than written.
examples: We have a verbal agreement, but nothing in writing.
The test measures both verbal and math skills.
etymology: From Latin verbalis, from verbum 'word'.

definition: In exactly the same words as were used originally.
examples: He quoted the instructions verbatim.
The article repeated the press release almost verbatim.
etymology: From Medieval Latin verbatim, from verbum, 'word'.

definition: Excessive or needlessly wordy language.
examples: Cut the verbiage and get to the point.
The contract is buried in legal verbiage.
etymology: From French verbiage, from obsolete verbeier 'to chatter'.

definition: Using more words than needed, in a wordy and tiresome way.
examples: The verbose email took five paragraphs to say the meeting was moved to noon.
His verbose explanations left the audience confused rather than informed.
etymology: From Latin verbosus, 'full of words', from verbum, 'word'.

definition: Green with lush plant growth.
examples: After the rains, the hills turned verdant.
They hiked through a verdant valley.
etymology: Perhaps from Old French verdeant, from Latin viridis 'green'.

definition: A green or bluish coating that forms on copper or brass over time.
examples: Verdigris has turned the old statue green.
Wipe the verdigris off the brass doorknob.
etymology: From Old French vert de Grece 'green of Greece'.

definition: Lush green vegetation, or its fresh green color.
examples: The valley was rich with verdure after the rains.
Spring brought new verdure to the park.
etymology: From Old French verdure, from verd 'green', from Latin viridis.

definition: An edge or border, or the point at which something is about to happen.
examples: The company is on the verge of bankruptcy.
I was on the verge of tears during the finale.
etymology: From Latin virga 'rod', via Old French.

definition: A thin, clear coating of ice on rock or ground.
examples: Climbers turned back when verglas coated the ledge.
A sheen of verglas made the trail treacherous.
etymology: From French verglas, from Old French verre-glaz 'glass ice'.

definition: Truthful, or corresponding accurately to reality.
examples: Was the memory veridical or reconstructed?
Philosophers debate whether perception is veridical.
etymology: From Latin veridicus, from verus 'true' + dicere 'to say'.

definition: The appearance of being true or real, especially in fiction.
examples: The film's costumes lend the story a convincing verisimilitude.
Dialogue that rings true gives a novel verisimilitude even when its plot is fantastic.
etymology: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verisimilis 'probable', from verus 'true' + similis 'like'.

definition: Realism in art or literature, especially portraying everyday or sordid life truthfully.
examples: The opera's verism shocked audiences used to kings and gods.
Roman portrait busts are famous for their unflattering verism.
etymology: From Italian verismo, from vero 'true', from Latin verus.

definition: Used to emphasize that a description is fitting; real or genuine.
examples: The garden is a veritable jungle.
The library holds a veritable treasure of maps.
etymology: From Old French veritable, from verite 'truth'.

definition: A true principle or belief, especially a fundamental one.
examples: The film questions every comfortable verity about family.
It's an old verity that pride comes before a fall.
etymology: From Latin veritas 'truth', from verus 'true'.

definition: Sour juice from unripe grapes, or sourness of temper.
examples: Chefs deglaze the pan with verjuice instead of wine.
His reply dripped with verjuice.
etymology: From Old French vertjus 'green juice'.

definition: Like a worm in form or movement, or marked with wavy lines.
examples: The stone was carved with vermicular patterns.
Vermicular trails crossed the wet sand.
etymology: From Latin vermiculus 'little worm', from vermis 'worm'.

definition: The everyday language spoken by ordinary people in a place or group.
examples: In the local vernacular, a sandwich is a 'hoagie'.
The poet wrote in the vernacular rather than Latin.
etymology: From Latin vernaculus 'domestic, native'.

definition: Relating to or occurring in spring.
examples: The vernal equinox falls around March 20.
Vernal pools fill with frogs after the rains.
etymology: From Latin vernalis, from ver 'spring'.

definition: A private viewing of an art exhibition before it opens to the public.
examples: Collectors sipped champagne at the vernissage.
She was invited to the vernissage of her friend's show.
etymology: From French vernissage 'varnishing', from the day artists varnished paintings before a show.

definition: Able to adapt easily to many different uses or tasks.
examples: A good cast-iron pan is versatile enough for frying, baking, and roasting.
She is a versatile actor who moves easily between comedy and drama.
etymology: From Latin versatilis, 'turning easily', from versare, 'to turn'.

definition: Experienced or knowledgeable in a subject.
examples: She is well versed in tax law.
Few voters are versed in the details of the bill.
etymology: From Latin versatus, from versari 'to be engaged in'.

definition: Causing or relating to dizziness, especially from great heights.
examples: The glass floor gave a vertiginous view of the street below.
Prices rose at a vertiginous pace.
etymology: From Latin vertigo, 'whirling'.

definition: A dizzy feeling of spinning or losing balance, often caused by heights.
examples: Looking down from the tower gave me vertigo.
The pace of change produces a kind of vertigo.
etymology: From Latin vertigo 'whirling', from vertere 'to turn'.

definition: Vigor, energy, and enthusiasm.
examples: The orchestra played the finale with tremendous verve.
She tackled the renovation with verve and good humor.
etymology: From French verve, 'vigor', originally 'form of expression'.

definition: Relating to, active in, or blooming in the evening.
examples: Bats begin their vespertine hunt at dusk.
The vespertine primrose opens as the sun sets.
etymology: From Latin vespertinus, from vesper 'evening'.

definition: Chaste and pure, originally relating to the Roman goddess Vesta.
examples: The bride wore vestal white.
Snow lay in vestal silence over the field.
etymology: From Latin Vestalis, from Vesta, Roman goddess of the hearth.

definition: Secured as a legal right, or having a personal stake in an outcome.
examples: Landlords have a vested interest in rent rules.
After four years, all her stock options were vested.
etymology: From vest, from Latin vestire 'to clothe'.

definition: A trace or remnant of something that is disappearing or no longer exists.
examples: The stone wall is the last vestige of the old farm.
Not a vestige of her earlier shyness remained.
etymology: From Latin vestigium, 'footprint'.

definition: A person with long experience in a field, or a former member of the armed forces.
examples: The veteran of thirty marathons gave us pacing tips.
Her grandfather is a Navy veteran.
etymology: From Latin veteranus, from vetus 'old'.

definition: The right or act of rejecting a decision or proposal.
examples: The governor used her veto to block the bill.
My sister has a veto over any movie with spiders.
etymology: From Latin veto 'I forbid'.

definition: To annoy, frustrate, or trouble someone.
examples: Slow internet can vex even the most patient person on a tight deadline.
The riddle continued to vex him long after the party had ended.
etymology: From Latin vexare, 'to harass, shake, trouble'.

definition: The study of flags.
examples: His love of vexillology began with a poster of world flags.
Vexillology fans debated the city's new flag design.
etymology: From Latin vexillum 'flag' + -logy.

definition: Capable of working successfully; practical.
